citation_text_en: [1]: Ignacio Odriozola [2] Verónica Jaramillo Fonnegra

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Argentina

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 14, Article 14 bis, Article 20. In the case of freedom of peaceful assembly, Art. 14 of the National Constitution states that “every inhabitant” of the territory, has a right “to associate with useful purposes." Art. 20 of the National Constitution expressly says that “Foreigners enjoy in the territory of the Nation all the civil rights of the citizen.” 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 5-6. The right of assembly is not only recognized and respected by local law, but it is also considered necessary for the integration of migrants, which is why article 17.C says that State should guarantee the freedom of assembly since “the State in all its jurisdictions, whether national, provincial or municipal, will favor initiatives aimed at integrating foreigners into their community of residence, especially those aimed at: c) To the knowledge and assessment of cultural, recreational, social, economic and religious expressions of immigrants." 3) Migrant Workers Convention (adopted as law by Law N° 26.202), Article 26. 4) Universal Declaration of Human Rights Article 20; American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man Article XXII; American Convention on Human Rights Articles 15 and 16, American Declaration on International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights Article 22. These international instruments were incorporated to the National Constitution by Art. 75.22 with constitutional hierarchy.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina emphasized their focus on the “equal civil rights of migrants.”

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No federal protection of this right. However, according to Argentina's Constitution Article 37, each of Argentina’s provinces has the right to establish its own electoral regime and the laws that regulate the regime, which includes granting voting rights to migrants. As of 2023, 23 out of 24 provinces in Argentina allow migrants to vote in local or regional elections. Formosa is the only province that impedes the exercise of this right. The conditions for voting vary slightly among the provinces, but, in general terms, the requisites are to be an adult, to have permanent residence (2 years MERCOSUR and 3 Extramercosur), to have an ID and be included in the register of voters.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 18, Article 75.22. 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Articles 3.g), Article 6, Article 12. The Immigration Act N° 25.871 has among its objectives the promotion of “the obligations, rights and guarantees of migrants, in accordance with the provisions of the National Constitution, international commitments and laws, keeping their humanitarian tradition open and open in relation to migrants and their families.” Particularly, Article 6 states that “the State, in all its jurisdictions, will ensure equal access to immigrants and their families in the same conditions of protection, protection and rights enjoyed by nationals, in particular as regards social services, public goods, health, education, justice , work, employment and social security.” Additionally, Article 12 ensures that "the State will comply with everything established in international conventions and all others that establish rights and obligations of migrants, who have been duly ratified."

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 18, Article75.22. The Argentinian Constitution ensures in article 18 that "the defense of the person and rights in court is inviolable." 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 86. The Immigration Act N° 25.871 states that "Foreigners who are in national territory and who lack financial means shall have the right to free legal assistance in those administrative and judicial proceedings that may lead to the denial of their entry, return to their country of origin or expulsion from Argentinean territory." In addition, article 86 of Decree 616/10 states that "the National Directorate of Migration, in the event of a complaint made by a foreigner, shall immediately intervene with the Public Ministry of Defence, ordering the suspension of any proceedings and of the deadlines underway in the administrative proceedings, until the aforementioned Ministry intervenes or the interested party receives the necessary legal assistance for the safeguarding of his interests." However, in a recent judgment titled "Zuluaga Celemin" (13 October 2022), the Supreme Court has indicated that there is no obligation of informing "personally and reliably" about the right to counsel, when the immigrant has not expressly asked for it. 3) Decree 616/10, Article 86. 4) Migrant Workers Convention, Article 18.3.d.. 5) Law N° 27.149 of the Public Ministry of Defense, Article 35.e.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina indicated it assigns a public defender to migrants who cannot obtain legal assistance, in pursuit of “the right to be represented” during removal proceedings in accordance with the American Convention on Human Rights.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) Immigration Act N° 25.871: Article 86 which ensures that foreigners “will be entitled to interpreter assistance if they do not understand or speak the official language." 2) National Penal Procedural Code, Article 268 which states that, in criminal proceedings, “the judge will appoint an interpreter when it is necessary to translate documents or statements that, respectively, are found or must be produced in a language other than the national one, even if he has personal knowledge of it.”3) Decree No. 616/10, Article 86. 4) Law No. 27.149 of the Public Ministry of Defense, Articles 16-25. 5) Migrant Workers Convention, Article 18.3.d. 6) Constitution, Articles 18 and 75.22.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina indicated migrants have “the right to the services of an interpreter free of charge” in accordance with the American Convention on Human Rights.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Immigration offenses can not be criminalized. However, irregular entry or stay can be fined or punished by expulsion, giving place to administrative sanctions. The Supreme Court confirmed that unauthorized entry is sanctioned with expulsion.
international_text_en: In a recommendation to the United States of America, in the course of its 2020 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina urged reconsideration of “measures that criminally penalize migrants who enter the country without authorization.”

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 14bis. 2) Immigration Act N°25.871, Article 6. 3) Housing Federal Act N° 24.464. Immigration Act and the Constitutional provisions do protect migrants right to housing since the federal housing system does not exclude based on nationality or migration status. However, there are no implementation of these guarantees to the extent that local governments exclude without impunity. Local laws may restrict access to housing programs based on immigration status. Some housing programs require native or naturalized citizenship, while others require permanent residency.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) International Covenant of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights Article 13, 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871 Articles 6-7. Article 7, guarantees full equal access to all educational institutions, both public and private, primary, secondary, tertiary, and university. 3) National Education Act N° 26.206, Article 4. This article recalls the inhabitants, citizens and foreigners, when saying that “The National State, the Provinces and the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires have the main and non-delegable responsibility of providing an integral, permanent and quality education for all the inhabitants of the Nation, guaranteeing equality, gratuity and equity in the exercise of this right, with the participation of social organizations and families.” 4) The National Constitution, in its Article 14, guarantees the right to "teaching and learning" to every inhabitant of the country.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Articles 6-7. 2) National Education Act N° 26.206, Article 4 which considers inhabitants as citizens and foreigners, and states that “the National State, the Provinces and the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires have the main and non-delegable responsibility of providing an integral, permanent and quality education for all the inhabitants of the Nation, guaranteeing equality, gratuity and equity in the exercise of this right, with the participation of social organizations and families.” 3) The National Constitution, in its Articles 14 and 75.22, guarantees the right to "teaching and learning" to every inhabitant of the country. 4) International Covenant of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights Article 13 and the Migrant Workers Convention Article 43 that are adopted into national law via Article 75.22 of the Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 29, Article 62. According to the Immigration Act, there could be two possible scenarios that will affect residence status when the migrant has criminal convictions. First, if a migrant would like to reside in Argentina, he/she will have to present himself/herself against the National Migratory Direction asking for a temporary residence. He/She will receive a “precarious residence” while the authority evaluates the documents required. In the case that he/she is being prosecuted for a criminal offense, is convicted for a crime or has criminal records, and any of these involves deprivation of freedom, i.e. not a “probation” nor an administrative offense, the National Migratory Direction will declare “irregular” the permanence of that person in the country and will order his/her expulsion -Art. 29-. On the other hand, if a migrant has a temporary or permanent residence, and he/she is convicted for a crime that involves deprivation of freedom, his/her situation will vary depending on the crime. If he/she is convicted for crimes of trafficking arms, people, narcotics, organs and tissues, or money laundering or investments in illegal activities, his/her residence will be canceled by the National Migratory Direction, his/her stay in the country will be declared irregular and he/she will be expel of the country. -Art. 62.b- However, in the case that the migrant is convicted for a crime different to those already mentioned and this one does not exceed five (5) years of deprivation of liberty or it is a deceitful crime, his/her temporary or permanent residence will not be immediately canceled. Instead, the National Migratory Direction will have the opportunity of avoiding this measure when the “foreigner invoke family reunification with respect to parent, child or spouse Argentine citizen” and “the time that the person has been legally residing in the national territory will be especially taken into consideration” -Art, 62 in fine-.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Art. 29. 2) Decree 616/10, Article 23.m.1, Article 23.m.2. 3) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 75.22 (incorporating Convention against Torture Art. 3 and American Convention on Human Rights Article 22.8 with Constitutional hierarchy). 4) Refugee Law N° 26165, Article 2, Article 7, Article 39. The Immigration Act N° 25.871, article 29, states that “humanitarian assistance” should be considered when evaluating the expulsion of a migrant from the country. Decree 616/10 further explains that “humanitarian assistance” involves: persons in need of international protection who, not being refugees or asylum seekers in the terms of the applicable legislation in the matter, are protected by the Principle of Non-Refoulment and cannot regulate their immigration status through the remaining criteria provided in Law No. 25,871 and in this Regulation,” and “persons for whom it is presumed that, if forced to return to their country of origin, they would be subject to human rights violations recognized in international instruments with constitutional hierarchy."

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 75.22 (incorporating American Convention on Human Rights Article 22.8 with constitutional hierarchy). The incorporation of the American Convention on Human Rights into the National Constitution is self executing and guarantees that no one can be deported: "in no case may the foreigner be expelled or returned to another country, whether of the origin or not, where his right to life or personal freedom is at risk because of his race, nationality, religion, social status or political opinion." 2) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Art. 29. 3) Decree 616/10, Article 23.m.1, Article 23.m.2. The Decree 616/10 that regulates the Act N° 25.871, indicates that “humanitarian reasons” involve: Persons in need of international protection who, not being refugees or asylum seekers in the terms of the applicable legislation in the matter, are protected by the Principle of Non-Refoulment and cannot regulate their immigration status through the remaining criteria provided in Act N° 25,871 and in this Regulation” and “Persons for whom it is presumably presumed that, if forced to return to their country of origin, they would be subject to human rights violations recognized in international instruments with constitutional hierarchy.“ 4) Refugee Law N° 26165, Article 2, Article 7, Article 39.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 29. 2) Decree 616/10, Article 23.m.1, Article 23.m.2. 3) Refugee Law N° 26.165, Article 2-3, Article 7, Article 29. The Immigration Act N° 25.871, article 29, states that “humanitarian assistance” should be considered when evaluating the expulsion of a migrant from the country. Decree 616/10 further explains that “humanitarian assistance” involves: persons in need of international protection who, not being refugees or asylum seekers in the terms of the applicable legislation in the matter, are protected by the Principle of Non-Refoulment and cannot regulate their immigration status through the remaining criteria provided in Law No. 25,871 and in this Regulation,” and “persons for whom it is presumed that, if forced to return to their country of origin, they would be subject to human rights violations recognized in international instruments with constitutional hierarchy."
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2008 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina indicated it utilized the perspective of “the full enjoyment of human rights” in its understanding and granting of refugee status.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. However, the General Act of Recognition and Protection of the Refugee N° 26.165, article 8, establishes that when a refugee has to be expelled of the country because “serious reasons of national security or public order justify it… the respective measure can only be made effective towards the territory of a State that guarantees its right to life, liberty and the security of its person as well that their protection against expulsion, return or extradition on the same terms as established in the previous article.”

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Immigration Law N° 25.871, Article 61-62, Article 69, Article 74, Article 89. These articles include the facts that may lead to expulsion, the procedure for reaching such a decision, and the remedies available to migrants.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina indicated that migrants have “the right to be notified of an expulsion order,” “the right to appeal against it,” and “the right to be heard by the competent authorities” in accordance with the American Convention on Human Rights.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 69, Articles 74-89. Particularly, article 74 of the Immigration Act allows migrants an opportunity to submit the reasons against a decision of the National Direction of Migration when they are definitive or when they totally prevent the processing of the claim, and "against the interlocutory of mere procedure that injure subjective rights or a legitimate interest, the review in administrative and judicial headquarters proceed, when: a) The admission or permanence of a foreigner is denied; b) The authorization of permanent, temporary or temporary residence is canceled; c) A foreigner is ordered to leave the country or his expulsion is decreed; d) Resolving the application of fines and sureties or their execution."

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 20. 2) Article 17 of the Stateless Act N° 27.512 states that "every stateless person has the right to naturalize, in accordance with Law 346, its regulatory and complementary norms, and the facilities granted in the present law." In addiition, Article 59 of said act states that, "in the case of unaccompanied or separated children who are stateless, the guardian and/or legal representative may submit an application for naturalization if it is considered to be in the best interests of the child." 3) Citizenship Act N° 346.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right, for immediate family members, in: 1) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 3.E, Article 10. 2) Decree N° 616/10, Article 22.B, Article 23.N. 3) Migrant Workers Convention (adopted as law by Act N° 26.202), Article 44. Decree N° 616/10 establishes that when the migrant has a “temporary residence” or a “permanent residence” - i.e. the migrant is settled - family reunification is possible with “a spouse, parent, unmarried child under the age of 18 years, not emancipated or older with a different capacity, of a permanent resident, taking into account principles of unity, support and with the scope of the right of family reunification established in the relevant legislation and in Article 10 of this Regulation.” However, for the purposes of this law, non-dependent family members are not considered family and therefore do not have the avenues to facilitate family reunification.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2008 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina recognized “the principles of family reunification” in the regulation of the Immigration Act of 2010.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Immigration Act N° 25.871, Art. 74, which entitles migrants the right to challenge at both administrative and judicial bodies any refusal of entry and residence.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 3.E, Article 10. 2) Decree N° 616/10. 3) The Same Sex Marriage Act N° 26.618 passed in 2010. Article 10 of the immigration act, and the subsequent passing of Decree N° 616/10 explicitly states the criteria for family members for the reunification framework. It states that, “the State will guarantee the right of family reunification of immigrants with their parents, spouses, minor unmarried children or older children with different abilities.” Same sex marriage was introduced to Argentina with the passing of Act N° 26.618, and with its passing, the term “spouse” is applied “regardless of whether the parties are same or different sex.”

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right. Temporary migrant workers' opportunities to switch to permanent status are unconditional on visa as outlined in the Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 17, 20, 22, and 23; and Decree 616/10 that supplements the Act N° 25.871, Article 22. C. After having a temporary residency with any type of visa, migrants can apply for a permanent one.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Immigration Act N° 25.871 - Article 17, and Article 61. Article 61 of the Immigration Act states that, "upon finding that the stay of a foreigner in the country is irregular, and taking into account the circumstances of the foreigner’s profession, his or her relationship with Argentine nationals, the proven period of stay and other personal and social conditions, the National Directorate of Migration shall order him or her to regularize his or her situation within the peremptory period set for this purpose, under penalty of ordering his or her expulsion. This period is 30 days (extendable to another 30 days). Upon expiry of the term without regularizing the situation, the National Direction of Migration shall decree his expulsion with suspensive effect and shall intervene and act as a party before the Judge or Court with competence in the matter, for the purposes of the review of the administrative decision of expulsion."

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) Employment Contract Law, Article 153 which does not establish differences based on the nationality of the worker. 2) Immigration Act N°28.871, Article 56 which establishes equality with nationals in the redress of workers.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. At this moment, the legal power to detain children is provided for in the Aliens Act. However, current government policy limits and prohibits detention of migrant children.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 6 and 8. Art. 6 of the Immigration Act N° 25.871 guarantees equal rights and treatment among foreigners and natives. Moreover, Art. 8 states that the State will ensure “access to the right to health, social assistance or health care to all foreigners who require it may not be denied or restricted in any case, regardless of their immigration status.” 2) International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, Article 12 which is incorporated into national law via Article 75.22 of the Constitution.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2012 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina indicated it had implemented programs to remove barriers that prevent migrant women from accessing health care services so that they may exercise their “reproductive and sexual rights.”

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No universal protection of this right. Election laws are handled at the local level in Argentina, and migrants can stand for election only in limited circumstances in some localities. In order to exercise the right to stand for election, the Constitution, at a national level, demand being native of Argentina or, eventually, naturalized. At a provincial level, in general terms, being native or naturalized is required. However, Buenos Aires Province is the only one that allows migrants to stand for elections. According to its Constitution, Art. 191.3, they can become Councilors.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Immigration Act N° 25.871 Article 13 which states: "for the purposes of this law, all acts or omissions determined for reasons such as ethnicity, religion, nationality, ideology, political or union opinion, sex, gender, economic position or physical characters, which arbitrarily prevent, obstruct, restrict, shall be considered discriminatory..." Furthermore, Articles 6-8 prohibit discrimination against migrants due to their migration status in regard to health, education, justice, social services, public goods, employment and social security.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina indicated that its National Institute to Combat Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism’s programming raises awareness about cultural diversity to ensure migrants “may exercise their rights on an equal footing with nationals.” In addition, in its intervention at the International Migration Refuge Forum, Argentina's Ambassador stated, “Our law places foreign citizens on an equal footing with nationals, migrants are guaranteed equal civil, social and economic rights, including the right to receive medical care, access to public education, work, and social security benefits. Migrants are also guaranteed access to family reunification. This is why the unrestricted respect for the human rights of migrants, their integration into Argentine society and their reception on an equal footing with nationals are fundamental principles of the legislation. nationals are fundamental principles of our country's immigration legislation. All of the above represents a ‘floor of rights’ for the Argentine Republic, existing in our legislation since long before the Global Compact for a Safe, Orderly, and Regular Migration, approved in December 2018. [...]”. Ambassador Pablo Tettamanti, Foreign Affairs Secretary, at the International Migration Review Forum, 21 June 2022.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) Act N° 25.871, Art. 13 which states, "for the purposes of this law, all acts or omissions determined on grounds such as ethnicity [...] or physical characteristics, which arbitrarily prevent, obstruct, restrict or in any way impair the full exercise on an equal basis of the fundamental rights and guarantees recognized in the National Constitution, international treaties and laws, shall be considered discriminatory." 2) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 75.22 which incorporates the international legal framework against discrimination into national law.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 14bis. Article 14bis of the Argentinian Constitution states that every "worker" - independently of their nationality - will "enjoy the protection of the laws, which shall ensure to the worker: dignified and equitable conditions of work [...] equal pay for equal work [...]." 2) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 5-6, Article 16, Article 56. Article 6 of the Immigration Act N° 25.871 states that the State will "ensure equal access for immigrants and their families to the same conditions of protection, protection, and rights enjoyed by nationals, in particular with regard to social services, public goods, health, education, justice, labour, employment, and social security." Article 56 states that employers have to ensure all migrant workers' rights regardless of their immigration status. 3) Migrant Workers Convention Article 25.1; International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights Article 6. 4) Work Contract Law, Article 81.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Migrant Workers Convention, Article 52.1 adopted by Act N° 26.602. 2) Act N° 25.871, Article 6, 16, 19, 23A and L. 3) Decree 616/10 that rules Act N° 25.871, Article 23A. The requirement to apply for a new work permit application while changing employment is only required in the first 3 years of a migrant worker (article 23.a). After 3 years, these migrants can get permanent residence and then they are completely free to choose employment. Additionally, most migrant workers get residence permits based on nationality grounds due to Mercosur Residence Agreement included in article 23.l, which makes them completely free to choose employment. Not all jobs, however, are available to migrants since the Public Employment Law (Law 25.164 Title II Art. 4) excludes foreigners from the possibility of holding public positions, with few exceptions.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution, Article 14bis. 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Art. 9, and Article 23.A. 3) Decree 616/10, related to Act N° 25.871, Article 23.A. 4) International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights Article 7, incorporated by Art. 75.22 with constitutional hierarchy. Migration law does not provide for any restrictions on the right to work for the spouse/life partner of the main migrant.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right, in a limited way, in: 1) Immigration Act N°25.871, Articles 23. A, L; 61 and 62.E, I, M. 2) Decree 616/10 that rules Act N° 25.871 Articles 23. I, M and 61. According to the Immigration Act, migrants who have temporary residence permit under migrant worker residence category (art. 23.a) would loose their immigration status if they can't get another residence status based on such category or any other (e.g., family ties; nationality of Mercosur State Party; humanitarian grounds; others). However, the Art. 61 of Decree 616/10 states that the migrant will have 30 days, extendable another 30 days, to regularize their migratory status within the country.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 14bis, and Article 75.22. 2) The Immigration Act N° 25.871 Articles 5-6, and 56. 3)Decree 616/10, Articles 5-6 and 56. The Constitution of Argentina states that "work in its various forms will enjoy the protection of laws, which will ensure the worker: decent and equitable working conditions, limited working hours; paid rest and vacations; fair compensation; mobile minimum living wage; Equal pay for equal work; participation in the profits of the companies, with control of the production and collaboration in the direction; protection against arbitrary dismissal; public employee stability; Free and democratic union organization, recognized by simply registering in a special register." These general conditions are reinforced by the Immigration Act, which states that nationals and foreigners have the same rights and should be treated equally.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National legislation in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 14 bis. The National Constitution states that social security benefits shall be comprehensive and inalienable. In particular, the law establishes mandatory social security, retirement and mobile pensions. 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871 - Art. 6. Both the National Constitution and Immigration Act N° 25.871 ensure equal acces to "social security" independent of a work permit. However, depending on the social security program, migrants will have to prove some period of legal residence in Argentina. 3) The Law on the Integrated Retirement and Pension System N° 24.241, Article 19 establishes that the interested party "must prove thirty (30) years of service with computable contributions in one or more systems included in the reciprocity system."

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) the Constitution of Argentina, Article 14bis. 2) The Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 6 which includes equal treatment on labor rights. 3) Employment Act N° 24.013. 4) Migrants Workers Convention Article 54 adopted by Act N°26.202. 5) Work Contract Act N° 24.013 Article 111 and ff which regulate requisites for unemployment benefits. These articles do not make any difference based on nationality. It is necessary to have a job as an employee in order to have unemployment insurance, and the number of months of benefits depends on seniority.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protect this right in the Immigration Act N° 25.871 Articles 17, 22, and 23; Decree 616/10 that rules the migration Act N° 25.871 Article 22. C. Article 22 of the Decree N° 616/10 establish five different avenues to change from temporary to permanent residence. One of these avenues require: "to have roots for having enjoyed temporary residence for two (2) continuous years or more, if he/she is a national of the countries of the Southern Common Market (MERCOSUR) or Associated States; and three (3)continuous years or more, in the other cases."

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) Identification Regime of the Newborn Act N° 24.540, Article 1 which states "Every child born alive or dead and his mother must be identified in accordance with the provisions of this law." Regardless the migratory status of the mother, the parents or the children, it is imperative to register the newborn. 2) National Constitution Article 20. 3) Citizenship Law 346 Articles 1, 2, 3. 4) Law 26413 (Law on Registration of Civil Status and Legal Capacity), Articles 27-40, Article 54.
international_text_en: In a recommendation to Ethiopia, in the course of its 2014 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina encouraged the issuance of birth certificates to newborn refugees.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 20, Article 22-26, Article 30-33. 2) Decree for the Law N° 25.871. Article 30.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in National Penal Code, Article 294. The National Penal Code considers the suppression or destruction "in whole or in part, a document so that it may be detrimental" to any person an illegal offense.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in Act N° 17.081 that adopts the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Moreover, Article 61 of Decree 616/10, states that "...the person’s right to information on consular assistance must be protected in accordance with the provisions of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations adopted by the Organization Of The United Nations(UN) on April 24, 1963 and approved by Law No. 17,081."
international_text_en: In a recommendation to the Netherlands, in the course of its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina urged it to ensure unaccompanied children are not deprived of liberty.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Argentina doesn't explicitly prohibit the detention of children on the basis of their migrant status, but has ratified Childs Convention Art. 9, 37, 40; Migrant Workers Convention Art. 17, 18; and Law No. 26.202, which adopts the Migrant Workers Convention, and Article 75.22 of the National Constitution, which incorporates the former Convention into domestic law with constitutional hierarchy.
international_text_en: In a recommendation to the United Kingdom, in the course of its 2012 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina urged “avoiding the use of detention” of asylum-seekers while determining their status.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Argentina does not explicitly prohibit the detention of migrants on the basis of their status as migrants, but Decree 616/10 of Law No. 25.871, Articles 70-71, and Law 25871, Articles 70-72 states that the detention of migrants could only be used as a measure of last resort. Until 2017, the detention of migrants could only be used as a measure of last resort, after all, legal remedies against expulsion had been exhausted. An executive decree (Decree 70 in 2017) expanded the scope of migration-related detention. The decree was considered unconstitutional and was repealed on 5 March to 2021 for Decree 138/2021. In practice, with the exception of a few cases, detention is only used at the very last stage before deportation (i.e. for about 24-48 hours). There is no specific institution for migration-related detention.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Constitution of Argentina, Article 43; Habeas Corpus Act N°23.098, Article 3; Immigration Act N°25.871, Article 70; Migrant Workers Convention, Article 22.4; Decree for the Law N° 25.871, Article 70. According to the Argentinian Constitution, “when the right injured, restricted, altered or threatened was physical liberty, or incase of illegitimate aggravation in the form or conditions of detention, or in the forced disappearance of persons, the action of habeas corpus may be brought by the affected party or by anyone in their favor and the judge will resolve immediately, even during the validity of the state of siege.“ Additionally, the Immigration Act establishes, in Article 70, that “in the event that the detained foreigner claims as a new fact to be a parent of a native Argentine minor or disabled person, the National Directorate of Migrations must suspend for two (2) business days the execution of the expulsion measure for the purpose of verifying the veracity of the facts and resolve whether or not to be granted in accordance with the provisions of articles 29 and 62 of this.”

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 66, Article 70; Migrant Workers Convention, Articles 16, Article 22; American Convention on Human Rights, Article 22.9. According to the Immigration Act, Article 66, "each case of expulsion shall be examined and decided individually”.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, which was incorporated into the constitutional hierarchy through article 75, paragraph 22 of the Constitution. The prohibition of torture and cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment has a constitutional protection (based on constitutional level of the UN Convention against Torture) and apllies to every inhabitant with no discrimination based on nationality and any other ground. Furthermore, Immigration Act 25.871, Art. 5 reminds that there is equality between nationals and migrants, and provisions should be applied equally.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. No national law in Argentina explicitly prohibits the use of force by its officials or agents to prevent migrants from entering the national territory. Nonetheless, the Art. 18 of the National Constitution states the "Principle of Innocence" as a guarantee for implicitly preventing or limiting the use of force in dubious situations, such as the supposed unlawful entrance to the country. In addition, the Art. 25 expressly says that the Federal Government "may not restrict, limit or levy with any tax the entry into the Argentina territory of foreigners who bring to work the land, improve industries, and introduce and teach science and arts." Additionally, Act N° 25871, establish the Migratory Auxiliary Police (Arts. 107 and ff.) without mentioning the possibility of using the force to prevent the entry of migrants, but precising that this Police will be build up by other forces (Argentine Naval Prefecture, the National Gendarmerie, the National Aeronautical Police and the Federal Police) which are able to use force according to their specific regulations. After exploring those specific regulations, none of them explicitly refers to the use of force to prevent migrants from entering to the state's territory but they do recall the idea of“proportionality.” The Art. 35 of the Decree 616/10, that regulates Act 25871, is not precise and is quite broad when tackling the “Border Rejection” regime. It ensures “When a foreigner's rejection is arranged at the border, the immigration authority will arbitrate the necessary means so that its reconduction outside the Argentine territory is carried out in the shortest possible time.” In short, the use of force is not forbidden explicitly, but the limits imposed by law discourage its use.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2008 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina indicated a shift away from “security and frontier control” and “restrictive immigration policies” that lead to a “loss of life” towards a more holistic view of the human rights of migrants.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. No national law in Argentina explicitly prohibits the use of lethal force by its officials or agents to prevent migrants from entering the national territory.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for both trafficked and smuggled migrants. National law in Argentina exempts trafficked migrants from prosecution as victims of trafficking, but there are no provisions for the protection and non-criminalization of smuggled migrants. National law in Argentina exempts trafficked migrants from criminal prosecutions in Art. 5 of the Act N° 26.364: "Non-punishability. Victims of trafficking are not punishable for the commission of any offense that is the direct result of having been trafficked. Nor shall the sanctions or impediments established in the migration legislation be applicable to them when the offenses are a consequence of the activity carried out during the commission of the offense that harmed them." Moreover, Argentina has ratified all the international conventions regarding these issues such as the Protocol against the Smuggling of Migrants by Land, Sea and Air; and the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children which was incorporated with constitutional hierarchy through Article 75 subsection 22 .

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: Nationa law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Citizenship Law N° 346. 2) Immigration Law N° 25871. There is no provision that allows the status of citizenship to be affected by criminal or other convictions.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Constitution of Argentina, Article 20 which states that any migrant may "obtain nationalization after residing two continuous years in the Nation; but the authority may shorten this term in favor of what it requests, alleging and proving services to the Republic." Other requirements, that do not alter these basic requirements, are further developed in the Citizenship Law N° 346, Article 2.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Constitution of Argentina, Article 20 which states that any migrant may "obtain nationalization after residing two continuous years in the Nation; but the authority may shorten this term in favor of what it requests, alleging and proving services to the Republic." Other requirements, that do not alter these basic requirements, are further developed in the Citizenship Law N° 346, Article 2.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Constitution of Argentina, Article 20 which states that any migrant may "obtain nationalization after residing two continuous years in the Nation; but the authority may shorten this term in favor of what it requests, alleging and proving services to the Republic." Other requirements that do not alter these basic conditions are further developed in the Citizenship Law N° 346. Additionally, the latter states that the spouse of an Argentine might get citizenship via naturalization in a shorter period than the two basic years required - Art. 2°(2)(7). Article 12 of Act 346 says that the children of people with citizenship automatically have citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right. No legal provision refers to dual nationality in Argentina's laws. However, the Supreme Court Justice of Argentina addressed this issue in the leading case "Padilla, Miguel" (10 April 2007) where it was stated that "obtaining a certain nationality different from that of origin is perfectly admissible ... a person can opt for Argentine nationality or naturalize Argentina without losing that of origin."

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 14, Article 20. National Constitution expressly says in Art. 14 that all "inhabitants" are guaranteed equal protection on these rights. Furthermore, Art. 20 states that “Foreigners enjoy in the territory of the Nation all the civil rights of the citizen; they can exercise…freely [their] cult.” 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 5, Article 6, Article 13, Article 14.C. The Immigration Act recognizes the equality of rights between nationals and foreigners, impeding any kind of discrimination based on religion. Art. 14.C of the Immigration Act obliges the State to respect and encourage “c) to the knowledge and assessment of cultural, recreational, social, economic and religious expressions of immigrants.” 3) Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; Article III of the American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man; Article 12 of the American Convention on Human Rights; and Article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. These international instruments have been incorporated into the National Constitution through Art. 75.22 with constitutional hierarchy. 4) Migrant Workers Convention Article 12, approved by Law N° 26.202 (2007).

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) Article 14 and Article 20 of the Constitution. The National Constitution expressly says in Art. 14 that all "inhabitants" are guaranteed equal protection to “publish [his/her] ideas by the press without prior censorship.” Furthermore, Art. 20 expressly says that “Foreigners enjoy in the territory of the Nation all the civil rights of the citizen.” 2) The Immigration Act N° 25.871 Article 5-6, Article 13, Article 14.C. 3) Migrant Workers Convention approved by Law N° 26.202(2007): Article 12. 4) Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; Article III of the American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man; Article 12 of the American Convention on Human Rights; and Article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. These international instruments have been incorporated into the National Constitution through Art. 75.22 with constitutional hierarchy.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina emphasized their focus on the “equal civil rights of migrants.”

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 14, Article 20. Art. 14 of the National Constitution states that “every inhabitant” of the territory, has a right to “publish [his/her] ideas by the press without prior censorship.” Art. 20 states "foreigners enjoy in the territory of the Nation all the civil rights of the citizen." 2) Migrant Workers Convention (adopted as law by Law N° 26.202): Article 26. 3) The Immigration Act N° 25.871: Article 5-6, Article 13, Article 14.C. 4) Universal Declaration of Human Rights Article 20; American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man Article XXII; American Convention on Human Rights Articles 15 and 16, American Declaration on International Covenant in Civil and Political Rights Article 22. These international instruments were incorporated to the National Constitution by Art. 75.22 with constitutional hierarchy.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina emphasized their focus on the “equal civil rights of migrants.”

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 14, Article 14 bis, Article 20. Art. 14 states that “every inhabitant” of the territory, has a right “to associate with useful purposes.” Furthermore, Art. 20 of the National Constitution expressly says that “Foreigners enjoy in the territory of the Nation all the civil rights of the citizen.” 2)Migrant Workers Convention (adopted as law by Law N° 26.202): Article 26. 3); Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 5-6. 4) Universal Declaration of Human Rights Article 20; American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man Article XXII; American Convention on Human Rights Articles 15 and 16, American Declaration on International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights Article 22. These international instruments were incorporated into the National Constitution by Art. 75.22 with constitutional hierarchy.
international_text_en: In its response to the Human Rights Council during its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina emphasized their focus on the “equal civil rights of migrants.”

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Immigration Act N° 25.871, Articles 3.E, Article 10; Decree N° 616/10, Article. 22. B, Article 23.N.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Article 20 which establishes that foreigners have the same civil rights as nationals. 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 5, Article 6. 3) Victims of Crime Act N° 27.372. If a migrant is a victim of a crime, he/she will have the right to access before criminal proceedings, as any other national, on the ground of this Act. This law only refers to “victims” without any distinction of nationality nor migratory status, and allows the participation of the individual through the whole procedure.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Argentina, Articles 18, Article 20. 2) Immigration Act N° 25.871, Article 23.m. 3) Decree 616/2010, Article 23.m. 4) Crime Victims Act N° 27.372. 5) Human Trafficking Act 26.364, Article 6.j. The Immigration Act, in its Art. 23 m) refers to "humanitarian reasons", a category that includes "...Persons who have been victims of trafficking in persons or other forms of slave exploitation and / or victims of the smuggling of migrants." These victims may benefit from a residence permit of 2 years.
international_text_en: In a recommendation to Belgium, in the course of its 2021 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina urged for an end to expulsion processes in the context of migrant women victims of domestic violence.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right in the Constitution article 75, subsections 22 and 23; Law No. 23.849 article 3, subsections 1; and Law No. 26.061 on "Integral Protection of the Rights of the Child and Adolescent"; and in Immigration Act 25.871 Articles 3, 10, and 29. There is no specific provisions that recognize the best interest of the child in the Immigration Act. However, the best interest of the child is recognized at the Convention on the Rights of the Childs, which is considered by Argentina's National Constitution as a self-executing treaty. Art. 75.23 states that the Parliament should “Legislate and promote positive action measures that guarantee real equality of opportunity and treatment, and the full enjoyment and exercise of the rights recognized by this Constitution and by current international human rights treaties, in particular with regard to children, women, the elderly and people with disabilities." However, the mentioned Convention was previously approved by the Parliament in 1990, so the "best interests of the child" should be considered in every decision adopted by authorities, including the administrative and judicial ones. The latter was reinforced by Act 26.061 which provides a more specific development of governmental obligations and duties towards children and adolescents. Article 29 of the Immigration Act ensures family reunification with migrant minors while allowing the suspension of a confirmed expulsion when the migrant to be expelled is the parent of a minor. Moreover, art. 3 includes the fulfillment of international human rights treaties. Additionally, on September 6th, 2022, in the Case "C.D., A. vs. National Direction of Migration", the Supreme Court referred to the above-mentioned rights and norms for stating that “the notion of "best interests" required an examination of the particularities of the case, taking into account, with special care and to the maximum extent possible, the real situation of the children involved, in order to find the solution that, among the possible alternatives, would be most beneficial to them, as subjects of preferential constitutional protection."
local_text_en: In a recent decision, the National Supreme Court of Justice stated that "The principle of the best interests of the child is constitutionally enshrined in Article 3 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (...). Its consideration must guide and condition all decisions of the courts called upon to cases involving children in all instances, including the Supreme Court, to which, as the supreme organ of one of the branches of the Federal Government, is responsible to apply - to the extent of its jurisdiction - the international treaties to which our country is a party (...)." See National Supreme Court of Justice, Case “C.G., A”, 6 September 2022, pp. 10-11.
international_text_en: In a recommendation to Belgium, in the course of its 2021 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina urged it to prioritize the “best interests of the child” in its decisions regarding migrant and refugee children. To the United Kingdom, in the course of its 2017 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina urged it to guarantee the “right to family reunification” for unaccompanied child refugees.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Argentina protects this right not in a universal way. National Constitution recognizes constitutional hierarchy to the CEDAW while it encourages the Parliament to promote positive action measures that guarantee real equality of opportunity and treatment with regard to women. Article 13 of the Immigration Act N° 25.871 additionally prohibits gender-based acts or omissions. Lastly, Article 3 of the Act N° 26.485 ensures all women an extensive catalog of rights and guarantees, such as "a) A life without violence and without discrimination; b) Health, education, and personal safety; c) Physical, psychological, sexual, economic or economic integrity; d) That their dignity be respected [...]" among others.
international_text_en: In a recommendation to Denmark, in the course of its 201 Universal Periodic Review, Argentina urged the unconditional granting of residence permits for women victims of domestic violence.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While the Constitution recognizes that the Parliament should adopt positive action measures to guarantee the rights of people with disabilities, there are no laws requiring authorities to take disabilities into account in the context of migration as a general matter. However, Article 23-h of the Immigration Act does provide temporary residence to those people that come to Argentina to address health problems in public or private health facilities, with authorization to remain in the country for one year, renewable, with multiple entrances and exits. Under this law, in the case of minors, disabled or sick people who due to the importance of their pathology should remain with companions, the temporary residence should be extended to direct family members, legal representative or curator.
