question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Australia

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The only non-citizens who are eligible to vote in a federal or state election are British subjects who were on the Commonwealth electoral roll immediately before 26 January 1984, at which time the eligibility requirements were altered. Also, non-citizens have the right to vote in some local government jurisdictions in Australia, for instance where they are a property owner or ratepayer.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are no express laws guaranteeing equal protection before the law for citizens or migrants in Australia. There is however, a common law right to natural justice/due process that his held equally by citizens and non-citizens: see Kioa v West (1985) 159 CLR 550. However, the content of the obligation to natural justice in certain cases (e.g., appeals over rejection of a visa) can be modified by statute. For instance, Part 7AA of the Migration Act 1958, provides very limited review rights to certain asylum-seekers; this is an example of a statutory override of certain migrants' rights to natural justice.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no right to free legal counsel. Section 193(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) provides that nothing in Australian law requires the Minister or any officer to allow a person in detention access to legal advice in relation to applications for visas, with the exception of where they have requested it (Section 256 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth)).

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right under Common Law. There is no right to an interpreter, but there is a presumption under common law that an interpreter should be provided where a judicial officer is not satisfied that the accused person understands the substance of the proceedings. It is well recognised that a criminal trial cannot be fair if the accused does not understand the language in which it is conducted: for example, Dietrich v The Queen (1992) 177 CLR 292. Additionally, while there is no right under national law, in Victoria, Queensland and the Australian Capital Territory the Human Rights Act 2004 (ACT), s 22(h), Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (VIC), s 25(2)(i), Human Rights Act 2019 (QLD), s 32(2)(i) provide for free interpretation in criminal proceedings.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 228B of the Migration Act 1958 provides that a non-citizen has no lawful right to come to Australia if they do not have a visa in effect. Section 228B(2) clarifies that this includes migrants seeking protection or asylum including whether or not they are found to be owed such protection. Civil and criminal sanctions may apply for unauthorised entry. In relation to criminal sanctions Section 235 provides for a criminal offence for presenting a false or forged document or making false or misleading representations in relation to entering or remaining in Australia. Additionally, Section 236 provides for an offence for using a visa granted to another person for the purposes of travelling to, remaining in Australia or identifying his or herself unless there is reasonable excuse.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no national legislation providing a right to public housing for citizens or migrants. This is governed at a state level. Most state legislation requires that a person be a citizen or permanent resident for a minimum number of years before being able to access public housing.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Australian Constitution does not contain a head of power for education under Section 51. Therefore, the regulation of school education falls within the residual power of states and territories. Public schools are generally free for citizens and permanent residents. School fees for dependents of temporary visas vary depending on the state or territory and depending on the visa subclass. Exemptions can apply and vary over time and across visa subclasses. For example, in New South Wales under 31A (1) and (2) of the Education Act 1990, ‘overseas students’ are liable to pay fees at a government/public school. ‘Overseas student’ is defined as a student who holds a visa under the Migration Act 1958, and does not include permanent visa holders.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Many temporary visas have a 'no study' condition which prohibits the holder from undertaking any form of study in Australia. For example, this includes bridging visas issued to certain cohorts of asylum seekers. To enrol at a public educational institution, a person must hold a valid visa without a no study condition attached to it. Subsidised access to universities and vocational colleges is available to citizens, permanent residents and New Zealand citizens. Generally only citizens are eligible for a low interest government loan to pay these subsidised fees (with exceptions for New Zealanders and permanent Humanitarian visa holders who satisfy additional residency requirements) under the Higher Education Support Act 2003 and VET Student Loan Act 2016.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. A visa (temporary or permanent) may be cancelled or refused under Section 501 of the Migration Act 1958 if the Minister reasonably suspects that the person doesn't meet the character test and the visa holder fails to satisfy the Minister that they do in fact pass the character test. This section provides that a non-citizen may fail the character test on the basis of their past or present general conduct. This allows the decision-maker to take into account "a broader view of a person's character where convictions may not have been recorded or where the person's conduct may not have constituted a criminal offence"

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. A non-citizen is entitled to a protection visa under the Migration Act, Section 197C if there is a real risk they would be subjected to torture, or cruel or inhuman treatment, or degrading treatment (except where that risk is faced by the population of the country generally and not faced by the non-citizen personally). This protection does not apply to those who do not apply for a Protection Visa. However, after the Migration Act was amended in 2014, a non-citizen who was found not eligible for a Protection Visa (on character or other grounds), could be removed despite the non-refoulement obligations under 197C. In 2021, Section 197C was amended to add Section 197C(3) providing that officers are not authorised to remove a non-citizen if, in the course of a protection visa application, a finding was made that they were owed protection. This amendment does not prevent refoulement of all people at risk of such harm because Section 197C(3) only applies to people who have made a valid application for a protection visa. The effect of Sections 197C(1) and (2) may be such that other non-citizens at risk, who have not applied and had a protection visa finally determined, may/must be removed. Moreover, even in relation to those protected from removal under s 197C(3), the Minister may determine under Section 197D that they are no longer a person in respect of whom a protection finding has been made.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. A non-citizen is entitled to a Protection visa under Section 36(2)(a) of the Migration Act if the Minister is satisified that Australia has protection obligations because they are a refugee, as defined in Section 5H. After the Migration Act was amended in 2014, a non-citizen who was not eligible for a Protection visa (on character or other grounds), could be removed despite Australia's non-refoulement obligations under 197C. However, in 2021, Section 197C was amended to add Section 197C(3) providing that officers are not authorised to remove a non-citizen if, in the course of a protection visa application, a finding was made that they were owed protection. This amendment does not prevent refoulement of all people at risk of such harm because Section 197C(3) only applies to people who have made a valid application for a protection visa. The effect of Sections 197C(1) and (2) may be such that other non-citizens at risk, who have not applied and had a protection visa finally determined, may/must be removed. Moreover, even in relation to those protected from removal under s 197C(3), the Minister may determine under Section 197D that they are no longer a person in respect of whom a protection finding has been made.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. A non-citizen is entitled to a Protection visa under the Migration Act, Section 197C if there is a real risk they would be arbitrarily deprived of their life or subject to the death penalty (except where that risk is faced by the population of the country generally and not faced by the non-citizen personally). After the Migration Act was amended in 2014, a non-citizen who was not eligible for a Protection visa (on character or other grounds), could be removed despite Australia's non-refoulement obligations under 197C. However, in 2021, Section 197C was amended to add Section 197C(3) providing that officers are not authorised to remove a non-citizen if, in the course of a protection visa application, a finding was made that they were owed protection. This amendment does not prevent refoulement of all people at risk of such harm because Section 197C(3) only applies to people who have made a valid application for a protection visa. The effect of Sections 197C(1) and (2) may be such that other non-citizens at risk, who have not applied and had a protection visa finally determined, may/must be removed. Moreover, even in relation to those protected from removal under s 197C(3), the Minister may determine under Section 197D that they are no longer a person in respect of whom a protection finding has been made.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protectoion of this right. Section 193 Migration Act 1958 specifically precludes such a right.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While Section 197C of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) now prevents secondary refoulement for those found to be owed protection obligations, this only applies to people who have gained entry and been immigration cleared in Australia and who are not barred from making applications for a protection visa. For people who arrive by boat to an excised offshore place, they may be removed to a country designated as a 'regional processing country' under s 198AB(2). The only condition for the exercise of the Minister's power to make that designation is that the Minister thinks that it is in the national interest to designate the country to be a regional processing country, though in considering the national interest, under s 198AB(3) the Minister must have regard to whether or not that country has given Australia assurances that it will not refoule the person.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law provides for the removal of unlawful non-citizens in s 198 of the Migration Act 1958.An unlawful non-citizen is a person who does not hold a lawful visa. Unlawful non-citizens may be expelled at the border based on discretionary screening interviews. If a person raises fears about being returned or claims asylum they cannot be turned around under policy guidelines. Where people hold visas in effect, they cannot be cancelled (giving rise to removal obligations) without access to procedural fairness.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in1) the Migration Act 1958. 2) The Australian Constitution s75(v). Most (but not all) decisions to issue or cancel a visa for persons inside Australia require some level of procedural fairness to be afforded. However, in some visa cancellation decisions, which may lead to eventual expulsion, a merits review is excluded and only judicial review is available. For example, where the Minister personally decides not to revoke a visa cancellation. However, judicial review is still available under Section 75(v) of the Australian Constitution.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, the Citizenship Act 2007, Section 21(8) states that stateless children born in Australia, who have never held citizenship of any country, and are not entitled to acquire citizenship in any other country are eligible for Australian citizenship. There are no provisions providing a right or access to citizenship to other stateless migrants (including children born overseas).

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia conditionally protects this right in the Migration Regulations 1994, sch 2. There are at least 14 visa subclasses which allow for the sponsorship of family members by permanent residents. However, refugees or workers who hold temporary visas (all refugees who arrived by boat since 2012) are not entitled to family reunion. There is also no ability to sponsor the residence of a family member who is not a spouse, parent or child, except for a very small number of visas available for 'aged dependent relatives' or 'remaining relatives'.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Migration Act 1958 Part 8.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in 1) Migration Regulations 1994 Sch 2. sets out requires for a Partner visa. 2) Migration Act 1958, Section 5CB defines de facto partner. Section 5F defines spouse. The Partner visa is available for any married spouses (including anyone in a valid marriage) or de facto couples (defined as 'whether of the same sex or a different sex').

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Migration Regulations 1994, Sch 2, there are some temporary visas, for instance the Temporary Protection visa for refugees who arrived in Australia by boat without authorisation, or the temporary visa for seasonal workers, for which it is not possible to transition to any permanent visa.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) s 13. The Fair Work Act provides protections for breaches of contract law and does not differentiate based on citizenship of the work. Furthermore, the Fair Work Legislation Amendment (Protecting Worker Entitlements) Act 2023 amends the Fair Work Act 2009 by inserting a new provision (s40B) which provides that the validity of a contract of employment or a contract for services is not affected by a breach of the Migration Act. According to the Explanatory Memorandum, the provision makes 'explicit the policy position that a migrant worker...would be entitled to the benefit of the FW Act regardless of migration status, including in relation to wages and entitlements conferred by the statute or a fair work instrument.' However, migrant workers do not have access to the Fair Entitlement Guarantee which provides compensation to the employees of companies which go bankrupt. There have been many recent cases of company's going into liquidation and migrant workers not being paid for months of work, whereas the local workers get compensation under this scheme.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Health Insurance Act 1973 (Cth), Section 6(1). Section 6(1), permanent visa holders are eligible for Medicare (free or subsidised public health care) on par with citizens. Temporary visa holders who have applied for a permanent visa may also be eligible with exceptions (eg Parent visa) if they on a visa allowing them to work, and their parent, spouse or child is an Australian citizen, a permanent resident, or a New Zealand citizen living in Australia. Temporary visa holders are also eligible if they live in a country that has a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement with Australia. Some temporary visa-holders (for instance asylum seekers or refugees who arrived in Australia by both without authorisation) have access to Medicare.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 34 of the Constitution states that, "Until the Parliament otherwise provides, the qualifications of a member of the House of Representatives shall be as follows: (i) he must be of the full age of twenty?one years, and must be an elector entitled to vote at the election of members of the House of Representatives, or a person qualified to become such elector, and must have been for three years at the least a resident within the limits of the Commonwealth as existing at the time when he is chosen; (ii) he must be a subject of the Queen, either natural?born or for at least five years naturalized under a law of the United Kingdom, or of a Colony which has become or becomes a State, or of the Commonwealth, or of a State."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no national law prohibiting discrimination on the ground of migration status. While there is a prohibition on the ground of nationality (Racial Discrimination Act 1975 Section 5), the decision from Addy v Federal Commissioner of Taxation (2021) 95 ALJR 911 [2021] HCA 34 struck down differential taxation of backpackers on the basis that this contravened the federal prohibition on discrimination on the ground of nationality (for backpackers from certain countries with whom a double tax agreement is in place). Therefore, the nationality clause is not settled law.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in 1) the Racial Discrimination Act 1975, Part II and Part IIA, implements Australia's international obligations under The International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD). 2) The Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Fair Work Act applies to all workers in Australia, and states that certain visa sublcasses also contain a requirement for equal pay to locals doing the same job. Additionally, all workers in Australia are entitled to the basic minimum wage under federal tribunal determination, or in a modern award (government pay rates in some jobs and some industries). However, there are no federal protections against discrimination on the basis of non-citizenship or immigration status. Therefore, migrants may be paid less than local workers doing the same work.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Migration Regulations 1994 Sch 2 and Sch 8 (Condition 8607). Where a migrant holds a Temporary Skills Shortage (TSS) visa, they are required to be sponsored by an employer and can change employers as long as the new employer becomes their sponsor within 60 days. Seasonal workers are required to be sponsored by a labour hire firm in a relevant industry. Temporary migrant workers on Working Holiday visas or student visas (which are far greater in number) have completely free choice of employment. Migrants on permanent skilled visas may either be restricted to employer sponsorship for a period of time, or to a region or unrestricted depending on the visa. In order to support Australia’s COVID-19 economic recovery, a less restrictive policy on visa condition 8107 was temporarily implemented. Under this policy, holders of 408 (COVID-19 Pandemic event) visas may change employment and work for more than one employer, including self-employment. Additionally, the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme was established in 2021. Under this scheme workers are restricted to working for their sponsoring employer in their nominated industry and region.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Migration Regulations 1994, Sch 2. Generally, condition 8607, which restricts work to certain occupations or employers, is only applied to the primary applicant, and not to family members. For example, a partner of a TSS visa holder (temporary sponsored worker) or permanent skilled visa-holder has unlimited work rights. A partner of an international student has work rights limited to 40 hours per fortnight while the primary visa-holder's course is in session.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Migration Regulations 1994, Sch 2. In almost all cases, permanent residence is not linked to ongoing employment in a particular industry or with a particular employer or at all. One very small exception is the permanent Regional Sponsored Migration Scheme visa which requires a migrant to make a genuine effort to work with a particular employer in a particular region for 2 years upon grant. Loss of employment for a TSS visa holder (temporary sponsored visa) will result in automatic loss of visa unless an alternative sponsor is found in 60 days. However, loss of sponsorship by a labour hire firm will result in loss of visa status for a seasonal worker.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in 1) Fair Work Act 2009. 2) National Employment Standards. However, there is no protection against discrimination on the basis of citizenship for migrants on any visa (temporary or permanent).

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in 1) Social Security Act 1991 (Cth), Sections 593, 7(2), ss 43, 94, 201AA, 500X. Generally only permanent residents can access social security benefits, but a waiting period of two years is often required (eg. Carer payment under section 201AA). Parenting payments require a waiting period of 4 years (section 500X). Other social security benefits (e.g. disability and old age pension) require a residence period of ten years.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in 1) Social Security Act 1991 (Cth), Sections 593, 7(2). Access to Newstart is available for permanent residents. It is not available to temporary visa holders, with the exception of a very small number of New Zealand citizens who have lived in Australia continuously for at least ten years since 26 February 2001 who can access a once only payment of Newstart Allowance, Sickness Allowance or Youth Allowance for a maximum continuous period of six months.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Migration Regulations, sch 2. There are a number of permanent visas, which are predicated on skills, employment or partnership with an Australian resident or citizenship which are available to most (but not all) temporary visa holders. Bars are usually applied against irregular migrant workers transitioning onto a substantive temporary or permanent visa (ie as opposed to a Bridging visa which may be availble to regularise their status pending their legal appeal or departure).

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right at the national level, but there are existing criminal laws in every state governing theft that provide this right, such as the Crimes Act of 1958 for the state of Victoria.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right at the national level. Registration of births and deaths is governed by state (not national) legislation

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to the Migration Act, Section 13, Australia holds visa information information electronically, and visa status information is now accessed through an online system, the Visa Entitlement Verification Online (VEVO). Work rights attached to a visa can also be checked through VEVO. However, there is no government mandated identity document issued to migrants. The government may issue ImmiCards to some migrants, upon their application, who don't have and cannot obtain a passport recognised by the Australian Government. The ImmiCard can be used as a 'commencement of identity' document, however this is only issued to certain visa holders, mainly those related to seeking or having sought protection.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While it is illegal to damage or interfere with an Australian passport under the Australian Passport Act, there is no equivalent prohibition in relation to other identity documents used migrants.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Consular Privileges and Immunities Act 1972 (Cth), Section 5 provides that certain articles of the Vienna Convention have the force of law in Australia, but it does not include Article 36.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Australia has a system of mandataroy detention, which applies to anyone who is in Australia without a valid visa, including children (Migration Act 1958, ss 189). However, Section 4AA of the Migration Act provides that children are to only be detained as a matter of last resort.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Under Australia's mandatory detention policies (according to the Migration Act 1958, Section 189), anyone whom an authorised immigration officer knows or reasonably suspects to be an unlawful non-citizen (i.e., who does not hold a valid visa) must be detained

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in 1) the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth). 2) The Australian Constitution s 75(v). However, under these provisions, migrants can only challenge legality, and can only challenge conditions in a limited way. There are no grounds for appealing proportionality, length or appropriateness of detention. In terms of conditions, there is limited scope to challenge these under the common law duty of care in tort law, where such conditions can be characterised as breaching that duty of care, according to the decision of AS v Minister for Immigration and Border Protection [2014] VSC 593.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Migration Act 1958, Section 189 states that detention is mandatory and automatic for anyone who does not hold a valid visa.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are some specific prohibitions on torture, cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment for individuals in some contexts, such for persons under arrest (according to Section 23Q of the Crimes Act 1914). But there is no genreral legal right to be free of torture and cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment for citizens, let alone for migrants.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Australia permits the use of force in the Maritime Powers Act 2013 (Cth), ss 37(1) and 72(4). Section 72(4) provides that a maritime officer may detain a person (who is, for instance, seeking to enter Australia) on a detained vessel and take the person to a place outside Australia. Section 37(1) provides that in exercising powers under this Act, a maritime officer may use such force against a person or thing as is necessary and reasonable in the circumstances.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protectionof this right. For instance, Sections 37(b)(i) and (ii) of the Maritime Powers Act 2013 (Cth) provides that the maritime officer must not do anything that is likely to cause the death of, or grievous bodily harm to, a person unless the person has been called on to surrender and the officer believes on reasonable grounds that the person cannot be apprehended in any other manner.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are no blanket exceptions from criminal prosecution of trafficked and smuggled migrants. While the act of being trafficked or smuggled is not criminalised, such persons can face criminal prosecution if they were complicit in the trafficking or smuggling of others, even in a minor way, or engaged in other criminal offences. There have been prosecutions of migrants who facilitated the travel of others when they themselves were fleeing harm. However, general defences under the Criminal Code such as sudden or extraordinary emergency may be applicable in those circumstances: see eg Nguyen v The Queen [2005] WASCA 22; Tran v Commonwealth (2010) 187 FCR 54; Warnakulasuriya v The Queen (2012) 261 FLR 260.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth) Sections 36A-L. Section 36D relates to 'Citizenship cessation determination for certain convictions'. Under this section the Minister is empowered to determine that a dual citizen ceases to be an Australian citizen if the person has been convicted of a terrorist related offence, under which they have been sentenced to a period of imprisonment of at least 3 years (as opposed to the 6 years under the previous regime). The Minister is empowered to make this determination if satisfied that the conduct demonstrates a repudiation of allegiance to Australia and that it would be contrary to the public interest for the person to remain an Australian citizen. It is important to note that under this section the power is enlivened only upon conviction by a court.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Australian Citizenship Act 2007 Section 21. Any migrant who is a permanent resident and fulfils other criteria (including a residence requirement, English language ability and passing a citizenship test) may apply for citizenship

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Australian Citizenship Act 2007 Section 21. Any migrant who is a permanent resident and fulfils other criteria (including a residence requirement, English language ability and passing a citizenship test) may apply for citizenship.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Australian Citizenship Act 2007 Section 21. Any migrant who is a permanent resident and fulfils other criteria (including a residence requirement, English language ability and passing a citizenship test) may apply for citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in the Australian Citizenship Act 2007, which contains no requirement that a migrant renounce their first nationality before receiving Australian citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no right to freedom of religion as such. This Consitutional protection in Section 116 prohibits the Commonwealth from laws which prohibit the free exercise of relation. Common law protections extend this to migrants on an equal basis with citizens, but they are only actionable in a limited way, as they only narrowly protect the right of freedom of religion.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are no laws in Australia providing nationals or migrants the right to freedom of opinions.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right [1&2] Australian Constitution; Nationwide News Pty Ltd v Wills (1992) 177 CLR 1; Australian Capital Television Pty Ltd v Commonwealth (1992) 177 CLR 106. There is no positive right to freedom of opinion or expression. However, there is an implied constitutional freedom to political communication which limits the power of parliament to curtail freedom of political communication in a way that is not reasonably appropriate and adapted to serve a legitimate end. The courts have read in a limited freedom of political communication into the Australian Constitution, but this is unlikely to extend to non-citizens as they are unable to vote.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: There is no general right to freedom of association for citizens or migrants in Australia. To the extent that national law in Australia protects this right, it does protects migrants on an equal basis with citizens. 1) Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Act 2009 (Cth) Section 166, which protects the freedom of workers in a workplace to become, or not become, members of industrial associations, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. 2) Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), which protects the rights of workers regardless of immigration status to be represented, or not represented, by industrial associations, and to participate, or not participate, in lawful industrial activities.3) Australian Human Rights Commission Regulations 1989. 'Trade union activity' is prescribed in the Australian Human Rights Commission Regulations 1989 as a ground for discrimination in employment that engages the power of the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986. This means that the Commission may investigate complaints about discrimination in employment based on trade union activity. No distinction is made in these laws between citizens and migrants.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Migration Regulations 1994 Sch 2, in order to sponsor a family member, the migrant must be a permanent resident. To sponsor parents or aged relative or humanitarian family entrants, it is necessary to have an assurance of support (and this may also be required for the sponsorship of children). An Assurance of Support is a legal agreement and provision of a bank guarantee to repay the Commonwealth any government payment to the family member.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are no specific provisions providing victims of crime (citizen or migrant) with any specific rights or guarantees in national law. However, some states offer such protection in the form of a Charter of Victims Rights or victims compensation schemes on an equal basis to citizens.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in 1) Migration Regulations, Division 1.5 (Special Provisions relating to family violence). 2) Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth) Sch 2. In relation to trafficking, relief is contingent on participation in criminal proceedings, where a Bridging Visa F - temporary, would be provided. In relation to family violence, victims applying for certain visas (subclasses 820, 309, 300 and 858) are able to obtain these visas even where the relationship has broken down if they experienced family violence during the relationship. This pathway was introduced to ensure that victims did not have to stay in an abusive relationship to regularise their status.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in 1) Migration Regulations 1994, Sch 4, cll 4016 and 4018. 2) Migration Act 1958 (Cth), s 4AA. 3) Immigration (Guardianship of Children) Act 1946. In Australian law, there is a general condition for most visas for which children are eligible, that requires the Department to be satisfied that there are not compelling reasons to believe that the granting of the visa would not be in the child's best interest. Also, the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) (including the provisions relating to the best interest of the child) is scheduled to the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission Act 1986 (Cth).

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Australia protects this right in Migration Act 1958, Schedule 2, sc 204 (Women at Risk Visa), which provides female refugees a visa when they do not have the protection of a male relative/partner and are in danger of victimisation.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Disability and health requirements can be used to refuse or cancel a visa per Migration Act 1958, Sch4, cll 4005-4007.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Kevin Fredy Hinterberger. [2]: Lukas Gahleitner-Gertz.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Austria

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Even though migrants enjoy all rights protected by Article 11 of the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which has been incorporated into Austrian law by application of Article 9 of the Austrian Constitution, provides a right of freedom of association for all people and does not distinguish between migrants and citizens, there are different aspects of the right of freedom of assembly in national law. In particular, there are additional rights of freedom of assembly afforded to citizens and laid down in the Versammlungsgsetz and which therefore do differentiate between citizens and migrants. For example, according to Section 8 of the Versammlungsgesetz only Austrian citizens are allowed to act as organizers or leaders of an assembly. For this reason, the right of freedom of assembly is limited in certain ways to migrants and not commensurate with the rights afforded to citizens.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While European Union citizens residing in Austria have the right to vote in local and European election, according to Article 117 Bundes-Verfassungsgesetz, other third-country nationals do not have this right.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Bundesverfassungsgesetz zur Durchf?hrung des internationalen ?bereinkommens ?ber die Beseitigung aller Formen rassischer Diskriminierung (BVGRassendiskr) states that all migrants are to be treated equally compared to other migrants, but not to citizens. Furthermore, the BVGRassendiskr also only applies to the government (execution) and the legislation, but not the judiciary.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 8a of the Verwaltungsgerichtshofsgesetz, which states that every person in an administrative law proceeding has the right to counsel at government expense, this is required to guarantee the right to a fair trial according to Article 6 of the European Charter of Human Rights, and Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. However, for asylum procedures Section 48-52a of the BFAVerfahrensgesetz (BFA-VG) provides specific counselling for asylum seekers (counsellors from NGOS, but not lawyers).

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 56, 126-127, 164, 381 of the Strafprozessordnung (StPO). According to Section 56 of the StPO, everyone has a right to free translation services in criminal proceedings. The law does not distinguish between migrants and citizens, and is interpreted to include both. Section 126-126 regulate the conditions the interpreter has to fulfill.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While there are no explicit criminal sanctions included in the criminal code, there are also no exemptions, either. In fact, there are sanctions stipulated in administrative criminal law for unlawful entry. For example, Section 120 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz (FPG) stipulates a fine of 500 up to 2500 Euros for migrants that stay illegally in the country. If the fine cannot be paid by the relevant persons, they can be imprisoned up to two weeks. In cases of repeated infringement, the migrants can be fined 2500 up to 7500 Euros or imprisoned for up to four weeks. In cases of persons applying for asylum after entering the country in an unauthorized manner, Article 31 of the Geneva Refugee Convention, which states that "the Contracting States shall not apply to the movements of such refugees restrictions other than those which are necessary and such restrictions shall only be applied until their status in the country is regularized or they obtain admission into another country," applies.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 8(4) of the “Wohnungsgemeinn?tzigkeitsgesetz” (WGG) stipulates that access to public housing is dependant on citizenship and length of stay. Non-profit building associations (public housing) primarily only provide housing to Austrian citizens, and foreigners who have been residing legally in Austria continuously for more than five years, and have a certificate from the Austrian Integration Fund.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Article 1 of the Schulpflichtsgesetz. For all children who are pemanently residing in Austria, starting from the age of 6, there is an obligation to attend school. The state is obligated to guarantee this access, but this right is not protected for irregular migrants, or those deemed not to be permanently residing in Austria.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Article 1 of the Berufsausbildungsgesetz. Generally, all natural persons can enter vocational training, including irregular migrants. As to public universities, the law does not differentiate on migrant status (meaning irregular migrants are applicable) for admission, but there is a differential fee structure.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Sections 7, 9 of the Asylgesetz (AsylG). According to Section 7(1) Nr 1 of the AsylG and Section 9(2) Nr 2 and 3 of the AsylG, refugees and beneficiaries of subsidiary protection lose their status if they are convicted of a criminal offense. One problem in practice, however, is that such procedures are often initiated before the person has been convicted. 2) Sections 11, 38 of the Niederlassungs und Aufenthaltsgesetz. Generally, a third-country national loses his/her residence status if he/she is convicted of a criminal offense (punishable by a sentence of imprisonment of at least one year).

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Articles 2-3 of of the European Human Rights Charter. If the authorities and Courts foresee a violation of these rights due to refoulement, the migrant in question can be granted residence status (subsidiary protection, § 8 AsylG); in case of criminal convictions the status can be revoked, a deportation is not possible when there is the risk of refoulement. These persons receive the status "Tolerated person" (Duldung). This status does not entail a legal stay, but the person cannot be fined for being in Austria. This special status can be revoked at anytime if the decision is made that that there is no risk of rights enfringement due to refoulement. 2) 45a and 50(1) of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz. The laws ban refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 3 of the Asylgesetz. Section 45a and 50(2) of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz. The laws ban refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to persecution based on race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular soical group, or political opinion.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Section Article 2 and 3 of the European Charter of Human Rights. 2) Section 45a and 50 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz. Section 45a (2) states that Aliens shall not be refused or deported back into a country or prevented from entering a country if there are good reasons to believe that their life or liberty there is restricted on grounds of their race, religion, nationality, membership of a certain social group or their political views would be threatened (Art. 33 Z 1 of the Convention on the Legal Status of Refugees, BGBl. No. 55/1955, in the version of the Protocol on the Legal Status of Refugees, BGBl. No. 78/1974), unless there is an internal flight alternative (§ 11 AsylG 2005).

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no specific mention of this provision in national law. Section 45a of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz (FPG, Aliens Police Law) if a person in an interview at the border mentions fear of being persecuted if they are returned to their origin, the case has to be investigated whether a rejection would violate the non-refoulement principle. But the migrant does not have to be informed about the possibility of lodging an asylum application.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Article 3 of the European Charter of Human Rights. 2) Sections 45a and 50 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz. According to the Supreme Administrative Court, the threat of a chain expulsion would constitute a violation of Article 3 of the European Charter of Human Rights (Verwaltungsgerichtshof 2006/19/0673).

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Section 52-53 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz. 2) Section 10 of the Asylgesetz. 3) Section 9 of the BFAVerfahrensgesetz (BFA-VG). In order to deport a person from Austria, the individual case has to be assessed and, based on this individual assessment, a return decision has to be issued. The return decision is admissable if state and public interests outweigh the individual right of private and family life guaranteed by Article 8 of the European Charter of Human Rights. Conforming to this stipulation, the authority has to check certain criteria (stated in Section 9 of the BFA-VG) such as the criminal record of the individual, his/her integration in Austria, time of stay in Austria, connections to home country etc.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Section 45 of the Allgemeines Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz. 2) Section 7 of the BFA-Verfahrensgesetz. 3) Section 9 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz. Specifically, Section 7 of the BFA-Verfahrensgesetz and Section 9 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz provide migrants with the right to lodge an appeal against explusion to the administrative court.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 3, 7(3) Z 2, 10(4) Z 2, 14(1) Z 1 of the Staatsb?rgerschaftsgesetz. In order to obtain citizenship, stateless persons have to be born in Austria, be stateless since birth, and have lived in Austria for 10 years (5 years without an interruption). The person must also not have been convicted of a major offense. The application for citizenship in the case of children has to be submitted between 18 months and a maximum of 3 years.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria conditionally protects this right in Section 46 and 52 of the Niederlassungs-und Aufenthaltsgesetz (NAG). Section 46 of the NAG provides settled migrants with a legal avenue for family reunification, but certain requirements have to be fulfilled. Favourable exceptions apply to family members of the European Union, EWR and Swiss citizens (Section 52 of the NAG) if they have made use of their right of free movement. A special regime applies to refugees and beneficiaries of subsidiary protection (see Sections 34-35 of the Asylgesetz). Economic migrants have to meet resource requirements, such as accomodations, for their incoming family members, while persons that have been granted asylum status do not have to fufill these preconditions as long as the time limit for applications are met.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 3 of the Niederlassungs-und Aufenthaltsgesetz, which states that an appeal against a negative decision against family reunification can be challenged with an appeal to an administrative court.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Section 2(1)Z, 9 of the Niederlassungs-und Aufenthaltsgesetz. 2) Verfassungsgerichtshof G 258/2017 ua. Family members are defined as someone who who is the spouse, registered partner, or unmarried child, including adopted or stepchildren (core family). Spouses and registered partners must have reached the age of 21. The Constitutional Court also recognized same-sex marriage in 2017 (Verfassungsgerichtshof G 258/2017 ua), meaning that, under the stipulations of the law, family reunification would be open to same-sex migrants.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The conditions to be eligible for a permanent status are set out in Section 45 of the Niederlassungs-und Aufenthaltsgesetz. For example, temporary migrant workers that are in Austria on grounds of a displaced person status are not eligible for permanent status.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Sections 54-56 of the Asylgesetz. As the requirements for regularization are very high, this right does exist, but generally for extraordinary cases. Section 56 of the Asylgesetz foresees a possibility of regularisation when the person is residing in the country for more than 5 years, of which half of the time - but at least 3 years - have to be on basis of a regular title of stay. 2) Section 11 of the Niederlassungs- und Aufenthaltsgesetz. Furthermore the person concerned has to either fulfill the "Integrationsvereinbarung" (Section 9 of the Integrationsgesetz) or be working (which is difficult to fulfill when a person is not residing lawfully). Additionally, obtaining a title via the regular migration scheme is not possible if a return decision has already been issued. If a return decision has not yet been issued it is possible to bring in an application in Austria.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Article 29 of the Ausl?nderbesch?ftigungsgesetz (AusIBG). Even if the work contract is unlawful (because the migrant does not have a work permit), Section 29(1) of the AuslBG states that those undocumented migrants have access to the same claims as if they would have a valid working contract. 2) Article 17 of the Gleichbehandlungsgesetz.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Articles 4-12 of the Allgemeines Sozialversicherungsgesetz (ASVG). 2) Article 23 of the Krankenanstalten-und Kuranstaltengesetz. Health care services are available for all persons who are working (employment-criteria), receive a pension or are family members of insured persons. Furthermore, persons who receive primary care ("Grundversorgung") or social welfare ("Sozialhilfe"/"Mindestsicherung") have access to health care. Therefore, in general health care services are guaranteed on an equal basis with citizens. Access to health care services are not denied by law to irregular migrants, however, irregular migrants do not generally receive primary care or social welfare and hence, do not have access since they are not allowed to work.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Only Austrian citizens are allowed to stand for national elections (minimum age 18 years). The same applies for local and regional elections, with one exception. European Union citizens residing and living in Austria are allowed to stand for election in the locality where they live, according to Articles 23a, 26, 95, and 117 of the Bundes-Vergassungsgesetz.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) the Bundesverfassungsgesetz vom 3. Juli 1973 zur Durchf?hrung des Internationalen ?bereinkommens ?ber die Beseitigung aller Formen rassischer Diskriminierung (BVGRassendiskr). According to the BVGRassendiskr, discrimination on grounds of race, skin color, or national or ethnic origin is prohibited. 2) The Gleichbehandlungsgesetz (GIBG). According to Section 2 of this law, migrants have the right to equal treatment in employment. Section 3 also provides equal treatment in all other aspects, such as education access. 3) The ArbeitnehmerInnenschutzgesetz. 4) Article 283 of the Strafgesetzbuch (StGB). The High Court ruled in 5.4.2017, 15 Os 25/17s, that a social media posting mentioning the personal approval of shooting of asylumseekers is illegal under Section 283 of the StGB. Even though the residence status of the person (asylum seeker) is not mentioned as one of the identifying criteria in the law directly the High Court says that incitement of hatred against a group of persons (residence status) is included in the criteria mentioned in the law (nationality).

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Articles 1 and 7 of the Bundesverfassungsgesetz zur Durchf?hrung des Internationalen ?bereinkommens ?ber die Beseitigung aller Formen rassischer Diskriminierung, which states that discrimination on grounds of race, skin color, or national or ethnic origin is prohibited. 2) Article 283 of the Strafgesetzbuch. 3) Article 20 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Art 7 B-VG; Bundesverfassungsgesetz vom 3. Juli 1973 zur Durchf?hrung des Internationalen ?bereinkommens ?ber die Beseitigung aller Formen rassischer Diskriminierung(BVGRassendiskr). 2) Article 20 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. 2) Section 17 of the Gleichbehandlungsgesetz (GlbG), which stipulates no one may be directly or indirectly discriminated against in connection with an employment relationship due to their ethnicity, religion or belief, age or sexual orientation.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in Articles 3-7 of the Ausl?nderbesch?ftigungsgesetz. A migrant generally needs a work permit to work, but different categories of migrants have different restrictions. Migrants on general work permits can change employers, but they must reapply for a new work permit. The only exceptions are migrants from the European Union, who have free choice of work without the need of a work permit.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Spouses do not have the right to work without applying for a work permit. The only group who are exempt are spouses of European Union citizens.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National low in Austria protects this right in Sections 11, 28 of the Niederlassungs-und Aufenthaltsgesetz (NAG), which states that certain residence permits are not invalidated with the loss of employment. However, one issue is that after a migrant loses their job, the possibility of obtaining a new residence permit will not be possible; see Section 41a of the NAG regarding the "Rot-Weiss-Rot Karte plus."

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protect this right in Article 17 of the Gleichbehandlungsgesetz and Article 7 of the Bundes-Verfassungsgesetz (GibG).

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this in 1) Article 14 of the Arbeitslosenversicherungsgesetz. 2) Article 221ff of the Allgemeines Sozialversicherungsgesetz (ASVG). 3) Allgemeines Pensionsgesetz (APG). The law does not differentiate between native and migrant workers. Instead, any person that has worked for more than a year in the last two years is eligible for social security protection. Prior work in the country of origin transfers to the Austrian system for work in European Union Member states and states where international agreements exist. Beneficiaries of international protection are eligible for social security protection like citiziens right after the title of stay was granted.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in Article 14 of the Arbeitslosenversicherungsgesetz. All workers have the same access to unemployment benefits disrespective of nationality or legal status. For the first time they apply, the person has to fulfill the precondition to work 52 weeks in the last two years. If the person is under the age of 25, the person must have worked 26 weeks in one year. For all other application periods, the right to unemployment benefits arises after half a year.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Articles 26, 45 of the Niederlassungs-und Aufenthaltsgesetz. Under certain circumstances, third-country nationals who have been resident continuously for the past five years can be granted a "permanent residence -European Union" residence permit.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) the Fremdenpolizeigesetz (FPG). 2) Asylgesetz (Asylg). 3) Niederlassungs-und Aufenthaltsgesetz (NAG). The right to not have identity documents confiscated by anyone, other than a public official duly authorized by the law is stated in all three laws (FPG, AsylG and NAG); documents can only be confiscated by the authority that issued it. Regarding each residence permit, there is a specific provision that stipulates in which cases a document may be confiscated (“Entziehung”).

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 9 of the Personenstandsgesetz, which obliges all parents to register their children within one week after birth regardless of status.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Niederlassungs- und Aufenthaltsgesetz (NAG). 2) Asylgesetz (Asylg). 3) Fremdenpolizeigesetz (FPG). Each law stipulates this right for different categories of migrants. AsylG deals with asylum seekers and refugees/beneficiares of subsidiary protection. FPG deals with all aliens (non-Austrian citizens). NAG deals also with all migrants but regarding their residency rights, whereas FPG deals with alien police matters like deportation but also documents like passports for refugees.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 229 of the Strafgesetzbuch. According to Article 229, it is generally prohibited to destroy documents, and provides a criminal sanction to anyone who destroys the documents of another person (not only migrants). Whoever destroys, damages or suppresses such a document, which they are not allowed to dispose of, must, if they act with intent, is to be punished with a custodial sentence up to one year or a fine.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Section 171 (4) lit c StPO (Code of Criminal Procedure). 2) Section 40 (2) Fremdenpolizeigesetz. Upon request of the concerned migrant, consular officials are to be informed about the migrants legal situation.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in Section 76(1) of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz which prohibits the detention of underaged minors (from 7 to 14 years).

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Sections 76-76 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz (FPG). 2) Article 5(1) of the European Convention on Human Rights. 3) Bundesverfassungsgesetz vom 29. November 1988 ?ber den Schutz der pers?nlichen Freiheit [Federal Constitutional Act on the Protection of Personal Freedom]. The law allows putting migrants without legal status into detention if the goal of the detention (securing the deportation or issuing measures that lead to deportation) cannot be reached by milder means. Detention can only be ordered if there is a risk of the migrant fleeing. Therefore, detention cannot be solely based on their immigration status, but the law does not explicitly prohibit it and there is a link to immigration status.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects the right in 1) Section 22a of the BFA-Verfahrensgesetz. 2) 82 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz. Detention and its circumstances can be appealed anytime during the detention. Upon release, the detention can still be challenged within 6 weeks.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 76 of the Fremdenpolizeigesetz. Detention requires an individualized decision by the authorities based on an examination of the migrant's personal circumstances, including a proportionality test.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Article 3 of the European Charter of Human Rights, which has been adopted as part of Austria's national constitution, which states that 'No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment'. 2) The ?bereinkommen gegen Folter und andere grausame, unmenschliche oder erniedrigende Behandlung oder Strafe (CAT).

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Article 2 of the Eurioean Convention on Human Rights. Austrian law does not explicitly prohibit the use of lethal force in these circumstances, but it does strictly regulate the use of force. The law requires that every measure taken has to be proportional, according to Articles 41(1) and 45 of the FPG ("Fremdenpolizeigesetz", Aliens' Police Law). Furthermore, Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, has been made directly applicable via in the Austrian Constitution, protects the right to life, hence the use of lethal force is only allowable in exceptional cases and is never proportional as a means of preventing entry.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protectects this right in Section 114 (5) of the Fremdenpolizeigeset, which states that "aliens whose unlawful entry or transit is promoted by the offence are not to be punished as participants (§ 12 Criminal Code). It is permissible to stay their return or deportation if and as long as this is necessary in order to interrogate them on the facts of the case."

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in "Staatsb?rgerschaftsgesetz" (StbG). According to the StbG, criminal and other convictions do not lead to the loss of citizenship status. However, two things have to be taken into account: first, a criminal conviction constitutes a ground for refusal to obtain citizenship (Section 10(1) Nr 2 StbG). Second, a person actively taking part in an armed conflict (e.g., ISIS) might lead to the loss of their citizenship. However, this only applies if the person will not be made stateless by the decision.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 10-11b Staatsb?rgerschaftsgesetz. Economic migrants have access if they fulfill certain requirements (e.g., 10 year-lawful-stay, etc).

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in §§ 10-11b Staatsb?rgerschaftsgesetz. The law does not differentiate between economic or humanitarian migrants. Any foreign national can access citizenship but there are recidency and income requirements. The applicant must also have a clean criminal record, and have no history of major administrative offenses.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Sections 7, 10-11b Staatsb?rgerschaftsgesetz. The pathway for minors is regulated in Section 7 of the Staatsb?rgerschaftsgesetz. Family migrants have access if they fulfill certain requirements (e.g., 6 year-lawful-stay, etc). Compared to economic and humanitarian migrants the requirements are a bit lower and easier to fulfil. Furthermore, minors can access citizenship by birth if their father or mother is an Austrian citizen (ius sanguinis).

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right for some migrants in Section 28 of the Criminal Code. Acquisition of Austrian citizenship by award presupposes that people applying for citizenship leave the previous state association insofar as this is possible and reasonable for them. However, it is possible to obtain dual nationality in exceptional cases; in cases where it is not possible or reasonable to leave the former state-associaton or where an exception was granted (Section 28 (1) of the Staatsb?rgerschaftsgesetz) because of best interest of the child, for example. In case that a child receives dual citizenship at birth, the child can keep both Austrian and their other citizenship (Section 7 and 28 of the Staatsb?rgerschaftsgesetz).

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Article 9 of the European Charter of Human Rights (ECHR), which has been incorporated into Article XXXX of the Austrian Constitution, and Article 14 of the Staatsgrundgesetz. Freedom of thought, conscience and religion is enshrined in Article 9 of ECHR, which was incorporated into Austrian Constitutional law and therefore includes all migrants on an equal basis with citizens. Article 14 of the Staatsgrundgesetz recognizes the same right.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Article 10 of the European Charter of Human Rights (ECHR) and Article 13 of the Staatsgrundgesetz. Freedom of expression is enshrined in Article 10 of the ECHR, which has been incorporated into Austrian Constitution, and therefore includes all migrants on an equal basis with citizens. Article 13 of the Staatsgrundgesetz recognizes the same right.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Article 10 of the European Charter of Human Rights (ECHR); in Article 13 of the Staatsgrundgesetz. Freedom of expression is enshrined in Article 10 of the ECHR, which was enshrined in Austrian Constitutional law and therefore includes all migrants on an equal basis with citizens. Article 13 of the Staatsgrundgesetz recognizes the same right.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Article 11 of the European Charter of Human Rights (ECHR), which has been incorporated into Austrian law as a constitutional provision. In addtion, Section 1 of the Vereinsgesetz likewise stipulates that any two persons can form an association, and does not differentiate between title of stay, or nationality. In addtion, Section 1 of the Vereinsgesetz likewise stipulates that any two persons can form an association, and does not differentiate between title of stay, or nationality.

question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are resource requirements for most migrants. For example, Sections 11, 46, and 52 state that, among other conditions, residence permits may only be issued to a migrant if the migrant has adequate health insurance coverage. Another requirement is that the stay of the foreigner cannot lead to a financial burden on a local authority. Exceptions can be found in cases where persons have been granted asylum. In these cases, family members can apply for family reunification within three months of the asylum decision. If an application is made within this time limit, said family members do not have to fulfill the resource conditions.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 61, 66 of the Strafprozessordnung. There is no distinction regarding the right of access before criminal proceedings between migrants and citizens. Section 66 of the Strafprozessordnung stipulates that victims rights are guaranteed for all victims of crimes. In connection with Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, this covers all victims - regardless of residence status or nationality.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in Section 57 of the Asylgesetz (AsylG). Section 57(1) Nr 2 and 3 of the AsylG states that a "special protection" residence permit can be granted to ensure prosecution of serious crimes and for victims of violence, to protect those victims from future violence. However, in practice this residence permit is almost never granted.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Austria protects this right in 1) Article 1 of the Bundesverfassungsgesetz ?ber die Rechte von Kindern" (BVG Kinderrechte), which protects minors in general. 2) Article 23 of the Reception Conditions Directive. 3) Sections 19(8) Nr 1, 21(3) Nr 1, 21a(5) Nr 1 NAG. 4) Section 41a(10) "Niederlassungs- und Aufenthaltsgesetz" (NAG). The provisions in the NAG provides that the best interest of the child has to be taken into account in relation to the fulfilment of requirements in Section 19(8) Nr 1, Section 21(3) Nr 1, Section 21a(5) Nr 1 and Section 41a(10). 5) Verfassungsgerichtshof 3.10.2019, E 3456/2019. According to this decision from the Constitutional Court ("Verfassungsgerichtshof" - VfGH), the best interest of the child has to be taken into account regarding expulsion decisions. 6) Article 8(2) European Convention on Human Rights. 7) Section 9(1) BFA-VG[2]: BVG Rechte von Kindern. 8) Section 40 of the Asylgesetz.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In context of migration, there are no rules specifically taking the vulnerability of women into consideration. For instance, Article 20 of the Asylgesetz, foresees that victims of sexual violence have the right to have an interviewer of the same sex. In practice, this targets mainly women, but is also a right for men who have suffered sexual violence.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are no specific provisions in the context of migration. From 2006, the Bundes-Behindertengleichstellungsgesetz has prohibited disciminatory treatment of persons with disabilities, in general, but provides no specific provision for the protection of migrants.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Bangladesh

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 37 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh recognizes this right only to the citizens.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 7 of the Voter Registration Act, 2009 provides that only citizens can be registered as voters.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. National law in Bangladesh protects this right for documented migrants in Articles 31-35 of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh under which documented migrants are entitled to equal criminal, civil and labor rights but not political rights such as freedom of speech, association including being candidates in any electoral exercises etc. Administrative tribunals in Bangladesh have very limited jurisdiction and specifically deal with disputes concerning the civil services. Hence, these tribunals are inapplicable to rights concerning migrants.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: There is no government sponsored legal aid mechanism in immigration proceedings.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Bangladesh protects this right in The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. However, there is no official post of interpreters in the judicial system. Proceedings are always conducted in Bangla and the only other language used would be English if the proceeding involves a migrant.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Unauthorized entry to the territory of Bangladesh is not exempted by any of the laws of Bangladesh, rather it is punishable offense under Section 14 of the Foreigners Act, 1946 (Act No. XXXI of 1946), and Section 4 of the Control of Entry Act, 1952 (Act LV of 1952).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Bangladesh protects this right in The Primary Education (Compulsory) Act, 1990. The Primary Education (Compulsory) Act, 1990 makes it obligatory for parents/guardians to enroll their children between the ages of 6-10 into primary schools.
