citation_text_en: [1]: Oleksandra (Sasha) Baglay. [2]: Joshua Blum.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Canada

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Sections 2 and 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states: "Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms: (a) freedom of conscience and religion; (b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication; (c) freedom of peaceful assembly; and (d) freedom of association." The term 'everyone' or 'every individual' under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been held to include territorially present non-citizens: Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 177. Section 15 provides that "Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability." Section 15 has been held to protect against discrimination on the ground of citizenship so long as the state action in question is outside of the immigration context: Lavoie v. Canada, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 769, 2002 SCC 23". However, note that section 34(1)(f) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act renders persons inadmissible to Canada purely for their 'membership' in an organization that has engaged in the subversion by force of any government (Section 34(1)(f) in combination with section 34(1)(b)) or any organization that has engaged in 'terrorism' (section 34(1)(f) in combination with section 34(1)(c)).

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 3 of the Canada Elections Act (S.C. 2000, c. 9) states that: "Every person who is a Canadian citizen and who on polling day is 18 years of age or older is qualified as an elector."

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states: "Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability." he Canadian Human Rights Act restricts complaints before it for discrimination for persons "lawfully present in Canada": section 40(5) of the Canadian Human Rights Act, (R.S.C., 1985, c. H-6)

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law only provides that counsel can be retained at a migrant's own expense: section 167(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act: "A person who is the subject of proceedings before any Division of the Board and the Minister may, at their own expense, be represented by legal or other counsel". Additionally, the Federal Court has held that there is no right to state-funded counsel in immigration proceedings: Austria v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 423.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Section 14 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states: "A party or witness in any proceedings who does not understand or speak the language in which the proceedings are conducted or who is deaf has the right to the assistance of an interpreter." Interpretation fees for criminal proceedings are paid for by the state: see discussion in McCullock Finney c. Canada (Attorney General), 2009 QCCS 4646 at para. 23.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 124 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act states that (1) Every person commits an offence who (a) contravenes a provision of this Act for which a penalty is not specifically provided or fails to comply with a condition or obligation imposed under this Act. That is, the entire IRPA functions as a parallel criminal enforcement act, rendering any contravention of the Act a potential criminal offence. This provision makes it a criminal offence to violate ANY aspect of the IRPA, a law which effectively only applies to non-citizens. Penalties are listed under Section 125 of the IRPA, which states that: "A person who commits an offence under subsection 124(1) is liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $50,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than six months, or to both."

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Public housing is administered under provincial jurisdiction and varies by province. In Ontario, refugee claimants have access to public housing but there are very long wait times.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no guarantee in national law, as education falls under provincial jurisdiction and policy varies between the provinces. While law and practice vary across provinces, nearly all provide free primary education to resident migrant children who are lawfully in Canada. For children without legal status, the situation varies. In Ontario, section 49.1 of the Ontario Education Act guarantees that 49.1: "A person who is otherwise entitled to be admitted to a school and who is less than eighteen years of age shall not be refused admission because the person or the person’s parent or guardian is unlawfully in Canada."

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law sets out the conditions for the issuance of study permits to migrants in Sections 212-222 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). Education and training programs fall under provincial jurisdiction, and are often limited to citizens and permanent residents. Permanent residents can typically access student loans and access adult institutions on part with citizens, but temporary residents must pay out of pocket for any such institutions and require a study permit which is subject to other conditions.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: Only major convictions (criminal offenses) can lead to loss of residence status. Section 36 (1) of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act states: a permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality for (a) having been convicted in Canada of an offence under an Act of Parliament punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years, or of an offence under an Act of Parliament for which a term of imprisonment of more than six months has been imposed; (b) having been convicted of an offence outside Canada that, if committed in Canada, would constitute an offence under an Act of Parliament punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years; or (c) committing an act outside Canada that is an offence in the place where it was committed and that, if committed in Canada, would constitute an offence under an Act of Parliament punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years."

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in 1) Section 7 and 12 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Section 7 states: "Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice." Section 7 also protects against refoulement to risks of torture and CIDT in all but the most exceptional (and as yet not defined) circumstances: Suresh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2002] 1 S.C.R. 3, 2002 SCC 1; India v. Badesha, 2017 SCC 44." Section 12 states: "Everyone has the right not to be subjected to any cruel and unusual treatment or punishment." 2) Section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act: "A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally (a) to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if (i) the person is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of that country, (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (iii) the risk is not inherent or incidental to lawful sanctions, unless imposed in disregard of accepted international standards, and (iv) the risk is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care."

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in 1) Section 115(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA): "A protected person or a person who is recognized as a Convention refugee by another country to which the person may be returned shall not be removed from Canada to a country where they would be at risk of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion or at risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment." But there is an exception to non-refoulement in Section 115(2: "(2) Subsection (1) does not apply in the case of a person (a) who is inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality and who constitutes, in the opinion of the Minister, a danger to the public in Canada; or (b) who is inadmissible on grounds of security, violating human or international rights or organized criminality if, in the opinion of the Minister, the person should not be allowed to remain in Canada on the basis of the nature and severity of acts committed or of danger to the security of Canada." 2) Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms requires an assessment of whether a refugee claimant faces persecution prior to deportation: Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 177 at para. 52; see also Ragupathy v. Canada (MPSEP), 2006 FC 1370 at paras. 24-27."

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in 1) Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which protects against deprivations of life, liberty and security of the person that are contrary to the principles of fundamental justice. 2) Section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which bans refoulement on the basis of serious deprivations of the right to life

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, individuals who are removal-ready may be able to file a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA, there are some conditions to be met, however; for example, for rejected refugee claimants, 12 months must have passed since the rejection). As a rule, individuals will be notified of their right to apply for a PRRA (although this is not expressly required by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act).

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The legislation does not contemplate such situations. The only potentially relevant provision is Art 4 of the Canada-US Safe Third Country Agreement whereby the country of last presence is responsible for determining the asylum claim. It can be considered to temper subsequent expulsion in a sense that the asylum claim needs to be examined first; the country of last presence cannot just send the claimant back to their country of origin. The Federal Court in cases about Palestinian refugees returned to places they are not a citizen of has gone so far as to say that Section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and its protection against chain refoulement is unconcerned by subsequent deportations after a refugee is deported from Canada: Qassim v. Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2018 FC 226 at paras. 60-61".

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Section 44 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) which provides that prior to a removal order an inadmissibility report must be written by an immigration officer based on facts relevant to the individual concerned and only pursuant to a decision reached in accordance with and authorized by law. The inadmissibility report is then transmitted to a delegate of the Minister of Public Safety who can either issue a removal order themselves, or in the case of inadmissibility based on security or criminality in Sections 34-37 of the IRPA, send the inadmissibility report to the Immigration Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board for a hearing on the facts of the individuals' case. Only after this process is complete, can the Immigration Division issue a removal order if the inadmissibility allegations are proven based on the facts and the relevant laws.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Sections 44, 45, 63 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Section 44 of the IRPA: "44 (1) An officer who is of the opinion that a permanent resident or a foreign national who is in Canada is inadmissible may prepare a report setting out the relevant facts, which report shall be transmitted to the Minister. Marginal note:Referral or removal order (2) If the Minister is of the opinion that the report is well-founded, the Minister may refer the report to the Immigration Division for an admissibility hearing, except in the case of a permanent resident who is inadmissible solely on the grounds that they have failed to comply with the residency obligation under section 28 and except, in the circumstances prescribed by the regulations, in the case of a foreign national. In those cases, the Minister may make a removal order." Section 45 of the IRPA: "The Immigration Division, at the conclusion of an admissibility hearing, shall make one of the following decisions: (a) recognize the right to enter Canada of a Canadian citizen within the meaning of the Citizenship Act, a person registered as an Indian under the Indian Act or a permanent resident; (b) grant permanent resident status or temporary resident status to a foreign national if it is satisfied that the foreign national meets the requirements of this Act; (c) authorize a permanent resident or a foreign national, with or without conditions, to enter Canada for further examination; or (d) make the applicable removal order against a foreign national who has not been authorized to enter Canada, if it is not satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible, or against a foreign national who has been authorized to enter Canada or a permanent resident, if it is satisfied that the foreign national or the permanent resident is inadmissible." Section 63 of the IRPA: "(2) A foreign national who holds a permanent resident visa may appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division against a decision to make a removal order against them made under subsection 44(2) or made at an admissibility hearing. Marginal note:Right to appeal removal order (3) A permanent resident or a protected person may appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division against a decision to make a removal order against them made under subsection 44(2) or made at an admissibility hearing." Additionally, before such a removal Is effecutated, there is a screening for fea of mistreatment, which provides a further opportunity to submit reasons against expulsion.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are opportunities for stateless migrants to be granted citizenship, but they are not guaranteed, and highly contingent on specific criteria not open to all stateless migrants and children of stateless migrants. Section 5(4) of the Citizenship Act states that: "despite any other provision of this Act, the Minister may, in his or her discretion, grant citizenship to any person to alleviate cases of statelessness or of special and unusual hardship or to reward services of an exceptional value to Canada." However, this does not guarantee that they will receive citizenship. Section 5(5) of the Citizenship Act also provides for citizenship based on bloodline connection for a person who meets the following conditions: "(5) The Minister shall, on application, grant citizenship to a person who (a) is born outside Canada after the coming into force of this subsection; (b) has a birth parent who was a citizen at the time of the birth; (c) is less than 23 years of age; (d) has been physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days during the four years immediately before the date of his or her application; (e) has always been stateless; and (f) has not been convicted of any of the following offences: (i) a terrorism offence, as defined in section 2 of the Criminal Code, (ii) an offence under section 47, 51 or 52 of the Criminal Code, (iii) an offence under subsection 5(1) or any of sections 6 and 16 to 22 of the Security of Information Act, or (iv) a conspiracy or an attempt to commit, being an accessory after the fact in relation to, or any counselling in relation to, an offence referred to in subparagraph (ii) or (iii)."

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada conditionally protects this right in Section 12(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which states: "A foreign national may be selected as a member of the family class on the basis of their relationship as the spouse, common-law partner, child, parent or other prescribed family member of a Canadian citizen or permanent resident." There are 2 core requirements for family reunification: "(1) eligible sponsor: Canadian citizen or PR, at least 18, resides in Canada (some exceptions); meets the threshold of minimum necessary income (some exceptions), signs an undertaking; is not on social assistance (some exceptions); not barred from sponsorship (eg, due to certain convictions, default on financial undertakings, being imprisoned, etc). (2) the sponsored relative must fall within one of the following relations to the sponsor: (a) the sponsor’s spouse, common-law partner or conjugal partner; (b) a dependent child of the sponsor; (c) the sponsor’s mother or father; (d) the mother or father of the sponsor’s mother or father; (e) [Repealed, SOR/2005-61, s. 3] (f) a person whose parents are deceased, who is under 18 years of age, who is not a spouse or common-law partner and who is (i) a child of the sponsor’s mother or father, (ii) a child of a child of the sponsor’s mother or father, or (iii) a child of the sponsor’s child; (g) a person under 18 years of age whom the sponsor intends to adopt in Canada if (i) the adoption is not being entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Act, (ii) where the adoption is an international adoption, the country in which the person resides is a party to the Hague Convention on Adoption and the Convention applies to their province of intended destination, the competent authority of the country and of the province have approved the adoption in writing as conforming to that Convention, and (iii) where the adoption is an international adoption and the country in which the person resides is not a party to the Hague Convention on Adoption or the Convention does not apply to the person’s province of intended destination (A) the person has been placed for adoption in the country in which they reside or is otherwise legally available in that country for adoption and there is no evidence that the intended adoption is for the purpose of child trafficking or undue gain within the meaning of the Hague Convention on Adoption, and (B) the competent authority of the person’s province of intended destination has stated in writing that it does not object to the adoption; or (h) a relative of the sponsor, regardless of age, if the sponsor does not have a spouse, a common-law partner, a conjugal partner, a child, a mother or father, a relative who is a child of that mother or father, a relative who is a child of a child of that mother or father, a mother or father of that mother or father or a relative who is a child of the mother or father of that mother or father (i) who is a Canadian citizen, Indian or permanent resident, or (ii) whose application to enter and remain in Canada as a permanent resident the sponsor may otherwise sponsor."

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Section 63(1) and 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Section 63(1) states that: "A person who has filed in the prescribed manner an application to sponsor a foreign national as a member of the family class may appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division against a decision not to issue the foreign national a permanent resident visa." Section 72(1) provides for an application for judicial review of any decision made under the Act.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in 1) Canada's Civil Marriage Act (S.C. 2005, c. 33), Section 2, which states that "marriage, for civil purposes, is the lawful union of two persons to the exclusion of all others." 2) Section 1(1)of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Section 1(1)of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations defines 'common law partner' in a way that does not distinguish between same sex and opposite sex relationships.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all temporary migrant workers. However, there are opportunities for temporary foreign workers to apply for permanent residence under the economic class. Such opportunities are more extensive for high skilled workers: they can transition to permanent residence status by applying under federal programs (like Canadian Experience Class or skilled worker class) as well as provincial nominee programs. Lower skilled workers have much more limited opportunities to transition to permanent residence status. Agricultural workers can apply under the federal Agri-food Pilot program (but it is capped at 2,750 application per year and is limited to a few eligible lower-skilled occupations). In addition, selected lower-skilled occupations in demand may be eligible for permanent residence under provinicial nominee programs. It may also be possible for temporary foreign workers to apply for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations (Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, section 25), the latter being subject to a highly discretionary decision.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in 1) Section 25 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which provides a discretionary route to permanent residence for anyone migrant in Canada if they can satisfy an immigration officer that a grant of permanent residence is justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations. 2) Section 24 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which provides for a Temporary Residence Permit (TRP) where it is justified by compelling and exceptional circumstances.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada conditionally protects this right in Canadian Human Rights Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. H-6), Section 3: "For all purposes of this Act, the prohibited grounds of discrimination are race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, family status, genetic characteristics, disability and conviction for an offence for which a pardon has been granted or in respect of which a record suspension has been ordered." The Canadian Human Rights Act applies only to private employers regulated by the federal government such as banks, trucking companies, telecommunication companies. In most cases, provincial human rights codes or provincial labour/employment legislation would be more relevant and redress should be sought under this provincial legislation.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Canada Health Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. C-6), Section 2 states that: "an insured person means, in relation to a province, a resident of the province other than a resident of the province who has not completed such minimum period of residence or waiting period, not exceeding three months, as may be required by the province for eligibility for or entitlement to insured health services." Health care in Canada falls under provincial jurisdiction and therefore health care coverage is administered under provincial law. In every province, permanent residents have full access to health care coverage on par with citizens (For Example the Regulations to the Ontario Health Insurance Act R.R.O Regulation 552, 1990, at section 1.2). Migrants without permanent status do not have public health care coverage. Certain migrants however - refugee claimants, resettled refugees, protected persons, and immigration detainees - have public health care coverage under the Federally administered Interim Federal Health Program (IFHP) under the Order Respecting the Interim Federal Health Program, 2012. The IFHP provides basic coverage that is not equal to what is available to citizens and permanent residents under provincial public insurance plans

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right at the national level. Section 65 of the Canada Elections Act (S.C. 2000, c. 9): “The following persons are not eligible to be a candidate: (a) a person who is not qualified as an elector on the date on which his or her nomination paper is filed… (under section 3 of the Canada Elections Act (S.C. 2000, c. 9): "Every person who is a Canadian citizen and who on polling day is 18 years of age or older is qualified as an elector.")" However, some provinces may allow non-citizens to run for office, while others do not. For example, in Ontario, only Canadian citizens can run for office in provincial and municipal elections. For national elections, all candidates must be Canadian citizens.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms provides for analogous grounds of discrimination and has found 'citizenship' to be a protected ground of discrimination outside the immigration context: Lavoie v. Canada, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 769, 2002 SCC 23. However, courts have consistently held that "immigration status" is not included in the prohibition of discrimination on the basis of citizenship in challenges to laws that provide a right to permanent residents that is not available to migrants without permanent status: Toussaint v. Canada (Attorney General), 2011 FCA 213 at para. 99; Canadian Doctors For Refugee Care v. Canada (Attorney General), 2014 FC 651 at paras. 860-870. Additionally, certain provincial human rights codes provide protection based on citizenship, i.e Ontario Human Rights Code, Section 1, which states that, "Every person has a right to equal treatment with respect to services, goods and facilities, without discrimination because of race, ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin, citizenship, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, age, marital status, family status or disability."

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in 1) Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which states that: "Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability." 2) Section 3(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act, which provides "For all purposes of this Act, the prohibited grounds of discrimination are race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, family status, genetic characteristics, disability and conviction for an offence for which a pardon has been granted or in respect of which a record suspension has been ordered."

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Section 203(3)(d) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations which provides that to be eligible to hire a temporary foreign worker the employer must demonstrate they pay a wage consistent with the "prevailing wage" for that job. Outside the cited provision, labour and employment are matters of provincial jurisdiction and so treatment will vary for workers in different provinces under different provincial labour law and anti-discrimination codes.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada conditionally protects this right in Sections 200-209 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) which explains that employment is tied to a specific employer; change of employer possible, but requires a new work permit application. Most migrant workers fall under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program and can only work for the employer who received a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) that was a precondition for the issuance of the work permit. For most workers, seeking new employment will require a new positive LMIA and a new work permit to be issued. Workers under the International Mobility Program can be open - allowing free choice of employment - but often with restrictions on the location or type of employment that can qualify.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Canada does not grant the spouse/partner of the principal migrant an automatic right to work, but pursuant to Section 207(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) they are eligible to apply for a work permit in some cases.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects protects immigration status despite the loss of employment for all migrants in Section 183(4)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, which states that "the period authorized for a temporary resident’s stay ends on the earliest of ... (b) the day on which their permit becomes invalid, in the case of a temporary resident who has been issued either a work permit or a study permit." Outside of permanent residents, migrant workers who have been laid off or lose employment are allowed to stay in Canada for the duration of their work permit (that is, until their work permit expires). This means that even if the migrant quits or is terminated by the employer, this does not invalidate his/her work permit, nor their temporary immigration status. However, because some work permits are tied to particular employers, some migrants will not be able to find alternative employment without requesting a new work permit.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While protections for equal employment conditions between migrants and citizens for some industries are regulated at the Federal level and are protected under federal laws, such as in Sections 3, 7, and 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, labor law generally is a matter of provincial jurisdiction, and therefore most industries are regulated at the provincial level. The governing regimes in provinces vary and therefore provide different, less rigorous, or no protections guaranteeig equal employment conditions. For example, in Manitoba, the Employment Standards Code provides protection to migrant farm workers for most key employment standards provisions, such as equal pay, but they are not covered by the general provisions on hours of work, overtime and holidays (Employment Standards Code, s.3). In Quebec, the province has not enacted any specific legislation on temporary foreign workers, but Quebec's minister of immigration must approve the employer's application and terms of employment before delivering a work permit.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada conditionally protects this right. Migrants have access to all types of social security protections and programs, but these programs attach special conditions specific to migrants. For example, national law in Canada protects migrant workers' rights to social security in Sections 3 and 4 of the Old Age Security Act (OAS) which provides that a full pension will be paid to someone who has legally resided in Canada after the age of 18 for at least forty years (3(1)(c) of the OAS), and a partial payment can be paid to someone who has legally resided in Canada at least ten years after the age of 18 (3(2)(b) of the OAS).

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada provides equal access to all types of unemployment benefits after a duration of stay to all regular migrants in in Section 7(2) of the Employment Insurance Act, which provides unemployment insurance to workers regardless of citizenship or immigration status so long as they have "had during their qualifying period at least the number of hours of insurable employment set out in the following table in relation to the regional rate of unemployment that applies to the person." Thus, equal access to all types of unemployment benefits is available, but only after a duration of stay.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right for all temporary workers except those engaged in manual labor or less specialized work in Section 87.1(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) which provides the prospect of permanent residence in Canada under the Canada Experience Class for those who have worked full-time in Canada for a year and meet other conditions. Temporary foreign workers can become permanent residents under the skilled worker program if they meet the various conditions of the Express Entry program (which allocates points for education, type of skilled work, language skills, region of work, etc) and under the Canada Experience Class program if they have worked over a year, speak English or French and doing what Canada allocates as desired professions under the National Occupational Classification (NOC) (See IRPR at section 87.1(2)(a). In practice this means that temporary workers doing manual or less specialized work cannot apply for permanent residence as they will never qualify under these programs. The only program that explicitly has no path to permanent residence is the Seasonal Agricultural Workers Program. Migrant workers who do not qualify for the Skilled Worker Program could still apply for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate considerations (IRPA at section 25) and this would be subject to a highly discretionary decision.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada explicitly protects this right in 1) Sections 140 (1) and 209.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Section 140 states that "An officer may seize and hold any means of transportation, document or other thing if the of ficer believes on reasonable grounds that it was fraudulently or improperly obtained or used or that the seizure is necessary to prevent its fraudulent or improper use or to carry out the purposes of this Act." 2) Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which "protects against unreasonable search and seizure from the state and would prohibit document seizure from a public official who is not duly authorized by law."

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Birth registration is a matter of provincial jurisdiction, and provincial laws require registration of birth but vary by province in the specifics. See for example, in Ontario, section 9 of the Vital Statistics Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. V.4 which requires birth registration without regard for immigration status.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Canada mandates the issuing of documents that recognize the status of permanent residents (Section 31(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act) and those authorized to work (Section 200(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations). However, migrants who do not fall into these categories are not granted the relevant issued federal ID. Refugee claimants in Canada are issued a Refugee Protection Claimant Document (RPCD), but it is not mandated by law.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Section 279.03 (1) of the Criminal Code, (R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46) which states: Every person who, for the purpose of committing or facilitating an of fence under subsection 279.01(1), conceals, removes, withholds or destroys any travel document that belongs to another person or any document that establishes or purports to establish another person’ s identity or immigration status ? whether or not the document is of Canadian origin or is authentic ? is guilty of (a) an indictable of fence and liable to imprisonment for a term of not more than five years; or (b) an of fence punishable on summary conviction.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Non-citizens arrested by the Canada Border Services Agency (i.e., immigration detention) are given a document called "Information for people detained under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act". This document states: "You have the right to contact your embassy or a representative of your country's consulate at your request". However, this document is not a legal document, and though Canada has incorporated some articles of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations in Section 3(1) of the Foreign Missions and International Organizations Act (S.C. 1991, c. 41), the Federal Court of Canada recognized in 2004 that Article 36 confers individual legal rights on Canadian nationals that they may rely on in domestic judicial proceedings: "Statutes should be construed to comply with Canada's international obligations....Specifically, the International Court of Justice's decision in LaGrand...states that the VCCR does create individual rights to the services requested by the Applicants in this case. See: Khadr v. Canada (Minister of Foreign Affairs), 2004 FC 1145, at paras. 26, 27, protections for non-citizens are not recognizes.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Although, the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27, Section 60 states: "it is affirmed as a principle that a minor child shall be detained only as a measure of last resort, taking into account the other applicable grounds and criteria including the best interests of the child," there is no formal prohibition on the detention of children based on their status as a migrant.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Canada sets out an immigration detention regime under which migrants are frequently detained under Sections 54-61 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and sections 244-250 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Section 55 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act provides for a list of circumstances when a foreign national or permanent resident can be detained without or without a warrant: "(1) An officer may issue a warrant for the arrest and detention of a permanent resident or a foreign national who the of ficer has reasonable grounds to believe is inadmissible and is a danger to the public or is unlikely to appear for examination, for an admissibility hearing, for removal from Canada or at a proceeding that could lead to the making of a removal order by the Minister under subsection 44(2). Arrest and detention without warrant (2) An officer may, without a warrant, arrest and detain a foreign national, other than a protected person, (a) who the officer has reasonable grounds to believe is inadmissible and is a danger to the public or is unlikely to appear for examination, an admissibility hearing, removal from Canada, or at a proceeding that could lead to the making of a removal order by the Minister under subsection 44(2); or (b) if the of ficer is not satisfied of the identity of the foreign national in the course of any procedure under this Act."

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Sections 57 and 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Section 57 states that within 48 hours after a permanent resident or a foreign national is taken into detention, or without delay afterward, the Immigration Division must review the reasons for the continued detention. At least once during the seven days following the review under subsection (1), and at least once during each 30-day period following each previous review , the Immigration Division must review the reasons for the continued detention." These reviews typically concern the grounds for detention rather than the legality or conditions of detention. Section 72(1) provides an application for judicial review in the Federal Court of Canada. Detainees can challenge the legality and the reasonableness of conditions of detention. The length of detention is not a standalone ground for review but is considered in reviewing the reasonableness of the Immigration Division Tribunal Member's decision to detain under section 248 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada requires an individualized determination of detention in Section 57 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which states: "Within 48 hours after a permanent resident or a foreign national is taken into detention, or without delay afterward, the Immigration Division must review the reasons for the continued detention." Section 58 states that: "the Immigration Division shall order the release of a permanent resident or a foreign national unless it is satisfied, taking into account prescribed factors, that (a) they are a danger to the public; (b) they are unlikely to appear for examination, an admissibility hearing, removal from Canada, or at a proceeding that could lead to the making of a removal order by the Minister under subsection 44(2); (c) the Minister is taking necessary steps to inquire into a reasonable suspicion that they are inadmissible on grounds of security , violating human or international rights, serious criminality , criminality or organized criminality; (d) the Minister is of the opinion that the identity of the foreign national ? other than a designated foreign national who was 16 years of age or older on the day of the arrival that is the subject of the designation in question ? has not been, but may be, established and they have not reasonably cooperated with the Minister by providing relevant information for the purpose of establishing their identity or the Minister is making reasonable ef forts to establish their identity; or (e) the Minister is of the opinion that the identity of the foreign national who is a designated foreign national and who was 16 years of age or older on the day of the arrival that is the subject of the designation in question has not been established."

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in 1) Section 12 of Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states that "everyone has the right not to be subjected to any cruel and unusual treatment or punishment." 2) Section 269.1(1) of the Criminal Code provides that "Every official, or every person acting at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of an official, who inflicts torture on any other person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years." 3) Section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27: A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality , their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally (a) to a danger , believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if (i) the person is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of that country, (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (iii) the risk is not inherent or incidental to lawful sanctions, unless imposed in disregard of accepted international standards, and (iv) the risk is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Sections 487-492 of the Criminal Code proscribe the conditions under which peace officers can take DNA and use necessary and proportional force to effect arrest. Section 138(1) of the Immigrant and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) states: "An officer, if so authorized, has the authority and powers of a peace officer ? including those set out in sections 487 to 492.2 of the Criminal Code ? to enforce this Act, including any of its provisions with respect to the arrest, detention or removal from Canada of any person."

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right by restricting the use of force by state officials, broadly, although there is no specific law or caselaw in Canada that directly addresses the application of these general restrictions in the context of attempted entry. Migrants are protected under Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which has been interpreted to prohibit lethal force in circumstances where law enforcement used lethal force in attempting to turn back migrants at the border. In addition, Section 25(4) of the Criminal Code sets out general considerations on when the use of force, including lethal force, is justified/allowed by a peace officer or anyone lawfully assisting a peace officer. In this context, except under the exceptional circumstances of a violent imminent threat, the use of lethal force would be grossly disproportionate to the immigration purposes of any power.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Sections 117 and 118 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) set out criminal punishment for smuggling (s.117) and trafficking (s.118). Smuggled or trafficked migrants engaged in mutual aid of one another with no profit motive cannot be caught under these provisions: R. v. Appulonappa, 2015 SCC 59. However, sections 122, 124, and 127 of the IRPA criminally punish illegal entry to Canada and the use of misrepresentation and false documents to enter Canada. Criminal punishment under these provisions can be deferred for an asylum-seeker while their claim is pending and if they are granted protection pursuant to section 133 of the IRPA. There is no deferral or exemption for a non-refugee and no exemption for a smuggled or trafficked person.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: Convictions do not affect citizenship status. Once citizenship is properly obtained, a conviction cannot lead to loss of status.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Section 5(1)(c)(i) which states: National law provides a pathway to citizenship for all permanent residents including economic migrants (so long as they meet the residency requirement, 1095 consecutive days within the five years prior to submitting the application, has knowledge of one of Canada's official languages, and be between the ages of 18 and 55) in Section 5(1)(c)(i) of the Citizenship Act.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in 1) Section 5(1)(c)(i) of the Citizenship Act which states: The Minister shall grant citizenship to any person who (c) is a permanent resident within the meaning of subsection 2(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, has, subject to the regulations, no unfulfilled conditions under that Act relating to his or her status as a permanent resident and has (i) been physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days during the five years immediately before the date of his or her application. 2) Section 25 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act provides pathways for citizenship specifically open to humanitarian migrants.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in 1) Section 12(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, which states htat: "A foreign national may be selected as a member of the family class on the basis of their relationship as the spouse, common-law partner, child, parent or other prescribed family member of a Canadian citizen or permanent resident." This allows for family reunification, which will then enable the family migrant to apply for citizenship through residence in Secont 5(1)(c)(i) of the Citizenhip Act. 2) Section 5(1)(c)(i) of the Citizenship Act which states: "The Minister shall grant citizenship to any person who (c) is a permanent resident within the meaning of subsection 2(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, has, subject to the regulations, no unfulfilled conditions under that Act relating to his or her status as a permanent resident and has (i) been physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days during the five years immediately before the date of his or her application".

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in the Citizenship Act which does not prohibit dual or even multiple citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Sections 2 and 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states: "Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms: (a) freedom of conscience and religion; (b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication; (c) freedom of peaceful assembly; and (d) freedom of association." The term 'everyone' or 'every individual' under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been held to include territorially present non-citizens: Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 177. Section 15 provides that "Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability." Section 15 has been held to protect against discrimination on the ground of citizenship so long as the state action in question is outside of the immigration context: Lavoie v. Canada, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 769, 2002 SCC 23".

citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Sections 2 and 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states: "Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms: (a) freedom of conscience and religion; (b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication; (c) freedom of peaceful assembly; and (d) freedom of association." citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Sections 2 and 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states: "Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms: (a) freedom of conscience and religion; (b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication; (c) freedom of peaceful assembly; and (d) freedom of association." Section 15 provides that "Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability." Section 15 has been held to protect against discrimination on the ground of citizenship so long as the state action in question is outside of the immigration context: Lavoie v. Canada, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 769, 2002 SCC 23". However, note that section 34(1)(f) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act renders persons inadmissible to Canada purely for their 'membership' in an organization that has engaged in the subversion by force of any government (Section 34(1)(f) in combination with section 34(1)(b)) or any organization that has engaged in 'terrorism' (section 34(1)(f) in combination with section 34(1)(c)).

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 133(1)(j) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations states: "A sponsorship application shall only be approved by an officer if, on the day on which the application was filed and from that day until the day a decision is made with respect to the application, there is evidence that the sponsor .....(A) has a total income that is at least equal to the minimum necessary income, if the sponsorship application was filed in respect of a foreign national other than a foreign national referred to in clause (B), or (B) has a total income that is at least equal to the minimum necessary income, plus 30%, for each of the three consecutive taxation years immediately preceding the date of filing of the sponsorship application."

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in 1) Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms: "Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability". 2) Sections 6, 7, 13, 14, 16, and 19(2) of the Canadian Victims Bill of Rights. Section 6 states that "Every victim has the right, on request, to information about (a) the criminal justice system and the role of victims in it; (b) the services and programs available to them as a victim, including restorative justice programs; and (c) their right to file a complaint for an infringement or denial of any of their rights under this Act." Section 7 states that: "Every victim has the right, on request, to information about (a) the status and outcome of the investigation into the offence; and (b) the location of proceedings in relation to the offence, when they will take place and their progress and outcome. Section Every victim has the right to have reasonable and necessary measures taken by the appropriate authorities in the criminal justice system to protect the victim from intimidation and retaliation." Section 13 states that: "Every victim has the right to request testimonial aids when appearing as a witness in proceedings relating to the offence. Section 14 states that: "Every victim has the right to convey their views about decisions to be made by appropriate authorities in the criminal justice system that affect the victim’s rights under this Act and to have those views considered." Section 16 states that: "Every victim has the right to have the court consider making a restitution order against the offender." Finally, Section 19(2) states that: "A victim is entitled to exercise their rights under this Act only if they are present in Canada or they are a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident."

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in section 24 (1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act states that "A foreign national who, in the opinion of an officer, is inadmissible or does not meet the requirements of this Act becomes a temporary resident if an officer is of the opinion that it is justified in the circumstances and issues a temporary resident permit, which may be cancelled at any time." While a temporary residence permit is not a guaranteed route to citizenship, it could potentially provide relief from expulsion.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in 1) Section 159.5(e) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) which provides an exception to the Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA) to permit unaccompanied minors to still claim refugee protection at the Canada-U.S Land Border. Section 248(f) of the IRPR, which requires the best interests of an affected child be considered before making a decision on detention or release. Note also sections 248.1 and 249 of the IRPR which provide further criteria for determining the best interests of the child in a given case, and for the application of the principle affirmed in section 60 of the Act that a minor child shall be detained only as a measure of last resort. Additionally, the definition of 'dependent child' under the IRPR which provides generally that persons under the age of 22 years old who are not married can be included in a parent's permanent residence application and acquire permanent residence when they do. 2) Rule 20 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules (RPD Rules} which mandate the designation of Designated Representatives to protect the interests of claimants under 18 years old. The RPD Rules are promulgated under the authority given to the Chairperson of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) under Section 161(1) of the IRPA. 3) Section 60 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) where "it is affirmed as a principle that a minor child shall be detained only as a measure of last resort, taking into account the other applicable grounds and criteria including the best interests of the child." Additionally, the decision in Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras. 34-41 4) has provided legal guidance in how to interpret Section 25 of the IRPA to take the best interests of the child into account when making immigration related decisions. 4) Finally note generally that national law in Canada in section 3(3)(f) requires that the IRPA be interpreted and applied in compliance with international human rights instruments that Canada has signed, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child."

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right in Section 25 of the Immigrant and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), which provides for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate considerations and can include consideration of discrimination against women in the country of origin and if the applicant has endured family violence in Canada or abroad. The failure to consider gender-based violence and vulnerability of the applicant can be grounds to quash a decision as unreasonable in the Federal Court but these factors must be raised by the applicant or her counsel in the TRP or H&C application.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Canada protects this right by allowing applications for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate considerations to be made based on "health considerations including inability of a country to provide medical treatment" under Section 25 of the IRPA. However, migrants with disabilities can be excluded in some cases under section 38 of the IRPA if "(1) A foreign national is inadmissible on health grounds if their health condition(a) is likely to be a danger to public health; (b) is likely to be a danger to public safety; or (c) might reasonably be expected to cause excessive demand on health or social services." In addition, in the context of refugee status determination, the Immigration and Refugee board of Canada has established Chairperson's Guideline 8: Procedures with respect to Vulnerable Persons, issued pursuant to section 159(1)(h) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), which establishes the ability of asylum seekers with disabilities to request procedural accommodation. While this guideline is not formally binding, disregarding the guidelines without justificationc an establish an abuse of discretion.
