citation_text_en: [1]: Oliver Wolf. [2]: Winfried Kluth

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Germany

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Federal Assembly Act guarantees the right of assembly to everyone, but Article 8 of the German Constitution guarantees this right only for German citizens. Accordingly, migrants can form and participate in associations, but the constitutional legal protection is restricted to subjects of the constitutional right of freedom of assembly, thus only German citizens.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Domestic Constitutional and Federal Basic Law, the right to vote for the German National Parliament is reserved to citizens, articles 38, 116 German Constitution in conjunction with section 12 Federal Election Law, with the exception of European Union (EU) citizens whom, according to Art. 28 paragraph 2 of the German Constitution, can vote in local/regional elections. Third-Country/foreign non-EU nationals, are thus migrants (as EU citizens are not migrants by definition, but right holders of unalienable guarantees of freedom due to the Movement within the European Union Act by birth) have no active voting rights whatsoever to vote for parliamentary representation.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in Articles 3, 19, 20 of the German Constitution. Article 3 of the Constitution forbids discrimination related to origin (except rights reserved to German citizenship, such as the right to vote for members of the German Parliament). Thus, every person, including migrants, have the right of equal protection in the law before all courts.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure stipulates when the government will provide counsel to the defendant. However, legal aid of this sort is only applicable if the migrant is already resident in Germany (e. g. has some kind of stable residence status, therefore undocumented persons are usually not eligible), cannot pay for counsel themself (as it is the case for all applicants, for example German nationals and European Union citizens), and not in all judicial constellations regarding immigration status (for example, applicable in case for permanency or naturalization, and not in expulsion/deportation cases, remedies against charges of migration-specific offenses, et. al.).

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Section 185 of the Courts Constitution Act. 2) Section 464c of the Criminal Procedure Code. 3) Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. 4) Article 103 of the German Constitution. The official administrative and court procedures language is German, but a translator has to be appointed if one party is a non-German speaker to comply with the right to a fair trial according to the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR). The ECHR also stipulates that the state has to provide, at the government's ex[emse, interpretation of court documentation. The European Human Rights Convention is directly applicable in Germany as a higher-ranked international obligation, as the Rulings of the European Court on Human Rights are binding in Germany (as long as the Federal Constitutional Court does not state otherwise) as part of International Public Law, incorporated into the Federal Law.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to the Federal Residence Act, there are both civil and criminal penalties related to unauthorised entry. However, Article 95 states exemptions to civil and criminal sanction, which include asylum seekers and refugees.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right for regular migrants in 1) Sections 3 of the Housing Allowance Act. 2) Section 27 of the Social Housing Act. 3) Section 5, 7 of the Conntrolled Tenancy Act. 4) Article 3 of the German Constitution. 5) Sections 1, 2 of the General Equal Treatment Act. 6) Sections 20, 22, 30a, 44 of the Federal Asylum Act. 7) Section 15 VI, 15a, 61 AufenthG. Even though social benefits for all groups of migrants are provided, including housing in the initial phase of residence in Germany, some migrants like asylum seekers and the undocumented are indeed not free to choose housing as there is a residence obligation for collective accommodations during their asylum procedure. For this reason, irregular migrants have no access to public housing programs. In case of such legal residence obligations (which include asylum seekers within the first six months after official application for asylum, asylum seekers coming safe origin/third countries/EU states/Dublin cases, and all illegal entries without asylum procedure), migrants are obliged to live in initial detention centers or collective shelters. Regarding financial housing benefits, migrants and foreigners are explicitly equalized to German citizens if housing support is applicable. The so-called Wohnberechtigungsschein/WBS (document certifying the eligibility to rent subsidized rental units), or financial support for housing like Wohngeld (housing benefits), are also often only applicable for a long-term residence so there is a waiting period for migrants to be eligible for those services. Generally, mandatory requirements to obtain housing include a pension insurance certificate, regular/stable employment, and a certain income threshold. For this reason, certain groups like refugees, asylum seekers, and undocumented people temporarily staying in Federal territory for humanitarian reasons are naturally disadvantaged. In cases of racial discrimination or unequal treatment related to the migrant status, one can file a lawsuit under the German Anti-Discrimination Act.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right for regular migrants in Article 7 of the German Constitution. There are laws which obliges children, young people and adolescents up to a certain age to attend school until completion. This regulation does not make any distinctions between citizens and migrants, though migrants need an adequate valid residence permit to access those public services.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right foe regular migrants in 1) Article 7 of the German Constitution. 2) The Federal Vocational Education and Training Act. 2) The 8th Social Code – Book on Child and Youth Welfare. 3) Sections 1, 2 of the General Equal Treatment Act. 4) Sections 25a-b, 60c, 12a, 18a, 50, 98, 43-45a of the Federal Residence Act; the Section on Integration Measures, includes the promotion of occupational German language learning, extension of the duty to participate in integration courses to certain groups of migrants, creation of a new right to stay in case of a successful vocational training, and regulation of administrative fines in case of non-information if the apprenticeship is terminated. 5) Sections 1 et seq., 4 of the Integration Act; the Integration Act brought major changes of the Aliens laws regarding educational opportunities (granting the possibility of language courses, vocational training and degree-level courses as a means for facilitated access to professional formation, apprenticeship and employment), as well as the obligation to provide an integration course and sanctions for insufficient integration efforts by the authority for prospective mid- to long-term residents. 6) Section 3 of the Federal Asylum Act. 7) Sections 34-34b, 63 of the 12th Social Code. 8) Section 8 of the Federal Training Assistance Act. 9) Sections 4, 8, 16, 17, 17a of the Federal Employment Directive. 10) Sections 5-5b of the Asylum Seekers Benefits Act. The regulations concerning education in Germany do not make any distinctions between citizens and migrants, but migrants need an adequate residence permit to have access to state facilities. Therefore, undocumented migrants, usually with the enforceable obligation to leave the country are usually restricted through administrative stamps on thier landing permissions, prohibiting participation in language and integration courses, and other qualification measures and education programs hosted by the Federal Labour Agency to ensure they are not able to enter the labour market.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany stipulates that only major convictions (e.g., criminal offenses) can lead to loss of residence status in Section 54 of the Residence Act.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 60, 74a of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 3a, 4 of the Federal Asylum Act. 3) Articles 1-2, Section 2 of the German Constitution. 4) Section 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which is binding international public law and incorporated into domestic law provisions, states that there is an absolute prohibition of push-back to countries where the refugee is either directly in danger of being subject to human rights violations, and/or is indirect risk of a chain of deportations.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Articles 3-5, 16a of the German Constitution. 2) Section 60 of the Federal Residence Act. 3) Articles 1, 5, 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. 4) Sections 3, 3a of the Federal Asylum Act.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National Law in Germany protects this right in 1) Section 60 III, V of the Federal Residence Act, which states that, "(3) If a foreigner may not be deported to a state because that state is seeking the foreigner for a criminal offence and there is a risk of the imposition or execution of the death penalty, the provisions on extradition shall apply mutatis mutandis. [...] (5) A foreigner may not be deported if the application of the Convention of 4 November 1950 for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ECHR, Federal Law Gazette 1952 II p. 685) shows that the deportation is inadmissible. [...]"

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Even though the most recent amendment of the Asylum Law in August 2019 provided for an independent and mandatory asylum advisory scheme for asylum seekers in Section 12a n., Federal Law still does not prescribe a legal duty for border authorities to advise on the right to seek asylum.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Section 60 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 26a, 27a, 29a of the Federal Asylum Act.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 53-55, 58-59, 79, 82, 83, 84, 11 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 42, 68, 80, 113, 124, 132, 146 et. seq. of the Administrative Court Procedures Code.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 53-55, 79, 82, 83, 84, 11 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 42, 68, 80, 113, 124, 132, 146 et. seq. of the Administrative Court Procedure Code. Preliminary internal remedy at the issuing authority, and subsequent legal action against administrative rejection, as a two-way review mechanism is provided for by law. Thus, according to general regulations, the expulsion-decision can be reviewed by the competent authority at the migrant’s request.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 25a, 25b, 27-36a , 104, 104a, 104b, 104c of the Federal Residence Act, which states the main prerequisites of for family reunification, which state that the temporary residence permit for family reunification purposes shall be granted to the foreign 1) spouse of a German, 2) minor, unmarried child of a German, 3) parent of a minor, unmarried German for the purpose of care and custody, if the joint habitual residence is in the federal territory. The main applicant must, 1) hold a permanent settlement permit, 2) an European Union (EU) long-term residence permit, 3) a temporary residence permit, 4) an EU Blue Card, 5) an ICT Card or a Mobile ICT Card, or 6) they must be entitled to stay in the federal territory, and 2) have sufficient living space available for the family member(s). A temporary resident permit will be granted to the parents of a minor foreign national in the Federal Territory if the child possess a temporary residence permit, a permanent settlement permit, or a permanent settlement permit after being granted a temporary residence permit pursuant, only if no parent possessing the right of care and custody is resident in the Federal territory. Finally, other dependants of a migrant may be granted a temporary residence permit for the purpose of subsequent immigration to join the migrant, if necessary in order to avoid particular hardship. 2) Article 6 of the German Constitution, which states that a temporary residence permit to enable foreigners to be joined by foreign dependents shall be granted and extended to protect marriage and the family, which includes both adult and minor dependents.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 83, 84 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sefctions 42, 75, 80, 123 of the Rules of the Administrative Courts. With regards to the administrative proceedings of a visa, there is a judicial remedy called 'Remonstration' available in every case. Thus, in each and every request for family reunification/formation in case of denial, a judicial remedy is possible.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Section 27 of the Federal Residence Act, which lists civil partnerships as equivalent to marriage. 2) Article 6 of the German Constitution. 3) the Civil Partnership Law, which guarantees complete equality to traditional marriage for same-sex couples. That being said, civil partnerships still experience inequality regarding the adoption of children, but there is no discrepancy regarding the legal recognition equivalent to a heterosexual marriage.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 4, 4a, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9-9a, 9b, 16-25, 37, 39, 41, 60a-d, 104-105 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) The Federal Employment Directive. The regulation does not refer to visa types. As for all residence permits for work purposes, a national residence permit according to Sections 4, 4a, 7 of the Federal Residence Act (Visa type D or similar residence titles) has to be issued within 3 months of residence in Germany after entry (on a short-mid term entry Visa Schengen type C with a validity of 3-6 months, according to Sections 4 and 6 of the Federal Residence Act).

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 25, 60a-d, 104-105 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 31-32 of the Federal Employment Directive. 3) Section 39 of the Federal Residence Act. 4) Section 55 of the Federal Asylum Act. There are several provisions for undocumented persons and asylum seekers with a pending protection status to legalize their stay if certain conditions are met. This can be done either through employment after 3 months, or other documented integrational efforts, such as via a two-stage immigration status of 1) an interim residence paper called tolerance certification by virtue of a temporary ban of deportation (thus though not being a residence permit, the stay is rendered legal for a limited time, and this status is extendable), and subsequently, 2) a residence permit for humanitarian reasons. The most recent amendment of the Federal Residence Act introduces an opportunity residence right (Artikel 1 Gesetz zur Einführung eines Chancen-Aufenthaltsrechts vom 21.12.2022), which created a humanitarian residence permit for humanitarian reasons after 5 years of legal stay without a residence permit. In particular, a tolerance permission holder is an undocumented migrant according to Section 60b through Section 103c of the Federal Residence Act.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 39, 41, 98a of the Posted Workers Act. 2) Section 25, 59 of the Federal Residence Act; Sections 406 et seq. of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 3) Section 266a of the Penal Code; Sections 1, 2 of the Labour Court Act. 4) Sections 1, 3, 13 of the Minimum Wage Act. 5) Sections 8-12 of the Law on Combating Illegal Employment. 6) Provisions of the Protection against Dismissal Act. 7) The Civil Law Code. 8) the Civil Procedure Code. 9) The Courts Constitution Act.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 2, 5, 291, 264 of the 5th Social Code, which states that all employed migrants have access to health care on an equal basis with citizens. 2) Sections 23, 27 of the 12th Social Code. Additionally, if they are unemployed but legally living in the territory (which means without a residence permit, but allowed to remain on a temporary basis), they have legal access to health care according to Section 27 of the 12th Social Code. 3) Sections 3, 4, 6 of the Federal Asylum, the Asylum Benefits Act guarantees equal basic health care for all beneficiaries, which means that refugees and irregular and undocumented migrants if certain conditions are met. It should be noted though, that the Asylum Seekers Benefits Act, if strictly applied, only includes acute “non-chronic" diseases, and so it only covers the minimum level of care regarding the prevention of death or severe health impairment. 4) Articles 1, 2, 3 of the German Constitution. 5) Sections 1, 2 of the General Equal Treatment Act.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Domestic Constitutional and Federal Basic Law, the right to being voted for the German National Parliament is reserved to citizens, articles 38, 116 German Constitution in conjunction with section 15 Federal Election Law, with the exception of European Union (EU) citizens whom, according to Art. 28 paragraph 2 of the German Constitution, can be voted in local/regional elections. Third-Country/foreign non-EU nationals, are thus migrants (as EU citizens are not migrants by definition, but right holders of unalienable guarantees of freedom due to the Movement within the European Union Act by birth) have no passive voting rights whatsoever to being voted for parliamentary representation.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Article 3 of the German Constitution. 2) Sections 130, 192a of the PenalCode. 3) Section 39 of the Federal Residence Act. 4) Section 131 of the 3rd Social Code. 5) Sections 1, 1a of the Asylum Seeker Benefits Act. 6) Section 22 of the Federal Police Act. There is an extensive ban on discrimination in domestic law in Germany, which also includes the prohibition of dicriminatory acts or any behavior with indirect discrimitory effects on the basis of origin, homeland, religion, language, and descent, though not expressively with regards to the feature ‘migration status.' However, the Federal Police Law currently still allows for ethnic/social profiling for border security and migration control measures, but those practices can be considered unconstitutional. A relevant decision on this matter from the Federal Constitutional Court is still pending.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Article 3 of the German Constitution. 2) Section 1 of the General Equal Treatment Act. 3) Sections 130, 192a of the Penal Code. There is an extensive ban of discrimination in domestic law in Germany, which also includes the prohibition of dicriminatory acts or any behavior with indirect discriminatory effects on the basis of ethnicity and race.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is a general equal pay rule for equal work for third-country migrants in relation to German or European Union (EU) Citizens laid down in Federal Residence Act, as well as for EU-citizens working in Germany. The Minimum Wage Act also provides stipulations to minimum pay in specific sectors where the law applies. This is enforcable by the labor jurisdiction in the case of legal disputes for everybody, thus also including migrants.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 4a, 39 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 34-35 of the Federal Employment Act. The right of free choice of employment depends on the residence status of migrants. In many cases, during the first time they are tied to a special employer. For instance, highly skilled workers have a right to free choice of employment, whereas other visa holders have more restrictions. Basic restrictions largely consist of the labour market test (which is given priority to German & European Union citizens) on the one hand, and some sectoral limitations for both qualified and unqualified jobs on the other hand as the job assignment has to meet criteria for several groups of jobs listed in the Federal Employment Directive. Administrative processes to change work permission, which is usually tied to a specific employer, has to be applied for and approved of by the immigrations office in each singular case where a position is changed.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in Section 1, 4a, 30 of the Federal Residence Act. As per Section 4a of the Federal Residence Act, normal restrictions on the right to work apply for all other residence permits; but the work permission is automatic for visas related to family reunification.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 4a paragraphs 1-3, 16a, 8 paragraphs 1-2, 11 paragraph 2, 16d-e, 17, 18 paragraph 2 sentence 1 numbers 1-2, 18a-20, 39-41, 51 paragraph 1 number 2, 81 paragraph 5a of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 1 et. seq., 34-36 of the Federal Employment Directive. 3) Sections 4-6 of the European Economic Area (EEU) Freedom of Movement Act. Protection of status due to loss of employment depends on the type of visa. The system of work permissions for all types of working Visa contains three types: a) employment which needs to be approved by the Federal Labour Agency, including either the necessity of a labour market test, or the approval of privileged employments without labour market test, and b) employments without the necessity of an approval by the Federal Labour Agency at all. The destiny of the validity of residence permit in case of loss of the present job depends either on the particular condition attached to the residence permit by the immigrations office, or on the approval required by the Federal Labour Agency: in case a special condition is imposed - work permission tied to a specific employer, for example - the residence permit either becomes invalid by law, has to be revoked or is not extended. In case of unconditioned work permissions for certain types of employments in particular highly-skilled labour, the residence permit can be re-issued/updated either upon approval by the Federal Labour Agency or by issuing of a new work permission by the immigrations office. The residence permit in case of start of an apprenticeship is automatically invalid upon loss of vocational training / cancellation of the formation contract. A request of approval of the change of the employer has to be submitted in each and every case; the stay in Germany is legal from submission of the application for new residence permit until (final) binding decision of the administration (temporary residence paper, the so-called Fiktionsbescheinigung, without permission to work during the pending phase of the residence status). For all other resident purposes, it is vice versa: a loss of the residence permit renders the resident status illegal with the duty to leave the country, which leads to the prohibition of work i. e. attached condition on the residence papers that work/self-employment is prohibited. Certain privileges are in place according to the facilitated mobility for Turkish working migrants and their families, holders of family reunion Visa to highly qualified migrants, settlement permits, EU-permanent residency and mobility permits, EU-Blue Card, long-term residence permission in other EU member states, and citizens of certain countries (so-called best friends states like Commonwealth nations). There is a jobseeking Visa and also a jobsearch residence permit for migrants already staying in Germany, most notably after cancellation of the current employment, from 6 months up to 1 year. Alternatively, most job-related residence permits allow for a switch of residency for example for humanitarian, family reunification, and educational purposes, but except a few entitlement cases (reunion with a German citizen family member, upgrade to Blue Card employment Visa), this regularly means undergoing the Visa procedure of exit and re-enter upon granting of a new national Visa for Germany.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Articles 2, 3, 12, 19 of the German Constitution. 2) Sections 1-2, 6-7, 8-9 of the General Equal Treatment Act. 3) Sections 4a, 39, 41, 98a of the Federal Residence Act.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 2, 5, 9, 21, 37 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Article 3 of the German Constitution. 3) Sections 1, 2, 6 of the General Equal Treatment Act. Access to public retirement pension schemes makes no distinction between citizens and migrants, but depends on length of employment.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 1, 5, 7, 8 of the Social Law Book II. 2) Section 137 of the Social Law Book III. 3) Sections 8, 23 of the Social Law Book XII. 4) Sections 1, 1a, 2 et seq. of the Asylum Seekers Benefits Act. 4) Article 3of the German Constitution. 5) Sections 1, 2, 6 of the General Equal Treatment Act. Social benefits apply to immigrants provided they can demonstrate lawful residence (asylumseekers, visa / residence permit holdes, humanitarian refugees), and this access begins after three months of legal residence.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 4, 4a, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9-9a, 9b, 16-25, 37, 39, 60a-d, 104-105 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) the Federal Employment Directive; Sections 39, 41 of the Federal Residence Directive. The majority of residence permits for work purposes, or other residence titles which grant the right to work are extendable for at least the same residence purpose as continued prolongation of a limited residence permit, or the change for a different type of visa, or a settlement permit, according to the general rules. However, certain types of occupations allow only a temporary stay in Germany by law, meaning after expiry of the maximum duration, the migrant worker is obliged to leave Germany and apply for a new visa from outside the territory.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 48, 50 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Section 55 of the Federal Residence Ordinance. 3) Sections 96, 4-5, 98 of the Federal Residence Act. 4) Sections 242, 246, 274 of the Penal Code. 5) Sections 823 et. seq., 854 et. seq., 1004 et. seq. of the Civil Code. The passport or passport substitute of a foreigner who is required to leave Federal territory is kept by the authorities until their departure, and upon request has to be handed over temporarily to Federal authorities. There is also a passport and identification obligation for migrants, but the state holds property on the documents issued. There is also a legal obligation of the employer to keep a copy of the identity document for the duration of the employment. It is an administrative offence with sanctions/fines for the migrant if they violates the identity/passport documentation duty, therefore illegal confiscation can be subject to restitutional claims (misappropriation of a deed, theft and misappropriation are usually implied offences related to crimes relating to smuggling/illegal migration).

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in Section 18 of the Civil Status Code, which states that every birth has to be registered within one week at the district office regardless of status.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 4, 4a, 12, 48, 60a, 78-78a of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 55, 63 – 64a of the Federal Asylum Act. 3) Sections 55-56, 59-61, 80 of the Federal Residence Ordinance. 4) Sections 34-36 Federal Employment Ordinance. Every migrant legally staying in Germany is delivered a document, which gives concrete information concerning their legal status, work status, and identity.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in Section 274 of the Penal Code.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in Section 62a of the Federal Residence Act, which permits embassy authorities to communicate with immigrants in detention facilities.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Federal Law doesn't explicitely prohibit the detention of minors. As a result, deportation and push-back detention is occasionally also imposed on children (minors below the legal age of 18), and thus regardless of their status as minors. However, this applies generally only to children over 16 years which means there is a de facto protection in place for minors under the age of 16. By law, deprivation of liberty to minors should be used only as an ultima ratio means, but this occurs regularly. Additionally, minor detentions can also be legally undertaken without a judge's order if the act doesn't exceed 48 hours.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The legal framework for detaining migrants based on their migration status is laid out in Sections 58 and 60 of the Federal Residence Act. Additionally, Article 2 II 2, 104 of the German Constitution creates guidelines for deportation based on situations where the migrant illegally enters the country, and introduces an accelarated asylum procedure for migrants from secure non-member states/safe countries of origin/EU-Dublin-Cases. It also states that migrants are to be generally detained or deprieved from their right of personal freedom to ensure they promptly leave the country through special collection centers until deportation decisions are made. Under this provision, detentions exceeding a duration of 48 hours can occur and sometimes qualify as a de facto deportation detention.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 62–62c of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Section 70 of the Act on Proceedings in Family Matters and in Matters of Voluntary Jurisdiction. 3) Sections 112 et. seq., 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Generally in cases of pre-trial detention, penal sentences, and deportation detention, individuals can appeal against the judicial resolution/order of custody under the provisions of ordinary jurisdiction regarding length, conditions and legality of detention.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 15, 50, 57, 58, 61, 60, 62b, 62c of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Article 104 of the German Constitution. 3) Sections 112 et. seq., 127 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Every detention has to be individual, respecting special circumstances, and according to administrative regulations. In general, a judge’s order is required prior to detention, in cases of imminent danger or special urgency, police and prosecutors can order the detention under the condition that the judge’s order is resumed within 24 hours after the detention. This provision is guaranteed in Article 104 of the German Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Articles 1 and 2 of the German Constitution. 2) Section 60 of the Federal Residence Act. 3) Article 3 of the European Convention of Human Rights in conjunction with articles 25, 59 German Constitution. 4) Sections 3a, 4 of the Federal Asylum Act. 5) Section 4 of the Asylum Seekers' Benefits Act.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. If migrants are legally not allowed to enter Germany, the Federal Police may use force according to the Administrative Enforcement Act in order to take the migrants into custody.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Section 12 of the Administrative Enforcement Act. 2) Sections 2, 9-12 of the Act on Direct Coercion in the Exercise of Official Authority by Federal Law Enforcement Officers. 3) Sections 14, 15, 70 of the Federal Police Act. 4) Section 106 of the Federal Residence Act. 5) Section 89 of the Federal Asylum Act; Article 2 of the German Constitution. The Act on Direct Coercion in the Exercise of Official Authority by Federal Law Enforcement Officers enables the restriction of the fundamental right to live under the constitution by use of weapons and firearms, but only when circumstances constitute an imminent and severe physical threat to other person(s) by an assault/attack of the migrant. Therefore, the use of force will almost be disproportionate and thus rendered illegal solely as a means of preventing migrants from entering the state's territory. However, there are no known cases applying this principal to the context of irregular entry.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Penal Code can prosecute victims of human trafficking and smuggling, which includes smuggled and trafficked migrants as alleged accomplices or participants of the crime.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 17, 28, 35, 42 of the Nationality Act. According to the Nationality Act, German citizenship can be revoked in the following cases: a German who, without the consent of the Federal Ministry of Defence or a body designated by the said Ministry, voluntarily enlists with the armed forces or a comparable armed organization of a foreign state whose citizenship he or she possesses or who actively participates in fighting by a terror organization abroad, automatically loses German citizenship unless he or she would otherwise become stateless.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 8, 9, 10 of the Nationality Act. 2) Federal Residence Act. National legislation generally and specifically provides a pathway for all regular non-circular work residence titles such as the residency card under the European Union (EU) Freedom of Movement Act, the EU Blue Card for highly skilled labor, and several other residence permits under the Federal Residence Act. Many permits issued for employment and/or self-employment have pathways to citizenship, but eligibility for German nationality requires that the migrant live in Germany and be able to support themselves for several years. This means that pathways to citizenship are for permanent, not temporary, visas.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 8, 9, 10 of the Federal Citizenship Act. Specifically, Section 10 of the Federal Citizenship Act lists humanitarian residence permits which preclude naturalization. 2) Section 25a-b of the Federal Residence Act, which created humanitarian residence permits, granting the ‘right to stay’ for migrants under 21 with 4 years of successful schooling/apprenticeship, or the ‘right to remain’ for those with 6-8 years of permanent residence, sufficient income.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in Sections 4-7, 8-10, 13-15 of the Nationality Act. All family reunion visas provide a legal avenue to German citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in Sections 10, 12 of the Nationality Act. According to Section 10 of the Nationality Act, dual nationality is not permitted, but Section 12 of the same law allows exceptions if the migrant is unable to give up his or her previous citizenship, or can do so only under very difficult conditions. It should be noted that, in about 50 to 70 percent of the cases, dual nationality is allowed. Additionally, there will be a legal change in 2023 to allow for dual nationality.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: Article 4 of the German Constitution guarantees the fundamental right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion to everyone and are subject to the Constitutional and Administrative Court’s protection. Thus, the German Constitution recognizes the right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief on an equal basis with citizens for foreigners as well.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) the German Constitution, Article 5, paragraphs 1-2, which provides migrants with full freedom to hold opinions commensurate with that afforded to citizens. 2) Federal Residence Act, Sections 47, 106 paragraph 1.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Article 5 of the German Constitution, which provides migrants with full freedom to hold opinions commensurate with that afforded to citizens. 2) Sections 47, 106 of the Federal Residence Act.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While migrants are able to join trade unions under Article 9, Section 3, they are not able to form trade unions. Migrants do enjoy some protections under Article 2, Section 1, of the Constitution, but are not fully protected under Article 9, Section 1 of the Federal Constitution in the same way as citizens.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. As the national law requires that all migrants demonstrate the ability to meet certain resource conditions (such as income, insurance, residence, etc.), including for family reunification. Therefore, the right to reunite with family members in Germany is conditional on the financial situation of the migrant as the initial residence right holder. For instance, in Book II or Book XII of the Social Code, if a migrant is reliant on social benefits for their livelihood, family reunification can be denied. It should be noted, though, that this precondition can be waived on discretion. There are also exceptions to the general rule requiring resource condtions, particularly to facilitate spouse and child reunion with German citizens, to Blue card holders, and for certain humanitarian residence purposes.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 25, 60a, 4a, 39-41, 95, 98, 98a of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Sections 266a of the Code on Penal Procedure. 3) Section 370 of the Federal Tax Code. 4) 284, 304 of the 3rd Social Code. 5) Sections 259, 374 of the Federal Code on the Criminal Procedure. 6) Articles 3, 101, 104, 19, of the German Constitution. Under the Federal Code on Penal Procedure, there is the possibility to file a civil claim for damages, which extends to migrants. Additionally, there is a constitutional right of access to justice and to have their case heard before a legally appointed judge commensurate with citizens. The only exceptions to this exist when the nature of the crime necessarily involves a connection to citizenship, then these accusations can only be brought forward by German citizens. Additionally, there is also a specific codified right for migrant workers subject to illegal employment to be granted access to Labour Courts to sue for a loss of wages.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 27, 29, 30, 31 of the Federal Residence Act; Sections 25, 60a of the European Union Freedom of Movement Act. 2) Sections 232-233a of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which states that any foreigner who has been the victim of a criminal offence should be granted a temporary residence permit for a temporary stay, even if they are enforceably required to leave the federal territory, should be granted a temporary residence permit for a temporary stay. The temporary residence permit may only be issued if, A) the public prosecutor's office or the criminal court considers his presence in federal territory to be appropriate in connection with criminal proceedings relating to said criminal offence, because it would be more difficult to investigate the facts of the case without their information, B) they have broken off contact with the persons accused of having committed the criminal offence, and C) they have declared their willingness to testify as a witness in the criminal proceedings relating to the offence. After conclusion of the criminal proceedings, the temporary residence permit could be extended for humanitarian or personal reasons or public interests require the foreigner's further presence in the federal territory. 3) Sections 1b, 11-12 of the Law on Combating Illegal Employment. 4) Section 15a of the Temporary Employment Act. 5) Sections 60, 60a, 3, 25 of the Federal Residence Act, Sections 3-4 of the Federal Asylum Act.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 25a, 27-37, 60a, 60c, 60d, 55,62, 62a of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Section 44 of the Federal Asylum Act. 3) Sections 4-6 of the Federal Citizenship Act.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Sections 25, 54, 60 of the Federal Residence Act. 2) Section 44IIa of the Federal Asylum Act. The Federal Residence Act provides for: A) a special pregnancy social grant and pre-/post-birth aid for female migrants, B) the right of tolerance certificate/suspension of expulsion for pregnant female migrants up to 6 months prior and after birth, and for abortion, C) a special humanitarian residence permit for criminal proceedings regarding sexual assault, D) reason for facilitated access to an independent marriage residence permit in cases of domestic violence, E) protection of expulsion, humanitarian residence permit, acknowledgement of asylum/refugee/subsidiary protection status in cases of severe gender specific persecution (female genital mutilation, honour killings, enslavement), sexualized violence and women-specific discrimination, F) right to appropriate housing/protected shelter in asylum shared accommodations (not codified) G) special protection with regard to pending deportation.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Germany protects this right in 1) Section 1 of the Federal Law on Equality and Equal Treatment. 2) Section 1 of the Law on Equality of the Disabled, which prohibits discrimination related to (amongst other features like race, religion, nationality etc.) disability. 3) Section 2 paragraph 2 of the Social Code No. 9. 4) Sections 4, 6 of the Asylum Seekers’ Benefits Act, which provides for special medical support. 5) Article 3 paragraph 1, paragraph 3 sentence 2 of the German Constitution. 6) Articles 21, 22 of Directive 2013/33/EU (adopted the by state laws on reception of asylum seekers). 7) Federal Residence Act, which provides a humanitarian residence permit/suspension of expulsion due to health reasons. This provision is not only just applicable to acute diseases or the like, but not expressively to disabilities as a permanent condition.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Greece

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for irregular migrants. However, national law in Greece protects this right for all regular migrants in the Migration Code (Law 4251/2014), Article 21A which states that: “Employees holding a uniform residence permit shall enjoy equal treatment with nationals in respect of: [...] (d) the right to strike and to be involved in trade unions in accordance with national law, freedom of association, accession and participation in an employee's or employer's organization or any professional organization, including the advantages provided by such organizations, including the right to negotiate and conclude collective labor agreements, and without prejudice to the provisions regarding public order and public security.” In Greece, the establishment of an association is controlled by the courts in accordance with the provisions of Article 78 of the Greek Civil Code. According to Greek jurisprudence, the constitutional right of freedom of association extends, in combination of article 12 and 25 of the Constitution, also to aliens.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 4 of Presidential Decree (PD) 26/2012 states that: ''the right to vote is provided only to Greek citizens who: Have reached the age of 17 (January 1st is considered the date of birth of all those born within the year). They are registered in the electoral roll of the country's municipality. They have not been deprived of the right to vote.'' Additionally, European Union citizens can vote in local elections, according to presidential decree 133/1997 which inserted the Council Directive 94/80/EC “Laying down detailed arrangements for the exercise of the right to vote and to stand as a candidate in municipal elections by citizens of the Union residing in a Member State of which they are not nationals” if they reside legally in Greece for two years.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in the Greek Constitution Article 8 and Article 20 §1. Article 8 (Right to legal judge) provides that "No one is deprived without his will of the judge appointed by the law. Judicial commissions and extraordinary courts, by any name, may not be established."According to Article 20 §1: “Everyone has the right to legal protection of the courts and can thereby express his/her views on his/her rights or interests, as provided by law.”

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Law 4939/2022. According to Article 76, Law 4939/2022 Article 76, "Applicants shall be provided [...] with free legal and procedural information regarding their case. In addition to the provision of information of the previous paragraph, in the event of a decision not to grant refugee status in the first instance, applicants are provided, upon request, with specific information regarding the reasoning behind the decision and the possibility to appeal against it. Applicants are provided, at their request, with free legal aid in the proceedings before the Appeals Authority [...]. In the event of an appeal before the Court, applicants may receive free legal aid, under the terms and conditions of L. 3226/2004 (Α? 24)." 2) Ministerial Decision 788502/2023 regarding the provision of legal aid to international protection applicants. According to Article 1: “1. Applicants of international protection are provided with free legal aid for the exercise of the appeal […]. 2. Applicants of international protection have the right to free legal aid during the second instance examination procedure […].

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Code of Penal Procedure, Article 95: "1. The suspect or accused is immediately informed about at least the following rights: a) the right to be represented by a lawyer, b) the right and preconditions of providing free legal advice, c) the right to information about the accusation, d) the right to interpretation and translation and e) the right to remain silent and not to incriminate oneself." According to article 101 “The suspect or the accused who does not speak or does not understand sufficiently the Greek language, has the right to interpretation, as well as to written translation of all the essential documents of the procedure […].” Moreover, article 233 states that: “1. At any stage of the penal procedure, when a suspect, an accused or a witness is to be examined, who does not speak or understand the Greek language sufficiently, interpretation is provided without delay. If necessary, interpretation is available for communication between the accused and their lawyers at all stages of the criminal proceeding. […]." 2) Law 4478/2017 which transposed Directive 2012/29/ΕΕ establishing minimum standards on the rights, support, and protection of victims of crime, Article 7 §1 (right to interpretation and translation): “Victims who do not understand or speak the language of the criminal proceedings in question are provided free of charge, upon request, with interpretation, in accordance with their role in the criminal proceedings [...], at least during each examination in the context of criminal proceedings before the investigating and judicial authorities, including police interrogations, as well as interpretation for their active participation in the hearing procedure before the court and in any necessary procedures of interim measures.”

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Law 3386/2005 Article 83 §1: “A third-country national leaving or attempting to leave Greek territory or entering or attempting to enter without the legal formalities is punished with an imprisonment of at least three months and a fine of at least one thousand five hundred euros (1.500e)..."

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Presidential Decree 80/4.12.2022, Article 17 (which codified article 3 of L. 4443/2016 on the principle of equal treatment): “2. Without prejudice to par. 3, 4 and 6, as well as article 18, the principle of equal treatment regardless of race, color, national or ethnic origin, descent applies to all persons, in the public and private sector, regarding: […] d) access to the availability and provision of goods and services available […] to the public, including housing […].” 2) L. 4251/2014 (Migration Code), Article 21Α (Equal treatment of employees - holders of a uniform residence [permit]): “1. Employees ? holders of a uniform residence [permit] enjoy equal treatment with nationals in terms of: […] θ) access to goods and services […], including procedures for obtaining housing […]. For EU Blue Card holders, Article 119 (equal treatment) of the Miigration Code (L. 4251/2014) says: “1. An “EU Blue Card” holder has the right to equal treatment with nationals regarding: […] g) Access to goods and services and supply of goods and services made available to the public, including procedures for access to housing […]. 2. Regarding par. 1 c) and g), the right to equal treatment is limited as regards […] the procedures for access to housing.” 3) L. 4939/2022, Article 31 (Access to accommodation): “Beneficiaries of international protection have access to accommodation under the conditions and restrictions applicable to third-country nationals legally residing in the country, taking into account the need to disperse them at national level and to ensure equal opportunities in terms of access to accommodation.” 4) For unaccompanied minors, this right is protected in: L. 4939/2022, Article 66KE (Field of application) “[…] 2. The Special Secretariat for the Protection of Unaccompanied Minors ensures housing and the respective services for unaccompanied minors, in a) Long-Term Accommodation Structures […], which are divided into: aa) Accommodation Centers for Unaccompanied Minors […] from six (6) to eighteen (18) years old and ab) Supervised Semi-Independent Living Apartments (SILs) for unaccompanied minors from sixteen (16) to eighteen (18) years old and b) emergency accommodation structures for unaccompanied minors living in precarious living conditions and are identified through the National Emergency Response Mechanism.” 5) For refugees, this right is protected in: Legislative Decree 3989/1959 (Ratification of the Geneva Convention of 1951), Article 21 (Housing): “As regards housing, the Contracting States […] shall accord to refugees lawfully staying in their territory treatment as favourable as possible and, in any event, not less favourable than that accorded to aliens generally in the same circumstances.”

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) L. 4251/2014 (Migration Code), Article 21 (Common rights of third-country nationals): “7. Minor third-country nationals, who reside in the Greek territory, are subject to compulsory education, as Greek nationals. Minor third-country nationals, who attend all levels of education, have, without restrictions, access to the activities of the school or educational community. 8. For the enrolment of minor third-country nationals in Greek schools of all grades, the corresponding documents as those demanded from nationals are required. Exceptionally, children of third-country nationals may be enrolled in public schools with incomplete documents, provided that: a) The are protected by the Greek State as beneficiaries of international protection and those under the protection of the United Nations High Commissioner. b) They come from areas where a state of emergency prevails. c) They have applied for international protection. d) They are third-country nationals residing in Greece, even if the legality of their residence has not been regulated […].” 2) L. 4939/2022, Article 55 (Education of minors) “1. Minor applicants and minor children of applicants during their stay in the country, are obliged to enroll in primary and secondary education units of the public education system. The competent authorities are obliged to provide the necessary and sufficient means to support and facilitate the relevant procedure..." 3) Article 130 (Education): “Beneficiaries of temporary protection who do not exceed 18 years old, are granted the right of access to public schools, in which reception classes […] operate or are planned to operate."

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) L. 4939/2022, Article 56 (Access to secondary education) and Article 58. According to Article 56: “Access to secondary education is not limited to minor applicants, but can also concern adult applicants, and for as long as there is no removal measure pending against them." Article 58 of L.4939/2022 relates to the right to vocational training and it says: " 1. Applicants have access to enroll and attend vocational training programs under the same conditions as Greek citizens, regardless of whether they have access to the labor market. […]" 2) Law 4251/2014 (Migration Code), Article 21: “10. Without prejudice to more specific provisions of the current legislation, third-country nationals graduated from secondary education in Greece have access to higher education under the same terms and conditions as nationals.” According to Article 21A: “1. Employees holding a uniform residence permit enjoy equal treatment with nationals in respect of: [...] (e) education and vocational training; (f) the recognition of diplomas / certificates and other professional qualifications in accordance with the relevant national procedures." In relation to seasonal employees, Article 21B states: “1. Seasonal employees enjoy equal treatment with nationals in respect of: [...] (e) education and vocational training...In terms of long-term residents, Article 97 of Law 4251/2014 states: "1. The long-term resident enjoys equal treatment with nationals in respect of: [...] b. Education and vocational training, including scholarships. c. The recognition of professional diplomas, certificates and other qualifications [...] 3. The right to equal treatment is limited regarding: b. Access to education and vocational training, for which the long-term resident may require to demonstrate the language skills required for this purpose. c. Access to Higher University or Technological Educational Institutions, for which a prior fulfillment of the educational requirements of the applicable legislation are required." 3) As to third country employees legally working in Greece: Presidential Decree 80/4.12.2022, Article 17 (which codified article 3 of L. 4443/2016 on the principle of equal treatment): “2. Without prejudice to par. 3, 4 and 6 as well as article 18, the principle of equal treatment regardless of race, color, national or ethnic origin, descent applies to all persons, in the public and private sector, regarding: c) education […]"

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Art. 16 L 4825/2021 provides that certain type of convictions can lead to loss of migrants' residence status (anaklisi or apolesi in greek language) specifically according to the specific article (a) the person in question should have been, or is, excluded from refugee status in accordance with Article 12; b) the falsification or omission of facts on the part of the person concerned, including the use of forged documents, was decisive for the granting of refugee status. 4. The ruling authority revokes or refuses to renew the status granted to a refugee when: a) it is reasonably considered that this person constitutes danger to the national security of the country, b) this person constitutes a danger to the society of the Country, due to his final conviction for committing a particularly serious crime.'' 2) Law 4251/2014 (Migration Code), Article 6: “The right of residence of third-country nationals legally entering Greece for one of the purposes of this Code is subject to the following conditions: [...] (c) They are not considered to be a threat to public order, internal security or international relations and are not registered as undesirable in national databases. Criteria for reasons of public order and security are considered the following [...]: (i) issuance of a final conviction for felony or misdemeanor for imprisonment of at least one (1) year; (ii) registration as an undesirable alien; such registration shall cease to be effective upon the granting or renewal of the residence permit; (iii) other reasons of public order, which should specifically [...] be mentioned in the relevant decision; (iv) particularly exceptional reasons, specifically justified, which relate to internal security matters.ξs revocation.” 3) Additionally, Article 13 of Law 4939/2022, which states: “1. Refugee status is revoked or not renewed by the Ruling Authority, as long as the person ceases to be a refugee, in accordance with article 10 of the present Code. […] 4. The Ruling Authority revokes or refuses to renew the status granted to a refugee when: a) it is reasonably considered that this person constitutes a risk to the national security of the country; b) this person constitutes a danger to the society of the country, due to a final conviction for the commission of a particularly serious crime […]. 5. The persons to whom par. 4 applies, enjoy the rights provided for or are analogous to those provided for in articles 3, 4, 16, 22, 31, 32 and 33 of the Geneva Convention, as long as they are in Greek territory.”)"

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Law 3386/2005 on the entrance, residence, and social inclusion of third-country nationals in the Greek territory, Article 78A of Law 3386/2005, Article 78Α, states that, "an expulsion is not ordered if reasons of non-refoulement apply and the return could subject the alien to torture under article 3 of the Convention against Torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment ratified by Law 1782/1988, or under Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights ratified by Law 2462/1997, or under Articles 31 and 33 of the Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees of 1951, ratified by Decree 3989/1959, or under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights ratified by Law 53/1974."2) Law 4939/2022, Articles 13, 20. Article 20 states that: "1. The competent authorities respect the principle of non-refoulement, in accordance with the country's international obligations."

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Law 3386/2005, Article 78Α. 2) Law 4939/2022, Article 20. Non-refoulement is highly regulated, and only allowable if the migrant represents a threat to national security, or public order (as stated by Law 4939/2022, Article 20). Additionally, Article 78A of Law 3386/2005 states that, "An expulsion is not ordered if reasons of non-refoulement apply and the return could subject the alien to torture under article 3 of the Convention against Torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment... or under Articles 31 and 33 of the Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees of 1951... or under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights..." 2) National law explicitly prohibits non-refoulment/return of the foreigner must not affect values of human civilization as they were formulated in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ratified by Law 2462/1997, document A), in the Geneva Convention on the Status of Refugees 1951 (cert. with Legislative Decree 3989/1959, Official Gazette 201/1959, document A), in the European Convention on Human Rights (regulatory with Legislative Decree 53/1974 Official Gazette 256/74, document A).

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Law 3386/2005, Article 78Α. 2) Law 4939/2022, Article 13. 3) Presidential Decree 3989/1959. 4) Presidential Decree 53/1974. Presidential Decrees 3989/1959 and 53/1974 incorporates the Geneva Convention on the Status of Refugees of 1951, and the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights which protects fundamental human rights. Additionally, Article 78A of Law 3386/2005 states that, "An expulsion is not ordered if reasons of non-refoulement apply and the return could subject the alien to torture under article 3 of the Convention against Torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment... or under Articles 31 and 33 of the Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees of 1951... or under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights..."

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in Law 4939/2022, Articles 39 and 70. Specifically, article 39 states clearly, that, “During the first 'Information' stage, third-country nationals or stateless persons are informed... for the possibility to apply for international protection.” Additionally, Article 70 says: “1. Third-country nationals or stateless persons, who are in detention centers or border crossing points, including transit zones, at the external borders, receive information about the possibility of applying for international protection. […]”

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right, in Law 3386/2005, Article 78Α. According to this article, “An expulsion is not ordered, if reasons of non-refoulement apply and the return could subjected the alien to torture under article 3 of the Convention against Torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment ratified by Law 1782/1988, or under Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights ratified by Law 2462/1997, or under Articles 31 and 33 of the Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees of 1951, ratified by Decree 3989/1959, or under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights ratified by Law 53/1974. In this case, the competent authority of article 76 §2 of Law 3386/2005 (Police Director or competent Police Officer) orders the non-removal of the alien on humanitarian grounds [...].”

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Law 3386/2005, Article 76. 2) L4825/2021, Article 2. 3) Law 4939/2022.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Law 3386/2005, Articles 76 and 77. According to Article 76: “2. Expulsion is ordered by decision of the competent Police Director [...] after previously giving the alien at least forty-eight hours to submit objections." Furthermore, Article 77 of Law 3386/2005 states that, "The alien has the right to appeal against the deportation order within five days from its notification before the Minister of Public Order or the authorized body." 2) Law 3907/2011, Article 28 which states that, "Third-country nationals have the right to submit an appeal in accordance with article 77 of L. 3386/2005 against return decisions issued by the police authorities." 3) Article 5 of Law 4825/2021 states that: ''1. Against the return decisions issued by the police authorities, the nationals of third countries can exercise the adversarial appeal of Article 77 of Law 3386/2005. Third-country nationals have the right to appeal against return decisions that are included in decisions to reject the request for the granting or renewal of a residence permit, as well as in decisions to revoke a valid residence permit, under Article 24 of Law 2690/1999 (A' 45) within an exclusive period of two (2) months from the service of the decision.''

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for both migrants and children of migrants who would otherwise be stateless. However, this right exists for children of migrants in: Greek Nationality Code (L. 3284/2004) Article 1“Anyone born on Greek soil acquires Greek nationality from birth, provided that:[…]Does not acquire a foreign nationality by birth nor can he/she acquire such with a relevant declaration of his/her parents to the competent foreign authorities. If the law of his/her parents nationality requires the submission of a similar declaration, or Is of unknown nationality, as long as the impossibility of establishing any foreign nationality acquired by birth is not due to the parent’s refusal to cooperate.”

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en:
National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Article 70 of the Migration Code (Law 4251/2014) which states that: "1. The citizen of a third country who resides legally in Greece for a period of two years is entitled to request, upon his application, the entry and residence in the country of his family members. The application is submitted and examined when these members reside outside the Greek territory. Any residence of these members in Greek territory, before the submission of the application for family reunification, is not a reason that prevents the submission of the application. 2. In order to exercise the right of the previous paragraph, the maintenance person should prove the family relationship with the members of his family for whom he is requesting reunification in Greece, as well as that he meets, cumulatively, the following conditions: a. Has accommodation capable of meeting the needs of himself and his family members for whom he is requesting reunification, as defined by a decision of the Minister of Health under the authority of Article 43 of Law 4025/2011 (A' 228), as applicable b. He has a stable and regular personal income, sufficient for himself and his family's needs, which does not come from recourse to the country's social assistance system. This income cannot be lower than the annual earnings of the person paid the minimum wage, according to national legislation, increased by 20% for the spouse and by 15% for each child. The above increase of 15% for each child is not required in the case where both spouses legally reside in Greece. c)c. He has full health insurance for all the risks covered for the respective categories of national workers, which can also cover his family members. 3. In case of polygamy, if the dependent already has a spouse living with him in Greece, family reunification with another spouse is not permitted. The family reunification of minor children of the breadwinner and another spouse is not permitted, except in cases where custody has been legally assigned to him.” The Migration Code's Article 1 §1 (λγ?) explains who are considered family members: “a) The other spouse, who has completed the age of 18, as well as their unmarried common children under the age of 18, including those who have been legally adopted in Greece by a Court decision or by a foreign court decision that is automatically enforceable or has been declared executor or its jurisdiction has been recognized in Greece, b) The other unmarried children under the age of 18 of the person concerned or of his/her spouse, including the adopted children, provided that each spouse is legally entrusted with the custody of his or her own children.” Articles 73, 76, and 80 of the Migration Code give further details such as Article 73 explaining the duration and renewal of residence permit within the context of family reunification. Article 123 talks about the right to reunification for family members of an EU blue card holder: "1. When the “EU Blue Card” holder moves from the first member state to Greece, according to the provisions of article 122, and when his/her family was already established in the first member state, his/her family members are allowed, to accompany or be reunited with him/her." 2) Presidential Decree 131/2006 (supplemented by P.D. 167/2008 and amended by P.D. 113/2013) as it relates to the right of family reunification for refugees. In Article 13, it says: 
 “An alien who is recognized as a refugee may at any time, for reasons of family reunification, request [...] the entry and settlement with him/her of the other spouse, who has completed the age of 18 and also their unmarried common children under the age of 18 and also the other unmarried children under the age of 18 of the applicant or of his/her spouse, including the adopted children, provided that each spouse is legally entrusted with the custody of his or her own children and also: 1. […] a. of his/her unmarried adult children or the ones of his/her spouse, provided that they cannot objectively meet their needs due to their health condition, b. of his/her parents, if the latter, according to a refugee's declaration, were living with him/her and maintained by him/her prior to their arrival in Greece and lack the necessary family support in the country of origin, and c. of his/her out-of-wedlock partner, with whom the refugee maintains a stable, long-term, and well-proven relationship. 2. If the refugee is an unaccompanied minor, family reunification is allowed with: a. his/her first-degree ancestors related by blood, irrespective of the conditions laid down in paragraph 1(b) and b. his/her legal guardian or other member of his/her family, provided that the minor has no ancestors with whom he/she is related by blood or that the latter cannot be located.” 3)Law 4939/2022 relates to family reunification for migrants who are in international protection status. Article 1 (Definitions) states: “lb) ‘family members’ of the beneficiary of international protection, provided that they are in Greek territory in relation to the application for international protection and that the family already existed in the country of origin, are considered the following: i. The spouse or his/her extramarital partner with whom he/she maintains a stable relationship duly proven, ii. His/her minor unmarried children, regardless of whether they were born in or out of wedlock of their parents or are adopted, iii. The father or the mother or other adult exercising custody of the applicant, in accordance with the Greek law, if the said applicant is a minor, iv. The adult unmarried children who suffer from mental or physical disability and cannot apply independently.” Article 22 emphasizes that "the competent authorities ensure that all necessary measures are taken to ensure the preservation of family unity..."

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right in: 1) Presidential Decree 131/2006, Article 12 (Right of appeal), which states that "2. For the decisions issued pursuant to the provisions herein and concern family reunification of third-country nationals legally residing in the Country, with the exception of refugees, an administrative appeal before the issuing authority is submitted, pursuant to article 24 of L. 2690/1999, as in force. Against the decisions concerning family reunification of refugees, an appeal before the Head of the Regional Asylum Office may be submitted within ten (10) days from its service." If the above appeals are rejected, applicants have the right to lodge an application for annulment before the competent Administrative Court of First Instance, according to article 15 of L. 3068/2002, which states that: “1. The jurisdiction of the […] Administrative Court of First Instance includes annulment applications which arise from infringement of individual administrative acts, issued pursuant to aliens’ legislation in general […].”Art. 25 of L4251/2014 provides that: ''Against the decision to reject the application for the granting of a residence permit, its revocation or non-renewal, issued pursuant to the provisions herein, an application for annulment shall be made before the competent administrative court, pursuant to the provisions of Article 15 of Law 3068/2002 (A' 274), as applicable.''

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Greece protects this right for family members of EU citizens under the right to free movement and residence, in: 1) Presidential Decree 106/2007, Articles 2-3 which states: ""2. Family members of an EU citizen are considered: (a) the spouse, (b) the partner with whom the European Union citizen has a relationship recognized by a civil union pact according to the law of a Member State, provided that the law of the host Member State recognizes the registered partnership relationship as equivalent to marriage, and in accordance with the conditions laid down in the relevant legislation of the host Member State." As Article 3 states: "2b.
