An enforcement objection shall not have suspensive effect on the enforcement of the return. 45/C § The aliens authority shall not expel an illegally staying third-country national who has submitted his or her asylum application pursuant to Section 71/A(1)(b) or Chapter IX/A of the Asylum Act. 46.§ (2) The decision ordering expulsion may be challenged in administrative proceedings within eight days, and the court shall decide within fifteen days. In relation to asylum procedures, legal remedy against expulsion is provided by the Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country-national, Art.46 (2). The decision ordering expulsion may be challenged in administrative court proceedings within eight days, and the court shall decide within fifteen days. Asylum seekers are not be ordered to be expelled so appealing is not applicable (see Art.45/C in Act II of 2007). There are several options for the appeals process, including an enforcement challenge, a prosecutorial review of legality and a request for suspension or postponement. The appeal can therefore be taken up by a body specifically empowered to do so and the decision of the administrative body can also be challenged in court. 2) Act I of 2007 on Union Citizens.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act LV of 1993 on Hungarian Citizenship. Article 3 states that, "unless proven otherwise, the child shall be deemed to be a Hungarian citizen (acquisition with rebuttable presumption): a) a child born in Hungary of stateless parents with a registered place of residence in Hungary, b) a child born of unknown parents found in Hungary." Furthermore, Article 4 states that, "a non-Hungarian citizen who has resided continuously in Hungary for three years prior to the submission of his/her application and who meets the conditions set out in points b) to e) of paragraph (1) maybe naturalized on preferential terms if d) has been recognized as a refugee by a Hungarian authority, or e) is stateless." 2) Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country nationals, which provides the procedures for determining statelessness.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right for migrants with residence rights in Act II of 2007 on the Entry and Residence of Third-Party Nationals. According to Article 19, "A residence permit may be issued on the grounds of family reunification to a third country national who is a relative of a third-country national who is in possession of a residence permit, immigration permit, permanent residence permit, interim permanent residence permit, a national or EC permanent residence permit, or - under specific other legislation - in possession of a residence card or permanent residence card (for the purposes of this Section hereinafter referred to as "sponsor")...The following persons may be granted a residence permit on the grounds of family reunification: a) family members of persons with refugee status, and b) the parents of unaccompanied minors with refugee status, or their legally appointed guardian...The following relatives of sponsors, the spouses of sponsors or persons with refugee status may be granted a residence permit on the grounds of family reunification: a) their parents who prodefendant; b) their brothers and sisters, if they are unable to provide for themselves due to health reasons."

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in Act II of 2007 on Entry and Residence of Third-Country Nationals, Articles 42, 88, 92/B. Article 42 allows for the migrant or sponsor to appeal against an expulsion decision, whereas Article 88/Q provides criteria for the appeals process. Article 9 states that, "(4): An appeal may be lodged against a decision to reject an application for an intended stay visa for a period not exceeding 90 days, to annul a visa or to revoke a visa."

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary conditionally protects this right on the basis of country of citizenship in EU Member States in 1) Act XXIX of 2009 on Registered Partnership, which allows for the formation of a registered partnership between two same-sex individuals over 18 years old who declare their intention before a registrar. Specifically, "3.§ (6) mandates the indication of marital status in the register, using terms such as 'married' and 'registered partner' for different statuses." 2) Act I of 2007 on the Entry and Residence of Persons Enjoying the Right of Free Movement and Residence, Article 2. Article 2 of this act defines family members, including the spouse of an European Economic Area (EEA) national and the EEA national or their spouse, which include dependent ascendants of the EEA national or their spouse, unless otherwise specified, and persons authorized as family members by the competent aliens' registration authority. It also recognizes the partner of an EEA national if they have established a registered partnership before a Hungarian authority or an authority of another EU Member State. This is a conditional right, since it only recognizes same-sex partnerships for migrants from the EU.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Act II of 2007, Article 18 states that a residence permit for season workers can be refused, "if the third-country national a) on the basis of the available data and facts is unlikely to leave the territory of the Member States of the European Union at the expiry of the residence permit, or b) has already held a residence permit issued for the purpose of seasonal employment for 6 months within a period of 12 months."

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In the case of third-country nationals who can work only when in possession of a work permit, but are employed without a work permit, this would be considered an unlawful stay in Hungary, and this infringement of the law can result in expulsion or similar measures following Article 43(2) of Act II of 2007 on the Entry and Residence of Third-Country Nationals. The relevant section states that, "the immigration authority shall order the expulsion of a third-country national under immigration laws who: a) has crossed the frontier of Hungary illegally, or has attempted to do so; b) fails to comply with the requirements set out in this Act for the right of residence; c) was engaged in any gainful employment in the absence of the prescribed work permit or any permit prescribed under statutory provision."

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country nationals. 2) Act I of 2012 on the Labour Code, Article 285. Particularly, Article 285 of Act I of 2012 states that, "(1) workers and employers may pursue their claims arising from the employment relationship or out of this Act, and trade unions and works councils may pursue their claims arising out of this Act or a collective agreement or a works agreement by judicial process. (2) By way of derogation from Subsection (1), employers may enforce their claims from workers arising from the employment relationship, if less than three times the mandatory minimum wage, by means of a payment notice. The payment notice shall be made out in writing. (3) A claim may be filed against a decision adopted by the employer within its right of discretion if the employer has violated the provisions pertaining to such decisions. (4)Employees may bring an action concerning their claims arising under Article 295 (posting) in connection with their employment in Hungary before the Hungarian court." The right of redress laid down in the Labour Code is granted to every worker irrespective of his/her nationality, according to Part IV (labour disputes), Chapter XXIII (Enforcement of Labour law Claims).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: Nation law in Hungary conditionally protects this right in 1) Act CLIV of 1997 on Health Care. 2) Act CXXII of 2019 on persons entitled to social insurance benefits and on the coverage of these benefits. 3) Act LXXXIII of 1997 on Compulsory Healthcare. In general, refugees, migrants with documents entitling them to permanent residence and EU citizens are privileged migrants, they are entitled to equal treatment with Hungarian nationals in the area of social security. Temporary migrants are subjected to limitations regarding economic and social rights (e.g. limited access to health care, access only for economically active insured persons). Irregular migrants have even more limited rights, access only to emergency healthcare and subject to reimbursement by the migrant after the intervention.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. The Constitution of Hungary, Article XXIII states that "(1)Every adult Hungarian citizen shall have the right to vote and to be voted for in elections of Members of the National Assembly, of local government representatives and mayors and of Members of the European Parliament. (2) Every adult citizen of another Member State of the European Union with domicile in Hungary shall have the right to vote and to be voted for in elections of local government representatives and mayors and of Members of the European Parliament. (3) Every adult person recognised as a refugee, immigrant or resident in Hungary shall have the right to vote in elections of local government representatives and mayors. (4) A cardinal Act may provide that only persons with domicile in Hungary may be granted the right or the full right to vote and to be voted for, and may specify further requirements for the eligibility to be voted for." Though EEA migrants have a right to vote in local elections, the law says nothing about their ability to stand as candidates.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In Hungary, the requirement of equal treatment is regulated by Act CXXV of 2003 on Equal Treatment and Promotion of Equal Opportunities (ETA) Act. The ETA Act protects equal treatment in general, including in employee-employer relations, which includes during the recruitment stage. By definition discrimination is prohibited if a person or group, because of their perceived or real characteristics, receives less favourable treatment than another person or group in a comparable situation receives, has received or would receive or is put at a significantly greater disadvantage (ETA Act, Article 8, prohibition of direct and indirect discrimination). Protected characteristics in the ETA Act are sex, race, skin colour, ethnic origin, age etc. and as a general clause, if the person has a special characteristic (according to Article 8 of the TEA). The ETA Act does not contain foreign nationality or migrant status as an expressly protected characteristic. However, there may be cases in which, for example, an employee suffers discrimination based on a status characteristic that also connects him to a vulnerable social group. Foreign citizenship can be an example of this. The Equal Treatment Authority (since 1 January 2021 Directorate-General for Equal Treatment as part of the office of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights) accepted the reference to foreign nationality as a protected characteristic in its decision EBH/46/2007.Consequently, so it is also considered as a protected characteristic even if it is not included in Article 8 of the Act.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) the Constitution of Hungary, which states that, "everyone is equal before the law. All persons have the capacity to exercise their rights. (2) Hungary shall ensure fundamental rights for all without discrimination on any ground such as race, colour, sex, disability, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status." 2) Act CXXV of 2003 on Equal Treatment and the Promotion of Equal Opportunities, defines discrimnation based on the following: "a provision shall constitute direct discrimination if, as a result of it, a person or group is treated less favourably than another person or group in a comparable situation is, has been or would be treated on grounds of any of the following characteristics, whether actual or presumed: a) sex, b) race, c) colour, d) ethnic origin, e) membership of a national minority, f)language, g) disability, h) state of health, i) religion or belief, j) political or other opinion, k) family status, l) motherhood (pregnancy) or fatherhood, m) sexual orientation, n) gender identity, o) age,p) social origin, q) property, r) part-time or fixed-term nature of the occupational relationship or other employment-related relationship, s) membership in a representative organisation, t) any other status, characteristic, or attribute (hereinafter jointly “characteristic”)."

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. National Law in Hungary protects this right for settled migrants in 1) Act I of 2012 on Labour Code, Article 12. Article 12 of Act I of 2102 on Labour Code states, "the requirement of equal treatment shall be respected in relation to the employment relationship, in particular in relation to remuneration for work. The remedy for any breach of this principle shall not involve any impairment of the rights of other workers...(3) In determining the equal value of work, account shall be taken in particular of the nature, quality and quantity of the work performed, the working conditions, the necessary qualifications, physical or mental effort, experience, responsibility and labour market conditions." 2) Act CXXV of 2003 on Equal Treatment and the Promotion of Equal Opportunities.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Migration status in Hungary is tied to a specific employer, and no change of employer is possible. Non-European Economic Area (EEA citizens (i.e. those who do not have the right to enter, reside and work freely in the EU/EEA) can, as a general rule, only be employed with a work permit, which precludes the freedom to choose where and what the third-country national wants to work. The exception to this is those who do not need a work permit because they are free to move to another place of work.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in Hungary protects this right in Government Decree No.445 of 2013, Section 15, "§ (1) No labour permit shall be required for the employment of a third-country national in the territory of Hungary within the framework of an employment relationship," Section 7, "for the employment of a spouse of a person recognised as a refugee, a person granted subsidiary protection or temporary protection, or a person with immigrant or settled status who has been living with the spouse for at least 1 year in Hungary." Section 8, "for the employment of a widow or widower of a person recognised as a refugee, a person granted asylum or refugee status, a person with the right of free movement and residence, who lived with the deceased spouse in Hungary for at least 1 year before the death of the deceased spouse, 17. for the employment of a family member of a third-country national holding an EU Blue Card who is subject to the rules on family reunification."

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Hungary conditionally protects this right in the Act II of 2007 on Entry and Residence of Third-Country Nationals, Article 29, "a third-country national shall notify the alien policing authority of his/her intention to establish an employment relationship with a specific employer if a) his/her employment is with a different employer or under different conditions than before, immediately after the termination of his/her previous employment relationship or a change in the employment conditions, but not later than five days or b) he/she holds the permits specified in paragraph (3) immediately after the… five days, or b) he/she holds the permits specified in paragraph (3), immediately after the conclusion of a prior agreement specified by law, but not later than 5 days." Article 37 goes on to state that, "A settlement, national settlement or immigration permit can be revoked by the alien policing authority if a) the conditions on the basis of which the permit was granted have changed so significantly that this would preclude the grant of the permit, provided that 5 years have not yet elapsed from the date of issue of the permit." The termination of the employment relationship has an impact on the migrant's status for two reasons: (a) if he/she becomes a social burden because he/she has no legal income and means of subsistence. The shared housing and earnings of another family member (sponsor/spouse), which is the basis for immigrant/settled status can temporarily replace this, together with the entitlement to social benefits for the third-country national. This may therefore be a problem for a single person without a family/sponsor if he/she does not meet the conditions for self-support for a longer period of time. If he/she is a guest worker whose purpose of stay is employment but who is employable without a work permit, he/she has limited chances of finding another job, including unemployment benefits that may be available, but for a third-country national who is subject to labour authorisation this usually means withdrawing the residence permit and leaving the country.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) the Constitution of Hungary, Article XVII which states that, "(2) As provided by law, workers, employers and their organisations shall have the right to bargain collectively and to conclude collective agreements and to take collective action in defence of their interests, including the right to strike. (3) All workers shall have the right to working conditions which respect their health, safety and dignity. (4) All workers shall have the right to daily and weekly rest periods and to annual holidays with pay." 2) Act I of 2012 on Labour Code. Article 12 (1) of the Labour Code lays down that the requirement of equal treatment must be maintained in relation to the employment relationship, and in particular regarding remuneration. Remedies for violations of this requirement must not violate or impair the rights of other employees. 3) Act CXXV of 2003 on Equal Treatment and the Promotion of Equal Opportunities (ETA Act), which protects equal treatment in general regarding the employment relationship (also during the recruitment stage), while the Labour Code protects the rights of workers in the employment relationship. Pursuant Article 8. point r) part-time and fixed term employment are protected characteristic, consequently part time workers and workers having a fixed term employment contract enjoy protection under the ETA Act irrespective of their nationality. Moreover, the temporary worker status has been by the decisions of the Equal Treatment Authority as a protected characteristic as well. As compared with the ETA, the Labour Code focuses on labour rights and on determining the equal value of work from the prospective of the principle on equal pay for equal work. This is valid irrespective of the nationality of the worker.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act III of 1993 on Social Benefits, Section 3, which states that "The scope of this Act shall, with the exceptions provided for in paragraphs (2) to (3), extend to the following persons living in Hungary: a) Hungarian citizens, b) immigrants and settled persons, c) stateless persons, d) persons recognised as refugees or persons granted protection by the Hungarian authorities." 2) Act LXXXI of 1997 on Social Security Pensions, Article 5/B, which reinforces that insured persons are only those entitled to old-age pensions. Irregular migrants have even more limited rights, access only to emergency-type healthcare. Migrants with a valid work permit qualify as insured persons as a main rule (if they are posted workers from another country to Hungary, they can remain under the competence of the sending state and then they are not part of the Hungarian social security system). Migrants who are insured persons are entitled to the full range of publicly funded(compulsory) healthcare services and invalidity benefits on the footing of equal treatment.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country nationals. 2) Act IV of 1991 on the Promotion of Employment and Unemployment Benefits. Although the law does not distinguish between foreign and national jobseekers, the conditions for applying for unemployment benefit rules cannot be met by a third-country national who is employed on the basis of a work permit. Firstly, the permit issued is for a specific job, so that when it is terminated, the permit expires. On the other hand, registration with the public employment service, daily cooperation, knowledge of Hungarian and 360 days of previous employment (paid within the previous 3 years, as the benefit is contributory-based) are required to be able to claim unemployment benefits. The situation is different for European Union (EU) citizens, because they could have completed the previous employment (contribution) in any other European Economic Area/EU state, and also for third country nationals living in Hungary who have resided as immigration permit holders or recognized refugees, because they retain their right of residence despite temporary unemployment.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act II of 2007 on Entry and Residence of Third-country Nationals. 2) Article 16 of Act I of 2007 on Union Citizens. Those who lawfully reside within the territory of Hungary for 3 or 5 years (depending upon their circumstances and relation to Hungary) can obtain permanent residence. In case of union citizens this is automatically granted (except in cases of being a threat to the public order etc.), in case of third-country nationals, the procedure is dependent upon the status of the third country national, the title of his/her residence, and there is a certain margin of discretion for the state to reject the application. Usually, Hungarian origin or being a family member of a Hungarian national shortens the waiting period. Additionally, under the provisions of the law, the work and residence permits may be granted consecutively, but there is no automatic conversion to another legal status. However, the migrant worker may apply for a long-term(open-ended) residence permit during the validity of his/her residence permit, if his/her housing and subsistence are stably secured and there are no public order or public security grounds against him/her

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country nationals, Article 29-30, 48(2). 2) Act I of 2007 on Union Citizens, Article 48/A. It is prohibited for an employer or employment intermediary to take or withhold an employee's documents or passport, as this constitutes forced labour and, from 1 July 2020, a criminal offence of trafficking in human beings. Only officials designated by law are entitled to confiscate the identity documents of migrants and only under specific circumstances and with specific purpose.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act II of 2007, Articles 33, 74, 94, and 157. Article 33 states that, “(3) If a child of a third-country national is born on the territory of Hungary to a third-country national who is a settled or immigrated third-country national, then, after the birth has been notified, the child shall be issued with a) a temporary settlement permit in the case of a parent with a temporary settlement permit holder; b) a national settlement permit in the case of a parent with a permanent/national settlement permit or an EC settlement permit.” Article 74 states that, “If a third-country national holding a visa for intended stay not exceeding ninety days, a visa for stay exceeding ninety days within one hundred and eighty days, a residence permit or a permanent residence/immigration permit holder gives birth to a child of a third-country national on the territory of Hungary, he/she shall notify the fact of the birth...” Article 157 states that, “The birth of a child of a third-country national shall be notified to the regional directorate competent for the place of residence or accommodation of the parent, by presenting the birth certificate of the child, on the form specified in a separate act, within three months of the birth of the child.” 2) Act I of 2010 on the Birth Registration Procedure, Article 61 which states that, “The birth shall, with the exception provided for in paragraph (3), be registered with the competent registrar of births not later than the first working day following the birth.”

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right in 1) Act I of 2007 on Union Citizens. 2) Act II of 2007, Articles 2, 7/A, 16, 53, 67, 71, 74, 74, and 88. 3) Government Decree 445/2013.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act II of 2007, Article 75, which states that, “(1) A third-country national shall report the loss, theft or destruction of his/her travel document and residence permit to the aliens' registration authority without delay…(2) Upon notification of a travel document believed to have been lost and of its discovery, the alien policing authority shall be notified without delay. (4) The third-country national shall be obliged to obtain a new travel document to replace the lost, stolen, destroyed or expired travel document, unless otherwise provided for in an international agreement.” 2) The Criminal Code, Article 346 which states that, “(1) Any person who - as regards any authentic instrument which does not belong to him or which is not exclusively his own: a) unlawfully acquires such authentic instrument from another person, without the consent of such person; b) unlawfully destroys or damages such authentic instrument; c) unlawfully commandeers or conceals such authentic instrument from its rightful holder; is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment not exceeding two years.”

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) the Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country nationals, which states: “[60. § (1) The third-country national in alien policing detention shall be informed of his/her rights and obligations in his/her mother tongue or in another language known to him/her. (2) The authority ordering detention shall, at the request of the third-country national or if a bilateral consular agreement makes this mandatory, notify the body responsible for the third country national's consular or diplomatic representation in Hungary directly and without delay of the detention or the obligation to stay in the designated place or the extension of the period of detention.” 2) Act XC of 2017 on Criminal Procedure. Relevant articles of this act include, Article 39, which states that, “§ (2) A suspected person in detention shall have the right to a) know the reason for his detention and any changes thereto, b) be informed of his detention by a person of his choice by the court, the prosecution and the investigating authority, c) contact his defence counsel and, if he is a foreign national, the consular representative of his State, and communicate with him in person, by post or by electronic means without any checks, (d) communicate with the person of his or her choice, before the charge is brought, before the public prosecutor's office, and thereafter by order of the court, in person and under supervision, and by post or electronic means, without control; (e) communicate with the person or authority specified in an international treaty promulgated by law, as specified in the international treaty.” Article 45, which states that, “§ (1) The person suspected/accused of having committed a criminal offence, his/her legal representative or a relative of the age of majority, or, in the case of a foreign national, the consular officer of his/her country of origin, may also authorise a lawyer to act as his/her defence.” Article 59, which states that, “§ (1) In order to represent or protect the rights and legitimate interests of the suspected/accused, the victim, the person interested in property and other interested persons under this Act, and to facilitate the exercise of rights or the performance of obligations under this Act, the following may participate in criminal proceedings as assistants: (a) the legal representative, the guardian ad litem, (b) the adult relative of the suspected/accused, (c) in the case of a foreign national accused/accused, victim and witness, the consular officer.” Article 383, which states that, “§ (4) At the request of the foreign national accused or suspected of having committed a criminal offence, their defence lawyer, or a foreign national victim or witness, a consular officer of his/her State may be present at the interrogation and other procedural acts in which he/she is involved.” Article 427, which states that, “§ (4) The foreign national suspected/accused, his/her defence lawyer or a foreign national victim or witness may, at the request of the foreign national, be present at the trial and the hearing by a consular officer of his/her State. Finally, Article 768, which states that, “§ (5) A consular officer of his/her State may also be present at the personal interview of the foreign national against whom the case has been brought.”

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Pursuant to Article 56 (2)-(3) of Act II of 2017 on Third Country Nationals, the detention of a third-country national who is a minor may not be ordered, but there are exceptions. Families with minors shall only be detained as a measure of last resort and for not more than thirty days where the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration, if the immigration authority is of the opinion that the objective of detention cannot be ensured by the confiscation of travel documents.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Immigration detention and detention preparatory to expulsion is regulated by Act II of 2017 on TCNS (Articles 54-56) while the asylum detention is laid down in Article 31/A. of Act LXXX of 2007 on the right to asylum. Detention is ordered by the immigration enforcement authority. Based on the currently effective legislation three types of detention can be ordered in Hungary: 1. Immigration detention, 2. Detention preparatory to expulsion, 3. Asylum detention. In its judgment of 17 December 2020 (Case C-808/18, Commission v Hungary), the Court of Justice of the European Union found that Hungary's legislation on the rules and practice in the transit zones situated at the Serbian-Hungarian border (Tompa and R?szke) was contrary to EU law. In particular, the Court identified breaches of provisions of the Asylum Procedures Directive (Directive 2013/32/EU), the Reception Conditions Directive (Directive 2013/33/EU) and the Return Directive (Directive 2008/115/EC).

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country nationals, Article 57 states that, “(1) The third-country national may not request the suspension of the detention procedure. (2) There is no right of appeal against the decision to detain. (3) A third-country national in detention may lodge an objection if the alien policing authority has failed to fulfil its obligations under § 60-61.(i.e. against the conditons in detention but not against the legal basis of detention) (4) The objection shall be examined by the local court competent for the place where the detention is carried out. (5) The court decides that the omitted measure must be made good or the offending situation must be remedied. (6) The court shall decide on the objection within eight days.”

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act II of 2007 54-56 on entry and residence of third-country nationals. Article 54 provides the criteria for detention; Article 55 provides the criteria for pre-deportation detention; and Article 56 provides stipulations and regulations about when detention is not admissable. 2) Act I of 2007, Article 40. 3) The Constitution of Hungary (2011) [Article IV (2), which states that, "No one shall be deprived of his liberty except for reasons and in accordance with procedures which shall be determined by law."

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) the Constitution (2011): Article II: Human dignity is inviolable, and every human being has the right to life and dignity, and Article III(1): which prohibits torture, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and holding individuals in servitude. Also prohibits trafficking in human beings. 2) Act CXLIII of 2011: promulgates the Optional Protocol to the Convention Against Torture, empowering the government to designate a body to liaise with the Committee against Torture. The national preventive mechanism, headed by the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights (Ombudsman), conducts regular visits to detention facilities to examine treatment and prevent torture or ill-treatment. 3) Act XXXIV of 1994 on the Police: Sets guidelines for police conduct, emphasizing the protection of human dignity and safeguarding human rights. Coercive measures may only be used within the boundaries of the law and with respect to the principle of proportionality. Police officers are prohibited from using torture, coercive, cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment and are required to take action against such conduct. 4) The Penal Code (Act C of 2012) also criminalizes assault, coercion, and unlawful detention in official proceedings. 5) Act CXI of 2011 on the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights (Ombudsman) grants the Commissioner the competence to investigate complaints against the police, ensuring accountability and examining potential fundamental rights infringements.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Act XXXIV of 1994 on the Police, which outlines the responsibilities of the police, including controlling border traffic, combating terrorism, crime prevention and detection, and immigration and asylum control. It also authorizes the use of physical force, coercive measures, and detention by the police, and specifies the conditions and reporting requirements for the use of coercive means.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Constitution (2011), Articles II and II. Article emphasizes the inviolability of human dignity and the right to life and dignity. Article III prohibits torture, inhuman or degrading treatment, punishment, and human trafficking. 2) The Act XXXIV of 1994 on the Police: Use of firearms, Sections 52(1), 54, 55. Section 52(1) establishes that the use of firearms by a police officer is allowed only in cases of legitimate defense and necessity. Section 54 specifies various situations where a police officer is entitled to use a firearm, such as preventing direct threats or attacks on life, preventing acts of terrorism, or preventing armed attacks on vital establishments or against the police. Section 55 prohibits the use of firearms, except in cases of armed attack, armed resistance, or when firing at an object or animal can achieve the purpose of police action. 3) Minister of the Interior Decree No. 30/2011 on Police Service Regulations: Use of firearms, Sections 47, 48, 49, 57, 94. Section 47 specifies the guidelines for firing a firearm, including directing shots at limbs whenever possible and limiting the discharge of firearms near state borders or against persons on border roads. Section 48 explains the conditions for firing a warning shot and shooting at objects or animals to eliminate a direct threat. Section 49 outlines the obligations of the police officer after using a firearm, such as providing first aid to the injured person, reporting the incident, and conducting an investigation into the legality and professionalism of the firearm's use. Similarly, Section 57 addresses the use of firearms against individuals in a crowd, stating that it is only permitted if the conditions for using firearms against individuals are met. Section 94 allows police officers who have passed an examination on weapon use to carry a weapon if their duty assignment justifies it.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right, in Act II of 2007 on the entry and residence of third-country nationals. This act states that, “[29. §(1) a humanitarian residence permit may be granted to a victim of trafficking in human beings if e) on the basis of a proposal of a court, the prosecution or the law enforcement and national security authorities, as well as the investigating authority of the National Tax and Customs Administration, a third-country national or, in respect of him or her, another third-country national who cooperates with the authorities in the investigation of a criminal offence in a manner that significantly facilitates the provision of evidence; f) on the application of a court, a third country national who has been employed under particularly exploitative employment conditions or a minor third-country national who has been employed without a valid residence permit or other authorisation entitling him/her to stay.”

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Hungary protects this right in the Constitution of Hungary states that "no one shall be deprived of Hungarian nationality acquired by descent or lawfully acquired." Subsequent acts, such as Act LV of 1993 on Hungarian Citizenship states that "(1) Hungarian citizenship may be withdrawn from a person who has obtained Hungarian citizenship by violating the law, in particular by providing false information or by concealing information or facts by misleading the authorities. No revocation is possible after 20 years from the date of acquisition of Hungarian citizenship...The President of the Republic shall decide on the termination of Hungarian citizenship by withdrawal, on the basis of a proposal by the Minister." For context, the President of the Republic decided to withdraw the Hungarian citizenship of 450 people until February 2022. The affected persons acquired Hungarian citizenship almost exclusively through simplified naturalization (beneficial naturalisation).

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Hungary protects this right in Act LV of 1993 on Hungarian Citizenship, Article 4. Though, there is no special scheme for economic migrants, Article 4 stipulates the criteria for all migrants who apply for naturalization, which include residency, a clean criminal record, and accommodation and financial requirements.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: The National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) Act LV of 1993 on Hungarian Citizenship, Articles 4, 23. In principal, any migrant can attain Hungarian citizenship if they meet the following requirements, as outlined in Article 4, which states, "upon application, a non-Hungarian citizen maybe naturalised if: a) he/she has resided continuously in Hungary for eight years prior to the submission of the application; b) he/she has no criminal record under Hungarian law and noncriminal proceedings are pending against him/her before a Hungarian court at the time of the assessment of the application; c) his/her livelihood and residence are secured in Hungary; d)his/her naturalization will not harm public security and national security in Hungary; e) he/she can prove that he/she has passed a basic constitutional knowledge examination in Hungarian or is exempted from this requirement by law." This includes refugees and other migrants; according to Article 23, "for the purposes of this Act, a non-Hungarian citizen who is a) an immigrant or a person with settled status, b) a refugee or a subsidiary protected person, and c) a person who exercises his or her right to free movement and residence in Hungary as defined in the Act on the Entry and Residence of Persons with the Right of Free Movement and Residence and has fulfilled his or her obligation to register shall be deemed to reside in Hungary as of the date of the application for residence."

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: The National Law in Hungary protects this right in Act LV of 1993 on Hungarian Citizenship, Article 4. Article 4(2) states that, "A non-Hungarian citizen who has resided continuously in Hungary for three years prior to the submission of his/her application and who meets the conditions set out in points b) to e) of paragraph (1) maybe naturalised on preferential terms if a) he/she has been living in a valid marriage with a Hungarian citizen for at least three years or the marriage has ended with the death of the spouse, b) his/her minor child is a Hungarian citizen, c) was adopted by a Hungarian citizen and is of age, d) has been recognised as a refugee by a Hungarian authority, or e) is stateless. (2a) If the conditions set out in points b) and d) of paragraph (1) are met, a minor who is not a Hungarian citizen and who has been adopted by a Hungarian citizen may be naturalised on preferential terms upon application." Article 4(3) also gives preferential treatment to some family members, as well; according to Article 4(3), "(3a) Upon application, a non-Hungarian citizen may be granted preferential naturalisation if a) he/she has been living for at least aa) ten years in a valid marriage with a person who was a Hungarian citizen at the time of submitting the citizenship application, or ab) five years in a valid marriage with a person who was a Hungarian citizen at the time of submitting the citizenship application and they have a child together, b)he/she meets the conditions set out in points b) and d) of paragraph (1), and c) he/she can prove his/her knowledge of Hungarian."

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in Article 2 of Act LV of 1993 on Hungarian Citizenship, which states that, "A Hungarian citizen who is also a citizen of another state shall be considered a Hungarian citizen for the purposes of Hungarian law, unless otherwise provided by law." The conditions on naturalisation do not mention termination of prior/actual citizenship. Since 1993, Hungarian law has consistently tolerated multiple citizenship in the naturalisation process (there is no requirement to renounce prior citizenship), thus preserving the applicant’s original citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) the Constitution of Hungary, Article VII, which "recognizes the right to freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, including the freedom to choose or change one's religion or beliefs, and the freedom to manifest or refrain from manifesting, practicing, or teaching them in public or private." Article VII also "allows persons of the same faith to establish a religious community for practicing their religion according to an organizational form determined by a cardinal law." Article VII states that "common rules for religious communities, conditions for cooperation, established churches, and detailed regulations shall be determined by a cardinal law (requiring a qualified majority for passage)." 2) Act CCVI of 2011 on the Right to Freedom of Conscience and Religion and on the Legal Status of Churches, Religious Associations and Religious Communities "(1) establishes freedom of conscience and religion as a fundamental right for everyone, not tied to any legal form," and "(3) prohibits subjecting anyone to advantages or disadvantages based on their conscientious or religious beliefs or modifications or practices thereof."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) the Constitution of Hungary, Article IX, which states that, "Everyone shall have the right to freedom of expression. (2)Hungary recognises and protects the freedom and diversity of the press, and ensures the conditions for the free provision of information necessary for the development of democratic public opinion. (3) In order to provide the information necessary for the development of democratic public opinion during the election campaign period, political advertising may be published in media services only without remuneration and under the conditions laid down in the cardinal law ensuring equal opportunities."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in the Constitution of Hungary, Article IX, which states that, "Everyone shall have the right to freedom of expression. (2)Hungary recognises and protects the freedom and diversity of the press, and ensures the conditions for the free provision of information necessary for the development of democratic public opinion. (3) In order to provide the information necessary for the development of democratic public opinion during the election campaign period, political advertising may be published in media services only without remuneration and under the conditions laid down in the cardinal law ensuring equal opportunities."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) the Constitution of Hungary, Article VIII, which states that, "(1) Everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly. (2)Everyone has the right to form and join associations. (3) Political parties may freely form and operate under the right of association. Parties shall contribute to the formation and expression of the will of the people. (4) The detailed rules for the operation and management of political parties shall be laid down in a cardinal law.(5) Trade unions and other interest-representing organisations may be formed and operate freely on the basis of the right of association." 2) Act CLXXV on hte Right of Association, Public Utility Status, and the Functioning and Support of Non-Governmental Organizations, which states, "(1) The right of association is a fundamental freedom right for everyone, based on which everyone has the right to create or join organizations and communities with others." The right of freedom of association is not confined to Hungarian citizens, it includes third-country nationals, as well. There are EU norms (e.g. Directive 2003/109/EC or 2011/98/EU) which contain references to the right of third-country nationals to freedom of association, including trade unions, which is properly implemented by Hungarian Law.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Act II 2007, family reunification is not possible in the absence of adequate financial resources and this support is not provided by the state.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Hungary protects this right in Act XC of 2017, Articles 50, 51, and 376. Article 51(2) states that, “the victim shall have the right to declare at any time what physical or mental injury or damage to property he or she has suffered as a result of the offence, and whether he or she wishes to have the accused found guilty and punished.” Additionally, Article 376 states that any person may file a crime report regarding a criminal offence subject to public prosecution.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, victims of trafficking can be provided immigration status in certain circumstances, in accordance with Directive 2011/36/EC on Preventing and Combating Trafficking in Human Beings and Protecting its Victims, and its implementation in Hungarian law.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National Law in Hungary protects this right in 1) The Child Protection Act (Act XXXI of 1997, § 3 (2)), which provides for equal treatment in child protection. Provisional measures can be taken by the guardianship authority in the absence of competence and jurisdiction (§ 4 (3)). General rules of procedure under the Act apply in the absence of an international convention (§ 4 (4)). The concept of unaccompanied minor and special rules: Act II of 2007, § 2(e) and (t) define "unaccompanied minor" and "persons requiring special treatment." 2) Various sections (§ 19(2), § 24(1), § 29(1), § 35(1)e, § 37(2)b, § 45(5), § 56(2)-(3), § 61(2)-(3)i.- j., 62.§(1)b-c, 86/J.§(3), 86/R.§(2)-(3), 99/A.§(1)e-f, 108/A.§(2)g) of the Act II of 2007 outline specific rules related to the protection of unaccompanied minors. 3) The Hungarian Constitution contains provisions (Articles XV (5), XVI (1)-(2)-(3), XVIII, XXIX (2)) related to the protection of children, protection of the family, and prohibition of child labour. 4) The Act XXXI of 1997 on the Protection of Children. 5) The Misdemeanour Act. 6) The Criminal Code. 7) Directive (EU) 2011/36 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and Directive on the protection of victims, provide protection and support for victims of trafficking. However, there are some exceptions, such as: Health care financed by social insurance or the state budget is subject to certain legal statuses, excluding emergency, life-saving care (43/1999, March 3 Government Decree, Health Care Act, § 3 s.). Attendance of public education free of charge is based on a residence permit of at least three months or a specific legal status (Act CXC of 2011 on Public Education, § 92).

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, there are some exceptions that give special treatment to pregnant women, or nursing mothers in the Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country nationals (TCNs) [§ 2.t.a pregnant woman requiring special treatment] provides exceptions taking into account the vulnerability of pregnant women. Act CXXXV of 2005 on Assistance to Victims of Crime and State Compensation [§ 1 (1) e. victim] ensures support and shelter for victims of trafficking in human beings, including migrant women who have suffered harm as a direct consequence of such acts. 114/2007 of 24 May Government Decree for the application of Act II of 2007 [§ 71/A] grants additional benefits to pregnant women or nursing mothers. According to Article XV (5) of the Fundamental Law, Hungary is committed to protecting families, children, women, the elderly, and individuals living with disabilities through separate measures. Article 2 (t) of Act II of 2007 on TCNs defines persons requiring special treatment, including vulnerable individuals such as minors, the elderly, disabled persons, pregnant women, single parents raising minor children, and those who have suffered torture or serious forms of physical, psychological, or sexual violence. Article 61 of Act II of 2007 on TCNs specifies that men and women placed under detention should be housed in separate quarters, and families with minors should be provided with separate accommodation to ensure privacy.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, Act II of 2007 on entry and residence of third-country nationals [§ 2.t.a person with a disability requiring special treatment] includes exceptions that take into consideration the needs of individuals with disabilities. Additionally, 114/2007 of 24 May Government Decree for the application of Act II of 2007 [§113 (2)] ensures a careful setting of a time limit for voluntary departure for all persons requiring special treatment, including migrants with disabilities. Also, according to Article XV (5) of the Fundamental Law, Hungary is committed to protecting families, children, women, the elderly, and individuals living with disabilities through separate measures. Article 2 (t) of Act II of 2017 on TCNs defines persons requiring special treatment, which includes individuals with disabilities who, after an individual assessment of their situation, can be determined to have special needs. Finally, Article 82 of the Code on Criminal Procedure recognizes disabled persons as defined by the Act on the rights of and ensuring equal opportunities for disabled persons, as well as persons who might qualify as such persons, as individuals requiring special treatment.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Binod Khadria. [2]: Shikha Silliman Bhattacharjee

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: India

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 19(1)(b)pf the Constitution of India protects the right to assemble peaceably and without arms. However, the fundamental rights under Article 19 apply only to citizens of India.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Only citizens may vote under the Constitution of India, Article 326.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in Article 14 of the Constitution of India, which states that: "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. Legal aid to the accused can be allowed only under certain cases in the Criminal Procedure Code, Clause no. 304. These exceptions are not specifically aimed migrant, but the deprived sections of the population.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Criminal Procedure Code, Clause no. 277-82, 333, which mandates that the state must provide an interpretor for interpretation of any evidence or statement.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in India enforces authorised entry through the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920, Clause 4(1),4(2): Power to arrest, and Foreigners Act, 1946, No. 31 of 1946, Article 3(2)(g). According to these provisions, any unauthorized entry can lead to to civil or criminal sanctions.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Central Government and various Indian States have enacted several schemes ensuring adequate housing for low and middle income strata of the populations, such as the National Urban Housing & Habitat Policy, the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal and the Indira Aawas Yojana. However, access to public housing does not extend to migrants.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right for only regular migrants in the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009, which provides for free and compulsory elementary education of equitable quality to all children of 6-14 years age. This right does not apply to irregular migrants.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. India is neither party to the 1951 Convention on Refugees nor the 1967 Protocol. The lack of specific refugee legislation in India has led the government to adopt an ad hoc approach to different refugee influxes. The status of refugees in India is governed mainly by political and administrative decisions, rather than any codified model of conduct.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no ban on refoulement. India is neither party to the 1951 Convention on Refugees nor the 1967 Protocol. The lack of specific refugee legislation in India has led the government to adopt an ad hoc approach to different refugee influxes. The status of refugees in India is governed mainly by political and administrative decisions, rather than any codified model of conduct.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no ban on refoulement, but in practice such protection is de facto provided under the "Right to Life" provided by the Constitution of India. India is neither party to the 1951 Convention on Refugees nor the 1967 Protocol. The lack of specific refugee legislation in India has led the government to adopt an ad hoc approach to different refugee influxes. The status of refugees in India is governed mainly by political and administrative decisions, rather than any codified model of conduct. In a decision by the Supreme Court of India on 8 April 2021 in Mohammad Salimullah and Anr v. Union of India and Ors., the court refused to grant interim relief in a petition seeking the temporary release of Rohingya refugees from detention in the State of Jammu and Kashmir and their pending deportation from India to Myanmar. In this judgment, the Supreme Court clarifies that India is not a signatory to the United Nations 1951 Refugee Convention and Protocol, indicating that this is sufficient for the non-compliance of the non-refoulement policy.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no obligation under Foreigners Act, 1946.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Foreigners Act, 1946 has no protections against expulsion on the grounds that a migrant is likely to be subjected to refoulement through a subsequent expulsion. India is neither party to the 1951 Convention on Refugees nor the 1967 Protocol. The lack of specific refugee legislation in India has led the government to adopt an ad hoc approach to different refugee influxes. The status of refugees in India is governed mainly by political and administrative decisions, rather than any codified model of conduct.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in India allows the Central Government to order the departure of an individual or group of foreigners in the Foreigners Act, 1946, Article 3(2)(C). In practice, these determinations are justified by facts relevant to the individual concerned and pursuant to the powers granted to the state. This is not formally required in all cases.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is a specific law for the expulsion of immigrants from Assam, i.e., The Immigrants (Expulsion from Assam) Act, 1950. However, there is no national law providing migrants with an opportunity to submit the reasons against expulsion and to have their case reviewed by the competent authority before being expelled.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Under the Passport Rules 1980, a "Certiicate of Identity" can be issues to a stateless person in India, who would be allowed to continue to stay in the country. However, there are no pathways for them to become citizens.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in India conditionally protects this right in 1) The Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920. 2) The Foreigners Act, 1946. 3) The Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. India has yet to recognize same sex marriage, though, this is an evolving issue. However, in 2011, a Haryana State court granted legal recognition to a same-sex marriage, involving two women. In 2018, the Supreme Court of India repealed Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, decriminalizing homosexuality.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: There is no established official procedures for foreign nationals of non-Indian descent to acquire Indian citizenship or permanent residence. India bestows citizenship in exceptional circumstances, subject to meticulous individual evaluations. The sole avenue for a foreigner to attain permanent residency in India is through investment-based pathways or thtrough naturalization to citizenship.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Irregular migrants are excluded from both registration and acquisition of citizenship through birth, registration, or naturalization, however, the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, No. 47 of 2019, provides a pathway to regularization for any migrant belonging to the Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi or Christian communities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh or Pakistan, and who were present in India on or before December 31st, 2014.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in 1) the Indian Contract Act, 1872. 2) Article 14 of the Constitution of India, which prevents the State from denying to any person the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. Under Indian law, there are no formal legal requirements as to the form and content of employment agreements and general rules governing contracts as laid in the Indian Contract Act 1872 are applicable to breaches or violations of any employment agreement. 3) Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Nirmal Kumar Gupta in the Court of Additional District Judge - 07, (Central District) TIS Hazari Courts, Delhi, 214/2016, 618236/2016. The plaintiff company was engaged in the business of providing satellite communication and broadcasting services including teleport services for TV Channels and OB Vans. The defendant was recruited as Engineer (Operation & Customer Support) vide appointment letter dated 01.07.2009 by accepting the terms and conditions of the Contract which restrained him from seeking alternative employment (as is the case with most migrant contract workers) for two years after leaving the job by giving one month's notice. The dendent resigned from the plaintiff company in 2014, and joined a competitor company. The plaintiff filed the case for compensation and restraint on the defendant. The defendant submitted that clauses no. 7 and 8(i) of the appointment letter dated 01.07.2009 violated Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, arguing that the said clauses were against the public policy and the same amounted to restrain of trade against the defendant and therefore, the same were void in terms of Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. The Court decided, in 2020, in favour of the defendant and against the plaintiff. Accordingly, the suit of the plaintiff was found not maintainable and hit by Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and was dismissed.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Constitution of India, Article 21, as interpreted in Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (AIR 1984 SC 802). Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees protection of life and personal liberty to all persons. In Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (AIR 1984 SC 802), the Supreme Court has held that the right to live with human dignity, enshrined in Article 21, derives from the directive principles of state policy and therefore includes protection of health.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Only citizens over 18 years old may run for publiuc office under Constitution of India, Article 58, 66, 124, 217 and Representation of the People Act, 1951, Part I(2)(e).

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 15 of the Indian Constitution bans discrimination on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, but this protection is reserved to citizens.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Constitution of India, Article 14 - Right to equality before law and equal protection of laws; Article 20 - Right to protection in respect of conviction for offences; and Article 21 - Right to protection of life and personal liberty. The Citizenship Amendment Act 2019 protects people from religious discrimination.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. India's Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, does not address wage discrimination on the basis of migrant status and applies only to preventing gender based wage discrimination.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) regulations, "the applicant [migrant] is not permitted to change employer for the entire duration of the employment visa." However, the MHA has clarified that this excludes a change of employers from a registered holding company to its subsidiary or vice versa, or between subsidiaries of a registered holding company.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Each individual must apply separately,

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Employment visas are subject to annual renewal conditional on producing necessary documents in support of continued employment.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: Constitution of India, Article 14, Equality before law and equal protection of laws applies to both citizens and foreigners, making foreigners (migrant workers) in India eligible for equal protection under Indian labour laws. Furthermore, India is a signatory of the International Labor Organization's (ILO) Equal Remuneration Act, 1979, page 8, Hours of Work (Industry) Convention, 1919, No. 1, Forced Labour Convention, 1930, No. 16 and Prevention of Major Industrial Accidents, Convention No. 174, and international treaties have been incorporated into Indian domestic law by the Constitution of India, 1949, Article 51(c) which states that to: “foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another; and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration," and the decision of Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1997 SC 3011, which holds that “it is now an accepted rule of judicial construction that regard must be given to international conventions and norms for construing domestic law where there is no inconsistency between them and there is a void in the domestic law."

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Employees Provident Fund (EPF) (Third Amendment) Scheme, 2008. Every foreign worker employed with an establishment to whom the EPF applies must become a member of the provident fund (PF) from the first date of his/her employment. There is no minimum period of stay in India for activation of PF compliance. However, Public Sector Social Security Schemes are not applicable in cases of non-citizens.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in 1) Article 14 of the Constitution of India, which states that: "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India." 2) Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act has been interpreted by the judiciary to include indicators of bonded/forced labour, "Any factor which deprives a person of a choice of alternatives and compels him to adopt a particular course of action," in People's Union for Democratic Rights and Others vs Union of India and Others [1982 II LLJ 454 SC (1982) 3 SCC 235].

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in Section 4(1) of Citizenship Act, 1955, which states that the birth of migrant children is required to be registered with a Foreign Regional Registration Officer (FRRO).

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, a foreign citizen can get an Aadhaar Card (UID or Unique Identity number) according to the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939 , which is a government-issued document that serves as proof of identity and residence address in India, not work status. This is not mandatory, though. Foreign citizens, can apply for an Aadhaar Card if they are staying in India for a considerable period of time. Wok Permit or Work Visa is the document mandated by the government of India that recognises a foreigners work status in India.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in 1) Indian Penal Code (IPC). Passport and travel are property of Central Government. Destroying government property is a punishable offense under Section 425 of Indian Penal Code (IPC). 2) Clause 17, Passport Act, 1967. 3) Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, which has been widely interpreted by the judiciary to include indicators of bonded/forced labour, including withholding/destroying identity documents by employers. 3) The decision in Bandhua Mukti Morcha (People’s Union for Democratic Rights) v. Union of India, A.I.R. 1982, S.C. 1473 (19 September 1982), which provided interpretation of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition Act, 1976). The issue before the Supreme Court was whether the forced labour provision of Article 23 of the Indian Constitution was applicable to a situation of workers being paid less than the minimum wage. The decision states, ”In the ordinary course ...where he is required to supply forced labour for no wage or for nominal wage, unless he has received some advance or other economic consideration from the employer, and unless, under the pretext of not having returned such advance or other economic consideration, he is either required to render service to the employer (and his subsequent generations of successors), or is deprived of his freedom of employment or of the right to move freely wherever he wants." The Court realized that it would be extremely onerous if every labourer had to prove that he had received an advance or other economic consideration from his employer. The labourer was likely to be illiterate and to have no documentary evidence of such an advance, and the employer was likely to deny ever having made the advance.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Though India is a signatory of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (VCCR), and international treaties have been incorporated into Indian domestic law by the Constitution of India, 1949, Article 51(c) which states that to: “foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another; and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration," and the decision of Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1997 SC 3011, which holds that “it is now an accepted rule of judicial construction that regard must be given to international conventions and norms for construing domestic law where there is no inconsistency between them and there is a void in the domestic law," these do not provide specific instances where this right can be assumed to be protected in all instances. Additionally, while the Model Police Manual prepared by the Bureau of Police Research and Development, Ministry of Home Affairs, Rule 565 calls for prompt consular access, this is not a statute but policy, and not all states have adopted the Model Manual.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While the rights to all children are protected under the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC, Article 37, page 10), Foreigners Act, 1946, Act No. 31 of 1946, Article 3(2)(g) grants powers to the central government to arrest, detain or confine any foreigner.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Foreigners Act 1946, Article 3(2)(g), grants powers to the central government to arrest, detain or confine any foreigner.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this in Article 14 of the Constitution of India, which states that: "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India." India's legal framework allows for the appeal of any decision, which means that migrants would be able to appeal legality, conditions, or length of detention.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Provisions of a Foreigners Act, 1946, Act No. 31 of 1946, Article 3(1),3(2)(g) allows Central Government orders to apply with respect to all foreigners or with respect to any particular foreigner or any prescribed class or description of foreigner.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in 1) the International Labor Organization (ILO) conventions on Right to Decent Work, arising from Forced Labour Conventions, 1930 and Abolition of Forced Labour Convention, 1957. 2) Article 21 of the Constitution of India, read with Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India. Article 21 extends equal protection of the law to both citizens and non-citizens. Maneka Gandhi interprets Article 21 of the Constitution of India to include not only the right to life, but the right to live with human dignity. This suggests prohibition of torture and cruel, inhumane, and degrading treatment. 3) United Nations Convention Against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman and Degrading Treatment or Punishment, read with Constitution of India, 1949, Article 51(c). International treaties have been incorporated into Indian domestic law in the Constitution of India, 1949, Article 51(c) which states that to: “foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another; and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration." Additionally, the decision of Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1997 SC 3011, holds that “it is now an accepted rule of judicial construction that regard must be given to international conventions and norms for construing domestic law where there is no inconsistency between them and there is a void in the domestic law."

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The application of force is allowed under the Border Security Force (BSF) Act 1968 and Rules 1969.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.
