Althought Article 21 of Constitution of India provides that: “No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to a procedure established by law," The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA), Article 4(a)1958, provides that lethal force may be used by security forces even in circumstances where they face no imminent risk of harm in designated "disturbed areas."

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Protocol against the Smuggling of Migrants by Land, Sea, and Air, Article 5, which establishes that migrants shall not become liable to criminal prosecution under this protocol for the fact of having been the object of smuggling. India ratified the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (UNTOC) and its three supporting protocols in May 2011. International treaties have been incorporated into Indian domestic law in the Constitution of India, 1949, Article 51(c), which states that to: “foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another; and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration." Additionally, the decision of Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1997 SC 3011, holds that “it is now an accepted rule of judicial construction that regard must be given to international conventions and norms for construing domestic law where there is no inconsistency between them and there is a void in the domestic law."

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in Citizenship Act, 1955, Sections 5(1)(a) and 10(1), (2)(d). Citizens who are naturalized, or registered under Section(5)(1)(a)(persons of Indian origin), can be deprived of citizenship by Central Government under Section 10(2(d) order if (d) that citizen has, within five years after registration or naturalisation, been sentenced in any country to imprisonment for a term of not less than two years.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Citizenship Act, 1955, Clause 5 and 6, and Schedule III. Economic migrants have pathways to citizenship through Registration (Clause 5) and Naturalization (Clause 6). Residency requirements, under Schedule III(d) sets out a residence requirement of 12 years within the last 15 years; however, this residency requirement can be waived under special circumstances specified in Schedule III (c) and the proviso at the conclusion of Schedule III.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Citizenship Act, 1955, Clause 5 and 6. Recently, the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) 2019 has provided a pathway for religiously persecuted non-Muslim undocumented migrants from neighbouring countries.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Citizenship Act, 1955, Clause 5 and 6. Citizenship Act Amendment (CAA) 2019 benefits are extended to family migtants.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in Article 25(1) of the Indian Constitution, which protects freedom of conscience, and the right freely to profess, practice, and propagate religion. This applies to all persons, and therefore includes citizens and foreigners.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Fundamental rights under Constitution of India, Article 19(1)(a) protect freedom of speech and expression, and includes the right to voice an opinion, seek information and ideas, and receive and impart information. However, the fundamental rights under Article 19 apply only to citizens of India.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Fundamental rights under Constitution of India, Article 19(1)(a) protect freedom of speech and expression, and includes the right to voice an opinion, seek information and ideas, and receive and impart information. However, the fundamental rights under Article 19 apply only to citizens of India.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution of India protects the right to form associations or unions. However, the fundamental rights under Article 19 apply only to citizens of India.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution, which protects the fundamental right to equality before law and equal protection of laws, and applies to both citizens and foreigners in India. Article 14 states: “The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.”

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Under the Foreigners Act, 1946 a petition can be filed for an expedited trial, and the victim can receive temporary relief from expulsion and be required to remain in country or to return to India to testify at trial. However, this right to remain in country to testify does not amount to an avenue to immigration status or long term relief from expulsion, except for those granted citizenship under the Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in the Convention on the Rights of the Child, 1989, Article 20 (1), which states that, "A child temporarily or permanently deprived of his or her family environment, or in whose own best interests cannot be allowed to remain in that environment, shall be entitled to special protection and assistance provided by the State." International treaties have been incorporated into Indian domestic law in the Constitution of India, 1949, Article 51(c) states that: “foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another; and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration." Additionally, the decision of Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1997 SC 3011, holds that “it is now an accepted rule of judicial construction that regard must be given to international conventions and norms for construing domestic law where there is no inconsistency between them and there is a void in the domestic law."

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in 1) National Commission for Women Act, 1990. The Commission has the right to review, from time to time, the existing provisions of the Constitution and other laws affecting women and recommend amendments thereto so as to suggest remedial legislative measures to meet any lacunae, inadequacies or shortcomings in such legislations. 2) The Indian Penal Code, Sections 366, 366A, 366B, 367, 370, 371, 372, 373, 374. includes a number of offenses that can be used to address trafficking, including kidnapping, abducting or inducing a woman to compel marriage (section 366), procuring a minor girl, importing a girl below 21 for sexual exploitation, kidnapping or abducting a person to grievous hurt, buying or disposing of a person as a slave (Section 367), habitually dealing in slaves (Section 371), selling minors for prostitution, or compelling forced labour (Section 372/373). The Indian Penal Code also includes other relevant offenses addressing the vulnerability of migrant women, including rape, sexual offenses, and outraging the modesty of a woman.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in India protects this right in 1) The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, which gave effect to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. 2) Protection for persons with disabilities is effectively upheld in that disability legislations takes precedence over administrative rules of the government, according to the decision in KritikaPurohit and Anr. v. State of Maharashtra and Ors.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Christopher Cason and [2]: Dodik Setiawan Nur Heriyanto

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Indonesia

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in the Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia, Article 28E; Law Number 39 of 1999 Concerning Human Rights, Article 24. Indonesia recognizes and protects the right to freedom of assembly of all people without exception, including migrants. This is a constitutional mandate which is the responsibility of Indonesia to protect the human rights of every person who is in Indonesian territory. However, in recent political situation post the presidential election 2019, the government tries to restrict this freedom. Based on the report of the Human Rights NGO, there were 1.056 cases of the freedom of assembly restriction.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 198 of Law Number 7 of 2017 Concerning General Elections states that only citizens of Indonesia can participate in elections.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in the 1945 Constitution [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/101646/uud-no--], 2nd Amendment, Article 28 D Paragraph 1; Law Number 48 of 2009 concerning Judiciary Power [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/38793/uu-no-48-tahun-2009] , article 4 paragraph (1); Law Number 6 Year 2012 concerning Ratification of the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39025], Article 7.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Immigration status decisions are considered administrative proceedings for which counsel is not guaranteed. Additionally, the Indonesian constitution does not specifically provide a right to counsel. Indonesian criminal procedural law (Law No. 8 on Criminal Procedure (UU8-1981) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/47041/uu-no-8-tahun-1981], Article 56(1)) only provides free counsel in death penalty cases and indigent defense for crimes punishable in excess of five years.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Translation services are provided by the courts, but there is no law mentioning whether these translation services will be paid for by the government. On the contrary, the burden of paying for these services is usually covered by the defendant. Article 177 of the Criminal Procedure Law (Law No. 8, 1981, on Criminal Procedure [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/47041/uu-no-8-tahun-1981] states: "If the defendant or witness does not understand Indonesian, the head judge at trial appoints an interpreter who swears or promises to translate everything that must be translated correctly." Likewise, Article 51 of the Criminal Procedure Law states, "The accused has the right to be clearly notified in a language he understands about what he is being charged with."

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: Unauthorized entry is considered as a criminal action. Law No. 6 on Immigration 2011 (UU6-2011) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011] expressly regulates criminal penalties for actions such as illegal entry, falsification of identity, providing false information to get a visa, and for detainees possessing firearms. The criminal penalties include imprisonment and fines, though, in practice, migrants are usually deported.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Government Regulation 103, 2015 (Peraturan 103-2015) on the Residential Home Ownership or Occupation by Foreigners Domiciled in Indonesia. 2) Executive Order No. 125, 2016 (Peraturan Presiden 125-2016), Article 24. For those with refugee status, Executive Order No. 125, 2016 (Peraturan Presiden 125-2016), requires that adequate shelter and other accommodations be provided by the agency in charge of a particular intake of refugees.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While the Constitution of Indonesia (UU1-1945), Amendment 3. Article 12 of Law No. 20 of 2003 Concerning the National Education System does not differentiate foreign nationals from becoming students in education systems, it does not guarantee access to free primary educational institution and services to migrant children commensurate with citizens.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law No. 20 on National Education, 2003 (UU20- 2003), which does not differentiate foreign nationals from becoming students in education units including higher education and equivalent institutions as long as they meet the admission requirements and regulations that are bound to them. 2) The Constitution of Indonesia (UU1-1945), Amendment 3. 3) The Job Creation Act of 2021. National law does not otherwise discriminate based on status, but adult education is not provided by the state under the National Law on Education or the Constitution. Only basic education is guaranteed to citizens, and is thus guaranteed to migrants.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Articles 52, 62 and 75 of Law Number 6 of 2011 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011]. 2) Article 159 paragraph (1) and (2) (c) of Government Regulation Number 31 of 2013 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/5363/pp-no-31-tahun-2013] as incorporate into Government Regulation Number 48 of 2021 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/161984/pp-no-48-tahun-2021]. All crimes which are punishable for more than 5 years, and crimes relating to drug possession can lead to loss of residence status.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Indonesia is not a party of the Refugee Convention 1951. To resolve refugee issues, Indonesia enacted Executive Order No. 125 of 2016 Concerning the Handling of Refugees from Abroad [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/41029/perpres-no-125-tahun-2016]. However, the non-refoulement principle is not mentioned in this law.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Indonesia is not a party of the Refugee Convention 1951. To resolve refugee issues, Indonesia enacted Executive Order No. 125 of 2016 Concerning the Handling of Refugees from Abroad [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/41029/perpres-no-125-tahun-2016], and there is no provision about non-refoulement principles included in the order.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Executive Order No. 125, 2016 (Peraturan Presiden 125-2016) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/41029/perpres-no-125-tahun-2016] provides no ban on refoulment on the basis of risk of serious deprivations of fundamental human rights.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Directorate General on Immigration Regulation No. IMI-0352.GR.02.07 on Handling of Illegal Immigrants Declaring as Asylum Seekers or Refugees [https://www.refworld.org/legal/legislation/natlegbod/2016/en/115630] makes no provision for advising or counseling other than to tell asylum seekers that they have access to legal counsel for the purpose of filing the necessary application for asylum.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Executive Order No. 125, 2016 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/41029/perpres-no-125-tahun-2016] (Peraturan Presiden 125-2016), Articles 37-39, 75, 78, 83, 85. 2) Law Number 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011] Articles 1, 208 209, 214, 236. 3) Government Regulation Number 31 of 2013 Concerning Implementing Regulations of Law Number 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/5363/pp-no-31-tahun-2013]. The existing law does not use the term expulsion but uses the term deportation. Deportation in Indonesia can only be imposed on migrants who are subject to detention; have been detained for 10 years; carry out activities and are suspected to be endangering security and public order or not obeying the laws and regulations; entered Indonesia to avoid threats or penalties in their home country; did not pay fines for violating the expiry of the Stay Permit and still remains in Indonesian territory for less than 60 days; and has been previously prohibited or denied entry into Indonesia.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Executive Order No. 125, 2016 (Peraturan Presiden 125-2016) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/41029/perpres-no-125-tahun-2016], Articles 37-39. However, this procedure is limited to an administrative appeal.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. As of January 1, 2020, national law in Indonesia does not guarantee citizenship to migrants or children of migrants who would otherwise be stateless in Law No. 12 on Citizenship of the Republic of Indonesia, 2006 (UU12-2006), Arts. 9, 19. The citizenship law and immigration laws limit visas to marriage and dependent children. Family members are subject to the same criteria as other residents seeking citizenship. There is no provision for "chain migration" in the sense there would be preferential treatment for families.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia conditionally protects this right in 1) Government Regulation Number 31 of 2013 on Implementing Regulations of Law Number 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration, Articles 102, 141, 166, 218. 2) President Regulation No. 125 of 2016 concerning Settlement of Refugees from Abroad, Articles 25, 28. Reunification of migrant families is legal in Indonesia, but only in some cases. Article 102 of Government Regulation Number 31 of 2013 Concerning Implementing Regulations of Law No. 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration, states that migrants who are allowed to unite with their family members in Indonesia on a Limited Stay Visa are: 1) migrants who join their husband or wife who are Indonesian citizens; 2) migrants who join with a husband or wife who hold a limited stay permit or permanent residence permit; 3) children resulting from legal marriages between migrants and Indonesian citizens; 4) children who are not eighteen years of age and are not married to foreigners who are legally married to Indonesian citizens; 5) children under eighteen years old, are not married, who join with their parents who hold a Limited Stay Permit or Permanent Stay Permit. For refugees, Indonesia applies the principle of family unification to its immigration examination, as stated in Articles 25 and 28 of Executive Order No. 125 of 2016 Concerning Settlement of Refugees from Abroad.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The national law in Indonesia does not provide a judicial remedy to appeal the refusal by the authorities to allow family formation/reunification in Law No. 12 on Citizenship of the Republic of Indonesia, 2006 (UU12-2006), Art. 13.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Indonesia does not recognize same-sex relationships under the family reunification framework in Law No. 1 on Marriage, 1974 (UU1-1974), Arts. 1 and 3; Law No. 23 on Population Administration, 2006 (UU23-2006), Art. 34(1).

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 6 On Immigration 2011 (UU6-2011), Article 62(2)(a). 2) Ministry of Human Right Regulation 443.77/1000/HR.2022.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Indonesia does not allow irregular migrant workers to regularize in Law No. 6 of 2011 on Immigration. On the contrary, there will be sanctions or fines imposed on the illegal migrants if they arrive in Indonesia. Specifically, they will be placed in a detention center and immigration authorities will process them for deportation.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 13 on Manpower, 2003 (UU13-2003), Articles 106, 183. Article 106 and 183 provide a system through which all laborers can seek redress for violations of the law. These sanctions include administrative and criminal liability, but these sanctions are imposed at the discretion of the Department of Manpower.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law No. 11 of 2021. 2) Law No. 4 of 2023. 3) Law No. 39 of 1999 on Human Rights. 4) Law No. 24 of 2011 on Social Security Administrator. Once migrant workers received their BPJS Ketenagakerjaan (Social Security Card) ID card, they will have an access to health services. This also includes anyone residing in Indonesia on a limited stay permit.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 182 of Law Number 7 of 2007 requires an individual election contestant to be an Indonesian citizen, and at least 21 years of age or older to run for public office in an election.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) the Constitution of Indonesia, Article 28D. 2) Law No. 6 of 2012 Concerning Ratification of the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families. The constitution generally prohibits discrimination of any type and migrants and citizens should be treated equally, without discrimination based on ethnicity, race, color, language, religion or creed, political opinions or otherwise, nationality, ethnic or social origin, citizenship, age, economic position, wealth, marital status, birth status or others.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) the Constitution of Indonesia, Article 28I. Article 28I stipulates that everyone has the right to be free from discriminatory treatment on any basis and is entitled to protection against discriminatory treatment, which includes migrants. This protection also has been adopted by Law No. 39 of 1999 on Human Rights. 2) Law No. 29 of 1999 on the Ratification of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination. 3) Law No. 39 of 1999 on Human Rights, Article 3.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law No. 11 of 2021. 2) Law No. 11 of 2020 on Job Creation, Article 80. 3) Law No. 13 of 2013, Article 47. However, the labor law restricts foreign workers to essentially performing work that cannot otherwise be performed by Indonesian Citizens.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 11 of 2021. In order for a migrant worker to perform labor of any sort in Indonesia, the migrant worker must have a work permit and associated visa sponsored by the employer. The regulation states that there is no provision for transferring the employment contract to another sponsoring entity.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. For spouses to work legally, Law No. 11 of 2021 on Job Creation requires a sponsored work permit for each individual regardless of marital status.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Law No. 11 of 2021 on Job Creation, upon termination of the contract/work permit, the visa holder must leave Indonesia within 7 days of the termination. This provision applies to residency on the basis of a work permit, not refugee residency, or marriage residency.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 11 of 2021 on Job Creation, Articles 47-80, 137, 169. All rights of local laborers are the same as migrant laborers, including pay, minimum wage, health and safety, as well as paid holidays. According to Article 47 of Law No. 11 of 2021 on Job Creation, these conditions cannot be "contracted away."

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 4 of 2023 on Development and Strengthening of the Financial Sector. Law No. 4 of 2023 states that all workers, including migrant workers, are required to enroll in the BPJS Manpower system. The benefits under this system would be on par with citizens based on the given years of contribution into the system. However, most migrants do not enroll in the system or are not employed for a sufficient period.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law No. 4 of 2023 on the Development and Strengthening of the Financial Sector. Law No 4 of 2023 states that migrant workers who are enrolled in the employment security department, BPJS Manpower, are eligible for unemployment benefits. However, because unemployment usually necessitates repatriation, there are effectively no benefits for migrant employees. 2) Law No. 6 on Immigration 2011.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law No. 6 on Immigration, 2011 (UU6-2011), Articles 52, 54, 62(2)(a). 2) Ministry of Human Rights Regulation 443.77/1000/HR, 2012. 2) Minister of Law and Human Rights Regulation Number 29 of 2021 on Visa and Stay Permit. To change the status of a limited stay permit to a permanent stay permit, migrants must be: (a) a migrants holding a limited stay permit as clergy, workers, investors, and more; (b) family due to mixed marriage; (c) husband, wife and / or child of a migrant holder of a Permanent Stay Permit; and (d) an Indonesian ex-citizens and ex subjects of dual citizenship of the Republic of Indonesia.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) the Constitution of Indonesia 1945 (UU1-1945) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/101646/uud-no--], Article 31. 2) Executive Order No. 125, 2016 (Peraturan Presiden 125-2016) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/41029/perpres-no-125-tahun-2016]. Article 25 of Executive Order No. 125 of 2016, regulates that refugees who are brought to the detention center may have anything confiscated, but not their travel documents, visa, and their documents detailing their permission to stay. 3) Law Number 6 of 2011 on Immigration [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011], Articles 106, 130. Article 130 of the Immigration Law prohibits and provides a criminal sanction to anyone who confiscates immigration documents belonging to another person.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law Number 24 of 2013 on the Citizen Administration (Amendment of Law Number 23 of 2006) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/38985/uu-no-24-tahun-2013], Articles 1, 27. 2) Presidential Regulation No. 96 of 2018 on the Requirements and Procedures for Civil Registration and Registration [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/97804/perpres-no-96-tahun-2018], Articles 32, 33. According to Article 32 paragraph of Presidential Regulation Number 96 of 2018 Concerning Requirements and Procedures for Civil Registration and Registration, every resident must register the birth event of their child. Residents are Indonesian citizens and non-citizen foreigners residing in Indonesia.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law Number 6 Concerning Immigration, 2011 (UU6-2011) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011], Articles 8-16, 53-57. Law Number 6 of 2011 states that all migrants with legal status are to be issued documentation of said status, either through notation on their passport, through a separate limited residency card (either printed or electronic). 2) Executive Order Number 125, 2016 (Peraturan Presiden 125-2016) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/41029/perpres-no-125-tahun-2016], Articles 35-36, which states that refugees should also be issued with a card for identification purposes and to confirm their status.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law Number 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011], Articles 129 and 131. Article 129 of the Immigration Law regulates the penalties for anyone who damages, changes, adds, reduces or eliminates, either in part or in full, immigration documents (including the document that recognize a migrants' residency status, work status, and identity). Article 131 prohibits anyone illegally destroying immigration documents of a migrant.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in Law Number 1 of 1982 of the Vienna Convention [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/46993/uu-no-1-tahun-1982]. As part of the mutual obligations under international relations and to respect the basic human rights, Indonesia facilitates the consular officials of other state to assist their nationals especially if they face problems with the immigration office. Additionally, as Indonesia has ratified both UN Convention on Diplomatic Relations and UN Convention on Consular Relation through Law No. 1 Year 1982, Indonesia is obligated to allow consular officials and migrants who are nationals of the consular sending state to communicate.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, the Indonesian government has issued a policy that refugees, including children, can no longer be detained in an immigration detention center. This policy is stipulated in the Circular Note of the Directorate General of Immigration, Ministry of Law and Human Rights, on returning the function of detention center for its initial purpose. No. IMI-UM.01.01-2827 (30 July 2018) [https://rudenimpontianak.kemenkumham.go.id/en/regulasi/surat-edaran-dirjen-imigrasi].

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Detention decisions are made by the Minister through designated immigration officers, and are regulated under Law No. 6 on Immigration, 2011 (UU6-2011) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011], Articles 77, and 83-85. Administrative procedures are usually arbitrary and rarely is there due process in the appeal of a decision for detention. Additionally, the provisions allow for deportation in lieu of detention and it is often the case that migrants without legal stay permits are deported without administrative hearings.However, Indonesia has issued a policy that refugees, including children, can no longer be detained in the immigration detention center. This policy is stipulated in the Circular Note of the Directorate General of Immigration, Ministry of Law and Human Rights, on returning the function of detention center for its initial purpose.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 6 on Immigration, 2011 (UU6-2011) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011] Articles 77, 83-85. Article 77 states that there is a right for migrants to be able to submit an objection to the Minister regarding their legal status as migrants when subjected to sanctions under immigration law. The response to such an objection is set forth through a Ministerial decision. However, there is no specific law governing the appeal of said detentions conditions, or length.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 6 on Immigration, 2011 (UU6-2011) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011] Art. 84, which requires an individual determination of a migrant by an immigration officer.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 24 on Treaty Ratification 2000 (UU24-2000) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/44991/uu-no-24-tahun-2000]; Executive Order No. 125, 2016 (Peraturan Presiden 125-2016) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/41029/perpres-no-125-tahun-2016], Article 16; Law Number 39 Year 1999 concerning Human Rights [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/45361/uu-no-39-tahun-1999], Article 33. Article 33 of Law Number 39 Year 1999 states that "everyone has the right to freedom from torture, or cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment or treatment." Indonesian law treats Indonesians and foreigners equally. This rule is considered more general and can cover migrant workers.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: The national law does not specifically mention the use of force by officers or agents as a means of deterring migrants from entering Indonesian jurisdiction.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Regulation of the Head of the Republic of Indonesia National Police Number 1 of 2009 Concerning Use of Force in Police Measures [https://www.policinglaw.info/assets/downloads/Regulation_No_1_of_the_Chief_of_the_Indonesian_National_Police_2009_(in_Indonesia).pdf]. 2) Law No. 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration, Articles 13, 91 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011]. 3) Law No. 2 of 2002 Concerning the Indonesian National Police, Article 19 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/44418/uu-no-2-tahun-2002]. 4) Regulation of the Head of the Republic of Indonesia National Police No. 1 of 2009 Concerning the Use of Force in Police Measures. 5) This is regulated in Article 19 paragraph (1) of Law Number 2 of 2002 Concerning the Indonesian National Police, and the Regulation of the Head of the Republic of Indonesia National Police Number 1 of 2009 Concerning Use of Force in Police Measures. Although there are no specific rules that govern migrants entering Indonesia, the prohibition on the use of lethal force by Indonesian authorities is strictly regulated. The police may only use weapons and violence with the principles of: legality, necessity, proportionality, general obligation, preventive, reasonable. So, as long as migrants do not threaten safety / unarmed and do not intend to harm others, the use of lethal force by the authorities is not allowed.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia exempts trafficked/smuggled migrants from criminal prosecution in Law No. 21 on Eradication of Human Trafficking, 2007 (UU21-2007) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/44418/uu-no-2-tahun-2002]; Law No. 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration, Articles 86-90; Law Number 14 of 2009 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011]; Law No. 21 of 2007 on Eradication of Human Trafficking, Articles 56, 57, and 58; Law of Number 5 of 2009 on the Ratification of UN Convention Against Transnational Organized Crimes [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/38586/uu-no-5-tahun-2009]; Law of Number 14 of 2009 on Protocol To Prevent, Suppress And Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women, And Children, Supplementing The United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/38615/uu-no-14-tahun-2009].

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law No. 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration, Article 62. 2) Law No. 12 of 2016 on Citizenship, Articles 23-30. Migrants convicted of a crime can only lose their Permanent Stay Permit. Law No.12 of 2016 on Citizenship does not include criminal conviction as a valid reason for the revocation of citizenship.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law No. 12 of 2006 on Citizenship, Article 9. 2) Law No. 6 of 2011 on Immigration, Article 59. Article 9 of Law Number 12 of 2006 Concerning Immigration provides requirements for a citizenship application, that is, at the time of submitting an application the applicant: has been residing in Indonesia for at least 5 consecutive years or at least 10 non-consecutive years, as evidenced by the applicant's Permanent Residence Permit. This document is valid for 5 years and can be extended under Article 59 of Law Number 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration. A limited stay permit holder is a worker, and must reside and settle in Indonesia as a resident of Indonesia to be eligible for a Permanent Residence Permit.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Indonesia is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol. Although Indonesia has passed Presidential Regulation No. 125 Year 2016 on the Handling of Refugees, they do not have any rights to access employment, start a business, or any pathway to get permanent residency or citizenship.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 12 of 2006 Concerning Citizenship, Articles 8-22. Article 9 of Law Number 12 of 2006 Concerning Immigration provides requirements for a citizenship application, that is, at the time of submitting an application the applicant: has been residing in Indonesia for at least 5 consecutive years or at least 10 non-consecutive years, as evidenced by the applicant's Permanent Residence Permit. This document is valid for 5 years and can be extended under Article 59 of Law Number 6 of 2011 Concerning Immigration. The citizenship law and immigration laws limit visas to marriage and dependent children. Family members are also subject to the same criteria as other residence seeking citizenship. There is no provision for "chain migration" in the sense there would be preferential treatment for families.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 26 of Law No. 12 of 2006 on Citizenship: "Indonesian citizens lose their citizenship if the person concerned: (a) obtains another nationality of his own volition; (b) does not refuse or does not give up other citizenship, while the person concerned has the opportunity to do so."

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 30 of 1999 on Human Rights, Article 24.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in Law No. 39 of 1999 Concerning Human Rights, Article 23. Article 23 of Human Rights Law guarantee that "(1) Everyone is free to choose and have his political beliefs; (2) Everyone is free to own, issue and disseminating opinions according to his conscience, orally and or writing through print or electronic media with pay attention to religious values, decency, order, public interest and the integrity of the nation."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Indonesia limits the protection of this right to citizens in Law No. 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Article 25, notwithstanding the broad protection in the Constitution of Indonesia, Article 28E.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in the 1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia, Article 28E paragraph (3); Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Article 24 number 1. Indonesia recognizes and protects the right to freedom of association of every person without exception, including migrants.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Applications for citizenship must demonstrate employment or adequate income/resources as part of the application process. The application for spouses states no such requirement, however, there is no provision for family reunification other than spousal reunification, which still requires the applicant to meet residency requirements.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law Number 8 on Criminal Procedure 1981 (UU8-1981) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/47041/uu-no-8-tahun-1981], Articles 51-53, 177. According to the Criminal Procedure Code everyone has equal access to obtain information related to their trial, the right to legal assistance, and other basic rights. 2) Law Number 6 Year 2012 Concerning the Ratification of the International Convention On The Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39025].

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Law No. 6 on Immigration, 2011 (UU6-2011) [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/39140/uu-no-6-tahun-2011], Arts. 87-88 only protects victims of human trafficking who would be subject to administrative procedures for deportation for illegally entering the country. However, there is no provision in immigration law or criminal procedure laws to allow for stay permits based on being the victim of a crime.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: Although the existing law related to child protection under Law No. 23 of 2002 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/44473/uu-no-23-tahun-2002] (amended by Law 35 of 2014 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/38723/uu-no-35-tahun-2014]) does not specifically provide that such protections cover migrant children. The Child Protection Law adopts the principle of protecting the "best interests of the child." Also, the Indonesian government has ratified certain human rights-related treaties, such as the Convention Against Torture (CAT) ratified in 1998 (Law No. 5 of 1998 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/45437/uu-no-5-tahun-1998], the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) ratified in 2006 (Law No. 12 of 2005 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/40261/uu-no-12-tahun-2005], and the Convention on the Rights of the Child ratified in 1990 (Presidential Decree No. 36 of 1990 [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/63923/keppres-no-36-tahun-1990] which include provisions for safeguarding the fundamental rights of refugees and asylum seekers. However, these laws do not provide special protections for migrant children above those that are provided to migrant adults.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No specfic protection of this right. The rules for the protection of women are specifically written in Executive Order No. 125 of 2006. However, this rule does not regulate the protection of women migrants. Law No. 12 of 2022 on Sexual Violence Criminal Offenses [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/207944/uu-no-12-tahun-2022] also does not specify the same protections for migrant women, even though the aim is also to provide protection to women against violence both at home and at work.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Indonesia protects this right in 1) Law No. 39 Year 1999 concerning Human Rights [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/45361/uu-no-39-tahun-1999] (Art. 41 par. (2)); 2) Law No. 13 Year 2003 concerning Employment [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/43013] (Art. 19 and Chapter X); 3) Law No. 8 Year 2016 concerning the Rights of Persons with Disabilities [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/37251/uu-no-8-tahun-2016]; 4) Government Regulation No. 39 of 2020 on Adequate Accommodations for Persons with Disabilities in the Judicial Process [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/142170/pp-no-39-tahun-2020]. 5) Government Regulation No. 42 of 2020 on Accessibility of Settlements, Public Services, and Disaster Protection for Persons with Disabilities [https://peraturan.bpk.go.id/Details/142301/pp-no-42-tahun-2020].

citation_text_en: [1]: Alan Desmond. [2]: John Stanley (2020 Coding) / James Buckley (Backcoded Questions)

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Ireland

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 40.6.1.ii of the Constitution of Ireland guarantees 'The right of the citizens to assemble peaceably and without arms.' Article 40.6.2 provides that laws regulating the manner in which the right of free assembly may be exercised shall contain no political, religious or class discrimination but it is unclear from the case law whether the protection of Article 40.6.1.ii in respect of migrants is commensurate with that afforded by it to Irish citizens. It is not possible to say that the word 'citizen' is equivalent to 'person' in this context (The State (Nicolaou) v An Bord Uchtala [1966] I.R. 567, per Henchy J.). In any particular case, one should consider whether the essence of the right relates to the essence of human personality and thus must be accorded to some or all migrants as a matter of constitutional equality, and, if it is to be accorded to migrants, consider whether a justifiable distinction may be made under Article 40.1 (equality) between citizens and lawful residents and non-citizens (N.H.V. v Minister forJustice and Equality [2017] IESC 35.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in Sections 9 and 10 of the Electoral Act 1992. According to Section 9: 'a person shall be entitled to be registered as a local government elector in a local electoral area if he has reached the age of eighteen years and he was, on the qualifying date, ordinarily resident in that area.'

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Articles 26, 40-44 of the Constitution of Ireland. Articles 40-44 of the Constitution of Ireland guarantee fundamental rights. Article 40.1 provides: "all citizens shall, as human persons, be held equal before the law." Unenumerated personal rights are protected by Article 40.3.1 which provides that the State "guarantees in its laws to respect, and as far as practicable, by its laws to defend and vindicate the personal rights of the citizen." Additionally, the equal protection clause of Article 40.1 has, however, been held to apply to non-citizens. 2) The State (Nicolaou) v An Bord Ucht?la [1966] I.R. 567. Some rulings from the Superior Courts impute consequence to the fact that throughout Articles 40-44, the word "citizen" is sometimes used, with "person" being used at other times, for instance, in the State (Nicolaou) v An Bord Ucht?la [1966] I.R. 567. 3) Quinn's Supermarket Ltd v Attorney General (1972) I.R. 1. The equal protection clause was interpreted by the Irish High Court in Quinn's Supermarket Ltd v Attorney General (1972) I.R. 1 to be based on personhood rather than citizenship status. It was held that the clause "is not a guarantee of absolute equality for all citizens in all circumstances but it is a guarantee of equality as human persons and...a guarantee against any inequalities" based on ethnic, religious, social or other backgrounds. 4) Article 26 and the Employment Equality Bill 1996 [1997] 2 I.R. 321. 5) NHV v Minister for Justice and Equality [2017] IESC 35. 6) Re Illegal Immigrants (Trafficking) Bill 1999 [2000] 2 I.R. 360. 7) Section 5(1) of the Illegal Immigrants (Trafficking) Act 2000, as amended by Section 34 Employment Permits (Amendment) Act 2014. 8) Sections 5 and 10 of the Illegal Immigrants (Trafficking) Bill 1999 [2000] 2 I.R. 360. 9) Murphy v Greene [1990] 2 I. R. 566. According to the ruling, "it is beyond question that every individual, be he citizen or not, has a constitutional right of access to the courts." However, it should be noted that migrants' right of access to the courts may be subject to conditions and limitations which would not apply to Irish citizens. Thus, Section 5(1) of the Illegal Immigrants (Trafficking) Act 2000 provides that a person shall not question the validity of certain immigration-related decisions and measures otherwise than by way of judicial review. Similar restrictions on judicial review of planning decisions show that the Oireachtas (Irish parliament) may lawfully restrict the right of access to the courts even by Irish citizens.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. However, applicants for international protection are protected in national law in Ireland in 1) Section 20(14) of the International Protection Act 2015. Section 20(14) International Protection Act 2015 provides that an international protection applicant detained under Section 20 is entitled to consult a legal representative and, where necessary, to the assistance of an interpreter for such consultation. 2) Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 which provides that international protection applicants may obtain legal advice and legal aid, inter alia in relation to immigration matters, subject to satisfaction of certain financial criteria. The Legal Aid Board is the statutory body which provides legal aid in Ireland. It provides confidential independent legal services to people applying for international protection in Ireland. It can assist with applications for international protection to the International Protection Office, appeals to the International Protection Appeals Tribunal, and with proposed removal to another EEA state under the Dublin III Regulation. Legal aid and advice is provided free of charge to persons who do not have the resources to pay for or contribute to the costs.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Section 3 of S.I. No. 564/2013 - European Communities Act 1972 (Interpretation and Translation for Persons in Custody in Garda S?och?na Stations) Regulations, 2013. Section 3, provides that an arrested person who does not speak or who does not understand the English language shall have the right while in custody to the assistance, at no cost, of an interpreter and to the translation, at no cost, of relevant documents. 2) Section 3 of S.I. No. 565/2013 - European Communities Act 1972 (Interpretation and Translation in Criminal Proceedings) Regulations, 2013. Section 3 states that a person (a) who appears before a court either charged with an offence or who, having been convicted of an offence, is appealing against that conviction or the penalty imposed on conviction, and (b) who does not speak or who does not understand the English language shall, where the proceedings are being conducted in the English language, have the right to the assistance, at no cost, of an interpreter as set out in these Regulations and to the translation of the documents specified in these Regulations

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Migrants found entering unauthorized are subject to punishment outlined in Section 6 of the Immigration Act 2004. The Immigration Act 2004 provides for various offences including the offences of (a) failing to have a transit visa; (b) failing to have an Irish visa; (c) failing to land at an approved port; (d) failing to present and apply for permission to land; (e) failing to be in possession of a valid passport or other equivalent document establishing identity and nationality; (f) failing to comply with a condition attached to a permission to land or be in the State. Section 13 provides that a person guilty of an offence under the 2004 Act shall be liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ?3,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or to both.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland conditionally protects this right in 1) Sections 20 and 40 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009. To be regarded as eligible for social housing on an equal basis with citizens, migrants must have a legal right to remain in the State on a long-term basis. Additionally, access to public housing programs is subject to an assessment made on the basis of Section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009. Section 40 of the 2009 Act empowers the relevant Minister to make regulations for the assessment. 2) The Housing Circular 41/2012 of December 2012. The Housing Circular 41/2012 of December 2012 sets out access to social housing support for non-Irish nationals. The circular clarifies that: (A) asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing support; (B) non-European Economic Area nationals must have five years' reckonable residence in the previous eight years on the basis of certain residence permissions, or have any length of reckonable residence and one of certain residence permissions on which the expiry date would permit their continued residence to an aggregate of five years in the previous eight years.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No explicit protection of this right in respect of non-citizens. Article 42.4 of the Constitution of Ireland obligates the State to provide free primary education. However, there has never been a legal case establishing this right to non-citizens.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Administratively, the government provides for a 'Free Fees Initiative' that, in effect, guarantees such access to educational institutions to many migrants. To avail of the free fees initiative, a student must either (A) be a national of a European Union Member State, a state which is a contracting state to the EEA Agreement, or the Swiss Confederation, (B) have refugee status in the State; (C) be a family members of a refugee granted permission by the Minister for Justice and Equality; (D) have permission to remain in the State as a family member of a European Union citizen under the Free Movement of Persons Regulations 2015; (E) have leave to remain in the State; or (F) have permission to remain in the State. Thus, while migrants with termporary permission, or who are in the State unlawfully or on a tolerated basis cannot avail of the scheme, settled migrants generally can.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. A criminal conviction can be the basis for a decision to deport (Section 3(2) of the Immigration Act 1999), even where the migrant is the parent of an Irish citizen child, according to FE (a minor) v Minister for Justice and Equality [2013] IEHC 93. A deportation order may also be made on the basis of a single serious offence (see FE (a minor) v Minister for Justice and Equality [2013] IEHC 93) or on the basis of a number of minor offences (see Falvey v Minister for Justice, Equality and Law Reform [2009] IEHC 528). A criminal conviction may also be one factor amongst others that weigh in favour of the making of a deportation order. While Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 provides the power to refuse permission to land or be in the State, these stipulations may only be exercised if an immigration officer is satisfied that one or more of the grounds apply. One of those grounds is that the non-national has been convicted (whether in the State or elsewhere) of an offence that may be punished under the law of the place of conviction by imprisonment of one year or more by a more severe penalty. However, in deciding whether to renew residence status, the Minister for Justice is not constrained only by criminal convictions, or other statutory criteria (Hussein v Minister for Justice and Equality [2015] IESC 104). This means that, at the Minister's discretion, any offense can lead to a rejection, or removal of a residence permit. That said, the Minister for Justice/immigration officers sometimes grant residence status and/or sometimes renew residence status notwithstanding that the migrant in question has minor convictions. The Supreme Court has stated that executive power operates within this legislative provision with the effect that the Minister's power in administering it is very broad and not subject to the express limitations in it (Hussein v Minister for Justice and Equality [2015] IESC 104.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Section 4(1) of the Criminal Justice (United Nations Convention Against Torture) Act 2000. 2) Sections 50(1) and 50A(1) International Protection Act 2015. Section 50(1) of the International Protection Act 2015 provides that a person who is or was an applicant for international protection under that Act shall not be expelled or returned in any manner whatsoever to the frontier of a territory where, in the opinion of the Minister for Justice and Equality, inter alia, there is a serious risk that the person would be subject to torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. 3) S.G. (Albania) v Minister for Justice and Equality [2018] IEHC 184. 4) S.G. (Albania) v Minister for Justice and Equality [2019] IESCDET 13.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Sections 50(1) and 50A(1) International Protection Act 2015. Section 50(1) of the International Protection Act 2015 provides that a person who is or was an applicant for international protection under that Act shall not be expelled or returned in any manner whatsoever to the frontier of a territory where, in the opinion of the Minister for Justice and Equality, inter alia, there is a serious risk that the person would be subject to torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Additionally, the act also provides for a detailed procedure for ascertaining if a person has a well founded fear of persecution on the basis of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, with persons found to have such a well founded fear being granted refugee status in the State. 2) S.G. (Albania) v Minister for Justice and Equality [2018] IEHC 184; S.G. (Albania) v Minister for Justice and Equality [2019] IESCDET 13.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Sections 2(1), 3, 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) Act 2003. Section 3 of the ECHR Act 2003 in effect obliges the Minister for Justice and Equality, when performing his or her functions in respect of deportation or removal, to do so in a manner compatible with the State's obligations under Articles 2 (Right to Life) and 3 of the ECHR and Protocol 13 of the ECHR. 3) McD v L [2009] IESC 81. 4) S v Minister for Justice, Equality and Law Reform [2011] IEHC 34. 5) MD v Ireland [2012] IESC 10. 6) Article 40.3.2 Constitution of Ireland. Article 40.3.2 of the Constitution of Ireland provides that the State shall by its laws protect as best it may from unjust attack and, in the case of injustice done, vindicate the life of every citizen. Notwithstanding that Article's express reference to 'every citizen', the Irish courts take it as the starting point for the vindication of a migrant's right to life in Irish law (Y.Y. v Minister for Justice and Equality [2017] IESC 81.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Deportation and expulsion methodology is outlined in 1) Sections 13 and 50 of the International Protection Act 2015. 2) Section 3 of the Immigration Act 1999. 3) Oguekwe v Minister for Justice Equality and Law Reform [2008] IESC 25 at para 31. 4) Dos Santos & Ors v The Minister for Justice & Ors [2014] IEHC 559. 5) The Immigration Act 2003. None of these provisions provide for an obligation or requirement that the person be advised of the possible availability of asylum before being expelled or prevented entry.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The process for explusion is outlined in the Immigration Act 1999, Immigration Act 2003, and International Protection Act 2015. None of these legal measures, or any other national law, expressly bans expulsion to a country where a migrant is likely to be subjected to refoulement through a subsequent expulsion. However, 'chain refoulement' may be considered in the context of the non-refoulement provision of section 50 of the International Protection Act 2015. However, Ireland is a state party to the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), and Article 3 of the ECHR prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The European Court of Human Rights has found against expulsion to states where an individual would face a risk of being subjected to refoulement through a subsequent expulsion in MSS (2011); Hirsi Jamaa (2012); Ilias and Ahmed (2019). Additionally, the ECHR has been indirectly incorporated into Irish Law by ECHR Act 2003, Section 2(1) of which requires Irish courts to interpret rules of domestic law in a manner which is in line with the State's obligations under the Convention. Section 4 of the Act also requires Irish courts to take account of judgments of the European Court. However, the Act allows Irish Courts to issue a declaration of incompatibility, as opposed to making a finding of a breach of the Convention, see McD v L [2009] IESC 81; S v Minister for Justice, Equality and Law Reform [2011] IEHC 34; MD v Ireland [2012] IESC 10.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Section 3(1) and Section 3(2) Immigration Act 1999. The statutory scheme for deportation under the Immigration Act 1999 requires that all considerations relevant to non-refoulement, humanitarian matters, and other matters relevant to the person concerned according to certain criteria set out in section 3(6) of the 1999 Act will be fairly examined before the Minister makes a deportation order. 2) Section 51 of the International Protection 2015 Act. The passing and entry into force of the International Protection Act 2015 on 31 December, 2016, brought into operation a new legal basis for the deportation of persons who have failed in their protection applications and applications for permission to remain under the International Protection Act. Section 51 of the International Protection 2015 Act is deemed to be a deportation order made under Section 3(1) of the Immigration Act 1999. 3) P. v. Minister for Justice Equality and Law Reform [2001] IESC 107 at para 35. According to the ruling of P. v. Minister for Justice Equality and Law Reform [2001] IESC 107, paragraph 35, the Supreme Court has held that where a large number of people apply, "on individual facts, for the same relief, the nature of the authorities consideration and the form of grant or refusal may be similar or identical. An adequate Statement of Reasons in one case may thus be equally adequate in others. This does not diminish the statements essential validity or convert it into a mere administrative formula."

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Sections 3 and 6 of the Immigration Act 1999. According to Section 3(3) of the Immigration Act 1999 provides that notification of an intention to make a deportation order has to be provided to the prospective deportee in writing. The notification of intention to deport must include the reasons for the proposed deportation and, where necessary and possible, the person shall be given a copy of the notification in a language that he or she understands. A person so notified has 15 working days to make representations in writing to the Minister. Section3(6) of the Immigration Act 1999, in determining whether to make a deportation order in relation to a person, the Minister shall have regard to: "(a) the age of the person; (b) the duration of residence in the State of the person; (c) the family and domestic circumstances of the person; (d) the nature of the person's connection with the State, if any; (e) the employment (including self-employment) record of the person; (f) the employment (including self-employment) prospects of the person; (g) the character and conduct of the person both within and (where relevant and ascertainable) outside the State (including any criminal convictions); (h) humanitarian considerations; (i) any representations duly made by or on behalf of the person; (j) the common good; and (k) considerations of national security and public policy, so far as they appear or are known to the Minister." 2) International Protection Act 2015. 3) Section 5 of the Immigration Act 2003. 4) S.E. -v- The Minister for Justice and Equality [2018] IESC 20, in this case the Supreme Court found that the State was not entitled to proceed to make a deportation order against a person to whom no invitation to make representations was sent because that person failed to provide an address for service.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for both migrants and children of migrants. There is no specific entitlement to citizenship for stateless persons, except that a child who is considered a ‘foundling’ (i.e., of unknown parentage), will be deemed to be entitled to citizenship by birth according to Section 10 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. In addition, Section 6(3)of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, provides that: a person born in the island of Ireland is an Irish citizen from birth if he or she is not entitled to citizenship of any other country. While a stateless migrant is not guaranteed citizenship, they can apply for citizenship per Section 16 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956 and Section 6(3)of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Additionally, Section 2 of the International Protection Act 2015, states that stateless persons are entitled to seek refugee status or subsidiary protection in respect of the country of their former habitual residence. A stateless person may also seek a waiver of the conditions of naturalisation pursuant to Section 16 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, however, the grant of such a waiver is at the “absolute discretion” of the Minister and is therefore a ‘privilege’ as opposed to a ‘right’.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland conditionally protects this right in 1) Sections 56 and 57 International Protection Act 2015. 2) Immigration Act 2004. Beneficiaries of international protection have a statutory right to reunification with immediate family members (Sections 56 and 57 International Protection Act 2015). However, immediate family members of all other settled migrants can only apply for a visa, entry to the State, and residence under the Immigration Act 2004, in which context there is no right to family reunification. Additionally, whether to grant the necessary visa/entry/residence permission in the case of the latter is a matter of discretion on the part of the Minister for Justice and Equality. Only settled migrants who are beneficiaries of international protection have a right to family reunification. In all other cases while there are administrative schemes, and even satisfaction of the criteria in those schemes does not guarantee family reunification as the relevant residency permission is ultimately a matter of discretion, not law. Important to note that the same applies for family members of Irish citizens. The only exception is residency for family members of EU citizens exercising EU free movement rights, who have relevant rights as set out in Directive 2004/38/EC (the Citizenship Directive), as given effect nationally in S.I. No. 548/2015 - European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Article 31 Directive 2004/38/EC. 2) Sections 56 and 57 International Protection Act 2015. 3) SI No. 548 of 2015. 4) Section 4 Immigration Act 2004. 5) Section 5 Illegal Immigrants (Trafficking) Act 2000. Refusal of family reunification in respect of beneficiaries of international protection under the International Protection Act 2015, or refusal of permission to be in the State under section 4 of the Immigration Act 2004, are challengeable by way of special rules for judicial review under section 5 of the Illegal Immigrants (Trafficking) Act 2000, as amended. With respect to family members of EU citizens, Article 31 Directive 2004/38/EC provides that, in the event of restrictions on the right of entry and the right of residence on grounds of public policy, public security or public health, the persons concerned shall have access to judicial and, where appropriate, administrative redress procedures in the host Member State to appeal against or seek review of any decision taken against them on the grounds of public policy, public security or public health. These rights are transposed in national law by SI No. 548 of 2015. In the context of family reunification under Sections 56 and 57 International Protection Act 2015, where the Minister is satisfied that the person for whom permission is sought is a "member of the family" of the sponsor, he has no discretion to refuse permission to enter and reside or to reside in the territory of Ireland.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Article 41.4 of the Constitution of Ireland. According to Article 41.4 Constitution of Ireland: 'Marriage may be contracted in accordance with law by two persons without distinction as to their sex.' The relevant primary legislation is applied in this constitutional context. 2) The Marriage Act 2015, which recognises same sex marriage, and the principle of non-discrimination requires that Ireland recognise same-sex marriages contracted in other states. 3) Permissions to land or be in the State are provided under Section 4 of the Immigration Act 2004, and the relevant implementing policy document (Policy Document on non-EEA Family Reunification) notes "eligible relationships for family reunification under the 2013 Guidelines include: marriage or civil partnership with no requirement as to a minimum duration; de facto partnerships (whether heterosexual or same sex) which must have existed in a relationship akin to marriage including cohabitation for 2 years prior to application for family reunification."

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Irregular migrants who wish to regularise their residence status in the State must do so by leaving the State and applying from outside the State for a 'D-class' long stay visa.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Section 4 Immigration Act 2004. 2) Luximon and Balchand v Minister for Justice and Equality [2018] IESC 24. 3) Reactivation Employment Permit (REP) Scheme, introduced by the Employment Permits (Amendment) Act 2014. 4) Reactivation Employment Permit Scheme (ISD). It is the general policy of the executive that irregular migrant workers present in the State who wish to become lawfully settled in Ireland, would have to leave the State and apply from outside the State for a 'D-Class' long stay visa (which is granted on a discretionary basis), on the basis of which, if obtained, they could then proceed to present for permission to land and be ultimately settled in the State. The executive had understood that the legislation did not allow it to 'regularise' temporary or irregular migrant workers, or other irregularly present migrants in the State other than in the context of proposing their deportation and allowing them to stay in the event that a deportation order was not made. The Supreme Court has clarified however that national law (the Immigration Act 2004) is capable of allowing the Minister for Justice and Equality to grant an enhanced residency permission that would have the effect of allowing a migrant present in the State in a restrictive manner to be considered for a residency permission that would in effect enable him or her to becomes lawfully settled in the State, according to the decision in Luximon and Balchand v Minister for Justice and Equality [2018] IESC 24.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) the Terms of Employment (Information) Acts 1994-2014. 2) The Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018. 3) The National Minimum Wage Act 2000. 4) The Payment of Wages Act 1991. 5) The Minimum Notice and Terms of Employment Acts 1973-1995. 6) The Industrial Relations Acts 1969-2015. 7) The Organisation of Working Time Act 1977. 8) The Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005. 9) The Employment Equality Acts 1998-2015. 10) The Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001. 11) The Protection of Employees (Fixed Term Work) Act 2003. 12) The Protection of Employment (Temporary Agency Work) Act 2012. 13) The Unfair Dismissal Acts 1977-2015. Where the term of an employment contract has been violated by an employer, a complaint can be brought to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC), an independent, statutory body which was established under the Workplace Relations Act 2015. The WRC provides information and assistance in making complaints in relation to contraventions of, and disputes as to entitlements under employment, equality and equal status legislation).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in Section 45 Health Care Act 1970. Eligibilty for health care services is predicated, inter alia, on the person being 'ordinarily resident' in the State (or being the spouse, civil partner, or dependant of the person ordinarily resident). Thus, access to health care services for settled migrants is on an equal basis with citizens.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: National Law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Section 12, Local Government Act 2001. Everyone ordinarily resident in Ireland and over the age of 18 can, regardless of nationality, stand for election in the local elections in Ireland, according to Section 12, Local Government Act 2001. However, a candidate must be 'ordinarily resident'. As that concept is open to interpretation, it cannot be said that there is an immediate right to run for public office in local elections. 2) Electoral Amendment Act 2009.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in the Employment Equality Act 1998, as amended, which includes an obligation of equal pay for work and prohibits discrimination between employees on 9 grounds, including on the grounds of race, skin colour, nationality or ethnic background.
