The prohibition of nationality based discrimination has been interpreted to include distinctions on the basis of migration status. In Hussein v. The Labour Court [2012] IEHC 364, the High Court found that section 2(1)-2(4) Employment Permits Act 2003 which prohibited absolutely the employment of a non-citizen in the absence of an employment permit had the effect of depriving irregular migrant workers of the benefit of all employment legislation by virtue of their illegal status, irrespective of where responsibility for that illegality lay. The High Court ruling in Hussein did lead to an amendment of the Employment Permits Act so as to allow irregular migrant workers to defend unlawful work by showing they took all reasonable steps to obtain a work permit. It furthermore empowered such workers to take a civil action to recover unpaid wages. The practical value of this amendment must be viewed as limited from the perspective of migrants whose very status and vulnerability may foment reluctance to take “all such steps as were reasonably open” to them to obtain work permits or to seek access to the civil courts for compensation.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) the Employment Equality Act 1998. Sections 19-20, and 29 of the Employment Equality Act 1998 includes an obligation of equal pay for like work and prohibits discrimination between employees on 9 grounds, including the ground of race, skin colour, nationality or ethnic background. 2) Equal Status Acts 2000-2018.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in Sections 6(2), 19, 20 and 29, Employment Equality Act 1998, which includes an obligation of equal pay for like work and prohibits discrimination between employees on 9 grounds, including the ground of race, skin colour, nationality or ethnic background. While there is no express entitlement for migrant workers to equal pay to that received by local workers doing the same work, nationality has been interpreted to include migration status. In addition, there is a right to equal pay for persons to do like work where any difference in pay is related to the person's race ('that they are of different race, colour, nationality or ethnic or national origins'). In Hussein v. The Labour Court [2012] IEHC 364, the High Court found that Section 2(1)-2(4) of the Employment Permits Act 2003, which prohibited the employment of a non-citizen in the absence of an employment permit, had the effect of depriving irregular migrant workers of the benefit of all employment legislation by virtue of their illegal status, irrespective of where responsibility for that illegality lay. The High Court ruling in Hussein did lead to amendment of the Employment Permits Act so as to allow irregular migrant workers defend unlawful work by showing they took all reasonable steps to obtain a work permit. It furthermore empowered such workers to take a civil action to recover unpaid wages. (See sections 3 & 4 Employment Permits (Amendment) Act 2014.) The practical value of this amendment must be viewed as limited from the perspective of migrants whose very status and vulnerability may foment reluctance to take “all such steps as were reasonably open” to them to obtain work permits or to seek access to the civil courts for compensation.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: Whether there are restrictions on a migrant worker's right to free choice of employment depends on the nature of the migrant worker's permission to be in the State. A work permit issued under the Employment Permits Acts 2006 to 2014 is issued in respect of a particular job. A change of employer is possible, but generally requires a new work permit application. By contrast, a migrant with a permission to be in the State pursuant to Section 4 of the Immigration Act 2004, Section 49 of the International Protection Act 2015, or by grant of executive power, on what is referred to as a 'Stamp 4' basis has a free choice of employment. European Union and European Economic Area citizens and their family members resident in the State on the basis of EU free movement rights have full access to employment on a par with Irish citizens. By contrast, holders of a General Employment Permit, for example, where it is the permit holder's first work permit in Ireland, he or she must stay with the employer for 12 months (save in exceptional circumstances). After 12 months he or she may move to a new employer, provided that a new application for a General Employment Permit has been made for a similar job, or to another eligible employment sector

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Migrants have rights if they are spouses of European Union (EU)/European Economic Area (EEA) citizens per, Employment Permits Acts 2003-2016, the Immigration Act 2004, and the International Protection Act 2015. However, spouses or partners of other settled migrants do not have a right to work on the basis of their being the spouse or partner of that person. Even the non-Irish national spouse or partner of an Irish citizen does not have such a right. The spouse or partner must have their own permission to be in the State, and this permission will not necessarily include a right to work. The partner or dependants of, for example, a General Employment Permit holder are not eligible to apply for a Dependant/Partner/Spouse Employment Permit but can apply for a General Employment Permit in their own right.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law protects the right in 1) the Employment Permits Acts 2003-2020. 2) The Immigration Act 2004. Whether loss of employment affects immigration status depends on the type of immigration status. It is only sometimes that loss of employment leads to loss of residence status. A migrant worker whose permission to be in the State is predicated on his or her having an employment permit under the Employment Permit Acts 2006 to 2014 who loses employment may also lose residency unless he or she gets a new work permit. For example, where the holder of a General Employment Permit who has not held such an employment permit for 5 consecutive years loses their job, they must notify the Employment Permits Section of the Department of Business, Enterprise and Innovation within four weeks of the redundancy. They will have six months from the date on which they were made redundant to find another job. By contrast, if a migrant with permission to be in the State under the Immigration Act 2004 otherwise than on the basis of a work permit loses his or her employment, whether this would affect his or her residence will depend on the particular terms of his or her residence permission. The term of residence permissions vary among the administrative schemes for residence. For some residence schemes (e.g., in respect of residency as the spouse or civil partner of an Irish citizen or Irish resident) loss of employment does not imply loss of the residency permission. By contrast, the residency scheme for 'workers made redundant' allows a grace period of six months within which the migrant must find another employer, or lose permission to be in the State. There are many administrative residence schemes, and whether and how loss of employment affects them depends on their terms. European Unio (EU) and European Economic Are (EEA) citizens and their family members resident in the State on the basis of EU free movement rights have full access to employment on a par with Irish citizens and do not lose any residence status due to loss of employment.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) the Employment Equality Acts 1998-2015. 2) Payment of Wages Act 1991. 3) Minimum Notice and Terms of Employment Acts 1973?2005. 4) Organisation of Working Time Act 1997. 5) Organisation of Working Time (Records) (Prescribed Form and Exemptions) Regulations 2001. In principle, all workers, including migrant workers, have the same rights and entitlements as local workers. However, and while there is a 'race' ground in employment equality/anti-discrimination law, there is no ground for protection against discrimination based on a person's residency status. Accordingly, as it cannot be excluded that migrants can be discriminated against by virtue of their status as migrants, it cannot be said that migrants have the same rights to employment conditions and protections as Irish citizens either in principle or in practice. The Supreme Court held in Sharda Sobhy v The Chief Appeals Officer & Ors. [2021] IESC 81, that a migrant worker who paid social welfare contributions at a time when they were working unlawfully, was not entitled to have same counted toward an entitlement to a maternity benefit, although they and their employer were entitled to a refund of those contributions.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) the Social Welfare and Pensions Act 2014. 2) Article 7(3)(a) of the Citizens Directive 2004. 3) The Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005. A European Union (EU) citizen who loses his or her job after working for more than 12 months and has registered as a job-seeker is entitled to job-seeker's allowance, according to Article 7(3)(a) of the Citizens Directive 2004. Non-EEA migrant workers who have been working for an employer for 2 or more years may be entitled to a redundancy payment if made redundant. A migrant worker who is 'habitually present' in the State has equal access to various social welfare payments, including unemployment assistance; child benefit; carer's allowance; disability allowance; and one-parent family payment.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Article 7(3)(a) of the Citizens Directive 2004. 2) The Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005. A European Union citizen or European Economic Area (EEA) citizen who loses his or her job after working for more than 12 months and has registered as a job-seeker is entitled to job-seeker's allowance, according to Article 7(3)(a) of the Citizens Directive 2004. Non-EEA migrant workers who have been working for an employer for 2 or more years may be entitled to a redundancy payment if made redundant. All migrant workers who are 'habitually present' in the State have equal access to various social welfare payments, including unemployment assistance; child benefit; carer's allowance; disability allowance; and one-parent family payment. 'Habitual residence' is predicated on the migrant worker having a permission to be in the State.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland conditionally protects this right in 1) Section 4 Immigration Act 2004. Section 4 Immigration Act 2004 allows the Minister for Justice to grant an enhanced residency permission allowing a migrant present in the State on a temporary permission to be considered for a residency permission that would enable him or her to become lawfully settled in the State. 2) The Reactivation Employment Permit (REP) Scheme, introduced by the Employment Permits (Amendment) Act 2014. 3) INIS, "Reactivation Employment Permit (REP) Scheme. Ireland has operated a number of ad hoc regularisation programmes allowing various categories of irregular migrant workers to acquire permission to be lawfully present for a limited period. Recently, for example, the Government put in place a sector specific "atypical worker permission mechanism" which allowed exploited undocumented workers to apply for an atypical worker permission after first obtaining contracts of employment. Similarly, The Reactivation Employment Permit (REP) Scheme, introduced by the Employment Permits (Amendment) Act 2014 enables migrants to work legally again if they were immigrants who entered the State on a valid employment permit but who fell out of the system through no fault of their own, or who were exploited in the work place. Under this scheme, a minimum of five years of reckonable residence, an individual may apply for long-term lawful residence.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Section 5(5)(c) of the Immigration Act 1999. Section 5(5)(c) provides that, where a person detained with a view to deportation is subsequently released from detention by a court, the court may make such release subject to a number of conditions including that the person in question surrender any passport or travel document in his or her possession. 2) Section 5(4)(c) of the Immigration Act 2003. 3) Section 17 of the International Protection Act 2015. In the context of documents provided by the state (as opposed to passports, or documents provided by foreign states that the third-country national takes with them), it should be noted that a 'temporary residence certificate' issued to applicants for international protection remains the property of the Minister, according to Section 17 of the International Protection Act 2015. 5) Section 14(1) of the Immigration Act 2004. 6) Section 23 of the Employment Permits Act 2006 (as amended). Section 23 of the Employment Permits Act 2006 (as amended) provides that neither an employer nor a person acting on his or her behalf shall keep any personal document belonging to an employment permit holder. Personal document for the purposes of section 23 includes a passport, a driving licence, an identity card, a document relating to any account held with a financial institution, a document relating to the skills, qualifications or experience of the foreign national and travel documents. A person who contravenes this rule is guilty of an offence. 7) Article 43 Constitution of Ireland.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in Section 19 of the Civil Registration Act 2004. Section 19 of the Civil Registration Act 2004 requires that when a child is born in the State, there is a duty to register the birth not later than 3 months from the date of the birth.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right, in Section 9 of the Immigration Act 2004; Section 17 of the International Protection Act 2015; Section 9 of the Employment Permits Act 2006; National Minimum Wage Act 2000. Section 9 of the Immigration Act 2004 requires that a migrant who has registered his or her permission to be in the State be issued with a 'registration certificate' that contain information re the migrant's identity and a stamp that denotes his or her residency status. Section 17 of the International Protection Act 2015 requires that an applicant for international protection be given a 'temporary residence certificate' that contains information re the person's identity and that denotes his or her status as an applicant for international protection. Section 9 of the Employment Permits Act 2006 provides that an employment permit shall specify a description of the employment in respect of which the permit has been granted and a statement of the remuneration and any deductions, where agreed, for board and accommodation or either of them in respect of the employment.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. It is a crime, though, to forge, fraudulently alter, or assist in those acts for such documents as per Section 23 of the Employment Permits Act 2006 (as amended); Section 20 of the Passports Act 2008; Section 17(6) of the International Protection Act 2015. There is no specific offence regarding the destruction of a temporary residence certificate, or a migrant's identity documents.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Section 16(1) of the Diplomatic Relations and Immunities Act, 1967. 2) Section 39(1) of the Prison Rules, 2007. 3) Prisons Act 2007. Section 6 of the Diplomatic Relations and Immunities Act of 1967 provides that the provisions of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations shall have the force of law in the State. This means, for example that consular officers shall be free to communicate with nationals of their State and to have access to them, and that those nationals shall have the same freedom with respect to communication with and access to their consular officers. This is reflected in, for example, in the Prison Rules, 2007 which provide that a foreign national shall be provided with the means to contact a consul and (Section 16(1)) and shall be entitled to receive a visit from his or her consul at any reasonable time or where he or she is a stateless person the consul of a state of his or her choosing who is willing to visit him or her (Section 39(1) of the Prison Rules). The Prison Rules are made by the Minister for Justice in exercise of the powers conferred on them by the Prisons Act 2007.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in: 1) Section 5(1) of the Immigration Act 1999. 2) Section 5 of the Immigration Act 2003. 3) Section 20(7) of the International Protection Act 2015. 5) Section 5(6)(c) of the Immigration Act 1999, as substituted by Section 78 of the International Protection Act 2015. Under Section 5(1) of the Immigration Act of 1999 and Section 5 of the Immigration Act of 2003, children under the age of 18 may not be detained for the purposes of (A) deportation or (B) removal. Furthermore, children under 18 who are applicants for international protection cannot be detained for reasons of immigration control in the manner that adult applicants for international protection can (Section 20(7) of the International Protection Act 2015).

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Pursuant to Section 5 of the Immigration Act 2003, various persons who have been unlawfully present in the State for less than (or who have been refused leave to land) three months may be may be arrested without warrant by an immigration officer or a member of the Garda S?och?na, and detained for a maximum period of 8 weeks for the purposes of removing them from the State. Various other powers of arrest and detention of migrants who are unlawfully present in the State for the purposes of their removal under Section 51A of the International Protection Act 2015; Regulation 22 of SI No. 548/2015; and Regulation 10 of SI No. 62/2018.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right 1) in Article 40.4.1 and 2 of the Irish Constitution. Article 40.4.1 of the Irish Constitution provides that 'No citizen shall be deprived of his personal liberty save in accordance with law.' Article 40.4.2 provides a mechanism to give effect to the right to liberty by permitting a judicial enquiry to ensure detention is lawful (i.e., habeas corpus). This remedy may be sought by any person, not just an Irish citizen (The State (Kugan) v O'Rourke [1985] I.R. 658). 2) Section 5 of the Immigration Act 1999. 3) Section 20 International Protection Act 2015. Detention for the purpose of immigration control in respect to applicants for international protection has a built-in periodic review by a court, as stipulated by Section 20 International Protection Act 2015. Section 20 states that, a District Judge must review the decision as soon as possible, and this review (and renewal) of detention orders must be made every 21 days. However, Irish NGO Nasc noted in 2018 that although "in theory Irish law provides opportunities for appeal and review of detention, the limited information received by detainees renders the majority of these options moot."

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) Section 5 of the Immigration Act 1999. 2) Section 5 of the Immigration Act 2003. 3) Sections 20 and 51A of the International Protection Act 2015. 4) Regulation 22 of SI No. 548/2015. 5) Regulation 10 of SI No. 62/2018. Detention of a migrant, whether for the purpose of deportation (Section 5 of the Immigration Act 1999), removal (Section 5 of the Immigration Act 2003) or immigration control of the person as an applicant for international protection (Section 20 of the International Protection Act 2015), requires an individualised determination on specified grounds.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in the Criminal Justice (UN Convention Against Torture) Act 2000. The Criminal Justice (United Nations Convention Against Torture) Act, 2000 incorporates the UN Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. It prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, regardless of citizenship status.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Code of Ethics for the Garda S?och?na (2020) by the Policing Authority states that Garda S?och?na have the discretion and authority to use significant police powers including powers to stop and search, detain and arrest people, use force, take samples and conduct surveillance. However, under Sections 2 to 4 of the Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997, unlawful use of force that does not result in death may amount to assault or assault causing harm or serious harm. Thus, while the national law does not prohibit use of force as a means of preventing migrants’ entry, the use of force is regulated and restricted.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects the right to life in Article 40.3.2 of the Irish Constitution, and in the general law restricting the use of lethal force by security officers. Murder is largely a common law offence in Ireland (albeit whose definition is supplemented by section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1964) and is not therefore fully defined in legislation. Strict policy conditions are laid down, including a requirement in all cases that all other means of achieving the purpose in question have been exhausted, before firearms may be used.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. With respect to smuggled migrants, there is no particular exemption from prosecution in legislation. It should be noted that there are provisions on arrest and detention in Section 5 of the Immigration Act 2003 for various persons who are suspected of being unlawfully present in the State for less than three months (or who have been refused leave or to land) on the basis that they have been smuggled. In such cases, if they were to make an application for international protection, they would be entitled to a temporary permission to remain under Section 16 of the International Protection Act 2015, which would change their status to a legal one ? albeit on a temporary basis for the sole purpose of the examination of their claim for international protection. Additionally, while Section 9(2) of the Ciminal Justice (Smuggling of Persons) Act 2021 excludes a person from the commission of an offence by the aiding, abetting, counselling or procuring of his or her own smuggling, it does not necessarily preclude prosecution of the smuggled party from prosecution for violation of national immigration laws. There is no domestic legal provision exempting trafficked migrants from prosecution. However, in the High Court case of Win Lin v. Governor of Cloverhill [2014] 1 I.R. 134 , it was held by Hogan J. that the courts were prepared to hold that prosecution of a victim of human trafficking constituted an abuse of process where an accused could show (a) that he or she was a victim of human trafficking and (b) that there was a real and substantial connection between his or her status as a trafficked person and the crimes that had been committed. On the facts of that particular case, it was found that the Applicant in question did not meet those criteria.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right. While Section 19(1) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956 provides that the Minister for Justice and Equality may revoke a certificate of naturalisation if he or she is satisfied, "that the person to whom it was granted has granted has, by any overt act, shown himself to have failed in his or her duty of fidelity to the nation and loyalty to the State," as of 2023, the Supreme Court decision in Damache v MJE [2020] IESC 63, [2021] 1 ILRM 121, struck this provision down as invalid. It has not been re-legislated and therefore there is no statutory procedure for the revocation of any grant of citizenship of naturalisation.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in Section 15(1) and 15A(1) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. Section 15(1) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956 provides that the Minister may grant an application for naturalisation if satisfied that the applicant, (c) has had a period of one year's continuous residence in the state immediately before the date of the application and, during the eight years immediately preceding that period, has had a total residence in the State amounting to four years; (d) intends in good faith to continue to reside in the State after naturalisation. In the case of applicants who have been married or in a civil partnership with an Irish citizen for at least 3 years, the residency requirement is reduced to a total of 3 years (in contrast with the 5 years required for applicants under s 15(1)). All periods of residence, in order to be reckonable, must be lawful.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in Section 15(1) and Section 16 Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. Section 15 (or, in the case of spouses or civil partners of Irish citizens, section 15A(1)) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended, provides for 'conditions of naturalisation' which apply to applicants for naturalisation, including humanitarian migrants (no distinction is made), and which provide for a residency requirement of one year's continuous residence in the State immediately before the date of the application and, during the eight years immediately preceding that period, a total residence in the State amounting to four years (a shorter latter period applies for spouses and civil partners of Irish citizens). Time spent in the state as an asylum seeker is not reckonable when calculating residence for granting naturalisation. If, however, an asylum seeker is granted refugee status, he or she may apply for naturalisation on the basis of 3 years of residence in the state with refugee status, a reduced temporal requirement equally applicable to stateless applicants for naturalisation (by contrast with the 5 years required under s15(1) Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956).

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in Section 15(1) and section 15A(1) Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. In the case of applicants who have been married or in a civil partnership with an Irish citizen for at least 3 years, the residency requirement is reduced to a total of 3 years (by contrast with the 5 years required for applicants under s 15(1)). Where a non-national naturalises as an Irish citizen, his or her non-national spouse or civil partner is entitled to apply for naturalisation on the same basis as the non-national spouse or civil partner of an Irish citizen under Section 15A(1) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. This is relevant to non-nationals who join their non-national partners in Ireland where the latter have been naturalised as Irish citizens. It is also possible for the minor children of non-nationals to apply for naturalisation, though the application must be made by their parent, legal guardian or a person acting on the child's behalf "in loco parentis."

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 44.2.1 of the Constitution of Ireland provides that freedom of conscience and the free profession and practice of religion are, subject to public order and morality, guaranteed to every citizen while 44.3 provides that the State shall not impose any disabilities or make any discrimination on the ground of religious profession, belief or status. Article 44.5 provides that every religious denomination shall have the right to manage its own affairs, own, acquire and administer property, movable and immovable, and maintain institutions for religious or charitable purposes. While Article 44.2.1 refers to freedom of conscience and religion in respect of citizens, it appears in practice that such freedom is also guaranteed in respect of non-citizens. However, it is unclear from case law (The State (Nicolaou) v An Bord Uchtala [1966] I.R. 567, per Henchy J.) whether the protection of Article 44.2.1 in respect of migrants is commensurate with that afforded by it to Irish citizens since it is not possible to say that the word 'citizen' is equivalent to 'person' in this context.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 40.6.1.i of the Constitution of Ireland, guarantees 'The right of the citizens to express freely their convictions and opinions,' however, it is unclear from case law whether the protection of Article 40.6.1.i in respect of migrants is commensurate with that afforded by it to Irish citizens. This is because, according to rulings found in The State (Nicolaou) v An Bord Uchtala [1966] I.R. 567, per Henchy J., it is not possible to say that the word 'citizen' is equivalent to 'person' in this, or all contexts.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 40.6.1.i of the Constitution of Ireland, guarantees 'The right of the citizens to express freely their convictions and opinions,' however, it is unclear from case law whether the protection of Article 40.6.1.i in respect of migrants is commensurate with that afforded by it to Irish citizens. This is because, according to rulings found in The State (Nicolaou) v An Bord Uchtala [1966] I.R. 567, per Henchy J., it is not possible to say that the word 'citizen' is equivalent to 'person' in this, or all contexts.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 40.6.1.iii of the Constitution of Ireland guarantees 'The right of the citizens to form associations and unions.' However, Article 40.6.2 provides that laws regulating the manner in which the right of forming associations and unions may be exercised shall contain no political, religious or class discrimination, but it is unclear from case law whether the protection of Article 40.6.1.iii in respect of migrants is commensurate with that afforded by it to Irish citizens. It is not possible to say that the word 'citizen' is equivalent to 'person' in this context (The State (Nicolaou) v An Bord Uchtala [1966] I.R. 567, per Henchy J.).

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. National law in Ireland protects this right for EU-citizens in S.I. No. 548/2015 - European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, transposing Directive 2004/38/EC (the Citizenship Directive) for EU citizens exercising their EU free movement rights. Rights to family reunification under Directive 2004/38/EC (transposed by SI No 548 of 2015) do not generally have explicit resource criteria where EU Treaty rights are being exercised, but where a person is not in employment or becomes an ‘unreasonable burden’ on public resources, a de facto resource condition is in being. Other EU-based residence rights also vary: e.g. Zhu & Chen type rights have resource criteria, but Zambrano-type rights do not. Under the 2013 Policy Document on Non-EEA family reunification, all adult sponsors are required to have a minimum level of earnings prior to being eligible to sponsor a family member. This will be set at a cumulative gross earnings figure of ?40k over 3 years where the sponsor is an Irish citizen and a higher level where the sponsor is a non-EEA national (and which increases commensurate with the number of children in the family). Social welfare payments will not be reckonable as earnings for this purpose. The financial thresholds will rise significantly where the application is made in respect of a dependent elderly parent. Any grant of immigration status in such cases will be subject to strict conditions aimed at protecting the public purse. These will include medical insurance and financial guarantees.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in The Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act 2017. Irish law makes no distinction between migrant and non-migrant victims of crime in the context of the right of access before criminal proceedings. 'Victim' in this context 'means a natural person who has suffered harm, including physical, mental or emotional harm or economic loss, which was directly caused by an offence.' This is not to say, however, that national law provides measures to safeguard migrant victims of harm from concerns they may have in respect of how such involvement might impact them if their status in the state is precarious. The Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act 2017 tranposes into Irish law Directive 2012/29/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2012 establishing minimum standards on the rights, support and protection of victims of crime, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2001/220/JHA. The latter states that its objective is to ensure that victims of crime receive appropriate information, support and protection and are able to participate in criminal proceedings. It provides that the rights set out in the Directive apply to victims regardless of their residence status.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Temporary status may be granted under provisions and exceptions in Administrative Immigration Arrangements for the Protection of Victims of Human Trafficking (March 2011) (Reference 2) and Second National Action Plan to Prevent and Combat Human Trafficking in Ireland (October 2016) (Reference 3); Section 3 of the Immigration Act 1999; Parhiar v Minister for Justice and Equality [2014] IEHC 445.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Irish law does not provide a 'best interests of the child' principle for migrant minors generally. However, there are exceptions. The International Protection Act 2015 stipulates that certain of its provisions (in particular re the asylum process, and family reunification) must be implemented having regard to the best interests of the child. Additionally, Regulation 9 of the 2018 Reception Conditions Regulations (which provide for reception conditions for applicants for international protection, giving effect to Directive 2003/9/EC (the Receptions Conditions Directive)) provides that in the application to minors of those Regulations, the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration. The 2018 Reception Conditions Regulations also provide for 'special reception needs' for 'vulnerable persons' such as a minor or an unaccompanied minor. Finally, minors generally may not be arrested and detained for the puposes of deportation or removal (Section 5(3) Immigration Act 1999 as amended; Section 5(2)(b) Immigration Act 2003), although minors may be detained for up to 12 hours prior to departure from the state so as to effect said departure.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are exceptions to the general position, but it is important to note that protections for victims of domestic violence and/or human trafficking are not designed exclusively for women, but may also be applied for the protection of men.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Ireland protects this right in 1) S.I. No. 230/2018 - European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018. 2) UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006).

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Ruvi Ziegler [2]: Avinoam Cohen

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Israel

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in HCJ 148/79 Sa'ar v. Minister of Interior. Freedom of assembly, as other civil rights, is afforded to all persons.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, those with temporary or permanent residence, including recognized refugees, can vote in local elections under Local Authorities (Elections)Act 5725-1965, Sections 6A, 11, and 13.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty 5712-1992, sections 2 &4. While the right to equality is not explicitly promulgated in Israeli constitutional arrangements, it has been read by the courts into the constitutional right to human dignity which is guaranteed to 'everyone' irrespective of their status. See CA 5535/12 Cabri v. The State of Israel (2013; Per Jusice Danziger): "In a decent society one cannot accept a double penal standard, since it does not compatible with the equality principle."

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right given that there is no general right to counsel, but pursuant to the prohibition of trafficking in persons (legislative amendments) Act 2006 the Legal Aid Act 1962 has been amended to include provision for victims of human trafficking (see section 1 of the Appendix to the Act). In addition, in (relatively rare) cases where immigration detention is considered as a consequence of criminal proceedings, appointed state defense attorneys may advise immigrant clients in proceedings where immigration detention follows criminal proceedings.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Public Defenders Act 5755-1995, Section 18. The right to interpretation in criminal proceedings is granted pursuant to meeting several tests, including the type of proceeding, severity of the offence, and financial status.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In Israel, civil or criminal sanctions for unauthorized entry are regulated by Law of Entry, 5712-1952; Prevention of infiltration (offenses and jurisdiction) Act 5714-1954 chapter B. Immigrants can, and sometimes are criminalized for illegal entry. The anti-infiltration Law applies to 'infiltrators', defined in section 1 as persons who are not residents and who enter Israel not through a border post. Section 10 creates a 'presumption of infiltration'. Chapter B lists offenses.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants, even though the foreign worker act requires employers to provide adequate housing to workers.The eligibility criteria for public housing effectively exclude migrants by requiring residence in public housing for at least five years, whereas residence in public housing requires an eligibility certificate for public housing issued by the Housing Ministry that would not be issued to a migrant pursuant to the criteria. The relevant legislation in relation to this issue are 1) Rights of a Resident in Public Housing Act 5758-1998; 2) Foreign Workers Act, 5751-1991.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Students Rights Act, 5761-2000, art. 3. Administrative Petition 29883-07-11 Manjan v. Eilat Municipality (District Court 2.8.2011).

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right for all persons; however non citizens may be subject to different tuition fees. See Student Rights Act 5767-2007, sections 3,4.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel regulates the authority of the Minister of Interior to grant or deny immigrant status. Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952, section 11(a)(2). That law has been interpreted as enabling the minister to condider migrants’ criminal and other convictions in this regard. Since ministeral discretion is extremely wide with regards to all types of residency and migration status, there is no limitation to the type of offense that can trigger the loss of status, of any kind. However, the consequence in terms of loss of status generally depends on the type of status. In cases of permanent residency, which applies almost exclusively to indigenous residents of East Jeruslaem, only major offenses may lead to loss of status, as was interpreted by the court. However, this category of status is generally unavailable to migrant workers. In case of weak and temporary classes of status, even minor offenses can lead to revocation or non-renewal of status.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in HCJ 4702/94 El Tai V. MInister of Interior (1995) ; Convention Against Torture. The right to non-refoulement has long been accepted as a principle of customary international law and is used in providing protection against return to torture in practice. Israel is a party to the Convention against Torture, but has not incorporated it into domestic law. Therefore, there is no specific legislation.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to persecution based on race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion in Ministry of Interior, 'General' section, PIBA, Refugee Status Determination Procedure No.: 5.2.0012 (Procedure for dealing with political asylum seekers in Israel- updated 21.3.2022). See also HCJ 4702/94 El Tai v Ministry of the Interior stating that the principle of non-refoulement is not limited to 'refugees' but rather applies in Israel in respect of any exercise of governmental authority relates to expulsion [7]. Israel is also a party to the Refugee Convention and Protocol, 1951 and 1967.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: The national law in Israel protects this right only in relation to the right to life but not on the basis of the risk of serious deprivations of other fundemental human rights. The courts in Israel have held the right of non-refoulement is not restricted to refugees fearing persecution but applies to all government action in the context of expulsion. See: HCJ 4702/94 El Tai v Ministry of the Interior.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no legislative or procedural requirement to inform persons that they are entitled to apply for asylum. The Ministry of the Interior occasionally publishes notices of a general nature on its website and displays notices in its offices, but the procedure does not require that the government will advise of the possibility of such grounds for status / protection.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Administrative Petition Appeal 8101/15 Cegata V. The MInister of Interior, provided that sufficient guarantees will be provided against subsequent expulsion.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Law of Entry, 1952. Although there is no formal requirement of an individualized assessment given the wide discretion granted to the Minister of the Interior under the Entry into Israel Act to revoke residence or other permits, general administrative law principles subject expulsion decisions to these general standards. See HCJ 282/88 Awad v. The Prime Minister PD 42(2) 424 (1988)in the context of permanent residents; HCJ 7302/07 Hotline for Migrant Workers V. MInister of Defense (Supreme Court, 7.7.2011) in the context of border pushbacks.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952, section 13X. The provision determines the right of an individual who considers themselves harmed by an authority's decision related to permits/residence/expulsion/citizenship to appeal to the appeals tribunal.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no provision for automatic citizenship for those born stateless.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel provides settled migrants with legal avenues to facilitate reunification with immediate or non-dependent family members in certain limited circumstances under Ministry of Interior, Procedure 5.2.2011: 'Procedure for giving status to foreign spouse married to a permanent resident' (updated 10.12.2020); and Citizenship Act 5712-1952. Most migrants in Israel cannot become permanent residents. Migrants with temporary residence permits, such as refugees, may sponsor a spouse to remain in Israel, but not to reunite with a spouse living abroad.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law Israel provides judicial remedy to appeal the refusal by the authorities to allow family reunification in Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952, section 13X(a).

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Israel recognizes same sex relationships under the family reunification framework in Ministry of Interior, Procedure 5.2.0009: 'Procedure for granting status to spouses of Israelis, including same-sex couples (updated 28.3.2022).

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: Does not apply

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. However, the Law of Entry, 1952, art. 3A (b1) provides the authority to the Ministry of the Interior to provide discretionary amnesties to irregular migrant workers. This has most commonly been applied with care workers who are sponsored by employers with a demonstrated need. There is no general right to regularize status for irregular migrants.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Labour courts Act 5729-1969, section 29. The section establishes the court's jurisdiction to hear cases involving labour disputes, including the determination of the existence of employment relations. General labour law applies to all workers equally.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While emergency health care is open to all, access to other health care services by migrant workers is only guaranteed on the basis of participation in private insurance plans. See: National Health Insurance Act 5754-1994 section 3; Patient's rights Act 5756-1996, Section 3(b).

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, those with temporary or permanent residence, including recognized refugees, can run for public office in local elections under Local Authorities (Elections) Act 5725-1965, Section 7.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel prohibits discrimination against migrants on the basis of their status as a migrant in Prevention of Discrimination in Products, Services, and Entry into Public Spaces Act 5761-2000 section 3(A). This anti-discrimination law protects migrants from discrimination, including on the basis of nationality, country of origin and personal status.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel prohibits discrimination against migrants on the ground of race or ethnicity in Prevention of Discrimination in Products, Services, and Entry into Public Spaces Act 5761-2000 section 3(A).

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in: 1) Equal Pay for Female worker and Male worker Act 5756-1996, Section 2. The Act was passed primarily to guarantee gender equality (as its title suggests) but its language makes it applicable to all workers. 2) Moreover, the Supreme Court in HCJ 2293/17 Gresgaher v Knesset (23 April 2020) struck down part the ‘deposit law’, which required asylum-seekers to deposit 20% of their salary in a dedicated fund which they can only access upon leaving Israel, holding it to be unconstitutional. However, some laws of general application (such as those regarding overtime pay) do not apply to some workers (such as care workers). See: Further Hearing (Supreme Court, extended panel) 10007/09 GLotten v. the National Labor Court (18.3.2013).

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in HCJ 4542/02 Kav La'oved et al v Government of Israel et al, 61(1) PD 346 (2006); Foreign Workers Act, 5751-1991. A 'binding arrangement' policy whereby migrant workers were bound to an individual employer was held to be unconstitutional by the HCJ in the cited judgment; sector 'binding arrangements' still apply in the care sector. On the other hand, NB new procedure, 10.1.0025, ‘handling the setting of condition for purposes of geographical delineation and licenses of asylum seekers and refugees’ introduced on 30 June 2022 and entered into force on 1 October 2022, prohibits asylum-seekers from working in most major cities in Israel (except in construction, agriculture, institutional care, hotels, or restaurants).

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects migrant spouse/partner of relevant high-skilled workers' right to work in Entry into Israel Act 5712- 1952, Section 2(c).

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952, Section 3A.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in HCJ 11437/05 Kav Laoved (Workers hotline) v. Ministry of Interior (13.4.2011). Generally all labor law protections apply, but not always, as in the case of work and rest (overtime hours). See: Further Hearing (Supreme Court, extended panel) 10007/09 Glotten v. the National Labor Court (18.3.2013).

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects migrant workers’ rights to social security protections in Expanding Ordinance (consolidated version) for Mandatory Pension 5771-2011. Only residents are entitled to national-security based plans of social security . Migrant workers are not considered residents and are explicitly excluded from the law. However, some social security protections that are mandated by labor law such as pension payments and workers protection regulations, apply to all workers, including migrant workers.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Eligibility for unemployment benefits is limited to residents under the National Insurance Act (Consolidated version) 5755- 1995, Section 2A(b)(3).The law excludes holders of foreign workers’ permits and therefore the vast majority of migrant workers from this protection.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Foreign workers Act 5751-1991, section 1.15(a) prohibts the holding of identity documents of migrant workers, which is a criminal offense.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel requires birth registration of migrant children, regardless of their status, in Population Registry Act 5725-1965, section 6.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Israel only mandates the issuing of documents that recognize migrants’ residency and work status but not identity in Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952, section 2.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in the holding and presentation of an Identification Card Act 5743-1982, Section 3 which requires a resident 16 years of age or older to hold an ID (or another official document pursuant to minister of interior regulation- section 6) and renders it an offense not to do so, subject to certain conditions. The Passport Act, 1952, section 8(a) prohibits anyone from destroying passports or identification documents; Penal Law, 1977, Section 376A prohibits the withholding of identification documents.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Israel signed the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations on February 25, 1964 but has not incorporated it into domestic law. Although customary international law provisions apply directly as provided in HCJ 279/51 Amsterdam v Minister of Finance, 6(2) PD 945 (1952), the government has never taken a position as to whether the obligation to allow consular communication is required as a matter of customary international law.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrant children. Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952, section 13 (detention) does not exempt migrant children from being subject to detention pursuant to the general conditions in the legislation. However, detention of children is regularly avoided. The Population Immigration and Border Authority (PIBA) regulations on treatment of unaccompanied minors (10.1.0016) prohibits the detention of unaccompanied minors under 14 and limits the detention of older children. In addition, courts regularly restrict the detention of minors, including accompanied minors.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Act authorizes detention of persons who are 'illegally present' until their departure or expulsion; pursuant to case-law, the prerogative under section 13F(a)(4) of the Act to release from detention persons held for more than 60 days is a mandatory requirement, unless the detainee is deemed to be non-cooperative with their removal. The courts have provided additional protections for asylum seekers. See: Administrative Petition Appeal 8101/15 Cegata V. Minister of Interior (Supreme Court; 28.8.2017). In Cegata, the court struck down a practice of detention aimed to persuade asylum sekeers to agree to be removed to another country of asylum, and in a trilogy of cases ending in Desta, the court ruled that prolonged detention or placement in a remote "open facility" of asylum seekers pending decision is unconstitutional (thus striking down legislation). Also see: HCJ 8665/14 Desta V. the Knesset (Israeli Parliament) (Supreme Court; 11.8.2015).

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in relation to all three aspects of detention (legality, conditions, or length of detention) in "Entry into Israel Act" 5712-1952, section 13D & 13N. This is also derived from the framework legislation in Basic Law: the Judiciary, section 15.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in HCJ 5100/94 Public Committee Against Torture (6 September 1999); HCJ 4702/94 El Tai V. MInister of Interior (Supreme Court; 1995); and Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952, section 13D.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right, in relation to risk of torture but not in relation to cruel, inhumane, or degrading treatment or punishment, in HCJ 5100/94 Public Committee Against Torture (6 September 1999) and HCJ 4702/94 El Tai V. MInister of Interior (Supreme Court; 1995), which recognized non-refoulement as an obligation in cases of risk of torture following removal. Israel signed the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment on 22 October 1986 and ratified it on 3 October 1991 but has not incorporated it into domestic law. Neverthless, there is a legal presumption that national law should be interpreted in accordance with International Law, and customary international law has direct effect in domestic law, as stated in HCJ 279/51 Amsterdam v Minister of Finance, 6(2) PD 945 (1952). There is a general prohibition on the use of torture by state authorities pursuant to the court's judgment (above). The judgment applies to state authorities' actions irrespective of who they are directed against. The judgment left open the possibility of ex-post-facto exoneration in a 'ticking-bomb' scenario.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Police conduct is generally governed by the Police Ordinance (The Police Ordinance (new version) 5731-1971 & criminal procedure law (consolidated version) 5742-1982) but no specific prohibition is included in the context of migration enforcement.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The right to life under the Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty 5752-1992 (sections 2,4,8,11) applies to 'everyone' and restricts state authorities. In turn, the principle of proportionality applies to all actions of public authorities pursuant to section 8, but no specific prohibition has been recognized in the context of migration enforcement.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for smuggled migrants. However, national law in Israel exempts trafficked migrants from criminal prosecutions in Prevention of Human Trafficking (legislative amendments) Act 5763-2003, section 375A; Prohibition of trafficking in persons (legislative amendments) Act 5766-2006; Art. 377A to the Penal Law (1977); and State Attorney Guidelines no. 2.32 (23.5.2017).

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel provides that convictions for criminal or other offenses leads to a loss of the citizenship status of naturalized migrants in Citizenship Act 5712-1952, Section 11. CITATION2: Citizenship Act 5712-1952, Section 11. Loss of citizenship requires a ministerial decision and court approval, and citizenship can be revoked in very few cases after convictions for serious terror-related offenses.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right as the Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952 sections 3A,4 restricts foreign workers' permits to a maximum 5 years (after renewals), except in the care sector. However, the Act gives the Ministry of the Interior discretion to substitute any residence permit for another permit, including permanent resident permit, but that does not constitute a right to have a pathway to citizenship or (permant) residence. Pathways to citizenship are set in the Citizenship Act 5712-1952, section 5.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, the Citizenship Act 5712-1952 gives the Ministry of the Interior discretion to substitute any residence permit for another permit, including permanent resident permit. There have been instances in which the Minister used this discretion to provide status for humanitarian migrants but the availability of this discretion does not constitute a right.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel provides pathway to citizenship for family migrants by meeting certain residence requirements in Citizenship Act 5712-1952 section 5. The law applies to partners of Israeli Citizens (including civil partners) provided that there are no security grounds for refusal. In addition, the Minister of the Interior can, at their discretion, relieve a spouse of an Israeli citizen from requirements under section 5. The requirements cited in section 5 include having some knowledge of the Hebrew language, minimum residence, renouncication of previous citizenship, intention to settle in the state, eligiblity to be a permanent resident.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel allows some migrants to obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin in Citizenship Act 5712-1952, sections 5, 7; but see section 2 (the route open for Jews and those of Jewish descent). For family migrants (or other special cases) where citizenship can be obtained, renunciation is required but dual nationality can be permitted upon request and decision of the Minister of Interior (generally allowed).

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in HCJ 73/53 Kol Ha'am v Minister of the Interior; Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty, Sections 2 and 4.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in HCJ 73/53 Kol Ha'am v Minister of the Interior; Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty, Sections 2 and 4.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in HCJ 73/53 Kol Ha'am v Minister of the Interior; Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty, Sections 2 and 4.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in: 1) Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty, Sections 2 and 4. 2) Collective Agreement Dispute 18/08 Builders Association- National Labor Association (2009). 3) HCJ 73/53 Kol Ha'am v Minister of the Interior.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Citizenship Act 5712-1952, sections 5,7. The law and procedures do not include resource-based requirements.The provision sets residence and other requirements which may or may not be waived in respect of family reunification candidates pursuant to section 7 thereof. The conditions in the provision are non resource-based.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Rights of Victims of Offences Act 5761-2001, Section 2. Even if the law is infrequently used by migrant victims, the provision does not distinguish citizens from non-citizens. It defines a 'victim of an offense' as anyone (irrespective of their legal status) who is the direct victim of an offense as well as family members (separately defined) of deceased victim.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel provides migrant victims of crime an avenue to immigration status or relief from expulsion as a result of being victim of a crime in Entry into Israel Act 5712-1952, sections 2 & 4; Population, Immigration and Borders Agency (PIBA) Procedure for granting status to victims of trafficking in women on humanitarian grounds, no. 6.3.0007; PIBA Procedure for granting status to victims of slavery and servitude on humanitarian grounds, no. 6.3.0008.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in Guardianship and Legal Capacity Act 5722-1962, section 17; Administrative Petition Appeal 10993/08 Ploni (John Doe) V. the State of Israel - MoI (Supreme Court, 10.3.2010), as well as by the Administrative Petition Appeal 9890/09 (2013) Nawa v. Ministry of Interior where the court required the best interest of the child.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Israel protects this right in the context of trafficked persons in Administrative Appeal Request 7938/17 Plonit (John Doe) v. PIBA (Supreme Court, 13.9.2018). In other contexts, courts have overturned immigration decisions when the vulnerability of women was not taken into consideration such as in Administrative Appeal Request 5040/18 (Supreme Court, 9.2.2020), but this is done on a case by case basis.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are general protections for persons with disabilities as outlined by the Equal rights for Persons with Disabilities Act 5758-1998, but no known cases where such protections were given special consideration in migration-related contexts. Israel is a party to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) but there are no special protections for migrants. Israel signed the CRPD on 30 March 2007 and ratified it on 28 September 2012. However, the convention does not have direct effect in Israeli Law which is a dualist system in terms of international law.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Adele Del Guercio. [2]: Chiara Favilli.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Italy.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) the Italian Constitution Articles 17, which grants everyone, citizens and aliens, the right to peaceful assembly. 2) Article 2 of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139).

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Migrants, generally, do not have a right to vote in Italy. The only exceptional migrants who have the right to vote in local or regional elections are citizens from the EU.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in 1) the Italian Constitution, Article 24. 2) Article 2(1) of the Legislative Decree No. 286/1998. In general, national law provides migrants with the right to equal protection before the law in administrative, civil and criminal courts and tribunals on the basis of equality with Italian citizens. However, Italian law does not recognize the right of appeal to the judge of second instance in the case of asylum seekers when they have had the denial of the protection by Territorial Commission (the competent administrative authority for the examination of requests for international protection). Asylum seekers only have the right of appeal to a judge in the first instance, and if the pronunciation of this is negative, they do not have the right to appeal to the judge of second instance.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) the Italian Constitution, Article 24, which recognizes the right to legal advocacy. For this right to be effective, the Italian government established rules to provide free legal aid to those who cannot pay, including migrants. 2) Legislative Decree No. 286/1998, Article 119 of the Aliens Act.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) Article 143, Procedural Criminal Law, which provides that free translation services are to be made available to all persons, including migrants, who request them during criminal proceedings. 2) Legislative decree 4 March no. 32 (implementation of directive 2010/64/EU).

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 10-bis of the Law on Immigration, unauthorized entry is punishable by an administrative sanction, a fine of ?5,000-10,000.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in Article 40 of the Aliens act, Legislative decree no. 286/1998, which states that migrants with a residence card and those who are legally resident in Italy, with a residence permit of at least two years and exercising a regular activity of subordinate work or self-employment, have the right of access, on an equal basis with Italian citizens, to accommodation in public residential buildings (Article 40.6). Irregular migrants do not have this right.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) Article 34 of the Italian Constitution, which states that primary education, lasting a minimum of eight years, is free and compulsory for any person, including foreigners. 2) Articles 2(5) and 38 of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139), which provide that primary public education is compulsory for minor foreign migrants in Italy.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right for certain visa types in Article 38 of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139). Only legally resident foreigners have the right to access public adult educational institutions and services for migrants (such as degree-level courses and vocational training) on an equal basis with citizens.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) Articles 380-381 of the Royal Decree 19 October 1930, no. 1398, Criminal Code, in OJ no. 251 of 26.10.1930. 2) Articles 13(1,2) and 15 of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139).

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in Art. 19(1.1) of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139). Article 19 prohibits refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Refoulement is also banned in the cases of foreigners living with relatives within the second degree or with a spouse of Italian nationality; of women who are pregnant or in the six months following the birth of a child; of foreigners who have particularly serious health conditions; and of unaccompanied minors; of asylum seekers integrated. In this last case they can obtain a resident permit for special protection.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in Art. 19(1.1) of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139). Article 19 of the law on immigration bans refoulement for those who risk persecution for reasons of race, sex, language, citizenship, religion, political opinions, personal or social conditions, or those who risk being sent back to a state in which they are not protected from persecution. In case of risk of return to persecution, asylum seekers can obtain the refugee status but if it is not possible because of the application of exclusion clauses he can obtain a resident permit for special protection.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) Art. 19(1.1) of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139). 2) Article 14 of Legislative Decree 19.11.2007, no. 251. 3) Legislative decree No. 18/2014, which provides international protection (which includes the prohibition of refoulement and the issue of a residence permit) in cases where there is a serious deprivation of fundamental human rights (such as the right to life). Asylum seekers can obtain a resident permit for special protection in case of vulnerabilities connected with the deprivation of economic and social rights in the country of origin, as the deprivation of house or water or food.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) Article 10-ter, Legislative Decree No. 286/1998. Art. 3(2). 2) 14(1) of EU Regulation 2016/399 of 9 March 2016 on a Union Code on the rules governing the movement of persons across borders (Schengen Borders Code).

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) Article 19, Legislative Decree No. 286/1998. 2) Legislative Decree 19.11.2007, no. 251.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in Articles 13-14 of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139).

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Italy protects this right in 1) Articles 13 and 14(8) of the Aliens Act (Decreto legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286, Testo unico delle disposizioni concernenti la disciplina dell'immigrazione e norme sulla condizione dello straniero, OJ no.191 del 18-8-1998, Suppl. Ordinario n. 139). Any order of expulsion must be validated by the judge, and the migrant who is affected by an expulsion order must be assisted by a lawyer who will also participate in the hearing.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for adult migrants. National law in Italy protects this right for children in Article 9(1)(e) of Law 91/1992, which guarantees citizenship to migrants and children of migrants who would otherwise be stateless conditional to 5 years of uninterrupted legal residency in Italy. Adult stateless persons may apply to acquire citizenship after five years of regilar stay, like refugees, according to Articles 9 and 16 of Law 5 febbraio 1992, no. 91, (Nuove norme sulla cittadinanza), in OJ no.38 of 15-2-1992).

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
