question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Kenya

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Article 37 of the Kenyan Constitution. Article 37 specifically states: "Every person has the right, peaceably and unarmed, to assemble, to demonstrate, to picket, and to present petitions to public authorities." 2) Article 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) further provides for the right to peacefully assemble with no restrictions except those imposed in conformity with the law in interests of national security or public safety, public order , protection of public health and morals or protection of rights and freedoms. Kenya has ratified the ICCPR in 1972 and the law is integrated into national law via Article 2(6) of the Constitution. Migrants can therefore enjoy the freedom to assemble, demonstrate, picket and petition equally just as other citizens do without being subjected to any discrimination.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. 1) Under Article 83 (1) of the Constitution, "A person qualifies for registration as a voter at elections or referenda if the person: (a) is an adult citizen; (b) is not declared to be of unsound mind; (c) has not been convicted of an election offence during the preceding five years." 2) Section 3 of the Elections Act, 2011.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Kenya (2010). Article 27(1) states that: "Every person is equal before the law and has the right to equal protection and equal benefit of the law." and Article 50 which states "Every person has the right to have any dispute that can be resolved by the application of law decided in a fair and public hearing before a court or, if appropriate, another independent and impartial tribunal or body." Article 47 stipulates that every person has the right to administrative action that is expeditious, efficient, lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair. The Court in Republic v Director of Immigration Services Ex-Parte Planet Motors Company Limited & another [2016] eKLR affirmed that these provisions apply to migrants as well when it stated that "In the instant case, there is absolutely no evidence to show that the applicants were heard or given an opportunity to be heard before the decision to watch list the 2nd applicant by the immigration department. Accordingly, without much ado, the provisions of Article 47 of the Constitution on the right to expeditious, efficient, lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair administrative action; and Article 50(1) of the Constitution on the right to a fair hearing was violated. In addition, the Fair Administrative Action Act No4 of 2015 was violated by the respondent."

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Kenya does not protect this right since asylum seekers and refugees are entitled to legal representation but at their own expense. There is no similar provision for other categories of migrants. 1) Section 12 (4) of the Refugees Act provides that, 'The Applicant(asylum seeker or refugee) in immigration proceedings shall present his claim in person but retains the right to be accompanied by legal practitioner if he or she desires, provided that the expense for legal representation shall not be borne by the Department.'

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Article 50 (1) (m) of the Constitution of Kenya which provides that in order to have a fair hearing, an accused person must have the assistance of an interpreter without payment if the accused person cannot understand the language used at the trial.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: Section 53 of the Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 makes it an offense for a person to unlawfully enter or be unlawfully present in Kenya in contravention of the Act. If convicted for the said offence, the person is liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand shillings or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three (3) years or to both. The Act also makes it an offence for a person not being a citizen of Kenya, engages in any employment, occupation, trade, business or profession, whether or not for profit or reward, without being authorized to do so by a work permit, or exempted from this provision by regulations made under the Act.COMMENT2:1. Migrants can be held civilly and criminally liable in Kenya under the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 and the Penal Code Chapter 63 Laws of Kenya. Section 51 (2) of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 allows civil and criminal sanctions in providing that In any prosecution for an offense under the Act, in any proceedings of a civil nature, and in any proceedings in the nature of habeas corpus or under Article 22 of the Constitution,2010, any document lawfully obtained from, any person by immigration officer in the exercise of his powers under this Act is admissible in evidence.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Article 43 (1) (b) of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, which states: "Every person has the right to accessible and adequate housing, and to reasonable standards of sanitation." 2) The Housing Act, Chapter 117 Laws of Kenya and the Regulations thereunder.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in 1) Article 43(1)(f) of the Constitution of Kenya which states: "Every person has the right to education." Furthermore, Article 53(1)(b) of the Kenyan Constitution guarantees every child, regardless of their nationality or immigration status, the right to "free and compulsory basic education." 2) Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act 2011, Section 36. 3) Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Regulations, 2012- Regulation 30(2). 4) The Basic Education Act 2014.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in 1) Article 43(1)(f) of the Constitution of Kenya which states: "Every person has the right to education." 2) Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act (2011), Section 36. 3) Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Regulations, 2012- Regulation 30. Although the regulations require a pass to be issued by immigration authorities before a migrant can attend an adult education institution, all categories of migrants, including irregular migrants, are in principle entitled to a pass if they meet the relevant conditions after being admitted to an educational institution.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Loss of residence status can be on minor administrative issues like failing to take up a job within 90 days of work permit approval.National Law in Kenya regulates the ability of migrants criminal and other convictions affecting residence status in Sections 38, 29, 41 and 42 of the Citizenship and Immigration Act.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Refugees Act, 2021- Section 29, which protects return if life, physical integrity or liberty would be threatened on account of external aggression, occupation, foreign domination or events seriously disturbing public order in part or whole of that country. 2) The Constitution of Kenya Articles 2 (5) and (6), 25 and 29. 3)The Prevention of Torture Act 2017, Section 21 (2) and the United Nations Convention Against Torture (CAT) and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Kenya ratified CAT on February 21, 1987, which is part of the laws of Kenya by virtue of Article 2 (6) of the Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) the Refugee Act No. 10 of 2021 under Section 29 (1) (a) which states that "No person shall be refused entry into Kenya, expelled, extradited from Kenya or returned to any other country or be subjected to any similar measure if, as a result of such refusal, expulsion, return or other measure, such person is compelled to return to or remain in a country where the person may be subject to persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion." 2) Constitution of Kenya under Article 2 (5) and (6) which makes the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees part of Kenyan law.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Section 29 of the Refugees Act No. 10 of 2021. This law protects against return for serious of fundamental human rights in circumstances that may not constitute persecution in protecting against return when the person's life, physical integrity or liberty may be threatened on account of external aggression, occupation, foreign domination or events seriously disturbing public order in part or whole of that country. The Court in the case of Kenya National Commission on Human Rights & another v Attorney General & 3 others [2017] eKLR held: "The basic principle of refugee law is, non-refoulement which refers to the obligation of States not to refoule, or return, a refugee to “the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.” 2) The 1969 the Organization of African Unity Convention Governing Specific Aspects of Refugee Problems in Africa, which was incorporated into national law via Article 2(5) and (6) of the Kenyan Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right specifically in national laws.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right for all migrants. There is a general obligation for the state to provide fair administrative action for all persons as outlined in Article 47 of the Constitution. More particularly, this right exists for refugees as outlined in Section 19 (3) of the Refugees Act, 2021. The Court in Kenya National Commission on Human Rights & another v Attorney General & 3 others [2017] eKLR recently affirmed the application of Article 47 to refugees when it granted "A declaration be and is hereby issued declaring that to the extent that the decision of the Government of the Republic of Kenya to close Daadab refugee camp was undertaken without giving the stakeholders and the affected parties an opportunity to make representations either in person or through their representatives, the right to a fair administrative action as guaranteed by Article 47 of the constitution has been denied, violated, infringed or is threatened, hence the said decision is null and void." Other categories of migrants are accorded this right under Section 40 of the KICA that provides that the Director is obligated to give written reasons for their decisions in issuing of permits to applicants for permits. Section 57 of the KICA further allows these migrants to file reviews and appeals to the Cabinet Secretary and the High Court.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right for all categories of migrants. Section 40 (3) & (5) of the Kenyan Citizenship and Immigration Act (KCIA) provides that in issuing permits to migrants, the applicant is allowed to submit an application together with supporting documents in order to satisfy the Committee that he has met the requirements relating to the particular class of permit. The Committee may request for additional information and where necessary, summon the applicants, require production of production supporting documents. This right for asylum seekers and refugees is provided under Section 12 (3) of the Refugees Act, 2021 which states that the Commissioner shall, on receiving an application, invite the applicant to appear before him or her, to provide oral or documentary evidence in support of the claim for asylum.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Kenya, 2010 which provides for citizenship by registration for stateless persons. Upon meeting residency requirements, such persons obtain citizenship and their children may subsequently be deemed citizens by birth. 2) Section 15 of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act (KCIA), 2011 provides that stateless persons who have been living in Kenya for a continuous period since 12th December, 1963, shall be deemed to have been lawfully resident and may, on application, in the prescribed manner be eligible to be registered as citizens of Kenya if those persons have adequate knowledge of Kiswahili or a local dialect; have not been convicted of an offense and have not been sentenced to imprisonment for a term of three years or longer; and intend upon registration as a citizen to continue to permanently reside in Kenya or to maintain a close and continuing association with Kenya; and the person understands the rights and duties of a citizen. A child of stateless persons who has attained the age of eighteen years and whose parents are or in the case of deceased parents were eligible to be registered as a citizen may, upon application be registered as a citizen of Kenya if among other things there is sufficient proof that the parents of that person fall within the class of persons referred to in the Act; the person was born in Kenya and has been continuously living in Kenya since birth; and the person does not hold and has never held a passport or identification documents of any other country. 3) Section 17 of the KCIA provides that a person who has attained the age of eighteen years and whose parents are or in the case of deceased parents were eligible to be registered as a citizen under stateless persons or migrants may, upon application in the prescribed manner be registered as a citizen of Kenya.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right for settled migrants in: 1) Sections 11, 14, 36 and 37 and Regulation 27 of the Kenyan Citizenship and Immigration Act (2011). The Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act (KCIA), 2011 only provides for the DEPENDANT pass, which can be utilized by families to facilitate reunification. A Dependent Pass can only be given where a party can actually prove dependence, age, marital status, health status, as well as some other criteria, according to Section 36 of the KCIA. According to Regulation 27, a person who is lawfully in or entitled to enter Kenya, by virtue of being a citizen of Kenya; having been issued with a permit; being an exempted person; being a person to whom section 34(3) of the KCIA applies; or being a permanent resident, may apply, on behalf of his or her dependant to an immigration officer, in Form 28 set out in the First Schedule, for a dependant’s pass.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Articles 22, 45, 50 and 165 of the Kenyan Constitution. Article 45 of the Constitution recognizes the family as the basic unit of the society which should be protected. As such no measures should be taken which are skewed together interfering with family formation or reunification. Furthermore, Articles 22, 50 and 165 guarantee all persons, including migrants, the right to redress in court. As such, migrants can apply to the High Court for a review of refusal by the authorities. The Court in Kenya National Commission on Human Rights & another v Attorney General & 3 others [2017] eKLR held: "Our Constitution makers in their wisdom thought that no fetters should be placed on the right of an aggrieved party to seek relief from this court under Article 22 of the constitution. Article 22 of the Constitution which I describe as the “heart and soul” of the Constitution guarantees the right to move the High Court for the enforcement of all or any of the fundamental rights conferred by chapter four of the Constitution."

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Kenya does not recognize same sex marriages. The Constitution of Kenya in article 45 recognizes the family unit as made up of one male and one female. Furthermore, the Penal code, Cap 63 of Laws of Kenya in section 162 and 165 criminalizes homosexuality with a punishment of 14 years. The Eric Gitari Case, a landmark case in Kenya, whose judgment was delivered on 24th May 2019 reiterates the above position on homosexuality being illegal in the country.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya provides temporary migrant workers with avenues to become lawfully settled without conditions (such as on visa type) in the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011- Section 37 (b) and Regulation 19 of the Regulations, 2012.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 40 (3) of the Act further provides that the Director shall not issue a permit of the required class to a person who is a prohibited immigrant or an inadmissible person. Section 11 of the Act also provides that prohibited immigrants may not acquire citizenship by marriage. Irregular migrant workers cannot regularize their status as long as this irregularity is discovered by the authorities.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right for migrants in regular status in Articles 27, and 41 as well as Section 5 (1) (b) of the Employment Act of Kenya. This act requires that the Cabinet Secretary, the Employment & Labour Relations Court and labor officers promote and guarantee equality of opportunity for a person who is a migrant worker or a member of the family of the migrant worker lawfully within Kenya. This includes ensuring the right to redress if the terms of an employee's contract have been violated. Article 27 lists the grounds for discrimination, but the list is not exhaustive, and Article 41 provides fair labor practices, generally, for both citizens and migrants.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Articles 43 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya (2010) which states: "Every person has the right: (a) to the highest attainable standard of health, which includes the right to health care services, including reproductive health care." Furthermore, Article 56 of the Constitution states: "The State shall put in place affirmative action programmes designed to ensure that minorities and marginalised groups: (e) have reasonable access to water, health services and infrastructure. 2) Kenya Citizenship & Immigration Act, 2011 provides that immigrants permitted to work or study in the country have access to public health sector services under the Kenya National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF), but permanent residents of Kenya have access to health insurance based on their residence and not their employment status.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In Kenya, the right to run for public office at the regional or national level is regulated by several laws and regulations including: 1) Constitution of Kenya: Particularly Chapter Seven on Representation of the People, provides the foundational framework for running for public office. It outlines the qualifications, eligibility criteria, and processes for various positions, including the presidency, parliamentarians, senators, governors, and members of county assemblies. It is a requirement for each of these positions for a candidate to be a Kenyan citizen for a given period of time. For instance a presidential candidate must be a citizen by birth, a governor as well as a member of county assembly and member of parliament must have been a Kenyan citizen for at least ten (10) immediately preceding the election date. 2) Election Act, 2011, Sections 22-25 which outline the processes, requirements, and timelines related to candidate nomination during elections. These provisions outline Kenyan citizenship requirements for various elected positions.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 27 of the Constitution talks about non discrimination: "The State shall not discriminate directly or indirectly against any person on any ground, including race, sex, pregnancy, marital status, health status, ethnic or social origin, colour, age, disability, religion, conscience, belief, culture, dress, language or birth." However, there is no mention of non-discrimination on the basis of status as a migrant.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in Article 27 (4) of the Constitution of Kenya, which says: "The State shall not discriminate directly or indirectly against any person on any ground, including race, sex, pregnancy, marital status, health status, ethnic or social origin, colour, age, disability, religion, conscience, belief, culture, dress, language or birth."

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Article 41 of the Constitution of Kenya (2010) which states: "Article 41 (1): Every person has the right to fair labour practices. (2): Every worker has the right?(a): to fair remuneration; (b): to reasonable working conditions. (c): to form, join or participate in the activities and programmes of a trade union; and (d): to go on strike." 2) Employment Act of Kenya (2007) in Sections 5 and 10. Section 5(5) of the Employment Act, 2007 states that an employer must pay his employees equal remuneration for work of equal value. Section 10(2)(h)(i) further states that a written contract service shall state the remuneration, scale or rate of remuneration, the method of calculating that remuneration and details of any other benefits and the intervals at which the remuneration is paid. Furthermore, section 5(1)(b) makes it a duty of the Minister in charge of Employment matters, respective labour officers and the Industrial Court (the Employment and Labour Relations Court) to promote and guarantee equality of opportunity for a person who is a migrant worker or a member of the family of a migrant worker lawfully within Kenya. Accordingly, migrant workers have the right to equal pay as that received by local workers doing the same work without discrimination and in contractual service. Their contract must set out the amount, rate and calculating method including benefits.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya regulates this right in: 1) Section 41(1) (c) of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 which provides that a migrant may have their work permit invalidated if they engage in any employment, occupation, trade business or profession, whether or not for remuneration or profit, other than the employment, occupation, trade, business or profession in respect of which the permit was issued. Employers are obligated under Regulation 22 (1) where the holder of a work permit ceases to engage in the employment in respect of which the work permit was issued, within fifteen days from the date of such cessation, to report, in writing, to the Director that the holder has ceased to engage in such employment.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. A spouse/partner of a principal migrant can only come into the country on a dependant pass. A dependant pass document is issued to a person whose spouse, parent or guardian is lawfully entitled to enter Kenya. A Dependant Pass does not entitle one to work. According to the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 under Section 45 it is a requirement for all non-Kenyans who wish to engage in employment in Kenya, whether gainful employment or for voluntary services, to apply for a work permit. For a spouse/partner of a principal migrant to work in the country, they must apply and obtain a work permit pursuant to the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 41 (1) (b) of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act (2011) provides that a residence or work permit will be invalidated where the migrant ceases to engage in the said employment, occupation, trade, business or profession. Employers are obligated to notify the Director of migrants who cease working under them within fifteen days of such cessation in the Regulations.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Article 41 of the Constitution of Kenya (2010) which states: "1) Every person has the right to fair labour practices. 2) Every worker has the right (b) to reasonable working conditions." 2) The Kenyan Employment Act which contains provisions that provide for the regulation of hours of work for each employee (section 27). Section 27(2) further provides that an employee should be allowed at least one resting day in every period of seven (7) days. In addition, every employee is entitled to sick leave under section 30 of the Act after two consecutive months of service with their employer. Such sick leave is with full pay if it does not exceed seven (7) days and thereafter to sick leave of a further seven (7) days with half pay. Furthermore, part VI of the Employment Act makes mandatory provisions in relation to termination of employment. As such, the termination process of every employee must fulfill the requirements laid out therein. 3) The Occupational Health & Safety Act which provides mandatory provisions that underpin employee safety and health while at the workplace.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Pensions Act which is primarily created for Kenya workers employed by the government on permanent and pensionable terms. 2) National Health Insurance Fund Act. 3) National Social Security Fund (NSSF) which is established under the NSSF Act is open to migrants but access/withdrawal of funds is cumbersome for migrants. 4) Migrant Workers (Supplementary Provisions) Convention, 1975.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Kenya does not have any specific law, regulations or provisions for unemployment benefits.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011, Section 37(b) which provides that any migrant who lives in Kenya continuously for a total of seven (7) years can apply for Kenyan citizenship.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011, Section 54 (1) which makes it an offense for any person:- "without any lawful cause confiscates, forcefully takes or detains a passport or travel document issued to another person." Under this act, only immigration officers are empowered to seize or suspend a person's passport, travel documents or document of identity including those of other countries. 2) Article 31 of the Constitution of Kenya. Article 31 stipulates that every person has the right to privacy which includes the right not to have their possessions seized, among others. Every person, including migrants, has the right to inherent human dignity and the right to have that dignity respected and protected.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Children Act (2022) Section 7 (2) which provides that every child has the right to be registered in the Register of Births immediately after birth in accordance with the Births and Deaths Registration Act (Cap. 149). This applies to every child regardless of their status as a migrant. 2) Under the Births and Deaths Registration Act, chapter 49 of the laws of Kenya, notification and registration of all births and deaths occurring within the country is mandatory. Section 9 of the Act further provides for compulsory registration of births pursuant to a Gazette Notice by the Cabinet Secretary in charge of matters births and deaths registration. 3) Article 7 of the United Nations Charter on the Rights of the Child (CRC) provides for mandatory registration of a child immediately after birth. Article 7(2) further stipulates that state parties should ensure the implementation of, among others, the right to registration, in accordance with their national law in particular where the child would otherwise be rendered stateless by not so doing. The UN International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) requires state parties to proceed with immediate registration of births and without discrimination of any kind regardless of the child's status or that of the child's parents. The registration of a child does not in and of itself confer nationality on that child although it saves the child from becoming stateless. Kenya has ratified both the CRC and the ICCPR and as such they have the force of law in light of Article 2(6) of the Constitution of Kenya. A child found in Kenya who is or appears to be less than eight years of age, and whose nationality and parents are unknown, is to be presumed to be a citizen of Kenya by birth and is to be so registered.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya provides for protection of this right for all categories of migrants. The registration of foreign nationals is governed by the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 which requires all foreigners that are resident in Kenya for a period exceeding ninety (90) days to be registered. Section 34 of the Act provides that a person who is not a citizen of Kenya or an asylum seeker shall not enter or remain in Kenya unless they have a valid permit or pass.According to section 26 of the Act, there are three main types of passes: a special pass, dependant pass and student/research/internship passes. Qualified persons are those who wish to enter or remain in Kenya for a limited period for the purpose of applying a review of a decision denying a permit, applying a permit/pass or those that are in the country to conduct any business, trade or profession temporarily; b) Work/Resident Permits ??“ work/resident permits are granted to foreign nationals who wish to reside in Kenya for purpose of engaging in gainful or voluntary service employment, trade, professional practice or business. Section 40 of the Act regulates the grant of permits. These permits are of various classes ranging from Class A-M; c) Permanent Resident ??“ section 37 of the Act provides that permanent residency may be issued in a number of circumstances including to Kenyans, their children or spouse who has previously lost their citizenship but the countries where they obtained citizenship do not allow dual-citizenship, spouses of Kenyan citizens who have been married for a period of not less than three (3) years and foreigners who have held work permits for a continuance period of seven (7) years. Upon approval, payment and issuance of the relevant immigration status, it is endorsed on the applicant's valid passport." Registration of refugees and asylum seekers is provided for under the Refugees Act, 2021. Section 28 (6) of the Refugee Act provides that 'A refugee and an asylum seeker shall have the right to identification and civil registration documents and such documents shall be sufficient to identify a refugee or asylum seeker for the purposes of access to rights and services under this Act and any other applicable law'. Section 23 of the Refugees Act continues to provide that a person who has submitted an application for refugee status in accordance with the Act along with every member of their family shall be issued with a temporary pass valid for ninety days and it shall be evidence that the person has applied for refugee status in Kenya. The temporary pass entitles them to remain in Kenya until his or her application is granted or rejected and no appeal has been filed with the Appeals Committee or until that person has exhausted his or her right of appeal. The Act does not require them to produce any documents before being issued with the temporary pass.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in Registration of Persons Act, CAP 107, Article 14 and Section 54 Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Kenya, article 2 (5 & 6) which incorporates the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations and the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations as part of Kenyan Laws. 2) Privileges and Immunities Act, chapter 179. Section 4, relating to diplomatic relations, provides that the Articles of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations are applicable in Kenya. Equally, section 5 of the Act, relating to consular relations provides that the Articles of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (including Article 36) shall have the force of law in Kenya. As a result, foreign nationals in the country are free to communicate with their consulates, embassies and high commissions.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right since the national law in Kenya allows detention of children where appropriate be they nationals or foreigners, although such detention is strictly regulated under law. The Constitution of Kenya, 2010 provides for the rights of a child during arrest and detention in the Bill of Rights under Chapter 4. In particular, Article 53 (1) (f) states that every child has the right not to be detained, except as a measure of last resort, and when detained, to be held for the shortest appropriate period of time; and separate from adults and in conditions that take account of the child's sex and age. Sub article 2 provides that a child's best interests are of paramount importance in every matter concerning the child. The Convention on the Rights of the Child, 1989, provides that if the detention of children is necessary in order to achieve a particular aim, then the length of detention should be the shortest appropriate period for the achievement of that aim. The Children Act, 2022 provides in section 8 (1) that in all actions concerning children, undertaken by public and private social welfare institutions, courts of law, administrative authorities or legislative bodies, the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration. Section 8 (2) states that all persons acting under the institutions shall treat the interests of the child as the first and paramount consideration to safeguard the rights and welfare of a child. Courts in Kenya have altered convictions and sentence of child offenders whose arrest and detention was contrary with Article 53 (1) (f). Additionally, courts have held that the sentencing of children was a constitutional matter of great concern and a child offender may only be detained as a measure of last resort for the shortest appropriate period of time and separate from adults.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Kenyan law permits the detention of migrants, on the basis of their status as a migrant, but subjects it to strong regulation. Section 49 (2) of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 allows an immigration officer or a police officer who has reasonable cause to believe that a person has committed an offense under the Act, or is unlawfully present in Kenya to arrest that person without warrant subject to the Bill of Rights and Criminal Procedures. Subsection (1) provides that within twenty four hours after a permanent resident or a foreign national is taken into detention, or without delay afterward, the person detained is to be produced before a judicial officer to review the reasons for the continued detention. At least once during the seven days following the review, and at least once during each thirty day period following each previous review, the detained person is to be produced before a judicial officer to review the reasons for continued detention. Under Subsection (4), a person other than a citizen of Kenya who, having been ordered to be deported from any country, enters Kenya on his way to his final destination, may be arrested without warrant by an immigration officer or a police officer and may be detained in prison or in police custody or immigration holding facility pending the making of arrangements for his departure from Kenya, and shall be deemed to be in lawful custody while so detained and such person needs to be taken to court within twenty four hours.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right, for all three aspects of detention, in: 1) The Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011; Section 57 which allows any person aggrieved by a decision of a public officer made under the Act to apply to the High Court for a review of the decision. This includes decisions by courts regarding detention of persons with immigration-related matters before the court at the first instance and decisions for continued detention; or persons awaiting the Cabinet Secretary's decision to remove them from Kenya. 2) The Constitution of Kenya (2010): the rights of arrested and incarcerated persons are provided for in the constitution from article 47 to 51. Right of appeal under Article 50 (2-Q) is a constitutional imperative and that means all persons regardless of their nationality or immigration status have these rights. Article 47 of the Constitution of Kenya, provides for fair administrative action for every person in Kenya that is expeditious, efficient, lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair. Moreover, Article 48 provides for access to justice for all persons. Article 22 further provides that every person has the right to institute court proceedings claiming that a right or fundamental freedom in the Bill of Rights has been denied, violated or infringed or is threatened. These court proceedings may be instituted by among others a person acting on behalf of another person who cannot act in their own or a person acting in the public interest. The Bill of Rights together with the international instruments that Kenya has ratified provide for the right to liberty as well as the right against arbitrary arrest and detention. Flowing from the above, any person, including migrants, has a right to appeal the legality, conditions and length of detention.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Section 43 (7) of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 which requires an individualized determination by the Cabinet Secretary on whether to remove a person from Kenya, and Section 49 (3) of the Act which makes reference to an individualized appearance in court where a detainee's matter will be handled and a determination issued. 2) The Constitution of Kenya article 50 on fair hearing and article 47 on fair administrative action.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Kenya. 2) UN Convention against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. 3) Prevention from Torture Act, 2017. Article 29(d) of the Constitution provides for freedom from torture whereas Article 29(f) provides for the right not to be treated or punished in a cruel, inhuman or degrading manner. These rights accrue to every person within the territory of Kenya irrespective of their status in the country. Article 25 of the Constitution which sets out rights and freedoms that cannot be limited has the freedom from torture as one of them. Kenya has enacted a legislation known as the Prevention from Torture Act, 2017 that gives effect to Articles 25(a) and 25(d) of the Constitution as well as the UN Convention against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. Particularly the Act lays down a legislative framework for preventing, prohibiting and punishing acts of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court in the case of Kenya National Commission on Human Rights & another v Attorney General & 3 others [2017] eKLR while affirming that this right applies to migrants as well held inter alia that: "International human rights law provides additional forms of protection in this area. Article 3 of the 1984 UN Convention against Torture stipulates that no State Party shall expel, return or extradite a person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he or she would be in danger of being subjected to torture... Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, this principle reflects the commitment of the international community to ensure to all persons the enjoyment of human rights, including the rights to life, to freedom from torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and to liberty and security of the person."

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Under the National Police Service Act, 2011, the police in appropriate circumstances and conditions may use force. Law enforcement officers, therefore, may use reasonable force to prevent migrants from entering the territory of Kenya. However, the Sixth Schedule of the Act states that the use of force should be proportionate to its intended objective, the seriousness of the offense, the resistance by the person against whom it is used and only to the extent necessary for those ends.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in 1) The Constitution of Kenya which guarantees the right to life, and that life should not be taken away arbitrarily by anyone. Article 244 of the Constitution also provides that the National Police Service is required to strive towards the highest standards of professionalism and discipline among its members. 2) The National Police Service Act: The National Police Service, under the Sixth Schedule, sets out guidelines that govern the use of force by police officers in the conduct of their functions and powers. Border surveillance is one of the broad functions of the Border Police Unit which is a branch of the Administration Police. The Police are prohibited against the use of excessive force in undertaking their functions. This therefore applies when preventing migrants from entering the state's territory. 3) Citizenship & Immigration Act, 2011. Immigration officers under this act are only required to arrest and prosecute violators of immigration laws, by following due process.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right, for trafficked migrants, in: 1) Section 14 of the Counter Trafficking in Persons Act, 2010 which avails a victim of trafficking immunity from being criminally liable for any offense related to being in Kenya illegally or for any criminal act that was a direct result of being trafficked. 2) The High Court on June 30, 2021 in the case of Geoffrey Mutemi Manzi v Republic [2021] eKLR affirmed Section 14 of the Counter-trafficking in Persons Act, 2010 where it upheld the decision of the lower court that held: "The victims herein, aliens, entered this country unlawfully. They were however protected from being charged and made witnesses to safeguard their rights as per Section 14 of the Act which provides for victim immunity from prosecution." However, national law in Kenya only protects this right for smuggled migrants if they identify and are willing to act as a state witness in the prosecution of the smuggler. 3) Section 54 of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 exempts smuggled migrants from being held liable only as long as they identify and are willing to act as a witness in the prosecution of the smuggler.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya regulates this issue in: 1) Article 17 of the Constitution of Kenya (2010) which provides for the grounds for revocation of citizenship by registration on the grounds of, among others, if the person has, within five years after registration, been convicted of an offense and sentenced to imprisonment for a term of three years or longer; or the person has, at any time after registration, been convicted of treason, or of an offense for which a penalty of at least seven years imprisonment may be imposed; or a more severe penalty may be imposed. 2) Section 21 of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act (2011) which reiterates the provisions of the Constitution and provides for the procedure to be followed by the Cabinet Secretary in revoking a person's citizenship. The Cabinet Secretary is required by notice, in writing, to inform any person whose citizenship is due for revocation of the intention to revoke his or her citizenship giving reasons. The Cabinet Secretary shall give a person who has been given the notice an opportunity to present the reasons why his or her citizenship should not be revoked. Where an appeal has been filed with respect to a decision to revoke citizenship, the person who has appealed shall be deemed to be lawfully present in Kenya until the appeal is determined. The person shall cease to be a citizen of Kenya on the date of the revocation or in any case upon exhaustion of appeal.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right by providing a pathway to citizenship for economic migrants via registration in Article 15 of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 and Sections 11, 13, and 14 of the Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011. If a person acquires a work permit under the provisions of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 and continues to have a lawful stay or presence in Kenya, he/she can acquire permanent residence which confers citizenship benefits by registration on application and upon satisfaction of the prescribed conditions.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right for humanitarian migrants via registration in: 1) The Constitution of Kenya under Articles 15. 2) Sections 15, 16 and 17 of the Kenyan Citizenship and Immigration Act (KCIA), 2011. Section 13 of the KCIA provides criteria for humanitarian migrants seeking naturaliztion. These include residency requirements (a continuous residency requirement of 7 years from the date of the application); has adequate knowledge of Kenya; is able to understand and speak Kiswahili or a local dialect; has not been convicted of an offence and sentenced to imprisonment for a term of three years or longer; has been determined, through an objective criteria, and the justification made, in writing, that he or she has made or is capable of making a substantive contribution to the progress or advancement in any area of national development within Kenya; and is not an adjudged bankrupt. Additionally, Section 34 recognizes a refugeee and an asylum seeker as lawfully resident in Kenya and they therefore do not need an additional permit or pass under the KCIA. The above Section 13 therefore equally applies to them on the conditions to be satisfied before grant of citizenship. 3) Article 34 of the Refugee Convention, which was integrated into Article 2(6) of the Constitution of Kenya in 1966, obligates countries or states to the Convention to facilitate in the assimilation and naturalization of refugees to citizens. With lawful entry and lawful stay in Kenya, they can therefore acquire permanent residence which confers citizenship benefits registration on application and upon satisfaction of the prescribed conditions.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right by providing a pathway to citizenship for family migrants in: 1) Article 15 of the Constitution of Kenya. 2) Section 17 of the Kenyan Citizenship and Immigration Act (KCIA), 2011. 3) Section 15 of the Refugee Act. The Constitution of Kenya in Chapter 3 together with the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act (KCIA), 2011 recognizes two ways of obtaining Kenyan citizenship that is either by birth or registration. Citizenship by birth as per article 14 of the Constitution and sections 6, 7 and 9 of KCIA is acquired if upon the date of birth of a child, both parents are Kenyans or if a child is found in Kenya whose age and parentage cannot be determined. Citizenship by registration, as per article 15 and sections 11, 13 and 14 of the KCIA, is acquired upon the lawful residence of seven years in Kenya, upon the application by a person who has been married for seven years to a Kenyan citizen or upon adoption of a child by Kenyan citizens. Section 15 of the Refugee Act contains provisions on families of refugees providing that a member of a family of a refugee shall be provided with a pass or card as applicable to enable the persons stay in Kenya, and ultimately apply for citizenship. Section 7 of the KCIA provides that a person born outside Kenya shall be a citizen by birth if on the date of birth that person’s mother or father was or is a citizen. This applies to citizens by registration or birth. Section 17 of the KCIA allows descendants of stateless persons and migrants who have attained the age of eighteen years and whose parents are or in the case of deceased parents were eligible to be registered as a citizen to apply to be registered as a citizen of Kenya.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in Section 20 of the Kenyan Citizenship and Immigration Act (KCIA), 2011. Section 20 of the KCIA allows for migrants to retain their nationality of origin when applying for Kenyan citizenship and are therefore considered dual citizens. They can also voluntarily renounce their nationality of origin.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Article 32 of the Constitution of Kenya which states: "(1):Every person has the right to freedom of conscience, religion, thought, belief and opinion. (2):Every person has the right, either individually or in community with others, in public or in private, to manifest any religion or belief through worship, practice, teaching or observance, including observance of a day of worship. (3): A person may not be denied access to any institution, employment or facility, or the enjoyment of any right, because of the person’s belief or religion. (4): A person shall not be compelled to act, or engage in any act, that is contrary to the person’s belief or religion." 2) The Court in Kenya National Commission on Human Rights & another v Attorney General & 3 others [2017] eKLR held: "The Bill of Rights therefore, guarantees fundamental rights to all including refugees."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in Article 33 of the Constitution of Kenya which states: "Every person has the right to freedom of expression, which includes: (a) freedom to seek, receive or impart information or ideas; (b) reedom of artistic creativity; and; (c) academic freedom and freedom of scientific research." While Article 33 primarily focuses on the right to freedom of expression, it encompasses the broader concept of the right to hold opinions without interference. This provision ensures that individuals in Kenya, including migrants, have the freedom to form and express their opinions without undue restrictions or censorship from the government or any other authority. Additionally, Article 32 provides that every person has the right to freedom of among other things opinion. The Court in Kenya National Commission on Human Rights & another v Attorney General & 3 others [2017] eKLR held: "The Bill of Rights therefore, guarantees fundamental rights to all including refugees."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in Article 33 of the Constitution of Kenya which states: "Every person has the right to freedom of expression, which includes: (a) freedom to seek, receive or impart information or ideas; (b) reedom of artistic creativity; and; (c) academic freedom and freedom of scientific research." This freedom is further entrenched in a various international instruments that Kenya has ratified and which are binding pursuant to Article 2(6) of the Constitution. These include the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) and the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights. The laws provided above are general laws that apply to every individual in Kenya, including migrants, regardless of their status.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Article 36 of the Kenyan Constitution which specifically states: "Every person has the right to freedom of association, which includes the right to form, join or participate in the activities of an association of any kind." 2) Kenya is also a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) which in Article 22 provides that everyone shall have the right to freedom of association with others including the right to join or form trade unions which therefore provides that migrants have the freedom to association as afforded to other citizens. International laws are integrated into national legislation with Article 2(6) of the Constitution and they are applicable to all people resident in Kenya without regard to their status in the country.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. As outlined in Section 36 of the Citizenship and Immigration Act, 2011 and Sections 26 and 27 (2) (c) of the Regulations of 2012, in order to get dependents' passes for family, the applicant must meet financial and residency requirements. Under the Kenya Citizenship & Immigration Act, for a migrant to confer a residency status to a family, they must prove a level of dependency demonstrating that the settled migrant is the one responsible for costs of the dependant.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in Article 22, 27, and 47-50 of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010. Article 27 provides for equality before the law. Article 48 further obliges the State to ensure access to justice for all persons and if any fee is required, it should be reasonable and shall not impede access to justice. Article 22 of the Constitution provides that every person has the right to institute court proceedings claiming that a right or fundamental freedom in the Bill of Rights has been denied, violated or infringed, or is threatened. Further in Article 22(2), court proceedings may in addition to a person acting in their own interest, also be instituted by a person acting on behalf of another person who cannot act in their own name, a person acting as a member of, or in the interest of, a group or class of persons, a person acting in the public interest or in association acting in the interest of one or more of its members.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) Counter Trafficking in Persons Act, 2010, Sections 14, 15 and 18: Section 14 guarantees relief from expulsion as a result of being a victim of a crime because the victims are not prosecuted for being in Kenya illegally or for any criminal act that was a direct result of being trafficked. Section 15 is relevant because it guarantees that such victims receive support in form of legal assistance or legal information, including information on the relevant judicial and administrative proceedings. This can be interpreted to include possible avenues to immigration status. Section 18 of this Act provides that the victims of trafficking are permitted to remain in Kenya until legal proceedings pertaining to such human trafficking are concluded and may by order of court in such proceedings be allowed to bring their children. 2) The Witness Protection Act, 2006: Should a person be a witness to a crime, the Witness Protection Act obligates the State to protect persons who are witnesses to crimes and who are likely to face intimidation on account of their testimonies. This Act does not differentiate between citizens and migrants in offering protection.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Kenya, 2010: Article 2 (5&6) which makes international law part of Kenyan law thus making all children rights conventions and protocols apply. Furthermore, Article 53 of the Kenyan Constitution of 2010 accords children special protection of the law. 2) Section 8 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. 3) The Children Act, 2022, Sections 8 and 9. Section 8 (1) of the Children Act provides that in all actions concerning children undertaken by public or administrative bodies, the best interests of the child shall be the primary consideration. This extends to the bodies overseeing immigration in Kenya. Section 9(1) of the Children Act goes on to provide that no person shall discriminate against a child, including migrant children, on the grounds of among other things language, colour, birth, social, political, economic or other status, race, tribe, local connection or any other status. Any person convicted of such discrimination shall be guilty of an offense under the Act.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, Article 2 (6) which provides for ratification of treaties among them the African Charter on Elections, Democracy and Governance. On 7th January, 2021 Kenya acceded to the African Charter on Elections, Democracy and Governance and deposited the same with the African Union on 4th February, 2022. Article 8 of the Charter obligates state parties to State Parties shall adopt legislative and administrative measures to guarantee the rights of women, ethnic minorities, migrants, people with disabilities, refugees and displaced persons and other marginalized and vulnerable social groups. It also obligates state parties to ensure literacy of women (Article 29) and their participation in decision-making and the electoral process (Article 43). State obligations under the Charter have been domesticated by various laws notably the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, the Elections Act, 2011, the Political Parties Act, 2011, the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Act, 2011 and the County Governments Act, 2012. Other relevant international treaties in effect include: 1) No. 10 of 2021 Universal Declaration of Human Rights Convention of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women. 2) The African Union Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol) The Solemn Declaration on Gender Equity in Africa.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Kenya protects this right in: 1) The Constitution of Kenya: Articles 2(6), 21(3), and 54. 2) No. 10 of 2021 Persons with Disability Act Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. 3) Article 8 of the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance (ratified in 2021) obligates State Parties to adopt legislative and administrative measures to guarantee the rights of vulnerable social groups including migrants, disabled individuals, refugees, and displaced people. Article 31 provides for state parties to promote participation of social groups with special needs, including the youth and people with disabilities, in the governance process. Article 43 provides for free compulsory basic education for children with disabilities and literacy of persons with disabilities who are above school-going age. These rights apply to all persons with disabilities regardless of their citizenship status.
