question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Republic of Korea

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for migrants. National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right only for citizens in Article 21(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea which indicates: (1) All citizens shall enjoy freedom of speech and the press, and freedom of assembly and association. (2) Licensing or censorship of speech and the press, and licensing of assembly and association shall not be recognized.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for migrants. National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right for citizens only in Article 24 of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea. However, local governments have the authority to determine whether non-citizens, including migrants, can participate in local elections. According to Article 34 (Preparation and Management of Registration Form of Foreigners) of the 'Immigration Act,' a non-Korean citizen registered in the relevant local constituency and who has had a resident visa for at least three years has the right to vote in local elections."

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right for refugees only in Article 14 and 15 (Interpretation and translation of public defense counsel's interview with the Defendant) of the Refugee Act.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In South Korea, the Labor Standards Act, articles 98-100, does not explicitly guarantee access to adequate, publicly supported housing to migrants independent of their status.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right for 1) legally resident foreign nations Refugee Act Article 33, as the right to free public primary education is primarily granted to South Korean citizens and legally resident foreign nationals, such as those holding valid visas or residency permits. 2) Refugees in Article 33 of the Refugee Act, which states, "(1) Where a recognized refugee or his or her child is a minor under the Civil Act, he or she shall receive the same elementary education and secondary education as the Korean people. (2) The Minister of Justice may support recognized refugees to receive necessary education in consideration of their age, learning ability, educational conditions, etc. as prescribed by Presidential Decree." Irregular migrants, including undocumented migrants, generally face challenges in accessing free public primary education.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. For those on valid work visas, there are opportunities to access education and training, but the level of access might not always be equivalent to that of citizens. Different visa categories also have different levels of access to different programs. For example, all migrants have equal access to language and integration programs (as in Article 39 of the Immigration Act), but refugees have explicit access to vocational training (as in the Refugee Act, Article 34) and degree-level education in public institutions (Article 35 of the Refugee Act).

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Korea protects this right in the Immigration Act, Article 85, "Even when a foreigner falling under any subparagraph of Article 46 (1) is in the course of enforcement of a sentence, the Commissioner of the competent Regional Immigration Service may take a procedure of deportation." South Korea has immigration laws and regulations that outline the grounds for visa cancellation, denial, or revocation. If a migrant is convicted of a serious criminal offense, particularly one that poses a threat to public safety or national security, their residence status may be adversely affected. Such convictions could result in deportation or the denial of visa extensions or renewals.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in South Korea protects this right in the Refugee Act of South Korea, which provides legal protection to refugees and incorporates the principle of non-refoulement. Article 3 (Prohibition of Compulsory Repatriation) states that no recognized refugee, humanitarian sojourner, nor refugee applicant shall be repatriated compulsorily against his or her will under Article 39 of the Refugee Convention and Article 3 of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: The Refugee Act of South Korea provides legal protection to refugees and incorporates the principle of non-refoulement. Article 3 (Prohibition of Compulsory Repatriation) states that no recognized refugee, humanitarian sojourner, nor refugee applicant shall be repatriated compulsorily against his or her will under Article 39 of the Refugee Convention and Article 3 of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in South Korea protects this right in Article 3 of the Refugee Act, which includes provisions that ban refoulement on the basis of a risk of serious deprivations of fundamental human rights, including the right to life.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in 1) the Immigration Act, Article 60 (Raising Objections), which states, "(1) If a suspect intends to protest a deportation order, the suspect shall file a written objection with the Minister of Justice through the Commissioner of the competent Regional Immigration Service within seven days after the suspect receives the deportation order. (2) The Commissioner of the Regional Immigration Service in receipt of the written objection under paragraph (1) shall submit it to the Minister of Justice with the written examination record and decision and the record of investigation attached thereto. (3) The Minister of Justice, in receipt of the written objection, etc. under paragraphs (1) and (2), shall examine and determine whether the objection is well-grounded and notify the Commissioner of the competent Regional Immigration Service of the determination thereon." 2) The Refugee Act, Article 21 (Objections), which states that "A person subject to a decision of non-recognition of refugee status under Article 18 (2) or 19 or a person whose refugee status is cancelled or withdrawn under Article 22 may raise an objection to the Minister of Justice within 30 days from the date on which he or she is notified thereof. In such cases, he or she shall submit an objection accompanied by materials explaining the grounds therefor to the head of the local immigration office or foreigner-related office."

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. South Korea does not have a specific provision in its national law that guarantees citizenship in all cases where a child would otherwise be stateless. Article 2(1) of the Nationality Act stipulates that ‘a person who was born in the ROK, if both of the parents are unknown or have no nationality’ shall be a national of the ROK at birth. Article 2(2) provides that ‘an abandoned child found in the ROK shall be recognized as born in the ROK’; thus, it is also eligible for the ROK nationality. Foreigners, including stateless persons, may attain the ROK nationality by ‘naturalization’ (Article 4) or ‘reinstatement of nationality’ (Article 9) if they are a former ROK national. The ‘persons with undetermined nationality’ may obtain the ROK nationality through the ‘determination of nationality’ (Article 20) procedure. However, while the South Korean government has taken steps to address the issue of statelessness, including granting citizenship to some individuals in specific circumstances, the granting of citizenship to prevent statelessness is not guaranteed universally.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The opportunity for temporary migrant workers to switch to permanent status is conditional on visa type.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: With the The Employment Permit System (EPS) the Government set the regularization process of undocumented migrant workers as follows: Undocumented migrants who had been in the Republic of Korea as of March 2003: a) For less than 3 years: eligible to sojourn status; b) Between 3 years and 4 years: eligible for visa issuance certificate but must first leave; c) the country until 15 November (2003). After that they should return to the RoK; d) within three months to be employed legally; e) For more than 4 years: no possibility to legalize their status and must leave the RoK by 15 November (2003) or will be deported.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The only protections listed in the Act on The Employment of Foreign Workers, is in Article 24-2 (Councils for Protection of Rights and Interests of Foreign Workers), which states that, "For the purpose of consulting on matters relating to the protection of the rights and interests of foreign workers, a council for the protection of the rights and interests of foreign workers may be established in an employment security office, wherein workers' organizations and employers' organizations in the relevant region participate in."

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in Article 23 of the Regional Public Health Act and Article 27(1) of the Medical Services Act. There is no distinction made between visa types, and all regular migrants have access to this system commensurate with citizens.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for migrants. Article 25 of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea gives this right to citizens only.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 11 (1) of the Constitution states that all citizens shall be equal before the law, and there shall be no discrimination in political, economic, social or cultural life on account of sex, religion or social status. Reference is made for the citizens, not including migrants before naturalisation.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right, however, the law does explicitly protect this right for wards of the state in the Framework Act on the Treatment of Foreigners Residing in the Republic of Korea, Article 10 (Safeguarding Human Rights of Foreigners, etc. in Korea) prohibits the State and local governments shall endeavor to take necessary measures, such as the conduct of education and publicity activities, to prevent unreasonable discrimination against foreigners in Korea and their children and to safeguard their human rights. Immigration Act Article 56-3 (Respect, etc. of Wards’ Human Rights), which states, the human rights of wards shall be respected to the utmost and discrimination against wards on grounds of their nationality, gender, religion, social position, etc. shall be prohibited.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in Article 22 (Prohibition against Discrimination) of the Act on Employment of Foreign Workers.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in a limited way in Immigration Act Article 46-9 and Article 21(1). Immigration Act Article 21 (Change and Addition of Work Place) states: (1) If a foreigner sojourning in the Republic of Korea intends to change or add his or her work place within the scope of his or her status of sojourn, he/ she shall obtain prior permission from the Minister of Justice: Provided, That a person prescribed by Presidential Decree who has expert knowledge, skill or ability shall report to the Minister of Justice within 15 days from the date on which he or she changes or adds his or her work place."

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in a conditional way in so far as loss of employment implies loss of immigration status unless a new job is found within a specified time period in the Immigration Act, Article 19 (Duty to Report by Employers, etc. of Foreigners), which states, "A person who employs a foreigner having the status of sojourn eligible for employment activities under Article 18 (1) shall report any of the following circumstances, if any of the following grounds occurs, to the Commissioner of the competent Regional Immigration Service within 15 days from the date on which he or she becomes aware of such circumstances: 1. Where he or she has discharged the foreigner or the foreigner has retired from the service or died; 2. Where the whereabouts of the employed foreigner becomes unknown; 3. Where important terms of an employment contract are amended."

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right for certain categories of migrants in Article 22 (Prohibition against Discrimination) of the Act on the Employment of Foreign Workers, which states the no employer shall unfairly give discriminatory treatment to a foreign worker on the ground that he/she is a foreign worker.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Korea protects this right in Act in Employment of Foreign Worker, Article 24-2 (Councils for Protection of Rights and Interests of Foreign Workers) which states that, for the purpose of consulting on matters relating to the protection of the rights and interests of foreign workers, a council for the protection of the rights and interests of foreign workers may be established in an employment security office, wherein workers' organizations and employers' organizations in the relevant region participate. Local councils in South Korea are involved in implementing social security programs, but the negotiation and design of these programs are largely managed by the central government.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in the Act on The Employment of Foreign Workers, Article 13 (Insurance and Trust for Departure Guaranty), Article 14 (Health Insurance), Article 15 (Insurance and Trust for Expenses for Return to Home Country). The type of visa a migrant worker holds can impact their eligibility for various rights and benefits, including social security protections and unemployment benefits.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Korea allows some temporary workers to apply by lottery for a permanent residency visa in the Immigration Act.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The government of the Republic of Korea only allows birth registration of Korean nationals according to the Act on the Registration etc. of Family Relationships, leaving children of undocumented foreign nationals outside the protection of the law (Act On Registration of Family Relations Section 2, Article 44).

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Korea protects this right in Article 56-4 of the Immigration Act, which outlines the specific conditions under which an officer is authorized to use force on immigrants. However, it is important to note that none of these conditions pertain to the situation of crossing the border.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Korea protects this right in Articles 56-4 of the Immigration Act. The use of lethal force by officers or agents as a means of preventing migrants from entering the state's territory is prohibited. According to Article 56-4, the use of force is allowed, but lethal force is prohibited.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in Nationality Act Article 14-3 (Decision on Loss of Nationality of the Republic of Korea). However, Nationality Act Article 14-3 (Decision on Loss of Nationality of the Republic of Korea) permits revocation of naturalization in certain circumstances that do not require a conviction. As discussed in the Act, "(1) If the Minister of Justice deems obviously inappropriate for a person with multiple nationalities to maintain the nationality of the Republic of Korea due to any of the following grounds, the Minister of Justice may decide on the loss of the nationality of the Republic of Korea after holding a hearing provided that this shall not apply to a person who has acquired the nationality of the Republic of Korea by birth: 1. Where the person conducts any act contrary to the national interests of the Republic of Korea, in respect of national security, diplomatic relations, national economy, etc.; 2. Where the person conducts any act prescribed by Presidential Decree which causes substantial hindrance in maintaining social order in the Republic of Korea."

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in Articles 4 and 7 of the Nationality Act. Article 4 states that, "An alien who has never acquired the nationality of the Republic of Korea may acquire the nationality of the Republic of Korea by obtaining permission for naturalization from the Minister of Justice." Article 7 states that, "3. A person acknowledged to contribute to the national interests of the Republic of Korea who has very excellent ability in a specific field, such as science, economy, culture, sport..." Under the naturalisation process, any person who has lived in South Korea for five consecutive years and have spent at least 183 days each year in South Korea, and able to complate necasary conditions of Ministry of Justice can apply for natiralisation.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in South Korea protects this right in the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Naturalization of Foreigners, which provides special considerations for individuals who have made exceptional contributions to the national interests of South Korea or possess outstanding abilities in specific fields. Additionally, under the naturalisation process, any person who has lived in South Korea for five consecutive years and have spent at least 183 days each year in South Korea, and able to complate necasary conditions of Ministry of Justice can apply for natiralisation.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in Nationality Act Article 5. According to the law, family migrants must have the ability to maintain living on his/her own assets or skills; or is a dependent member of a family capable of the feat. Applicants must have basic knowledge befitting a Korean national; such as understanding of the Korean language, customs and culture.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in Nationality Act, Article 12 (Obligations of Persons with Multiple Nationalities to Choose One Nationality). This right is dependant on bilateral agreements with other countries.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for migrants. National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right for citizens in Article 19 (freedom of conscience) and Article 20 (1) (freedom of religion) of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 21 of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea guarantees this right, but only for citizens.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Though Article 21 of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea protects this right, it is only for citizens.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in the Republic of Korea protects this right in the Constitution of the Republic of Korea, Article 33 (1) that states: To enhance working conditions, workers shall have the right to independent association, collective bargaining and collective action. This right is also regulated in Article 5 of South Korea’s Trade Union and Labour Relations Adjustment Act, which states that “all workers have the right to freely form or join labour unions.” Additionally, Article 2(1) of the Labour Standards Act defines a “worker” as “a person who offers work to a business or workplace to earn wages, regardless of [the] kinds of jobs he/she is engaged in.” Thus, by definition, this includes both regular and irregular migrant workers.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Korea protects this right in the Constitution of the Republic of Korea, Article 12, which states that, "Anyone who is arrested or detained shall have the right to receive assistance of counsel immediately. However, when a criminal defendant is unable to secure a defense counsel by oneself, the state shall assign a defense counsel according to the provisions of the law."

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Korea protects this right in the Immigration Act, Article 55, 3(2), which lists pregnant women as individuals requiring special protection.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Lebanon

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Article 13 of the Lebanese Constitution, which states that "The freedom to express one's opinion orally or in writing, the freedom of the press, the freedom of assembly, and the freedom of association shall be guaranteed within the limits established by law." 2) Article 21 of the International Covenant for Civil and Political Rights, which provides that "The right of peaceful assembly shall be recognized. No restrictions may be placed on the exercise of this right other than those imposed in conformity with the law and which are necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security or public safety, public order (ordre public), the protection of public health or morals or the protection of the rights and freedoms of others." Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception."

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 21 of the Lebanese Constitution states that "Every Lebanese citizen who has completed his twenty-first year is an elector provided he fulfills the conditions stated by the electoral law."

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Article 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure which stipulates that "the right to have recourse to a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law that guarantees a fair trial for Lebanese and migrants is enshrined in Lebanese law." Also, Article 7 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that "all are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to equal protection of the law. All are entitled to equal protection against any discrimination in violation of this Declaration and against any incitement to such discrimination." 2) Article 26 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights that "All persons are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to the equal protection of the law. In this respect, the law shall prohibit any discrimination and guarantee to all persons equal and effective protection against discrimination on any ground such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status." Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception."

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Article 78 of the Lebanese Code of Criminal Procedure, which states that if a defendant appearing before the investigating judge is unrepresented, the judge either designates a lawyer or refers designation to the president of the competent Bar association. Article 78 goes on to stipulate that “If the defendant is unable to appoint a lawyer, the Investigating Judge shall appoint one or ask the President of the Bar Association to do so.” 2) Article 425 of the Lebanese Code of Civil procedures (LCCP), states that "If one of the opponents is unable to assume the charges and fees of the trial due to financial difficulties, he can apply for Legal aid". Article 426 states that "Legal aid is granted to natural persons of the Lebanese nationality, as well as foreigners residing usually in Lebanon on condition of reciprocity." 3) Chapter 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure stipulates that "individuals, who are Lebanese or foreigners usually residing in Lebanon, and cannot pay the charges and fees of a trial, and where their country would grant reciprocal right to a Lebanese, may apply for legal aid in order to sue or defend in the first instance or in appeal." According to Article 435, the state legally covers the expenses and fees of legal aid, while both bar associations of Beirut and Tripoli cover lawyers’ fees through bar revenues.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right through Article 81 which stipulates that “If the defendant is not proficient in the Arabic language, the Investigating Judge shall appoint a qualified interpreter. Article 254 also states: “If the defendant does not understand the Arabic language, the President of the Court shall appoint a qualified interpreter, who shall begin his work after taking an oath to perform his duties honestly and with integrity.”

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 32 of the 1962 law on entry, stay and exit of foreigners provides for criminal charges against any foreigner who illegally enter the territory i.e. without any of the authorizations provided for in Article 6 of the said law (i.e. visa and/or residency permit).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no public housing system in Lebanon

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon proteccts this right in 1) Article 28 of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child which stipulates that “state parties recognize the right of the child to education, provided that they make primary education compulsory and available free of charge to all.” 2) As of July 7, 2020, National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 2 of the Decree no 9706/2022 Concerning the Regulation and Conditions of Compulsory Free Education, which states that primary education shall be compulsory and free of charge for every child in Lebanon, without discrimination of any kind, irrespective of the child's sex, age, religion, sect, place of residence, national or social origin, or his parents' political or economic, or ideological beliefs, or because of any disability afflicting the child, or any other status. Free of charge education is compulsory for stateless children, and those whose citizenship is under study. However, according to this decree, for foreigners legally residing in Lebanon, the rules of reciprocity apply to them; and in order to implement the provisions of this decree, it is required that the student holds a resident card valid for one year, or a permanent residence permit (valid for three years). 3) Article 28 of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child which stipulates that “state parties recognize the right of the child to education, provided that they make primary education compulsory and available free of charge to all.”

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 19 of the decree n°8590/2012 "Regulating vocational and technical education fields stages and certificates," provides that priority is given to Lebanese students if the number of candidates for admission exceeds the capacity of the institution.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Article 88 of the Penal Code, which stipulates that "Every foreigner who was convicted (of a major criminal offenses) will lose his residence status and he will be subject to expulsion". Any migrant sentenced to a crime (serious criminal infractions sentenced to death, life imprisonment, fixed term imprisonment of a period not less than 3 years, fixed term hard labour) may be expelled from Lebanese territory pursuant to a special provision of the judgement. If they are sentenced to a penalty for a misdemeanor (penal infractions with penalty of less than 3 years imprisonment), they may not be expelled except in the cases prescribed by law. The deportation order shall either be permanent or for a period ranging from 3 to 25 years.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Article 26 of The 1962 Law Regulating the Entry and Stay of Foreigners in Lebanon and their Exit from the Country (Law of Entry and Exit), which provides that "Any foreigner who is subject of a prosecution or a conviction by an authority that is not Lebanese for a political crime or whose life or freedom is threatened, also for political reasons, may request political asylum in Lebanon." 2) Article 3 of the United Nation Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment to which Lebanon has adhered provides that "No State Party shall expel, return ("refouler") or extradite a person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he would be in danger of being subjected to torture. Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception."

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1)Article 26 of the 1962 Law on Entry and Exit of Foreigners, which provides protection only for those fleeing persecution for political reasons and those fearing torture. Article 26 states that 'any foreign national who is the subject of a prosecution or a conviction by an authority that is not Lebanese for a political crime or whose life or freedom is threatened, also for political reasons, may request political asylum in Lebanon." Article 31 provides protections for the non-refoulement of former political refugees: "In the event that a former political refugee is deported, he or she may not be removed to the territory of a country where his or her life or freedom is threatened." 2) Article 3 of the United Nations Convention against Torture and other Cruel Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, provides a blanket protection for all refugees. Article 3 stipulates that "No state party shall expel, return (refouler) or extradite a person to another state where there are substantial grounds for believing that he would be in danger of being subjected to torture." Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, whcih provides that "Everyone has the right to seek and to enjoy in other countries asylum from persecution." Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception." Paragraph 'B' of the preamble of the Lebanese Constitution, states that “Lebanon is a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall uphold these principles in all fields and areas without exception. The jurisprudence of the Constitutional Council in Lebanon affirms that the preamble of the constitution is an integral part of the Lebanese constitution. We cite from decision No 2 of the Constitutional Council dated 10/15/2001: “International agreements explicitly mentioned at the beginning of the constitution constitute with the preamble of the constitution an integral part of the constitution, and together they enjoy a constitutional force.” Article 2 of the Code of Civil Procedures in Lebanon mentions that “the courts shall comply with the principle of the rules of hierarchy. In the event of conflict between the provisions of international treaties and those of ordinary law, the former shall take precedence over the latter”.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Article 31 of The 1962 Law Regulating the Entry and Stay of Foreigners in Lebanon and their Exit from the Country (Law of Entry and Exit), which states that "in the event that a former political refugee is deported, he or she may not be removed to the territory of a country where his or her life or freedom is threatened." 2) Article 3 of the United Nation Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment and Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that "Everyone has the right to seek and to enjoy in other countries asylum from persecution." Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception."

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights providing that "Everyone has the right to seek and to enjoy in other countries asylum from persecution." Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception."

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Articles 37, 88, and 179. of the Lebanese Penal Code. Article 37 states that, “The customary penalties for felonies are: 1. Death; 2. Hard labour for life; 3. Life imprisonment; 4. Fixed‐term hard labour; 5. Fixed‐term extended imprisonment.” Article 88 states that "Only major convictions can lead to expulsion and loss of residence status." Article 179 stipulates: “An offence is defined as a felony, a misdemeanor or a contravention and is accordingly punishable by a penalty for a felony, a misdemeanor or a contravention.” 2) The 1962 Law on Entry and Exit of Foreigners, Article 32, which provides that migrants shall be under penalty of imprisonment of between one and three months, or of a fine of LBP 2500 to 12500 and of expulsion from Lebanon, if: a) the migrant entered Lebanon without complying with the provisions of Article 6 of the present law (i.e. holding valid documentation, a visa, and legal entry through one of the posts of General Directorate of General Security); b) the migrant made a false declaration to conceal their true identity or who may have used forged identity papers. In all such cases, the court shall not be authorised to grant the foreigners a reprieve from sentence or sentence them to imprisonment of less than one month.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in the Lebanese Code of Civil Procedure and Lebanese Code of Criminal Procedure, which provide for appeal procedures of decisions issued by judicial bodies for both Lebanese and foreigners. However, there are no provisions under Lebanese law that deal explicitly with the appeal of the decisions of the Director General of the General Security that are taken based on Article 17 of the 1962 Law on Entry and Exit of Foreigners, which provides for the expulsion of foreigners on the grounds that they constitute a threat to general safety or security. Nonetheless, such decisions are considered administrative decisions (executive orders) and can be challenged before an administrative judge within two months of the notification of the decision.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, Article 1 of the Lebanese Nationality law (Decision No.15 of 1925) does state that those considered Lebanese do have access to citizenship. Article 1 states that: "A) Every person born of a Lebanese father. B) Every person born in the Greater Lebanon territory and did not acquire a foreign nationality, upon birth, by affiliation. C) Every person born in the Greater Lebanon territory of unknown parents or parents of unknown nationality," have access to citizenship. Therefore, the right is only available to those born in Lebanon, and can prove Lebanese ancestry from the male line.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in the 1962 Law Regulating the Entry and Stay of Foreigners in Lebanon and their Exit from the Country (Law of Entry and Exit). The General Directorate of General Security may grant the family members of a certain category of migrant authorized to reside in Lebanon a one-year residency permit if the family members sign a notarized promise not to work or, if they are minors, provide a notarized undertaking of financial support from the head of the family. The aforesaid migrants who are entitled to such a right are: (I) Migrants whom residency is issued based on their financial capabilities, i.e., based on bank certificate showing a bank account of a value of no less than three hundred million Lebanese pounds (equivalent to US$ 200,000) or a certification of a monthly income that is estimated to more than five million Lebanese pounds (equivalent to US$ 3,300) from financial transfers or retirement funds from abroad, or any other legal funds. (II) Migrants who have an annual residency permit for work (only for jobs classified under class I and class II which exclude all migrant domestic helpers and migrant workers who earn a monthly salary ranging between the minimum salary wage and twice the said amount i.e. ranging between 450US$ to 900US$).

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in Article 69 of Law No. 10434 of 14 June 1975 (the Statute of the State Council), which stipulates that the claimant has two months from the date of adoption or notification of the administrative act to submit his claim. The decision of the Director of the General Security regarding the refusal by the authorities to allow family reunification can be challenged before the administrative judge within two months as of the issuance date of the decision.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Homosexuality is often criminalized under the article 534 of the Penal Code.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: N/A

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 21 of the Law of 1962 on Organizing the Work of Foreigners provides that any infringement of the provisions relating to the requirement of prior approval for a work permit shall be subject to the penalties provided under Article 32 of the Law of 1962, On the Entry and Exit of Foreigners (imprisonment, fines and expulsion) along with other penalties (imprisonment and fines) for breach of other provisions of the Law of 1962 on Organizing the Work of Foreigners.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which stipulates that "The right to have recourse to a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law that guarantees a fair trial for Lebanese and foreigners is enshrined in Lebanese law." 2) Decree No. 3572 of 10/21/1980 considered every dispute arising from a labor relationship - as defined in the Article 624 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts ? to be within the jurisdiction of the labor councils - and this applies to cases of domestic workers, but in the latter case, the labor councils would apply the Code of Obligations and Contracts, not the Labor Code. In addition, according to Article 79 of Lebanese Labor Law, “Arbitration Labor Council deals with: (a) Disputes arising from the assessment of the minimum pay, (b) Disputes arising from labor accidents covered by Legislative Decree No 25 of May 4, 1943, (c) Disputes arising from dismissal, abandonment of work, imposition of fines, and in general, all disputes that arise between employers and employees regarding the application of the provisions of this law.”3) Article 59 of the Labor Code, which provides that "Upon termination of their employment, foreign workers shall enjoy the same rights as those enjoyed by Lebanese workers on condition of reciprocity and must obtain a work permit from the Ministry of Labor."

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 9 of the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) law of 1963 limits access to health care services at government expense to only those migrants who come from countries that have reciprocity agreements with Lebanon as set out in the Labor Code. It should be noted that Law No. 128 dated 24/8/2010 amended Article 9 of the Social Security Law and exempted Palestinians from the requirement of reciprocity to benefit from social security contributions, and exempted them from the contributions of sickness and maternity funds and family allowances. Migrant workers who do not benefit from the NSSF Law are still able to access private health care establishments, provided they are privately insured or personally funded.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 7 of the Lebanese Electoral Law of 2018 provides that "A candidate standing to be a member of the Parliament shall be a Lebanese citizen who has attained 25 years of age and maintains their civil and political rights."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 2 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights states that "The States Parties to the present Covenant undertake to guarantee that the rights enunciated in the present Covenant will be exercised without discrimination of any kind as to race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status." Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception." The jurisprudence of the Constitutional Council in Lebanon affirms that the preamble of the constitution is an integral part of the Lebanese constitution. This Court in its decision No 2/2001 states that “International agreements explicitly mentioned at the beginning of the constitution constitute with the preamble of the constitution an integral part of the constitution, and together they enjoy a constitutional force.” Paragraph 'B' of the preamble of the Lebanese Constitution, states that “Lebanon is a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall uphold these principles in all fields and areas without exception.” In addition, article 2 of the Code of Civil Procedures in Lebanon mentions that “the courts shall comply with the principle of the rules of hierarchy. In the event of conflict between the provisions of international treaties and those of ordinary law, the former shall take precedence over the latter”. Finally, the decision from Single Criminal Judge in Metn, Decision no 15, dated 26/01/2017, states that, "Given that the principle of equality among people, which is one of the fundamental pillars of any democratic society that respects human dignity and identity, grants every individual the right to enjoy all rights and freedoms without any discrimination or preference based on color, religion, race, or any other status, especially since these rights are considered 'natural' rights inherent to human beings and do not need to be acquired. Likewise, an individual does not lose these rights due to their beliefs or way of life, even if that way of life is rejected by the majority of society.”

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination which was ratified by Lebanon in 1971. Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception."

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. Though Article 23 paragraph 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that "Everyone, without any discrimination, has the right to equal pay for equal work," and Article 7 paragraph (a) also states that "remuneration which provides all workers, at a minimum, with: (I) Fair wages and equal remuneration for work of equal value without distinction of any kind, in particular women being guaranteed conditions of work not inferior to those enjoyed by men, with equal pay for equal work," domestic workers are specifically excluded from the benefits provided by their employer, such as minimum wage, health care, 48 work hours per week and holidays.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 15 of the Decree Law 17561/64 on Organizing the Work of Foreigners in Lebanon, which states that it is prohibited for any holder of prior approval or work permit to change the nature of their job or to change employer before having obtained the prior approval of the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The General Security requires that the spouse signs an agreement that they will not to work while in Lebanon, and can only work if they apply for their own residency permit.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 7 and Article 15 the Decree Law 17561/64 on Organizing the Work of Foreigners in Lebanon. Article 7 provides that "the work permit is an extension of the prior approval and complementary condition to the latter. Article 15 states that it is prohibited for any holder of a prior approval or work permit to change the nature of their job or to change employer before having obtained the prior approval of the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs. If the validity period of the permit is elapsed or if the renewal is refused, the effect of the prior approval is equally suspended and the party concerned shall be required, in this event, to obtain a new prior approval to work in Lebanon." If a migrant loses their job and does not find new employment within the validity period of their residency permit, and also does not receive prior approval from the Ministry of Labor for a new job, they shall lose their immigration status.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 8 of the Lebanese Labor law. However, Article 7 excludes certain groups from the protections and guarantees provided in the Labor Law (minimum wage, rules governing arbitrary dismissal, the number of working hours, annual leave, and other public order provisions). While the text of the law does not exclude migrant workers, it includes sectors which predominately employ migrants and therefore practically exclude many migrants from protections. The groups excluded in the text of Article 7 are: (i) Domestic workers. (ii) Agricultural unions that have no relationship with trade and industry, who are subject to special legislation. (iii) Institutions where only members of the family are employed by the father, mother or guardian. (iv) Government departments and municipal bodies with respect to daily and temporary workers who are not subject the state personnel system and who will be subject to special legislation. Article 8 provides that all employers and employees are subject to the provisions of this law except those excluded by a special text.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, Article 9 of the Social Security law, which states that "The aforementioned foreign wage earners shall be entitled to the benefits stipulated in the social security law provided that they are holders of work permits in accordance with the laws and regulations in force, and that their country of origin grants Lebanese nationals the same treatment accorded to its own nationals with regards to social security." The states that treat Lebanon in a reciprocal manner are: France, Belgium, England and Italy. Access, therefore, is restricted based on reciprocity.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: Nationa law in Lebanon protects this right. Lebanese Law does not explicitly stipulate the right to prevent the confiscation of documents from migrants. However, Lebanon is bound by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) and International Convent on Civil and Political rights (ICCPR), which uphold the rights of individuals, including migrants, to freedom of movement. Treaties ratified by Lebanon are binding on the country. This is explicitly mentioned in paragraph 'B' of the preamble of the Lebanese Constitution, which states, “Lebanon is a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall uphold these principles in all fields and areas without exception.” The jurisprudence of the Constitutional Council in Lebanon affirms that the preamble of the constitution is an integral part of the Lebanese constitution. In the case of domestic workers in Lebanon, the Ministry of Labor has introduced a unified employment contract between the employer and the domestic worker. This contract explicitly states that employers are not allowed to confiscate the worker's identity documents. If an employer does confiscate these documents, the worker has the right to terminate the contract. In the event of any disputes between the parties, a complaint can be filed directly with the Ministry of Labor, either through a hotline or by initiating a claim before the relevant labor arbitration council. Domestic workers can also benefit from the Penal Code if they are victims of any crime deprivation of liberty (article 569), and they can file a complaint with the relevant authorities in that regard.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 11 of Law on Documenting Personal Status of 1951, which states that that "birth must be declared at the Personal Status Officer within 30 days of the date of birth." The birth certificate shall be drafted and signed by the father, mother, guardian, doctor or midwife who assisted the birth, and the "mukhtar" shall ratify the signature". However, in practice and in order to register the birth of migrant children, Lebanese authorities require a valid residency permit for both parents in case they are both migrants. Such requirement makes it impossible for many migrants (especially Syrian refugees who do not hold residency permit) to register the birth of their child.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right through Article 397 of the Lebanese Penal Code which provides a one year to three year imprisonment for anyone who burns or destroys, even if partially, the records, drafts or originals of the instruments of the public authority.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this obligation in Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Lebanon has ratified Vienna Convention on Consular Relations on 26/12/1970 by Law No 17.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Juvenile Law 422 ensures the best interest of the child through the emphasis on fair and humane treatment of the underage migrant in conflict with the law, the adoption of amicable settlements and solutions, taking measures most suitable to the juvenile, avoiding judicial proceedings if possible, and resorting to sentences depriving of liberty only as a last resort. However, it does not prohibit the detention of children on the basis of their status as a migrant.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The 1962 Law Regulating the Entry and Stay of Foreigners in Lebanon and their Exit from the Country (Law of Entry and Exit) does not prohibit the detention of migrants solely based on their immigration status. On the contrary, Article 32 provides that migrants shall be under penalty of imprisonment of between one and three years and of a fine of LBP 2500 to 12500 LBP and of expulsion from Lebanon, if: a) the migrant entered Lebanon without complying with the provisions of Article 6 of the present law (i.e. holding valid documentation, a visa, and legal entry through one of the posts of General Directorate of General Security); b) the migrant makes a false declaration to conceal his true identity or who may have used forged identity papers. In all such cases, the court shall not be authorised to grant the migrant a reprieve from the sentence or sentence him to imprisonment of less than one month.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in the Lebanese Criminal Procedural Code (CPC), which provides for appeal procedures regarding the legality, conditions and length of the detention (Articles 107, 108, 117 and 135 of the CPC provides for the right to appeal the decisions of the Investigation Judge and Article 192 of the CPC provides for the right to appeal decisions of the judge of first instance).

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The 1962 Law for Foreigner does not require an individualized determination for detention of a migrant. Article 32 provides for criminal charges against any person who enters the territory without proper authorization/visa.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right by being part of the United Nations Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhumane and Degrading Treatment. Lebanon has ratified the United Nation Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment by Law No 185 dated 24/05/2000. Additionally, in the rationale of the Lebanese Law No 65/2017 on the punishment of torture and other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment, it is mentioned that the UN Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, following its ratification in 2000, has become an integral part of Lebanese law and is directly enforceable.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Code of Conduct issued by the General Security was developed in cooperation with the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. It provides that the general security forces "shall refrain from performing, enticing, or overlooking any act of torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment during investigations or the execution of any functions they are entrusted with" and "they shall refrain from resorting to force except where it is necessary and in a way that is proportional to the foreseen risks, without exaggeration in assessing risks, in line with the lawfulness and the necessity of the situation, and after exhausting all non-violent means."

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 221 of Law 17 of 6/9/1990, Police officers shall only use firearms when it is absolutely necessary after taking all possible precautionary measures and after exhausting all other means. Therefore, though the use of firearms are restricted, it is not banned. According to the Code of Conduct of the General Security, the use of firearms is allowed only in cases of utmost necessity according to the law, in a way proportional to the risks, and after exhausting all non-violent means. When using firearms, the General Security officer shall ensure that damages and human injuries are as limited as possible and he/she shall provide the necessary first aid to the injured.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for smuggled migrants. Law 164/2011 regulates the criminalization and punishment of human trafficking. The law on human trafficking does not criminalize the victims of this crime. According to this law, victims of human trafficking are generally exempt from criminal liability. However, these victims can still face prosecution if they have committed any act punishable by law, or they have violated the conditions of their residency or the conditions of their work permit. In the latter case, these victims can be exempted from punishment if they can prove that they were forced to commit the offense or to breach their work permit and their residency conditions. In principle, victims of human trafficking are exempt from criminal liability. However, these victims can still face prosecution if they have committed any act punishable by law or violated the conditions of their residency or the conditions of their work permit. Prosecuted victims can be exempted from punishment if they can prove that they were forced to commit the offense or to breach their work permit and their residency conditions. On the other hand, in the absence of a clear framework for migrant smuggling, migrants who enter Lebanon illegally may be held criminally liable under Law 1962 regulating the Entry and Stay of Foreigners in Lebanon and their Exit from the Country.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right. Neither the Lebanese Criminal Code nor the Lebanese Nationality law contain provisions pursuant to which convictions can affect citizenship status.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Lebanese Nationality Law (Decree No.15 of 1925) and its amendments do not permit the granting of nationality to foreigners except for those of Lebanese origins. Lebanese nationality is acquired only according to blood association and exclusively when proving the Lebanese origin.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Lebanese Nationality Law (Decree No.15 of 1925) and its amendments do not permit the granting of nationality to foreigners except for those of Lebanese origins. Lebanese nationality is acquired only according to blood association and exclusively when proving the Lebanese origin.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Lebanese Nationality Law (Decree No.15 of 1925) and its amendments do not permit the granting of nationality to foreigners except for those of Lebanese origins. Lebanese nationality is acquired only according to blood association and exclusively when proving the Lebanese origin.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in The Lebanese Nationality Law, which does not provide for restrictions on dual nationality.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 9 of the Lebanese Constitution which provides that "there shall be absolute freedom of conscience. The state in rendering homage to the God Almighty shall respect all religions and creeds and shall guarantee, under its protection the free exercise of all religious rites provided that public order is not disturbed. It shall also guarantee that the personal status and religious interests of the population, to whatever religious sect they belong, shall be respected". Paragraph (B) of the Preamble of the Lebanese constitution provides that Lebanon is also a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception." Paragraph (C) of the preamble of the constitution provides that Lebanon is a parliamentary democratic republic based on respect for public liberties, especially the freedom of opinion and belief, and respect for social justice and equality of rights and duties among all citizens without discrimination. The right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief of migrants was mentioned in a Judicial Decision No. 51 issued by the First Instance Judge on 31/01/2019. In this decision, the judge upheld the right of the Palestinian defendant to exercise his freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, including the right to change their religion and create a video addressed to several Christian believers in Sweden, in which he shared his life testimony about his conversion from Islam to Christianity. The judge determined that this video does not constitute the offense of “inciting sectarian strife and of contempt of religious rites”, as alleged by the Public Prosecution in Lebanon. As part of the Judge’s reasoning, the Judge stated that “the defendant, like any citizen or foreigner residing on Lebanese territory, has the full freedom to choose the religion that satisfies their beliefs”.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Article 13 of the Lebanese Constitution, which provides that "The freedom to express one's opinion orally or in writing, the freedom of the press, the freedom of assembly, and the freedom of association shall be guaranteed within the limits established by law." 2) Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) providing that everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of nationality. Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) Article 13 of the Lebanese Constitution provides that the freedom to express one's opinion orally or in writing, the freedom of the press, the freedom of assembly, and the freedom of association shall be guaranteed within the limits established by law. 2) Article 1 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights provides that each State Party to the present Covenant undertakes to respect and to ensure to all individuals within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction the rights recognized in the present Covenant which include the right to freedom of expression. Paragraph B of the Preamble of the Lebanese Constitution provides that Lebanon is "a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall embody these principles in all fields and areas without exception."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Though Article 13 of the Lebanese Constitution provides that "The freedom to express one's opinion orally or in writing, the freedom of the press the freedom of assembly, and the freedom of association shall be guaranteed within the limits established by law," Article 92 of the Lebanese labor law provides that migrant workers cannot be elected to unions, or vote for union leadership positions. Migrants in Lebanon can form other types of associations, according to the Lebanese Law of Associations.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The 1962 Law Regulating the Entry and Stay of Foreigners in Lebanon and their Exit from the Country (Law of Entry and Exit) stipulates that the General Directorate of General Security may grant the family members of a certain category of migrant authorized to reside in Lebanon a one-year residency permit if the family members sign a notarized promise not to work or, if they are minors, provide a notarized undertaking of financial support from the head of the family. The aforesaid migrants who are entitled to family reuinification schemes are are: (I) Migrants whom residency is issued based on their financial capabilities, i.e., based on bank certificate showing a bank account of a value of no less than three hundred million Lebanese pounds (equivalent to US$ 200,000) or a certification of a monthly income that is estimated to more than five million Lebanese pounds (equivalent to US$ 3,300) from financial transfers or retirement funds from abroad, or any other legal funds. (II) Migrants who have an annual residency permit for work (only for jobs classified under class I and class II which exclude all migrant domestic helpers and migrant workers who earn a monthly salary ranging between the minimum salary wage and twice the said amount i.e. ranging between 450US$ to 900US$).

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in Article 8 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which states that "Everyone has the right to an effective remedy by the competent national tribunals for acts violating the fundamental rights granted him by the constitution or by law". 2) Article 5 of the Lebanese Code of Criminal Procedure, which grants access to criminal proceedings for any aggrieved party.?

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In general, Lebanese law does not provide migrant victims of crime an avenue to immigration status or relief from expulsion as a result of being a victim of a crime. The one exception is if the crime is categorized as a political crime, according to Article 26 of the 1962 Law on Entry and Exit of Foreigners.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Lebanon protects this right in 1) the 1962 Law for Foreigners, particularly Article 23. 2) The Convention on Rights of the Child ratified by Lebanon on October 20, 1990, Article 22 which provides that the state shall take all appropriate measures to ensure that a refugee child receives appropriate protection. Treaties ratified by Lebanon are binding on the country. This is explicitly mentioned in paragraph 'B' of the preamble of the Lebanese Constitution, which states, “Lebanon is a founding and active member of the United Nations Organization and abides by its covenants and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Government shall uphold these principles in all fields and areas without exception.” The jurisprudence of the Constitutional Council in Lebanon affirms that the preamble of the constitution is an integral part of the Lebanese constitution. Lebanon has ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child on 30/10/1990 (Law No 20). Lebanon has ratified join the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the sale of children, child prostitution and child pornography on 05/06/2002 (Law No 414).

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The 1962 Law Regulating the Entry and Stay of Foreigners in Lebanon and their Exit from the Country (Law of Foreigners) does not have provisions that take into consideration the vulnerability of women in the context of migration.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Lebanon adopted in 2000 Law 220 on the Rights of Disabled Persons (Law 220/2000). The law is mainly built around a set of rights integrating citizens with disabilities into social and economic life, through employment, transport and housing quotas, and guarantees of health and educational services but the 1962 Lebanese law relating to the Entry and Exit does not provide special protection for migrants with disabilities in comparison to other migrants.
