Article 22 states that: "Any person who has acquired Moroccan nationality may be stripped of it: 1° - if convicted : - either for an attack or offense against the Sovereign or members of the royal family ; - or for an act qualified as a crime or misdemeanor against the internal or external security of the State; - or for an act constituting a terrorist offence; - or for an act qualifying as a felony, to a sentence of more than fivey ears' imprisonment; 2° if they have evaded their military obligations." Article 23 addresses the procedural procedures for stripping citizenship, such as the necessity of withdrawing it by decree in the case in which it was granted by decree, and withdrawing it by decree in the normal case, with the need for the competent authorities to be obligated to inform the concerned personof the merits of the measures intended to be taken. Article 24 relates to the collective impact of deprivation of citizenship, which could include the wife and minor children.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Morocco protects this right in Law No. 06-62 is the Nationality Law, issued on March 23, 2007, Official Gazette No. 5513, April 2, 2007, Chapters 11 and 12. Chapter 11 relates to determining the conditions for foreigners to acquire Moroccan citizenship through naturalization, which are mainly regular residence for more than five years upon submitting an application, physical and mental integrity, a good reputation and the absence of a criminal record, as well as sufficient knowledge of the Arabic language and the availability of sufficient means of subsistence. Chapter 12: In exceptional cases, Moroccan citizenship is granted to a foreigner who has suffered a disability or illness as a result of work he performed in the service of Morocco, or to a foreigner who has performed or is performing exceptional services for Morocco, or whose naturalization results in an exceptional benefit to Morocco.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in Articles 11 and 12 of the Nationality Law. Article 11 states that, "Conditions for naturalization Subject to the exceptions set out in article 12, foreign nationals wishing to acquire Moroccan nationality by naturalization must demonstrate that they meet the following conditions: 1° - have been habitually and regularly resident in Morocco for the five years preceding the submission of the application, and remain resident in Morocco until a decision is taken on the application; 2° - be of legal age at the time the application is submitted; 3° - be of sound mind and body; 4° - be of good conduct and morals and not have been convicted of : - crime; - infamous offence; - acts constituting an offence of terrorism; - acts contrary to the laws of legal residence in Morocco; - or acts entailing forfeiture of commercial capacity. not erased in all cases by rehabilitation; 5° - provide evidence of sufficient knowledge of the Arabic language; 6° - provide evidence of sufficient means of subsistence. A commission has been set up to rule on applications for naturalization. Its composition and operating procedures are determined by the administration."

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Morocco protects this right in Chapter 7, 9, 10, and Article 18 of the Moroccan Nationality Law. Chapter 9 relates to the conditions for acquiring citizenship through birth and residence in Morocco, as well as the conditions for obtaining this citizenship through sponsorship, while Chapter 10 of the law specifies the acquisition of citizenship through marriage. It should be noted in this context that only the Moroccan husband has the right to grant citizenship for his foreign wife, while this possibility is not available to the Moroccan wife, although the wife is able to pass on her citizenship to her children. Article 18 states that, "Minor children of persons who acquire Moroccan nationality under article 9 of the present Code become Moroccan at the same time as their parents. The unmarried minor children of the reinstated person, when they actually live with the latter, recover or acquire Moroccan nationality at the same time as their parents. The naturalization deed may grant Moroccan nationality to the naturalized foreigner's unmarried minor children. However, naturalized minor children who were at least sixteen years of age at least sixteen years of age at the time of their naturalization may renounce Moroccan nationality between their eighteenth and twentieth birthdays."

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: All immigrants can acquire Moroccan citizenship while retaining their original nationality, as the conditions outlined in the Nationality Law do not mandate renouncing one's original nationality upon obtaining Moroccan citizenship. Specifically, legislation regarding Moroccan nationality lacks any provisions prohibiting dual nationality. Therefore, the prevailing principle, in the absence of explicit prohibition, is permissibility and acceptance.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Morocco does protect right in Article 25 of the Constitution, to freedom of thought, of opinion and of expression under all their forms. However, although Article 3 of the Moroccan Constitution, adopted in 2011, guarantees, ‘free practice of religion for everyone,’ the Constitution prohibits conversion to religions other than Islam. " In addition, Chapter 220 of the Moroccan Criminal Code, which criminalizes anyone who “uses means of seduction to shake the faith of a Muslim or convert him to another religion”, and this has been interpreted broadly.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Morocco protects this right in Articles 25 and 28 of the Moroccan Constitution. Article 25 states that, "The freedoms of thought, of opinion and of expression under all their forms[,] are guaranteed. The freedoms of creation, of publication and of presentation [exposition] in literary and artistic maters and of scientific and technical research[,] are guaranteed." Article 28 of the Constitution states that “All have the right to express and to disseminate freely and within the sole limits expressly provided by the law, information, ideas and opinions. “ Likewise, the law relating to the press and publishing did not include any distinction between Moroccans and foreigners residing in Morocco with regard to the procedures andcontrols for exercising these rights, as Restrictions on freedom of expression in various national legislation must be adhered to by everyone, regardless of nationality or residency status.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Morocco protects this right in Articles 25 and 28 of the Moroccan Constitution. Article 25 states that, "The freedoms of thought, of opinion and of expression under all their forms[,] are guaranteed. The freedoms of creation, of publication and of presentation [exposition] in literary and artistic maters and of scientific and technical research[,] are guaranteed." Article 28 of the Constitution states that “All have the right to express and to disseminate freely and within the sole limits expressly provided by the law, information, ideas and opinions. “ Likewise, the law relating to the press and publishing did not include any distinction between Moroccans and foreigners residing in Morocco with regard to the procedures andcontrols for exercising these rights, as Restrictions on freedom of expression in various national legislation must be adhered to by everyone, regardless of nationality or residency status.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While Article 29 of the Constitution states that, "The freedoms of reunion, of assembly, of peaceful demonstration, of association and of syndical and political membership [appartenance], are guaranteed. The law establishes the conditions of the exercise of these freedoms. The right to strike is guaranteed." However, while migrants can join associations and strike, they cannot lead or chair political organizations.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 16 of Law No. 02.03 states that: "A residence card may be issued to any foreigner who can prove at least 4 years' uninterrupted residence on Moroccan territory, in compliance with current laws and regulations. The decision to grant or refuse the residence card is taken taking into account the means of subsistence availableto the foreigner, including the conditions of his professional activity and, where applicable, the facts he can invoke in support of his intention to settle permanently on Moroccan territory.The residence card may be refused to any foreigner whose presence on Moroccan territory constitutes a threat to public order." Additionally, Article 16 of Decree No. 2.09.607, issued on April 1, 2010, for the implementation of Law No. 02.03 concerning the entry and residence of foreigners in the Kingdom of Morocco and measures against illegal immigration, published in Official Gazette No. 5831 on April 19, 2010, specifies that "a foreigner wishing to reunite with a family member must provide documentation to establish the family relationship in the case of marriage, filiation, or lineage until the child reaches the age of majority. In the case of caring for parents or sponsoring children, it is required that the individual has adequate means of subsistence."

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: Moroccan national law safeguards this right under Article 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, explicitly stating that 'Every crime entitles the right to initiate a public lawsuit for the application of penalties, and the right to initiate a civil lawsuit to seek compensation for the damage caused by the crime.' The criminal law and rules in Morocco demonstrate no differentiation between foreigners and citizens in accessing the courts. Criminal procedures guarantee automatic judicial assistance to victims, irrespective of their immigration status.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Morocco provides an avenue to relief from expulsion to victims of trafficking in Article 4 of Law 27.14 relating to combating human trafficking - Official Gazette No. 6501, September 19, 2016, p. 6644, which stipulates the possibility of granting temporary residency to immigrant victims of human trafficking within the framework of physical and psychological rehabilitation and recovery, according to available capabilities.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Morocco protects this right in 1) Clause 8 of Article 26 and Clause 3 of Article 29 of Law 02.03 wherein migrant children are exempt from deportation and expulsion to the border. 2) Provisions of the International Convention for the Protection of the Rights of the Child, which Morocco signed on January 20, 1990, and issued ratification and accession papers on June 21,1993, Official Gazette No. 4440 December 19, 1996, p.1477. 3) Article 30 of the Moroccan Constitution of 2011, which states in its preamble that Morocco commits itself “to comply with theinternational conventions duly ratified by it, within the framework of the provisions of theConstitution and of the laws of the Kingdom, within respect for its immutable national identity, andon the publication of these conventions, [their] primacy over the internal law of the country, and toharmonize in consequence the pertinent provisions of national legislation.”

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National Law in Morocco protects this right in Clause 7 of Article 26 and Article 29 of 02-03 Law. Clause 7 of Article 26 states that no pregnant woman should be deported. Article 29 states no pregnant woman should be deported. Additionally, Morocco ratified the International Convention to Combat All Forms of Discrimination against Women in 1993, and published in the Official Gazette in 2001, Official Gazette No. 4866, January18, 2001. This has been incorporated into Moroccan law by the provisions of the Moroccan Constitution of 2011, which emphasizes on the supremacy of international agreements ratified by Morocco.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Gerrie Lodder. [2]: Coder 2

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: The Netherlands

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Article 8 and 9 of the Dutch constitution. Article 8 states, "the right of association shall be recognised. This right may be restricted by Act of Parliament in the interest of public order." Article 9 states that "the right of assembly and demonstration shall be recognised, without prejudice to the responsibility of everyone under the law. Rules to protect health, in the interest of traffic and to combat or prevent disorders may be laid down by Act of Parliament."

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: Lawful presence does not create a legal right for third country national migrants to vote in the Netherlands. However, national law in the Netherlands provides the right to vote for members of the municipal council elections if they have a residence card and have resided in the Netherlands for a period of 5 years. Furthermore, Article 130 of the Dutch Constitution states that the right to vote for members of a municipal council and the right to be a member of a municipal council may be granted by Act of Parliament to residents who are not Dutch nationals provided they fulfil at least the requirements applicable to residents who are Dutch nationals. Furthermore, national law provides for a right to vote in local elections for EU citizens resident in a municiaplity in the Netherlands.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 1, 17 and 18 of the Constitution. Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution states that all persons in the Netherlands shall be treated equally in equal circumstances. Discrimination on grounds of religion, belief, political affiliation, race or gender or on any other ground is not permitted. Article 17 of the Constitution states that everyone has the right to a fair trial before an independent, unbiased judge. Article 18 of the Constitution provides for the right for everyone to seek legal and administrative assistance. 2) The Legal Aid Act, which provides legal aid to citizens in need of aid, and does not make distinctions between migrants and citizens. 3) Article 10(2) of the Aliens Act, which provides rights to legal aid which also explicitly applies to irregular staying migrants.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 43(2) of the Legal Counsel Act. Migrants other than Asylum Seekers are not entitled to legal aid during the application procedure, but can be entitled to funded legal aid after refusal of the application in an administrative appeal, or appeal before the Court, if they fulfill the general criteria in regard of income or capital and residence. 2) Article 10(2) of the Aliens Act, which provides legal aid for irregular staying migrants. 2) Article 8 of the Decree of the Legal Counsel Act. 3) Article 3.109 of the Aliens Decree, which provides legal aid for asylum seekers. Asylum seekers are entitled to free legal aid during the whole application procedure and after a negative decision in an appeal procedure before the Court.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 6 (3) European Convention of Human Rights, which is directly applicable in national law based on Article 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution; 2) Directive 2010/64/EU and Directive 2010/64/EU both provide for a right to (free) interpretation in criminal proceedings. 3) The international obligations are also implemented in national law in Articles 27(4), 29(b), 191, 260, 274-276, 325, 346, 362 and 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (wetboek van strafvordering). 4) The Instruction of assistance from interpreters and translators in the investigation and prosecution of criminal offenses. The right to interpretation at government expenses exists in the following situations: a) the suspect must be able to consult with his counsel with the help of an interpreter; b) the government is obliged to summon an interpreter at a number of essential times (including when the suspect is heard by the police or on the occasion of the handling of a claim for pre-trial detention); c) he suspect must be informed in writing in a language that he understands about the charge; d) the suspect must be given the opportunity to receive a translation of some crucial parts of the file, if this is necessary to prepare the defence.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Unauthorised entry in itself is strictly speaking not punishable as a crime, but it can lead to criminal sanctions in certain circumstances. Article 108 of the Aliens Act lists all the action which are punishable by criminal sanctions. Article 5 of the Aliens Act obliges a migrant who is refused entry at the border to leave the Netherlands immediately and follow the instructions of the Border guards. Article 6 obliges a migrant who is refused entry at the border to stay in a designated location. Article 46(2)(b) refers to all the obligations of a migrant in respect to border control. A migrant who does not comply with any of these regulations or obligations can be punished with a criminal sanction. In addition, migrants can also be subject to administartive sanctions for unauthorized stay in certain circumstances. Article 66a of the Aliens Act permits the administrative sanction of issuing a re-entry ban to iregular staying third country nationals who haven't complied with the obligation to leave the territory within a given time. Article 67 of the Aliens Act states that a migrant can be declared an undesired migrant if he has violated multiple times aprovision of the Aliens Act, like irregular stay. A criminal sanction can be imposed on a foreigner who has been declared undesirable and is found on Dutch territory.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right for all regular migrants in 1) Article 10 Huisvestingswet (Housing Act), which states that all migrants with a legal residence status have access to public housing programs commensurate with citizens. Irregular migrants are excluded from public housing programs. This provision also states that an alien who is not lawfully resident may not claim benefits and facilities provided by means of an order of an administrative body.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right for all migrants in 1) Article 40(1) of the Primary Education Act, which states that acces to a primary school may not be made dependent on legal residence. 2) Articles 28-29 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which have been incorporated into Dutch law by [CITATION]. 3) Article 14 Directive 2008/115/EG, which has been incorporated into Dutch law by [CITATION]. 4) Article 23 of the Dutch Constitution. 5) The Compulsory Education Act. 6) Article 8.4 (1)(b and c) Wet voortgezetonderwijs 2020 (Secondary Education Act), which states that children under 18 have access to secondary education regardless of the legal status of children over 18, who are allowed to finish the type of secondary education they started before they turned 18.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right for regular migrants in 1) Article 7(1)(c) of the Equal Treatment Act, which states that educational institutions are not allowed to discriminate against migrants in offering services in the field of education. 2) Article 7.32 (5)(c) Wet op het hoger onderwijs en wetenschappelijk onderzoek (Higher and Scientific Education Act). 3) Article 8.1.1(1)(c) Wet educatie en beroepsonderwijs (Education and Vocational Education Act). For the higher and scientific Education, every alien with a legal residence status can register as a student. Irregular students can only register before they turn 18, and can not register or apply after. However, they can continue and complete schooling they began before they turned 18 after they turned 18.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right for all convictions except criminal offenses in 1) Articles 16(1(d), Article 18(1(e), Article 19. Article 21(1)(c), Article 22(2)(c) of the Aliens Act 2000. 2) Article 3.86 of the Aliens Decree. A residence permit can be revoked as a consequence of a criminal conviction, depending on the length of stay; seriousness of the crime committed; right to family and private life.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in 1) Article 29(1)(b) of the Aliens Act, which provides for a residence right for people who fear (sub b, 2) torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. 2) Furthermore the prohibition follows from international instruments like the European Convention of Human Rights, the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights and EU law which are all applicable in the Dutch legal system based on Articles 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution and for EU law based on Article 288 TFEU.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 1, and 29(1)(a) of the Aliens Act. Article 29(1)(a) provides for a residence right for people who are a refugee, based on the United Nations Refugee Convention. The definition of a refugee, as formulated in this Convention is listed in Article 1. The protection applies to a persons who fears persecution on the basis of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion. 2) Furthermore, the Netherlands are bound by the Refugee Convention and EU legislation which contains the same prohibition of refoulment and has been incorporated into Dutch law based on Articles 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution and for EU law based on Article 288 TFEU.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 29 (1)(b)(1 and 3) Aliens Act, which provides for a residence right for people who fear for the death penalty or execution. Article 29 (1)(b)(3) also provides for a residence right for people who’s life is at risk as a consequence of an armed conflict. 2) This prohibition also follows from international instruments like the European Convention of Human Rights and other EU Instruments, which have been incorporated into Dutch law based on Articles 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution and for EU law based on Article 288 TFEU.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law does not require that a migrant be advised of the possible availability of asylum before being expelled or prevented entry. However, if entry is refused or a migrant is to be expelled this person will get a motivated decision which the migrant can contest.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 3.106a (c and d) of the Aliens Decree, which states that rejection of a request for asylum because the migrant enjoys such protection in another country, requires that it is ascertained that that country will respect the principle of non-refoulement. 2) Article 29 of the Aliens Act. 3) Article 3 of the European Convention of Human Rights, which are directly applicable in Dutch national law based on Articles 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Articles 61-66 of the Aliens Act, which contain the rules for the voluntary return and expulsion of migrants who (no longer) have legal stay in the Netherlands. Migrants without legal stay are obliged to leave within a certain time frame. If they do not leave, they can be expelled. A migrant can only be expelled after a request for residence has been denied (first residence or extension, and no appeal has filed or the appeal has been rejected), or their legal residence has expired, or after a return decision has been issued. In all these situations an individualised decision is required.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Articles 27(1), 45(1), 62-62b, 69, and 72(4) of the Aliens Act. The decision to refuse a residence right includes the legal ground for expulsion (decision to return) (Articles 27 (1) and 45 (1)). This decision can also be contested according to Article 69. The return decision filed against migrants who have not applied for a residence permit (Articles 62 to 62b) can also be contested based on Article 72 (4) and Article 69.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Article 3(2), 6(1)(b), and 8 of the Dutch citizenship Act. Article 3(2) provides for Dutch citizenship for the child found abandoned or abandoned in the territory or seagoing ship of the Netherlands unless within five years, counting from the day on which it was found, it appears that the child possesses a foreign nationality by birth. Article 6(1)(b) provides that the foreign national born in the Netherlands, who has had legal and main residence for an uninterrupted period of at least three years and has been stateless since birth acquires Dutch citizenship through the "option" procedure, and Article 8 allows stateless migrants to naturalize after 3 years instead of 5 years.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law provides settled migrants with legal avenues to faciliatate family reunification with immediate family members in 1) Article 15 of the Aliens Act. 2) Articles 3.13 - 3.24 of the Aliens Decree. Article 3.14 states that the eligible family members of a settled migrant are the minor children of the settled migrant or of his/her spouse and the spouse and unmarried partner. 3) EU Directive 2003/86, which has been incorporated into Dutch national law by Articles 93 and 94 of the DUtch Constitution. 4) EU Directive 2004/38, which has been incorporated into Dutch national law by Article 15 of the Aliens Act and Article 3.13 of the Aliens Decree. 5) Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which is directly applicable in Dutch national law by based on Articles 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution. For EU migrants, the conditions are relaxed.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 7:1 and 8:1 of the General Act on Administrative Decisions and Procedures (Algemene Wet Bestuursrecht), which contains general provisions on the possibility to have one's case reviewed and to submit reasons against administrative decisions, which include refusals of requests for family reunification. 2) Articles 69 to 92 of the Aliens Act.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 3.14 and 3.15 of the Aliens Decree. The Aliens Decree defines eligible sponsor and family member as the marital spouse who entered into a, according to Dutch International Private Law, valid marriage. Family reunification is also possible between registered partners and between partners who have a duly atested and durable relationship. In these situations the partners can also be same-sex partners. 2) Article 30 of the Civil Code, Book 1. According to the Dutch Civil Code, a marriage can be entered into by two people of different or of the same sex.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Having resided irregularly for a certain period of time in the Netherlands in principle does not make that person eligible for regularization. Only in very exceptional circumstances, in which it is established that the government was aware of this particular person’s presence in the Netherlands but failed to take any action to expel this person, even though there were no obstacles for doing so, may lead to the state viewing said migrant's presence as “tolerated” and thus an irregular migrant may become eligible for humanitarian status. In this case, such a migrant must have developed a substantive family or private life that is connected to the Netherelands. It is therefore not possible to ‘earn’ regular residence by working, or simply being present.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 610 of the Civil Code, Book 7, which regulates contracts between employers and employees, and includes protections on the right to redress for all employees, including migrants. 2) Article 23 Wet arbeid vreemdelingen (Aliens Employment Act), extends the right to redress to irregular migrants. 3) Article 5 of the Law on Equal Treatment. 4) Directive 2009/52/EC, which has been incorporated into Dutch law by, [CITATION].

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution. 2) Article 7 of the General Equal Treatment Act. 3) Article 2.1.1 of the Wet Langdurige Zorg (Act on long term care). 4) Article 2(1) of the Zorgverzekeringswet (Act on Health Insurance). Netherlands operates a system of obligatory health insurance which gives access to health care and creates an obligation for a health insurer to accept a request to provide health insurance. The obligation to acquire health insurance applies to all inhabitants of the Netherlands including migrants with legal residence status. Irregular migrants are excluded from this obligation and the possibility to acquire health insurance. This limits their access to paid health care. Irregular migrants have restricted access to medical care, meaning care that is only provided if this is considered medically necessary or necessary for the prevention of breaches of public health.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: Lawful presence does not create a legal right for third country national migrants to stand in elections in the Netherlands. However, national law in the Netherlands provides the right to stand as members of the municipal council if they have a residence card and have resided in the Netherlands for a period of 5 years. Furthermore, Article 130 of the Dutch Constitution states that the right to vote for members of a municipal council and the right to be a member of a municipal council may be granted by Act of Parliament to residents who are not Dutch nationals provided they fulfil at least the requirements applicable to residents who are Dutch nationals. Furthermore, national law provides for a right to stand in local elections for EU citizens resident in a municiaplity in the Netherlands.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution, which states that all persons in the Netherlands shall be treated equally in equal circumstances. Discrimination on the grounds of religion, belief, political opinion, race or sex or on any other grounds whatsoever shall not be permitted. Migrants and migrant status are covered under this provision which is confirmed in a ruling in ECtHR 6 November 2012, Hode and Abdi v. the UK, No. 22341/09.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Article 1 of the Constitution, which states that all persons in the Netherlands shall be treated equally in equal circumstances. Discrimination on the grounds of religion, belief, political opinion, race or sex or on any other grounds whatsoever shall not be permitted.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution. 2) Article 5 (1) of the Algemene wet gelijke behandeling (Equal Treatment Act), which provides for equal working conditions in general, including equal pay. Article 1 states that a distinction made on the basis of nationality is forbidden. This provision also includes migrants regardless of status.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects the right of free choice of employment, but requires that applicant apply for a new work permit in Article 2 (1) Wet arbeid vreemdelingen (Migrant Labour Act). The general rule, as laid down in the Migrant Labour Act, is that an employer is only allowed to employ a migrant worker if he has a work permit or a combined work and residence permit to work with a specific employer. Migrant workers with a common work permit are tied to a specific employer. If they want to change their employer, the migrant worker and new employer have to apply for a change of the residence and work permit. After five years of legal work and residence this migrant worker has free access to the labour market. Some categories of migrants always have free access to the labour market. The main groups are: a. EU migrant workers and their family members; b. Migrants with a residence permitfor asylum and most migrants with a residence permit for family migration; c. Highly skilled workersdon't need a work permit (only a residence permit); within the limits of certain conditions like an income criterium, they have free access to the labour market.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in a limited way in Article 7.1 Besluit uitvoering Wet arbeid vreemdelingen (Decree implementing the Foreign Nationals Employment Act. For family members of migrant workers (who need a work permit and residence permit) the labour market position is the same as for the principal migrant. Family migrants who stay with Dutch nationals or migrants with permanent residence have completely free choice of employment. The same applies to holders of international protection status and their spouses/partners. Family members of highly skilled workers are free on the labour market. Family members of EU migrant workers also have free access to the labour market. Family members of a migrant with a common work permit and of students are not allowed to work without a work permit.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 18, 19 and 22 Aliens Act. 2) Article 3.91 Aliens Decree for regular legal migrants (further elaborated in Sections B5/5 and B6/5 of the Vreemdelingencirculaire (Aliens Circular) and for EU citizens and their family members in Article 8.12 (2) of the Aliens Decree. According to Article 3.91 of the Alines Decree and Sections B5/5 and B6/5 Aliens Circular, most types of work related temporary residence permits, a period of three monthis is granted to find a new job. For migrants with a permanent residence status, loss of employment is never a reason for loss of residence status. For a temporary residence right, loss of residence can follow from no longer complying with certain conditions. For family migrants, employment is not a condition, so this cannot lead to a loss of residence status. Sufficient income is a condition for residence, so the loss of employment could lead to loss of residence status if the income requirement can no longer be fulfilled (but this will always be balanced against the interest of the family).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in 1) Articles 1, and 5(1) of the Equal Treatment Act, which states that it is forbidden to make a distiction on the basis of migrant status when an employer offers a position; job placement; entering into and terminating an employment relationship; formal working conditions; access to education and (vocational) training; promotion and conditions at the workplace. Article 1 also states that discrimination on the basis of nationality is forbidden. 2) Article 8(1)(d)(e) of the Act on Migrant Labour. 3) Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 6 of the Algemene Ouderdomswet (Old Age Act), which provides access to pensions to migrants. 2) Article 3(1) and (3) of the Werkloosheidswet (Unemployment Act), which provides access to social security in case of unemployment and illness . 3) Article 8 (1) of the Wet werk en inkomen naar arbeidsvermogen (Work and Disability Act), which provides migrants access to disability payments. 4) Article 1:1 (b)and 3:1 Wet arbeid en zorg (Work and Care Act), which provides migrants with access to maternity leave. Article 1:1 (b) and Chapter 4, 5 and 6 of the Wet arbeid en zorg (Work and Care Act) also provides migrants with access to short- and long-term care leave.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 3(1) and 3(3) of the Unemployment Act. 2) Articles 10 and 11 of the Aliens Act. 3) Article 7a of the General Equal Treatment Act. 4) Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution. Migrants who have legal residence in the Netherlands have immediate equal access to unemployment benefits. Although a prior duration of stay is not a condition as such, a condition for all employees is a certain duration of employment prior to the first day of unemployment. Entitlement to benefits arises for the worker if he has at least worked one hour per week in at least 26 weeks within a period of 36 weeks immediately preceding the first day of unemployment.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Articles 21 and 45b Aliens Act. Migrant workerswith a residence right with a temporary character can apply for one of the non-temporary character residence rights if they fulfil the conditions. Subsequently, they could apply for a permanent residence right.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Articles 50b and 55 of the Passport Act, which states that only officials duly authorized to consider requests for identity documents and border/immigration control officials may confiscate travel and identity documents.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Article 19e of the Civil Code Book 1 (Burgerlijk Wetboek (BW) Boek 1), which states that the duty to register the birth of a child (within 3 days after the birth) rests on the father of the child; the mother of the child is authorised to register the birth of her child. If no father is known or able to register the birth, the duty to register falls on any other person who have witnessed the birth. This duty exists regardless the status of the child. The duty to register a child is on the parents or other person who witnessed the birth. The relevant authority will effectively always register the child if a parent or other person reports it.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Article 9 of the Aliens Act, which states that there is an obligation to provide a document to migrants with lawful stay. This can be either a residence permit on all possible grounds or lawful stay awaiting the decision on an application for a residence permit, if the migrant is allowed to await the decision in the Netherlands (this applies in general to asylum seekers). The document provides information about the right to work, and the document can serve as an identity document.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands does not explitly make it illegal for anyone to destroy documents. However, it explicitly states that migrant documents are property of the state and must always be returned to the state in 1) Article 4.52 of the Aliens Decree. 2) Article 4.15a of the Voorschrift Vreemdelingen (Aliens Regulation). 3) Additionally, Article 57 of the Passport Act states that travel documents must be destroyed only by the authorities and only in a limited number of circumstances: if a document has not been collected within three months after having become available; if a document has been handed in; if the travel document has been cancelled and there is no right to appeal; if the document can no longer be used due to wrong information; if the document has been found and cannot be returned to its owner. 4) Article 67 of the Passport Regulation.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 56 (3) of the 'Penitentiaire Beginselenwet' (Act concerning principles with regard to imprisonment). 2) Regeling model huisregels penitentiaire inrichtingen, Bijlage point 3.8.3 (Appendix tot to Ministerial regulation containing house rules for prisons). 3) Article 5.5 (2) of the Aliens Decree. 4) The articles of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, are binding on all persons and are directly applicable in the Dutch legal system under Article 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution. Detained migrants have the right to contact consular officials of the sending state and to be visited by them.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are two grounds for aliens detention: Article 6 of the Aliens Act provides for detention of migrants who seek to enter the territory without the proper documents. Article 59 fo the same act provides grounds for detention for irregular staying migrants who are to be expelled. In both situations there is not a general prohibition on detention of minors. Families with minor children and unaccompanied minors who apply for asylum at the border, cannot be placed in border detention based on Article 6 of the Aliens Act, according to the guidelines (A1/7.3 A5 Aliens Circular). In other situations of refusing entry at the border and detention for expulsion families with minor children and unaccompanied minors are placed in a special facility where they can't leave the territory but have freedom of movement on the territory.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: Article 15 of the Dutch constituion and Article 6 of the ECHR are the basic provisions which prohibit detention. Detention is only alowed if there is a legal ground in national law. There are two grounds for aliens detention: Article 6 Aliens Act provides for detention for migrants who seek to enter the territory without proper documentation. The Articles 59, 59a, 59b, 59c Aliens Act are the ground for detention for irregular staying migrants who are to be expelled. This right is protected in national law (in the provisions listed above) by limiting detention to two circumstances; 1) migrants who are to be expelled and for whom there is a reasonably prospect of expulsion; 2) irregular migrants who pose a danger for public policy and security, including a risk of absconding. Detention to be expelled is only allowed as long as there is a reasonable prospect of expulsion, however, not all migrants who seek access to the territory irregularly, or who are to be expelled can be detained.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects the right of migrants to appeal the legality and duration of detention in in Articles 94 - 96 Aliens Act. National law in the Netherlands protects the right to appeal against the conditions of detention in Articles 60 to 69 of the Penal Principles Act (Penitentiare Beginselenwet) (for aliens detention with a view to expulsion) and Article 14-19 Border detention regulation (Reglement regime grenslogies). Migrants can appeal the initial legality of the detention in a first appeal procedure. If the migrant doesn't file an appeal themselves, a notification will be sent to the court within 28 days after the start of the detention which will be regarded as an appeal to the court. If the appeal is unfounded, the migrant can appeal the (legality of the) continuation and length of the detention. Migrants can also file complaints about the circumstances of their detention. Both the aliens who are detained on the basis of Article 6 of the Aliens Act 2000 and the aliens who are detained on the basis of Article 59 of the Aliens Act 2000, have the right of complaint against decisions made by the director of the institution where they reside. Aliens who are in detention pursuant to Article 59 of the Aliens Act can file a complaint under Articles 60 to 68 of the Penal Principles Act. Pursuant to Article 69 of this Act, it is also possible for them to appeal the decision of the Complaints Committee to the Council for the Application of Criminal Justice and Youth Protection. However, once a decision is made on their complaint, they cannot appeal said decision.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 6, 59, 59a, 59b and 59c of the Aliens Act. These provisions all regulate that the detention of a migrant should be based on a specific grounds, particular to each case\. 2) Articles 5.1a, 5.1b, 5.1c, and 5.3 of the Aliens Decree. Article 5.2 specifies that a migrant should be heard before placed in detention. Article 5.3 specifies that a decision to place a migrant in detention should state reasons and that the migrant should be notified of these reasons

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 11 of the Constitution, which states that 'Everyone shall have the right to inviolability of his person, without prejudice to restrictions laid down by or pursuant to Act of Parliament'. This is not the same formulation as the prohibition of torture, inhuman and degrading treatment. However, international conventions like Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 3 of the Anti-Torture Convention of the United Nations are directly effective in the Dutch legal system and have precedence over national rules (see Articles 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution) so the Netherlands are also bound by the prohibition of these international treaty provisions which entails the here listed forbidden treatments. As these rights apply to everyone, including migrants. 2) Article 3 of the European Convention of Human Right. 3) Article 3 of the Convention Against Torture.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Border control is excersied by the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee (military police). According to Article 7 paragraph 1 and 8 of the Police Act, the use of force by police officials in general, including officials of the Royal Dutch Marechaussee, is legitamate if it is necessary and proportionate. The use of force by police officials is further regulated in the 'Ambtsinstructie voor de politie, de Koninklijke marechaussee en andere opsporingsambtenaren' Official instruction for the police, the Royal Dutch Marechaussee and other investigating officers. Border control is regulated in the EU Schengen Border Code. This code does not entail a general prohibition of the use of force as means of preventing migrants from entering the (EU) territory. The Schengen Border Code stipulates in article 15 that "Member States shall deploy appropriate staff and resources in sufficient numbers to carry out border control at the external borders, in accordance with Articles 7 to 14, in such a way as to ensure an efficient, high and uniform level of control at their external borders.” However, in article 4 the Schengen Border Code prescribes that Member States shall act in full compliance with fundamental rights and article 7 (1) stipulates that 'Border guards shall, in the performance of their duties, fully respect human dignity, in particular in cases involving vulnerable persons.' Article 288 on the functioning of the EU gives general rules for the implementation and working of EU law in the member states. According to this provision a Regulation works directly in the legal order of the EU member states and member states are not allowd to implment these rules.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Article 7-10a Ambtsinstructie voor de politie, de Koninklijke marechaussee en andere opsporingsambtenaren ( Decree containing official instructions for police officers of various divisions, including border control officers). The use of lethal force by public officers in general is restricted to specific (dangerous) circumstances. These do not include the prevention of migrants from entering the state's territory.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right in national law for trafficked and smuggled migrants.However, in Dutch policy regulations trafficked, but not smuggled, migrants are excempted from criminal prosecutions in Section 3.2 of the 'Aanwijzing Mensenhandel' (Directions for the prosecution of human trafficking). The 'Aanwijzing Mensenhandel' contains the formal policy regulations for the prosecution of human trafficking. According to these rules victims of human trafficking are exempted from criminal prosecution of offences committed under force during a situation of trafficking. Offences committed voluntarily can be prosecuted.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands provides that only major convictions can lead to loss of citizenship status in Articles 14(1), 14(2), 14(3), and 14(4) of the Dutch Citizenship Act. Only very serious crimes, like crimes against members of the Royal Family, ministers and state secretaries or public institutions, international war crimes and terrorist crimes can lead to loss of Dutch nationality.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Articles 6, 8 and 9 of the Dutch Citizenship Act. There are three ways to obtain Dutch citizenship: by operation of law (not so relevant for economic migrants), by using an option on Dutch citizenship, or by naturalisation. Migrants with a non-temporary residence right and at least 5 years lawful residence (for married couples with a Dutch partner a shorter period applies) can apply for Dutch nationality through the regular naturalization process. Other requirements are the integration diploma, willing to make a declaration of commitment and renounce other nationality. In specific situations, Dutch citizenship can be obtained through a shorter and easier process: 'option' instead of the normal naturalization process.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 6, 8, and 9 Dutch Citizenship Act (Rijkswet op het Nederlanderschap). 2) Article 8 Dutch Citizenship Act. 3) Annex 3 to Article 8(1)(b) in the Handbook on the Application of the Dutch Citizenship Act. Migrants with a residence permit based on non-temporary humanitarian grounds can obtain Dutch nationality after 5 years of residence (see answer above). A problem that may arise in this respect is that humanitarian migrants are not always able to submit legal documents proving their birth/identity. The absence of such documents do not stand in the way of obtaining humanitarian residence status, but it is an obstacle for becoming a Dutch citizen.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 6, 8 and 9 of the Dutch Citizens Act. 2) Articles 3 and 8 of the Dutch Citizenship Act. Migrants with a non-temporary residence right and at least 5 years lawful residence (for married couples with a Dutch partner a shorter period applies) can apply for Dutch nationality. Other requirements are the integration diploma, willing to make a declaration of commitment and renounce other nationality. In specific situations, Dutch citizenship can be obtained through a shorter and easier process: 'option' instead of naturalization. When a migrant is married to a Dutch citizen, naturalization is possible after 3 years.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: Protection of this right is conditional on a migrant being unable to renounce their prior citizenship or other narrow exceptions. Article 9(1)(b) of the Dutch Citizenship Act provides that an applicant for citizenship be refused if "the applicant possessing a foreign nationality has not made every effort to renounce that nationality and/or is not prepared to make such effort after his or her naturalisation, unless this cannot reasonably be expected of him or her." The principal rule is that persons who become Dutch citizen departs their former nationality. However for some countries it is not possible to renounce their nationality and for some categories it is not obliged to renounce the former nationality: for example for persons who are married to Dutch citizens, for recognised refugees, for persons who have to pay a considerable amount of money to be able to renounce their former nationality and some other categories, Section 3 in the Handbook on the Application of the Dutch Citizenship Act (Handleiding Rijkswet op het Nederlanderschap 2003).

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Articles 1 and 6 of the Dutch Constitution. Article 6 (1) states that everyone shall have the right to profess freely their religion or belief, either individually or in community with others, without prejudice to their responsibility under the law.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 1, 6, and 7 of the Dutch Constitution. There is no specific provision in the constitution that grants the freedom to hold opinions, neither for citizens nor migrants. This right is considered to be included in the provisions protecting freedom of expression. 2) Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which has been incorporated into Dutch national law by Articles 93 and 94 of the Dutch Constitution. In this convention, the freedom to hold opinions is provided by Article 9: Freedom of thoughts, conscience and religion.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Articles 1 and 7 Dutch Constitution. Article 7(1) states that no one shall require prior permission to publish thoughts or opinions through the press, without prejudice to the responsibility of every person under the law.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in Article 8 Dutch constitution, which states that the right of association shall be recognized. This provision includes the right to join a trade union.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 16 (1)(c) of the Aliens Act and Article 3.22 Aliens Decree lay down the condition of resources for family reunification. In principal for family reunification, the sponsor must have sufficient and durable income, not being social assistance.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Article 51a(1)(a) of the Criminal Proceedings Code, defines the term 'victim' as "person" in criminal proceedings without distinguishing between citizens and migrants. 2) Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution, which prescribes equal treatment in general: “All those in the Netherlands are treated equally in the same situation. Discrimination on the grounds of religion, belief, political affiliation, race, gender or on any grounds whatsoever is not permitted.”

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands provides for this right in 1) Articles 8(k), 17.1(d) of the Aliens Act. 2) Articles 3.48(1), and 3.50 (1)(h,i,j) of the Aliens Decree. Suspected victims of human trafficking can be granted a period of lawful residence of, at max, 3 months to consider whether they want to press charges (reflection period). Victims of human trafficking, labour exploitation, honour-related violence and domestic violence are also eligible for residence status. The temporary residence status for victims of human trafficking and labour exploitation is connected to criminal proceedings. In case no criminal proceedings are started, or continued, victims do not have a right to residence except for very serious humanitarian reasons. A residence status may also be granted to persons who operate as a witness or reporter of human trafficking. For migrant victims of other types of crimes, there is no specific provision which grants a residence right.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right Article 3.15(3) (c) Vreemdelingenbesluit 2000 (Aliens Decree). This provision refers specific to the best interest of the child. The best interests of the child are also reflected in special, more favourable, provisions for children, for example in Vreemdelingenbesluit 2000 (Aliens Decree) Sections3.48(g), 3.50, 3.58(2), 3.109(b), 3.109(d), 6.5, 8.22. .2) and Voorschrift Vreemdelingen (Aliens Regulation): Sections 3.24aa, 3.34a, 3.45a. 3) Article 3 (1) of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. 4) Article 6 of Regulation (EU) No 604/2013; Art. 25 Directive 2013/32/EU.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While national law in the Netherlands provides special protections for migrants who fear honour related violence or domestic violence in Article 3.48 (1)(e, f) of the Aliens Decree, this is a blanket protection, and not specific to women.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in the Netherlands protects this right in 1) Articles 3.10b, 3.22(2), 3.94, and 8.22 of the Aliens Decree. Articles 3.22 (2) and 3.94 offer migrants who are disabled (not able to work) an exemption from the sufficient income criterion for family migration (exemption applies to the sponsor resident in the Netherlands) and for applying for permanent residence. 2) Articles 5 and 6 (1) of the Integration Act, which offer an exemption from the integration obligation to migrants who have a psychological or physical impediment, or a mental handicap, that causes them to permanently be unable to pass the integration exam. 3) B1/4.1, 4.7 and C1/2.2 of the Aliens Regulations. 4) Article 64 of the Aliens Act.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Francis Collins. [2]: Stewart Dalley

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: New Zealand

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, Section 16, which states that, "everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly."

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. However, national law protects this right for permanent residents in the Electoral Act 1993, Sections 73-74 and the Local Electoral Act 2001, Section 20. In accordance with Sections 73 and 74 of the Electoral Act 1993, migrants who have become permanent residents who have at some time resided continuously in New Zealand for a period of not less than 1 year can vote in both local and national elections.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for immigration proceedings. In general, migrants have the right of equal protection of the law in all administrative, civil and criminal courts. However, the Immigration Act 2009 limits the right of equal protection in relation to immigration matters. Appeals or judicial reviews stemming from decisions of the Immigration and Protection Tribunal first require the High Court (or upper courts if denied at first instance) to grant leave to appeal or judicially review the decision. Section 186 of the Immigration Act 2009 also limits a migrants right to appeal to the courts against a decision in relation to the grant of a temporary visa. Section 392 provides that no complaint can be made under the Human Rights Act 1993, which relates to unlawful discrimination.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to the legal Services Act 2011, Sections 7 and 12, legal counsel at government expense (Legal Aid) in cases that involve the detention of migrants is available to New Zealand residence visa holders who have been made liable for deportation, for those claiming refugee status (including related appeals), and who are unable to pay for their own legal services. Irregular migrants, and those on temporary visas cannot apply for legal aid.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in 1) the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, Section 24g, which guarantees that anyone charged with an offence "shall have the right to have the free assistance of an interpreter if the person cannot understand or speak the language used in court." 2) Legal Services Act 2011, Section 6.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right, as there are no specific civil or criminal sanctions for unauthorized entry. The Immigration Act 2009 Section 154 specifies only that a person who is unlawfully in New Zealand, i.e. including migrants who have mande an unauthorized entry, are liable for deportation.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right conditional on migrant status in the Housing Restructing and Tenancy Matters Act 1992 and the Social Housing Ammendments of the Ministerial Direction of 2020. However, there are exceptions, as not all migrants can access public support for housing. Only New Zealand Citizens and Permanent Residents are eligible for public housing programs. According to the Ministerial Direction on Continued Eligibility for Social Housing 2014, "the basic residential qualifications are that the person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand and- (a) is a New Zealand citizen; or (b) is a permanent resident who has been in New Zealand for more than two years since he or she became a permanent resident." Additionally, recognised refugees and those persons granted a residence visa as a victim of the Christchurch terrorist attack or those eligible to receive payment under the Christchurch Mosque Attack Welfare Program can access social housing.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in 1) the Education and Training Act 2020, which provides that "every domestic student is entitled to free enrolment and free education at any state school during the period beginning on the student’s fifth birthday and ending on 1 January after the student’s 19th birthday." Some migrant children are considered domestic students for the purposes of the Education and Training Act, according to Section 10, which states that a domestic student includes citizens, holders of a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009, and a person of a class or description of persons required by the Minister, by notice, to be treated as if they are not international students. 2) The Education Act 1989, Section 159(1), which provides that a person is considered a domestic student for tertiary education purposes if they are a New Zealand citizen, a resident visa holder, or a class of person required by the Minister of Education to be notified by Gazette such as to treat them as domestic students. Otherwise, the migrant will be considered an international student and be required to pay the fees associated with that to attend a public adult education institution.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right based on visa status in the Education and Training Act 2020, Section 10, and other person designated by notice of the Minister. Domestic students are provided a tuition subsidy which substantially reduces the cost of enrolment in most adult educational institutions; international students are ineligible for this and can be charged the full cost of their courses.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to the Immigration Act 2009, residence class visa holders can be liable for deportation as a result of several types of criminal convictions: a) if, when they were on a temporary visa, they committed a crime that they were subsequently convicted of that would lead to a sentence of 3 months or more; b) convicted of an offence that could lead to a sentence of 2 years or more within the first 5 years or residence; c) an offence of 5 years or more after 5 years but until 10 years of residence; d) an offence related to workplace exploitation if the offence was committed before 10 years of residence. In additoon, regarding administrative offenses, Section 160 also states that a residence visa holder may be liable for deportation based on past administrative offences related to the holding or acquisition of temporary or resident visas.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 130, 131 and 164. Refoulment is generally banned. However, in accordance with section 164(3) of the Immigration Act 2009, a recognised refugee can only be refouled if a refugee or a claimant for recognition as a refugee if Articles 32.1 or 33 of the Refugee Convention allows the deportation of the person. Further, Sections 164(4)(a) and 164(4)(b) of the Immigration Act 2009, a protected person (protected person status being gained if it is found that the person has substantial grounds for believing that they would be subject to torture as defined in Article 1 of Covenant Against Torture if returned, according to Section 130(5) of the Immigration Act; or pursuant to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, has substantial grounds for believing that they would be in danger of being subjected to arbitrary deprivation of life or cruel treatment if deported from New Zealand, according to Section 131(1) of the Immigration Act) may only be deported to any place other than a place in respect of which there are substantial grounds for believing that the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture (as defined by Article 1 of Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CAT)) or has substantial grounds for believing that they would be in danger of being subjected to arbitrary deprivation of life or cruel treatment if deported. Additionally, a person designed as a threat to national security by the Minister of Immigration can be deported, if the Governor-General by way of Order in Council, issues a deportation order against them.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act, Sections 164. Generally, refoulment is banned. However, Section 164(3) of the Immigration Act 2009 provides that a refugee or a claimant for recognition as a refugee may be deported only if Article 32.1 or 33 of the Refugee Convention allows the deportation of the person. Such persons have the right to appeal on humanitarian grounds according to Section 206(1)(d) of the Immigration Act 2009.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 131 and 164. For persons recognised as holding refugee or protected status, refoulement is banned if he or she would be in danger of being or subjected to arbitrary deprivation of life if deported. In making deportation decisions, attention must be given to the existence in the country concerned of a consistent pattern of gross, flagrant, or mass violations of human rights.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Immigration Act 2009, Section 133 states that, "A person has to signify his or her intention to seek recognition as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand to a representative of the Department (Immigration New Zealand) or to a constable." The notification of the possibility of asylum is not required.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. This right is only partially protected in connection with the "protection elsewhere" principle set out in AH (Egypt) [2013] New Zealand Immigration and Protection Tribunal 800268-272, which provides that the Immigration and Protection Tribunal has an implied power to refuse to recognise persons as refugees or protected persons on the same grounds as set out expressly in respect of the powers of a refugee and protection officer in Section 138(2) of the Immigration Act 2009. Section 138(2) covers situations where the person has the protection of another country or has been recognised as a refugee by another country and can be received back and protected there without risk of being returned to a country where he or she would be at risk of circumstances that would give rise to grounds for his or her recognition as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealnd protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 154-167, and in Part 6. Part 6 details a wide range of ways in which migrants can be liable for deportation; all of these entail decisions in accordance with or authorized by the law and in relation to evidence.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 193-208 and in Part 7. Appeals can be made in relation to decisions on residence class visas, recognition as a refugee or a protected person, and liability for deportation. In relation to temporary visa applications, legal appeals are not possible but there is a procedure for migrants who are lawfully in New Zealand to seek reconsideration of a decision by a different immigration officer. Sections 193-200 provide for such a right in appealing decisions relating to recognition as a refugee or protected person. Sections 201-208 provide for when other migrants may appeal on facts or on humanitarian grounds (or both). This right is, however, somewhat circumscribed for those who are making a subsequent claim for refugee status or who hold a limited visa and are making a refugee claim. Where a migrant is undocumented, they have no right of appeal, unless they appeal within the strict time limits applied as to when they first became undocumented.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Citizenship Act 1977 states that the Minister may (but does not have to) grant citizenship in special cases where a person would otherwise be stateless.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Immigration New Zealand Operational Manual explains a number of different conditions that apply to family reunification in New Zealand. These conditions are changed from time to time. At the time of writing, there are avenues for New Zealand residents or citizens to sponsor partners and dependent children, although these applications can be declined on health and character grounds. Parents of migrants can gain residence either if they have substantial investment capital (currently $0.5 million) and ongoing income (currently $60,000 per annum). The Parent Category resident visa allows adult children to sponsor residence applications of their parents. In addition to applicants meeting the eligibility, health and character requirements, sponsors must commit to sponsoring their parents for 10 years, including covering a range of maintenance and other costs. Sponsors must meet minimum income requirements, starting at 1.5 times the national median income for one sponsor sponsoring one parent. However, this is government policy, and not protected in the law.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 186-188, 245, 247 and 249/249A. Section 187 provides that most persons declined a resident visa have the statutory right of appeal to the Immigration and Protection Tribunal on the facts or special circumstances of the case (according to 188(1)(f)). And thereafter, per Sections 245, 247, and 249-249A, if they remain dissatisfied, to the High Court on appeal or judicial review (or both). However, Section 186(1) provides that there is no right of appeal in relation to any temporary visa application. Similarly, Section 186(3) provides that there is no right to bring judicial review proceedings to court in respect of any temporary visa application made from outside of New Zealand.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While there is no protection in domestic law, the Immigration New Zealand Operations Manual (which is a matter of government policy), E4.1.20 and F2.5 states clearly that partnership includes marriage, civil union or de facto relationship whether opposite or same sex.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Holders of Recognised Seasonal Employer Work Visas are not permitted to apply for other visas including residence visas and thus they are excluded from pathways to become lawful permanent residents.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Immigration Act 2009, Section 61, provides that the Minister of Immigration may grant a visa of any type to a person who is unlawfully in New Zealand if that person is not subject to a deportation or removal order, however, the decision to grant a visa in such cases is entirely at the Minister's discretion.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Employment Relations Act 2000, Part 9, which does not distinguish between migrant and local workers when it comes to rights to redress when employment contracts are violated. However, temporary migrants can experience difficulty in seeking redress due to their vulnerability when their visa is tied to a specific employer.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
