citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right, in the Health and Disability Services Eligibility Direction 2011, Part B, which provides that access to free public health care in New Zealand is limited to citizens, permanent resident, work visa holders who are eligible to be in New Zealand for 2 years or more, those under 17 and their parent or guardian is eligible, refugee claimants, and victims of people trafficking. All other migrants would be required to pay for treatment which would otherwise be free. Where a migrant does not fit eligibility criteria, there are some limited medical free access in certain situations such as personal injury which is covered under New Zealand's Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC), or emergency care where treatment is necessary to alleviate a risk to health.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 25 and 47(3) of the Electoral Act 2001 states that candidates for election in national or local body elections, respectively, need to be New Zealand citizens.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Immigration Act 2009 specifically allows for discrimination against migrants on the ground of migration status in relation to the Human Rights Act 1993. Section 392 prohibits complaints being made under the Human Rights Act 1993 "in respect of (i) the content or application of this Act or any regulations made under this Act; or (ii) the content or application of any immigration instructions made in accordance with section 22." Section 392 (3) is particularly clear: "This section recognises that immigration matters inherently involve different treatment on the basis of personal characteristics."

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in New Zealand broadly protects the right of migrants to be free from discrimination in the Human Rights Act 1993, Sections 21(1)(e), 21(1)(f). Sections 21(1)(e) provides it is unlawful to discriminate against any person on the grounds of race, and s21(1)(f) provides it is similarly unlawful to discriminate on the grounds of ethnic or national origins, which includes nationality or citizenship. However, migrants are explicitly excluded from protection against discrimination in the application of immigration law in the Immigration Act 2009, Section 392, which "recognises that immigration matters inherently involve different treatment on the basis of personal characteristics" and preclude claims made based on the Human Rights Act in relation to the Immigration Act 2009.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in 1) the Equal Pay Act 1972. The Equal Pay Act 1972 does not distinguish between migrant and citizen workers. 2) The Wages Protection Act 1993. 3) The Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022, which provides the basis for "bargaining for fair pay agreements that specify industry or occupation-wide minimum employment terms" - this act does not distinguish between citizen and migrant workers. There is, however, no specific protection against unequal pay for migrants compared to citizens.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. However, the Immigration New Zealand Operational Manual provides rules and regulations providing some migrants with the right for workers to change their employer. In relation to major categories: working holiday visa holders can change employer freely and choose region and occupation but under some schemes can only work for an employer for three months; essential skills work visa holders (general work visa category) can only change employers after applying for a variation of conditions from Immigration New Zealand, if essential skills workers wish to change occupations they must apply for a new work visa; partnership work visa holders can work without restrictions and can change employers; post-study work visa holders can work without restrictions and can change employers; seasonal horticultural and viticultural workers (Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme) can only change employer to another RSEapproved employer and must apply for a variation of conditions from Immigration New Zealand, they cannot work outside horticulture and viticulture.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Spouses/partners of a principal migrant on a temporary visa is required to apply for a work visa either on their own right or as the partner/spouse and to be granted a work visa before they can work. Generally, work visas can be granted when spouses/partners can demonstrate a genuine relationship and have been living together. At the time of writing plans to cease granting work rights to spouses/partners of Accredited Employer Work Visa holders from December 2022 have been postponed with no date yet announced for when these changes will occur.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 157 and 159. Loss of employment only effects immigration status if the migrant's visa is tied to the employment, as opposed to having an open work visa permitting the migrant to work for anyone or no one. V3.115 of Immigration New Zealand's "Operational Manual" provides that visitor visas can be granted (subject to meeting other criteria) to migrants and their family members, if they held a work visa specific to an employer who are dismissed during a 90-day trial period. Under section 157 of the Immigration Act 2009, all other employer specific work visa holders would effectively no longer be eligible for the visa they hold and could accordingly be made liable for deportation for breaching their visa conditions, unless granted another visa (work or otherwise). Similarly, where continued employment was a prerequisite for a specified time period on a resident visa, loss of said employment could result in deportation for breaching their visa conditions, per Section 159.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in 1) the Employment Relations Act 2000, Part 6, which provides for most of these terms of employment, and defines who are employees. No distinction is made between migrant and local employees. Thus, generally migrant workers have the same rights to equal employment conditions and protections as local workers. 2) The Holidays Act 2009. 3) The Parental Leave and Employment Protection Act 1987. 4) The Health and Safety at Work Act 2015. 5) The Human Rights Act 1993. Migrant workers are not protected from discrimination on the basis of migration status under the Human Rights Act 1993 as outlined in Section 392 of the Immigration Act 2009. In practical terms too, the linking of work visa status to employers means that it is more difficult for migrant workers to pursue their rights in relation to employers as has been evident in numerous cases of workplace exploitation in recent years in New Zealand. 6) The Privacy Act 1993.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: Protection of this right depends on migrant status. However, some are available to all migrants that are lawfully present. 1) the Accident Compensation Act 2001, applies to all persons lawfully in New Zealand for workplace injury and diseases to the same degree as citizens. 2) The Parental Leave and Employment Protection Act 1987, does not distinguish entitlements between persons holding work visas, residence class visas or citizens. Other social security protections differentiate on the basis of visa type. 3) The Social Security Act 2018 includes a residential requirement (Section 16), which specifies that social security is only available to New Zealand citizens or persons holding a residence class visas for two years or more, thus excluding work visa holders. 4) The Kiwisaver Act 2006 covers eligibility for workplace savings schemes, including employer and government contributions - only New Zealand citizens and persons with the right to live indefinitely (e.g., have a valid residence visa) in New Zealand are eligible, work visa holders are thus ineligible. 5) The New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001, specifies residential requirements that make work visa holders ineligible for this scheme.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 17 of the Social Security Act 2018 provides that only New Zealand citizens or holders of residence class visas who are ordinarily resident in New Zealand, or recognised refugees or protected persons are eligible for benefits. Section 19 specifically states that a person is not entitled or eligible to receive a benefit if the person is lawfully resident or present in New Zealand but only by virtue of holding a temporary entry class visa. Section 205 does, however, permit the grant of emergency benefit and other support to person lawfully inside New Zealand who have made a claim for refugee or protected person status and are awaiting the outcome.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: No legal protection of this right. However, according to the New Zealand Operational Manual, which is government policy, temporary migrant workers can apply for residence and become lawfully settled if they meet certain criteria. These criteria vary by category (skilled, business, family, humanitarian), are modified regularly, and updated in the Immigration New Zealand Operations Manual. In relation to migrant workers, residence-class visas normally involve applications to the Skilled Migrant Category within which points are awarded on the basis of English language ability, age, skilled employment, work experience, qualifications, partners qualifications, remuneration.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 281b, 351 and the Customs and Excise Act 2018, Section 259. The right to not have identity documents confiscated is only specified in relation to cases where an employer is "allowing an unlawful employee or temporary worker to work in the employer’s service"; in those situations it is characterized as an offense under the Immigration Act 2019 to take or retain “possession or control of a person's passport, any other travel or identity document, or travel tickets." Section 281b of the Immigration Act 2009 specifies that certain public officials including immigration officers can seize or confiscate identity documents, explicitly stating protection of this right in this context.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right, in Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Act 1995, Section 5. The act states that "Every birth in New Zealand shall be notified and registered in accordance with this Part."

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While visas generally recognize both residency and work status, they need not be documents, but can be electronic and therefore are not required to be issued to migrants. In addition, the law provides for the discretionary issuance of identity documents only in cases where a migrant is unable to obtain one from their country of citizenship. The Passport Act 1992, Section 16 stipulates that the Minister of Internal Affairs "may issue a certificate of identity to any person, not being a New Zealand citizen, if the Minister is satisfied that the person is unable for any reason to obtain a travel document from the Government or other appropriate authority in the country of his or her nationality." Similarly, pursuant to Section 27A of the Passport Act, a Refugee Travel document can also be issued to persons recognized as refugees by New Zealand.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009 Section 345, which makes it an offence to destroy documents that recognise a migrants' residency status, work status, and identity. The penalty for doing so will be imprisonment for a term not exceeding 7 years, a fine not exceeding $100,000, or both.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. New Zealand ratified the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations in 1974. However, Section 4 of the Consular Privileges and Immunities Act 1971 (as amended) does not list Article 36 as one of the articles within the Convention that has force of law in New Zealand.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Immigration Act 2009 Sections 309 and 310 do not distinguish between adults and children in relation to immigration detention. Immigration is a civil rather than criminal matter and as a result the rights of children to have immunity from detention due to age do not apply. Section 317, however, specifies that in cases of mass arrival warrants permitting detention that persons under the age of 18 can only be detained if they have a parent, guardian or relative that arrive and are detained as part of a "mass arrival" of 30 or more persons.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Immigration Act 2009 provides for detention of persons liable for deportation as a result of their immigration status. Section 310 outlines a number of circumstances where a migrant can be detained on the basis of their status as a migrant, such as being liable for turnaround; liable for deportation; suspicion of being liable for turnaround or deportation where contrary evidence fails; where the migrant constitutes a threat or risk to security. Additionally, if someone is found to have somehow entered NZ without coming through the usual border route, they would likley be detained pending deportation.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in 1) the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 324, 324A. Sections 324(3) stipulates that those migrants detained under a warrant of commitment can apply to the District Court to vary conditions or release on conditions. This section does not however allow for those detained as part of a mass arrival (discussed below) to apply to review their condition or term of detention. 2) The Judicial Review Procedure Act 2016. 3) The High Court Rules 2016. A detained migrant can exercise their rights to seek judicial review related to the legality of their detention to the High Court pursuant to the Judicial Review Procedure Act 2016, or to make an appeal against the District Court's decision in accordance with the High Court Rules 2016.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 317 of the Immigration Act provides for an individualized determination for the detention of migrants. However, when an application is made to the court in respect of the detention of persons arriving collectively (defined as a mass arrival), Sections 317A-317E provides that the application is assessed as a whole, rather than individually.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in 1) the Crimes of Torture Act 1989, which implements New Zealand's obligations under the Convention Against Torture and the Optional Protocol to the Convention. It prohibits acts of torture and provides for a National Preventive Mechanism (NPM) to inspect and monitor places of detention. While migrants are not specified within the act, protection against torture is considered absolute. The Crimes of Torture Act 1989 Section 16 specifies "premises approved under the Immigration Act 2009" under its list of places of detention. However, in the absence of its own dedicated detention facilities, Immigration New Zealand has regularly detained asylum seekers and some migrants in correctional facilities, as outlined in an Amnesty International report in 2021 and an independent review of Immigration New Zealand's 'Restriction of Movement of Asylum Claimants’, which recommended changes to Part 9 of the Immigration Act 2009 and a range of changes to processes and procedures pending this legislative change. 2) New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, Section 9, which states, "Everyone has the right not to be subjected to torture or to cruel, degrading, or disproportionately severe treatment or punishment."

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 123 of the Immigration Act 2009 provides immunity from civil proceedings where the person used reasonable force in good faith in accordance with Sections 101 or 118 of the Immigration Act 2009. Section 285(2) of the Immigration Act 2009 grants an immigration officer with the power to enter a place located on the border - as defined in s 285(3) - by force, if necessary, with or without a warrant, where they have reasonable cause to believe a person who is liable for deportation or turnaround is located.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The immigration legislation is silent on lethal force. Section 39 of the Crimes Act 1961 provides that police officers or those assisting police officers can use lethal force when executing any sentence, warrant, or process, or in making or assisting to make any arrest. The Crimes Act does not expressly state the grounds by which the use of lethal force would be measured. The Immigration Act provides only that the use of force be deemed reasonably necessary, but does not address whether the use of lethal force to prevent entry is reasonably necessary.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in the Crimes Act 1961, Sections 98B-98F, which states that only the acts of trafficking and smuggling migrants are criminalized. Though the law does not explictly exempt trafficked and smuggled migrants from criminal prosecution, the law is explicit in that only the smuggler or trafficker are liable for criminal sanction.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand Protects this right in the Citizenship Act of 1977, Sections 16, 17, and 19. Criminal convictions gained after a person has New Zealand citizenship will not generally result in the depravation of citizenship. However, Section 16 of the Citizenship Act 1977 provides that persons of at least 18 years of age and of full capacity can be deprived of their New Zealand citizenship if they are a citizen of another country or have exercised the privileges or performed other duties of another country of which they are a citizen or national, if it is determined that they acted in a manner that is contrary to the interests of New Zealand. Section 17 provides that New Zealand citizenship can also be deprived if it is established that it was procured by fraud false representation, or wilful concealment of relevant information, or by mistake. For the latter (mistake), deprivation will not occur if to do so would render that person stateless. Where Sections 16 or 17 are invoked, Section 19 provides that the person must be first given the right to appeal the decision to the High Court for a declaration that there are insufficient grounds to deprive them of citizenship.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Citizenship Act 1977, Sections 8, 9a, and 71. Section 8 provides that persons 16 and over can apply for citizenship if they are a New Zealand resident visa holder, and resided in New Zealand for a minimum of 1,350 days during the 5 years immediately preceding the date of the application, and for at least 240 days in each of those 5 years; albeit, there is some ability to waive or reduce the residence requirements.According to Section 9a, applicants must also have sufficient English language skills and be of good character

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Citizenship Act 1977, Sections 8, 9-9a, and 71. All persons who have held residence visas for 5 years or more and demonstrated a commitment to New Zealand can be granted citizenship. In addition, Section 9 of the Citizenship Act 1977 provides that a person can also be granted citizenship status if the relevant Minister is satisfied that granting New Zealand citizenship to the applicant would be in the public interest because of exceptional circumstances of a humanitarian or other nature relating to the applicant, or if the person would otherwise be stateless.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Citizenship Act 1977, Sections 3, 6-8, 71. According to Section 6, persons are citizens by birth, if born inside New Zealand and if at least one of their parents was a New Zealand resident visa holder or citizen at the time of their birth (or per Section 3, later adoption). Otherwise, per Section 7, they are a New Zealand resident by descent if born outside of New Zealand to at least one parent who was a New Zealand citizen at the time of their birth (or if the parent was a citizen by descent, citizenship would only pass on if that person would be stateless otherwise). Absent Sections 6 or 7, Section 8 applies, and each applicant of citizenship must satisfy the relevant criteria in their own right, which for migrants would be by holding a resident class visa for 5 years and residing in the country for the required period of time in each of those 5 years.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Citizenship Act 1977. All citizens can have dual citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, Section 13, which states that "everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience, religion, and belief, including the right to adopt and to hold opinions without interference."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, Section 13, which states that "everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience, religion, and belief, including the right to adopt and to hold opinions without interference."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, Section 14, which states that, "everyone has the right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to seek, receive, and impart information and opinions of any kind in any form."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right, in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, Section 17, which states that, "everyone has the right to freedom of association."

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Resource conditions are required for the sponsorship of parents (income, investment capital), siblings (income, job offer) and adult children (income, job offer). These requirements vary by type of visa applied for and applicant; requirements are outlined in the Immigration New Zealand Operational Manual.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in 1) the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, Section 27. The right to justice is affirmed for everyone in the New Zealand Bill of Rights. 2) The Victims' Rights Act 2002, Section 4. A victim in the context of the Victims' Rights Act does not distinguish between migrants or citizens.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 61, 61A, and 207. The only crimes where an avenue to immigration status is specifically provided for is where the migrant has been the victim of family violence, perpetrated by a New Zealand citizen or resident, where certain eligibility criteria are met (see WI7 and S4.5 of Immigration New Zealand’s “Operational Manual"), or victims of people trafficking (V13.5 and WI.16 of Immigration New Zealand’s "Operational Manual"). Further, in the wake of terrorist attacks in Christchurch on 15March 2019, immigration status can also be granted to those persons who were victims and their immediate family, see Section 4.30 of Immigration New Zealand "Operational Manual." The Immigration Act 2009 does not specify these visas; such visas are a matter of government policy, which is outlined in Immigration New Zealand's Operational Manual, which is published pursuant to sections 22-25 of the Immigration Act. There is, however, no overall relief to expulsion as the victim of crime. A migrant that was due to be deported may have the right to appeal deportation. However, the fact that they had been a victim of a crime would not necessarily in isolation result in their deportation being cancelled, pursuant to section 207 of the Immigration Act 2009.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in New Zealand protects this right in 1) the Immigration Act 2009, Sections 375, 377 and 398. The Immigration Act 2009 states that in proceedings related to deportation, recognition as refugee or protected person, appeal/review of immigration proceedings or detention that minors are to have a responsible adult to represent their interests (Section 375) and that the views of minors are to be considered (Section 377). The Immigration Act 2009 Section 398 also provides for the financial assistance to be provided to dependent children and/or partners of a deported migrant. 2) The Immigration New Zealand Operational Manual, Section A16.1. Visas are provided for dependent children of temporary and permanent visa holders in the Immigration New Zealand Operational Manual. Section A16.2.15 specifies the application of the Immigration Act 2009 in relation to children and young persons under the age of 18 and in relation to UNHCR guidelines and UN Convention on the rights of the child. This includes prioritizing the interests of the child, that the child is not to be separated from their parents against their will (except where it is in their best interests/welfare) and the general avoidance of detention of children and young persons. Section A16.1 of the Immigration New Zealand Operational Manual (updated 22/12/2022) specifies that applicants for the 2021 Resident Visa category will be prioritized if the applicant is separated from their offshore partner and/or dependent children due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Migrant women who have been the victim of family violence perpetrated by a New Zealand citizen or resident, can obtain both temporary and resident visas due to such family violence, where certain eligibility criteria are met. The Immigration Act 2009 does not specify these visas; such visas are a matter of government policy, which is outlined in Immigration New Zealand’s Operational Manual, which is published pursuant to sections 22-25 of the Immigration Act.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Immigration New Zealand policy instructions (Operational Manual) provides at A4.10 that all resident visa applicants are subject to health criteria, and can be denied a visa if they are deemed to be an unacceptable standard of health. A4.10(b) of the Operational Manual provides that a migrant is considered to have an unacceptable standard of health if they have a medical condition or group of conditions that are deemed to impose significant costs and/or demands on New Zealand’s health and/or education services. This generally calls for an individualized assessment. However, the current policy provides at A4.10.1 that migrants with severe hearing, vision or developmental disorders or severe cognitive impairments are pre-deemed to be an unacceptable standard of health. Accordingly, those with such disabilities will only gain a visa if an immigration processing officer grants a medical waiver; wherein, per A4.70 of instructions, various countervailing factors are taken into account (such as degree of costs of medical condition on New Zealand, family ties to New Zealand, the visa they are applying for etc.) alongside the medical condition, in determining whether to waive the medical condition; if waived, the visa application can then be otherwise assessed against the specific criteria of the visa applied for. A4.60(iii)provides that those migrant visa applicants who have a physical, intellectual, cognitive and/or sensory incapacity that requires full time care, including care in the community are not eligible fora medical waiver, and, as such, will have their visa application denied.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: Coder 1: Linda Ekeator; Coder 2: Joseph Onele

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Nigeria

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 40 of the 1999 Constitution which allows everyone to assemble freely and associate with other persons.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does not provide the legal right for migrants who are not citizens of Nigeria to vote. See sections 77(2) and 117(2) of the 1999 Constitution both of which reserve voting rights to Nigerian citizens who have attained the age of 18 years, and section 12 of the Electoral Act, 2022 which requires citizenship for any person to be registered as a voter.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in Section 36 of its Constitution and in section 101 of the Immigration Act 2015.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 10 of the Legal Aid Act 2011 which provides that persons are entitled to legal aid on the basis of a resource condition so long as their "income does not exceed the national minimum wage." However, in exceptional circumstances, legal aid services may also be granted to a person whose earning exceeds the national minimum wage, subject to the approval of Governing Board of the Legal Aid Council.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in Section 36(6)(e) of the 1999 Constitution which provides that, "every person who is charged with a criminal offence shall be entitled to have, without payment, the assistanvce of an interpreter if he cannot understand the language used at the trial of the offence." This right is also protected in Section 63 (c) of the Trafficking in Persons Prohibition Act 2015 which provides that, "a victim of trafficking shall be provided with counselling and information as regards (the) victim's legal rights in a language that the victim can understand."

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right as the Immigration Act 2015 in its section 56 (1) (b) makes it an offense for any person to enter and remain in Nigeria having been refused entry, and prescribes penalty for the offense in section 56(4). However, section 62 of the Trafficking in Persons Prohibition Act 2015 prohibits detention or prosecution of a trafficked persons for any offense relating to being a victim of trafficking, including non-possession of valid travel documents, or the use of false travel or other documents.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right, for smuggled migrants and refugees, in section 100 of the Immigration Act 2015 and Article 21 of the Articles of the Convention applicable to the Status of Refugees which is the First Schedule of the National Commission for Refugees Act. The Immigration Act provides for the establishment of 'Transit shelters' as facilities for caring for smuggled migrants, and mandates the Nigeria Immigration Service to ensure that "steps are taken to maintain and rehabilitate facilities provided for smuggled migrants"; while the National Commission for Refugees Act requires that the authorities provide shelter for refugees legally staying in the territory with housing in a manner as favorable as that provided for nationals.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in sections 2, 3, and 5 of the Compulsory, Free Universal Basic Education Act 2004 which provides for free, compulsory and universal basic education for every child of primary and junior secondary age enrolled in public primary and junior secondary school; and this applies to all children who are resident in Nigeria. Also, section 18 (3) (a) & (b) of the 1999 Constitution; Article 17(1) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples Rights (Ratification and Enforcement) Act make similar provisions.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in Section 18 (3) (c) & (d) of the 1999 Constitution; Article 17 (1) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples Rights (Ratification and Enforcement) Act. See also the National Universities Commission Act and the National Board for Technical Education Act.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria regulates how migrants' criminal and other convictions affect their residence status. Section 58 the Immigration Act 2015 makes it an offense for any employer of persons liable to repatriation to discharge any such persons without giving notice to the Comptroller-General of Immigration (CGI), or for any such employed person to be re-designated, or to change his employment, without the approval of the CGI; and upon conviction, the employer (if not a citizen of Nigeria), the employed person and his dependants shall, if the Minister of Interior thinks fit, be deported and the business of the employer be wound up as described under the Act. The foregoing may be considered an administrative offense which renders the offender liable for loss of residence status. Section 1 (2) of the National Commission for Refugees Act Chapter N21 (LFN) 2004 provides that a refugee may be expelled if they pose any danger to the security of Nigeria, or if they are convicted by a court or tribunal for committing any serious crime as stipulated under the Act.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria bans refoulement but not on the basis of a risk of return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. See section 3 (2) of the Extradition Act 2004 and section 1(1) of the National Commission for Refugees Act, LFN, 2004. The stated laws protect against refoulement if the personal liberty of the concerned person is threatened or if the person would be prosecuted as a result of nationality, race or religion. Risk of torture, cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment are not mentioned under those provisions.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 3 (2) of the Extradition Act 2004 and section 1(1) of the National Commission for Refugees (NCR) Act, LFN, 2004. Section 3 (2) of the Extradition Act 2004 prohibits the extradition of even a fugitive criminal "if it appears to the Attorney-General or a court dealing with the case (a) that the request for his surrender, although purporting to be made in respect of an extradition crime, was in fact made for the purpose of prosecuting or punishing him on account of his race, religion, nationality or political opinions or was otherwise not made in good faith or in the interest of justice; or (b) that, if surrendered, he is likely to be prejudiced at his trial, or to be punished, detained or restricted in his personal liberty, by reason of his race, religion, nationality or political opinions." Section 1 (1) (a) of NCR Act provides to the effect that no person who is a refugee within the meaning of the Act shall be refused entry into Nigeria, expelled, extradited or returned in any manner whatsoever, to the frontiers of any territory where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular group or political opinion.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in Article 33 of the First Schedule to the National Commission for Refugees Act - Prohibition of Expulsion or Return ("refoulement").

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 8, specifically sub-sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, of the National Commission for Refugees Act.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this law in section 3 of the Extradition Act and section 1 of the National Commission for Refugees Act. Under these provisions, expulsion to a country where a migrant could be subjected to refoulement through a subsequent expulsion is not one of the categories prohibited.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in sections 44, 45, 46, 47 and 50 of the Immigration Act 2015. Sections 44 (2) and 45 requires conviction of an immigrant accompanied by a deportation order before deportation can be effectuated. Additionally, for migrants seeking asylum or refugee status, this right is further protected in section 8 of the National Commission for Refugees Act which provide that where refugee status is denied, the Eligibility Committee shall give reasons for its decision, the applicant has the right to appeal against the decision and if the applicant is finally refused a refugee status, they shall be given reasonable time to seek admission as a refugee into another country.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 46 of the Immigration Act 20015 [where Order of Deportation of an Immigrant has been issued]. In addition, for migrants seeking asylum or refugee status, this right is protected in section 8 (6), (7), (8) & (9) of the National Commission for Refugees Act; and section 13 (1), (2) & (3) of the National Commission for Refugees Act [where asylum/refugees status of a migrant is withdrawn].

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no specific legal provision granting citizenship to stateless persons under Nigerian law. Citizenship to non-Nigerians generally is provided under sections 26, 27 and 28 of the 1999 Constitution and none of those make any reference to statelessness.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does not recognize same sex relationships under the family reunification framework as mentioned in section 1 of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, 2014.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in Section 96 of the Immigration Act 2015 which provides for the juridiction of the Federal High court to hear and determine any matter arising from any aspect of the provisions of the Act, and that does not exclude matters relating to family formation / reunification, and such matter can be instituted by any affected person of any category of migrants. National law provides additional rights for refugees in the form of a judicial remedy to appeal the refusal by the authorities to allow family formation/reunification in section 10 of the National Commission for Refugees Act which prohibits court proceedings against a person or any member of their family for unlawful entry into or unlawful presence within Nigeria, provided that the appelant has been granted a refugee status or has a pending application for the grant of a refugee status..

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does not recognize same sex relationships under the family reunification framework as mentioned in section 1 of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, 2014.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: The opportunity for temporary migrant workers to switch to permanent status is conditional on migrant being an investor who had imported an annual minimum threshold of capital as specified in the current national visa policy or any other relevant policy.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in sections 45 and 46 of the Labour Act 2004.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in sections 1(1)(c)&(d), 20, and 30(1) of the National Health Act, 2014. Section 1(1) (c) provides to the effect that a national health system shall be established to provide for people living in Nigeria the best possible health services within the limits of available resources. This provision is without discrimination against migrants. Section 20 prohibits the refusal of emergency healthcare to any person and for any reason. This section again does not exclude migrants from benefiting; and Section 30(1) allows any person (not excluding migrants) to lay a complaint about the manner of treatment received in a health establishment and have the complaint investigated.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does not provide for migrants’ right to stand for election. Sections 131(a) and 177(a) of the 1999 Constitution require citizenship by birth for election into the office of the President and Governor, respectively. Sections 65(1)(a) & (b), 106 (a) also require Nigerian citizenship for membership of the National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly, respectively.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 98(a) & (h) of the Immigration Act 2015; Article 3 of the First Schedule and Article 4 of the Third Schedule to the National Commission for Refugees Act. Article 3 of the First Schedule to the Act mandates that refugees be treated without discrimination as to race, religion or country of origin; and Article 4 of the Third Schedule to the same Act mandates treatment of refugees without discrimination as to race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinions. In the Immigration Act 2015, section 98 (a) prohibits subjecting a smuggled migrant to discriminatory treatment on any account including his status as a smuggled migrant, while (h) prohibits "the use of any person's history of being smuggled to discriminate or cause harm to such person, his family or his friends in any way whatsoever, particularly with regard to freedom of movement, marriage or search for gainful employment."

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria prohibits discrimination against migrants on the grounds of race or ethnicity in the National Commission for Refugees, Migrants, and Internally Displaced Persons (NCFRMI) Act 2022, which applies to all migrants and effectuates non-discrimination provisions of various international treaties. While the constitutional protections against non-discrimination to not apply to non-citizens, there are additional non-discrimination provisions protecting victims of smuggling and trafficking: A) Section 98 (a) of the Immigration Act 2015 mandates the Nigeria Immigration Service to ensure that, "a smuggled migrant is not subjected to discriminatory treatment on account of race, colour, gender, age, language, religion, political or other opinion, cultural beliefs or practices, national, ethnic or social origin, property, birth or other status, including his status as a smuggled migrant." B) Section 61 (a) of the Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act 2015 mandates the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons to ensure that "a trafficked person is not subjected to discriminatory treatment on account of race, colour, gender, sex, age, language, religion, political or other opinion, cultural beliefs or practices, national, ethnic or social origin, property, birth or other status, including his status as a victim of trafficking or having worked in the sex industry."

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria protects this right only for regular migrant workers in Section 17 (3) (e) of the 1999 Constitution which provides for equal pay for equal work without discrimination as long as every migrant has a work permit. In addition, the law protects this for refugees and migrants from the Economic Community of West African States, because they do not need a work permit to be able to work in Nigeria.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria makes provision for this in section 58 of the Immigration Act 2015. What is required to change jobs is not necessarily a new work permit but the expatriate quota of the new organization that intends to employ the migrant. The expatriate quota is a limit of number of foreigners that a company is allowed to employ per time, and it is issued by the Ministry of Interior.The permit application is required from the employer to ascertain that the employer has not exceeded its permitted quota of foreign employees.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does not protect migrant spouse/partner’s right to work in section 36 of the Immigration Act 2015. Citizens of ECOWAS member countries are exempted from this requirement under section 37 (13) of the Immigration Act 2015.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: According to the section 38(4) of the Immigration Act 2015, loss of the employment for which residence permit was granted means an automatic loss of that residence permit and the immigrant would then be expected to leave the country. However, by section 37 (8) of the Act, the Comptroller-General of Immigration has discretionary power to issue a temporary work permit.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 17 (3) of the 1999 Constitution and section 33(2) of the Labour Act, 2004.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 11 (c) of the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) Act 2004. Any non-Nigerian who is employed in Nigeria for a period of 6 years or more is able to contribute to and benefit from the Fund. However, if that migrant is required to contribute to or is entitled to benefit from the social security scheme of another country or any other scheme which would be more beneficial to him than his potential benefits from the NSITF, then they are exempted from benefiting from the Fund.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does not make provision for this right in the Labour Act 2004 or any other law.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 37(10) of the Immigration Act, 2015 which provides for the issuance of Permanent Residence Visas to foreign nationals who are investors and have imported an annual minimum threshold of capital over a period of time according to specifications under the extant National Visa Policy or any other such policy.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right in the Immigration Act 2015 nor in the Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act 2015.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria requires birth registration of every child (including migrants) in Section 153 (1) (j) and Para 24 (b) of Part 1 of the Third Schedule to the 1999 Constitution. Section 153 (1) (j) of the 1999 Constitution establishes the National Population Commission (NPC) while Paragraph 24 (b) of Part 1 to the Third Schedule requires the NPC to establish and maintain a machinaery for continuous and universal registration of births and deaths in all parts of the country. The use of the term "universal" envisages that all births and deaths are to be registered including those of migrants.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria mandates the issuing of documents that recognize migrant's residence status and work status in sections 20, 36 and 37 of Immigration Act 2015 which provide for the issuance of visas, work permit and residence permit, respectively. Additionally, the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) Act 2007 in its section 14 establishes a National Identity Database, section 15 mandates the issuance of a multipurpose identity card, and section 16 requires that the identity of every person including non-Nigerians who are resident in Nigeria be registered in the database. See also Regulations 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 40, 41 and 43 of the Immigration Regulation 2017.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria makes it illegal for anyone to destroy documents that recognize migrants' residency status, work status and identity in Section 74(2) of the Immigration Act 2015 which criminalizes tampering with an immigrant's document (intended to be exhibited as evidence) by falsification, conversion, destruction or forgery and prescribes punishment for same.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does, however, protect this right for smuggled migrants in section 98 (c) of the Immigration Act 2015 which provides that the Nigeria Immigration Service shall allow a smuggled migrant access to the embassy or consulate of the country of which he/she is a citizen or where there is no embassy or consulate, to the diplomatic representative of the State that takes charge of the country's interest or nationals, to protect them.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does not prohibit the detention of anyone (there is no mention of children) in the Immigration Act 2015. However, section 99 of the Act prohibits the detention of a smuggled migrant. Again, that section makes a general provision without mentioning "children."

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Immigration Act 2015 in section 26 provides for the detention of a person whom an Immigration Officer considers to be a prohibited immigrant as the person awaits deportation. Sections 50, 52 and 53 provide for detention of a migrant while finalization or execution of a deportation order is being awaited or in lieu of such order, respectively. Additionally, the 1999 Constitution in section 35 (1)(f) allows personal liberty to be curtailed for the purpose of preventing the unlawful entry of any person into Nigeria or for effecting the expulsion, extradition or other lawful removal from Nigeria of any person or the taking of proceedings relating thereto.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en:
National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 96(1) of the Immigration Act 2015 which grants the Federal High Court the jurisdiction to hear matters relating to migrants. Additionally, the 1999 Constitution in Section 35 (1) (f) permits the curtailment of liberty of a person with respect to immigration offences "Provided that a person who is charged with an offence and who has been detained in lawful custody awaiting trial shall not continue to be 
 kept in such detention for a period longer than the maximum period of imprisonment prescribed for the offence." Section 35 (4) allow migrants to appeal length of time while 35 (6) allows them to appeal legality.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 32 (1) of the Immigration Act 2015 which states that, "A person required or authorized to be detained under this Act may be detained in such places as the Minister may direct."

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in sections 65 (2), 66 (2), 66 (3,b,i), 68 (2), 73 (2) and 95 (1) of the Immigration Act 2015; as well as in Section 34 (3) of the Immigration Regulation 2017. This right is also protected for all, including migrants, in Section 34 (1) (a) of the 1999 Constitution which protects the right to be free from torture, inhuman and degrading treatment for all.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Sections 19, 26 and 27 of the Immigration Act 2015 provides agents the power to refuse entry, to control immigrants' entry into Nigeria and to remove immigrants, respectively. Section 35(1)(f) of the 1999 Constitution provides for the curtailment of personal liberty for certain purposes that may involve immigrants and does not prohibit the use of force. Section 44 (5) of the Trafficking in Persons Prohibition Act 2015 provides that, “Any officer of the Agency [National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP)] or a duly authorized law enforcement officer who uses such force as may be reasonably necessary for any purpose in accordance with this Act, shall not be liable in any criminal or civil proceeding, for having, by the use of reasonable force, caused injury or death to any person, or damage to or loss of any property.”

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Sections 19, 26 and 27 of the Immigration Act 2015 provide for power to refuse entry, control of immigrants entering Nigeria and removal of immigrants, respectively. None of the three sections either prohibit or encourage the use of any kind of force in preventing, controlling or removing the immigrants. Section 35 (1) (f) of the 1999 Constitution as amended provides to the effect that every person shall be entitled to his personal liberty and no person shall be deprived of such liberty save in certain cases and in accordance with a procedure permitted by law in different cases and for different purposes including (f) for the purpose of preventing the unlawful entry of any person into Nigeria or of effecting the expulsion, extradition or other lawful removal from Nigeria of any person or the taking of proceedings relating thereto. This section provides for the curtailment of personal liberty for certain purposes that may involve immigrants, but it does not prohibit the use of force (lethal or not) in doing the same.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria does, however, exempt trafficked persons from criminal prosecution in section 62 of the Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act 2015. The section provides that, “Where the circumstances so justify, trafficked persons shall not be detained or prosecuted for offense relating to being a victim of trafficking, including non-possession of valid travel documents, use of false travel or other document.”

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Nigeria provides that convictions for criminal or other offenses can lead to a loss of the citizenship status of a naturalized migrant in section 30 (1) & (2) of the 1999 Constitution. Sub-section (1) relates to withdrawal of citizenship from a naturalised citizen who within 7 years of naturalisation is sentenced to a prison term of not less than 3 years while sub-section (2) relates to cases in which the naturalised citizen is found to have been disloyal to Nigeria or to be trading or communicating with an enemy of Nigeria by assisting the enemy at war with Nigeria or by communicating with the enemy in a way that is detrimental to the interest of the country. The President shall deprive such a person of the citizenship if he is satisfied from the records of proceedings of a court of law or other tribunal or after due inquiry in accordance with regulations that the person is guilty of any of the offences. In addition, section 56 (4) of the Immigration Act 2015 provides that, “Any person who commits any of the offences prescribed under subsection (1) and (2) of this Section (referring to section 56) is liable to imprisonment for a term of ten years or a fine of Two Million Naira or both." Some of the offences mentioned in section 56 of the Immigration Act 2015 are minor offences.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 27 (2) (e) of the 1999 Constitution which provides to the effect that citizenship by naturalization could be issued to a person who has fulfilled certain conditions including showing that he has, "made or is capable of making useful contribution to the advancement, progress and well-being of Nigeria." Also, section 37 (10) of the Immigration Act 2015 provides that, "The Comptroller-General of Immigration may authorize the issuance of Permanent Residence Visas to foreign nationals ... who are investors who have imported an annual minimum threshold of capital over a period of time as may be specified from time to time in the National Visa Policy or any other such policy: Provided that the Residence Permit can be withdrawn whenever the investor withdraws his investment or fails to comply with any other condition that may have been prescribed for the issuance of the Residence Permit."

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 27 (2) (e) of the 1999 Constitution which provides to the effect that citizenship by naturalization could be issued to a person who has fulfilled certain conditions including showing that he has, "made or is capable of making useful contribution to the advancement, progress and well-being of Nigeria."

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right, in the form of citizenship by registration, in section 26 (2) of the Constitution to "(a) any woman who is or has been married to a citizen of Nigeria; or (b) every person of full age and capacity born outside Nigeria any of whose grandparents is a citizen of Nigeria."

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria allows migrants to obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin in section 28 of the 1999 Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 38 of the 1999 Constitution under which every person is entitled to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including freedom to change his religion or belief, and freedom (either alone or in community with others, and in public or in private) to manifest and propagate his religion or belief in worship, teaching, practice and observance. Additionally, Article 4 of the First Schedule to the National Commission for Refugees Act mandates that refugees in Nigeria be accorded treatment at least as favourable as that accorded to Nigerians with respect to freedom to practice their religion and as regards the religious education of their children.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 39 of the 1999 Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 39 of the 1999 Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 40 of the 1999 Constitution which guarantees persons’ rights to assemble freely and associate with other persons, and in particular to form or belong to any political party, trade union or any other association for the protection of their interests.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in sections 20 (4) (d) and 37 (10) of the Immigration Act 2015. Section 20 (4) (d) allows the Comptroller-General of Immigration or any officer acting on his behalf to issue appropriate visa to the dependents of a foreign national who has a subsisting contract of employment in Nigeria. Section 37 (10) allows the Comptroller-General of Immigration to authorize the issuance of Permanent Residence Visas to foreign nationals who are married to Nigerians.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in section 36 of the Constituiton, sub (4), which protects the right to a fair hearing. In addition, Section 63 (b) of the Trafficking in Persons Prohibition Act 2015 provides a victim of trafficking the right for their views and concerns to be presented and considered at appropriate stages of criminal proceedings against the traffickers.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right, in a limited way, in section 98 (e) of the Immigration Act 2015 which only provides for a smuggled migrant to not be denied temporary residence visa during the pendency of a related legal action (civil or criminal).

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in Sections 33 (4) of the Immigration Act 2015. Specifically, by virtue of Section 33(4) of the Immigration Act 2015, a person who is under the age of eighteen years, is allowed to enter Nigeria with just a valid passport and visa and permitted to remain in Nigeria for as long as the parents are in the country, without going through the hassle of obtaining a residence permit as is expected of adult migrants.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in Sections 15 (3) of the Immigration Act 2015 which has a provision to the effect that only a female immigration officer may search the body of a woman or girl.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Nigeria protects this right in Article 24 of the First Schedule to the National Commission for Refugees Act, LFN 2004 (NCR Act) which in practise applies to all categories of migrants within the country, not just the refugees. In addition, there are special protection for persons with disabilities (including migrants) under the Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act 2018 which seeks to provide for the full integration of persons with disabilities into the society. Under the Disabilities Act 2018, there are provisions relating to 'assisted service' and guaranteeing the right of persons with disability to access the physical environment and buildings.
