question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of that right. According to Article 33 of the Labor Law, the spouse of a foreign worker must obtain their own visa and work permit to be able to work.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia stipulates that loss of employment implies loss of immigration status unless a new job is found within a specified time period in Article 27 of the Residence Law.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia stipulates that migrants have a right to most of the employment conditions and protections for citizens in the Labor Law. Provisions on overtime, work hours, weekly rest, paid holidays, sick pay, health and safety at work apply to the migrant workers and Saudi nationals alike. However, in the case of dismissal of a worker, Saudi nationals enjoy more protections, and domestic workers are subject to separate regulations and do not benefit from the same protections as other categories of foreign workers.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 9 of the Social Security Law states that Social Security benefits are reserved for Saudi Arabian citizens, only.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia protects this right in the Premium Residency Law of 2019, Article 3, which states that the Premium Residency Card, which allows eligible self-sponsored foreign nationals to obtain a residence permit for up to one year (renewable) or an unlimited period of time.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia protects this right in 1) the Saudi Arabian Council of Ministers Decision No. 166 of 12/7/1421 AH Regulating Relations between Migrant Workers and Their Employers, Supreme Economic Council, which prohibits the confiscation of passports by the employer. 2) Article 64.2 of the Labour Law of 2005, which requires that employer (sponsor) must return to the worker all certificates and documents that are in their possession (following the completion of their immigration process).

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia protects this right in Article 12 of the Residence Law, which states that all migrant are issued a Work visa, Residence permit and an ID card as part of their process toenter and remain in Saudi Arabia

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia protects this right in 1) the Labor Law (Royal Decree No. M/51, 27 September 2005) under Part III “Employment of non-Saudis. 2) The Ministerial Order No. 166 & 4786 Dated 28/12/1436H, which protects the right of migrant workers to not have their identity documents destroyed in any way or by any person other than officials. The Ministerial Decrees Nos 166 and 4786 only relates to the confiscation of documents. However, it is assumed the destruction of documents would be considered as identical to the confiscation of documents by the law. 3) Article 59 of the Residence Law of 1956.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Though Said Arabia is a signatory of the Viennat Convention on Consular Relations, national law in Saudi Arabia does not entail an obligation to allow consular officials and migrants to communicate.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Child Protection Law of 2015 which safeguards the rights of children stipulates that a child may be detained if they are accused of a crime that requires arrest.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 116 of the Criminal Procedure Law of 2013 stipulates that a detainee must be informed of the reasons of their detention, but the law does not stipulate that an individualized determination for detention is required.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia protects this right in Article 2 of the Criminal Procedure Law of 2013, which prohibits the use of torture, cruelty, or inhumane treatment.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Art. 5 of the Cabinet Decision 933-1394 on the approval of the draft Border Security Law permits recourse to force in certain circumstances, but Saudi Arabia does not otherwise regulate and restrict the use of force by law enforcement officials.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Anti-Trafficking in Persons Law (Royal Decree M40 of 2009) does not exempt trafficked and smuggled migrants from criminal prosecutions. However, articles 15.6 and 15.7 stipulate that police protection may be provided to a victim, if necesary, and that residency and work status may be granted at the discretion of the relevant authority.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia protects this right in 1) Articles 21, and 22 of Cabinet Decision 4 of 1954, on the Approval of the Saudi Arabian Nationality Law. 2) Saudi Arabian Nationality Regulations 1374H Resolution No (4) dated 25/1/1374 article 12, 13, 21-23, which states that Major convictions such as being affiliated and/or declared terrorist lead to loss of citizenship status.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Saudi Arabia protects this right in the Saudi Arabian nationality Law Article 9 and Article 20. The criteria for obtaining Saudi citizenship inlcudes: - age above 18; - generally mentally competent; -have had legal residence for 10 years continuously; - have legal ways of earning a living; considered generally moral; - have no criminal record/no sentencing history for more than 6months; and - must read, write and speak Arabic fluently.

citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all categories of migrants. However, national law in Saudi Arabia provides a pathway only for females who marry Saudi Arabian male citizens in the Saudia Arabian Nationality Law, Article 7.

However, the majority of migrant women in Saudi Arabia are domestic workers who have not been covered by the recent legislative reforms aimed to provide more protection for migrants in general, and are subject to separate regulations and visa process.

However, according to Article L-9 of the labor code, migrants can only assume the leadership of a union if they meet certain conditions, including the possibility for Senegalese nationals to access it in their country of origin and to be domiciled in Senegal for at least five (5) years. 3) Article 8 of the Constitution, which protects freedom of association for all people in Senegal.

question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: National law in Senegal protects this right in Article 4 of Law No. 71-10 dated January 25 regarding the conditions of admission, stay, and settlement of foreigners.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Senegal protects this right in Law No. 99-33, which ratified and brought into the domestic legal frameowrk, the Protection of Migrant Chirldren and Cooperation in International Adoption of May 29, 1993.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Senegal protects this right in the Multilateral Agreement on Regional Cooperation Against Trafficking in Persons.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Eugene K B Tan. [2]: June Lim

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Singapore

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law does not recognize and protect the right of freedom of assembly commensurate with that afforded to citizens. Article 14(1)(b), of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore provides that only citizens are guaranteed the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. However, migrants generally havea right to assemble where there is no express prohibition, but their rights are not constitutional ones.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: Being lawfully present in Singapore does not create a legal right for migrants to vote in national elections. Only Singapore citizens have the right to vote in elections in Singapore.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Section 12(1), which states, all persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law. There is no distinction between migrants and citizens.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: Migrants do not have a right to counsel at government expense in proceedings related to their legal status as a migrant. While migrants do not have a legal right to counsel at government expense, they will be assigned counsel at government expense under the Legal Assistance Scheme for Capital Offences (LASCO) if faced with a capital offence (e.g. murder, drug trafficking). Migrants may also avail themselves of criminal legal aid through Pro Bono SG, if they meet the eligibility requirements.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in 1) State Courts Act 1970 (2020 Rev. Ed.). Section 14, State Courts Act 1970 states that: "There are to be attached to the State Courts such commissioners for oaths, interpreters, clerks, bailiffs, process servers and other officers as may appear to the Chief Justice to be necessary for the administration of justice and the due execution of all powers and duties which are vested in the State Courts." 2) Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1969 (2020 Rev. Ed.), which provides that: "There are to be attached to the Supreme Court commissioners for oaths, interpreters, clerks, process servers and other officers as, from time to time, appear to the Chief Justice to be necessary for the administration of justice and the due execution of all powers and duties which are vested in the Supreme Court." 3) Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (CPC), Sections 22(4), 23(3A), and 288(1), which ensure that an accused person is not disadvantaged because he/she does not understand the official languages used in the investigation process and in court proceedings.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: National law does not exempt migrants from civil or criminal sanctions for unauthorized entry. Section 15 of the Immigration Act 1959 state that migrants who unlawfully enter or remain in Singapore after cancellation of their passes shall be found guilty of a criminal offence, and may be liable to a fine, imprisonment and/or caning.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law does not guarantee access to adequate, publicly supported housing to migrants, independent of status, commensurate with citizens. Public housing is available to citizens and permanent residents only.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law does not guarantee access to free primary educational institutions and services to migrant children commensurate with citizens. Only the children of citizens of Singapore and permanent residents are guaranteed enrolment in national primary schools. If there are spots available after the first two groups are serviced, they are they granted to other migrants.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law does not guarantee access to public adult educational institutions and services to migrants (such as degree-level course and vocational training) commensurate with citizens.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: Convictions for criminal or other offenses could affect migrants’ residence status. Acccording to Section 8(3)(d) of the Immigration Act 2010 (2020 Rev Ed), which defines "prohibited immigrants" as those convicted of a criminal offence and an imprisonment term under Singapore law, as those who may be removed from Singapore by order of the Immigration Controller. Nevertheless, migrant workers may also have their work passes cancelled for contravention of their work permit conditions which may be an administrative offence.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore does not explicitly protect this right although the Extradition Act 1968 (2020 Rev Ed), Part 3, especially sections 8 and 9, provides for restrictions on surrender of persons to foreign States and declared Commonwealth states. Similarly, section 10(2) of the Extradition Act provides that "If the Minister is satisfied that, by reason of (a) the trivial nature of the offence that a fugitive is alleged to have committed or has committed; (b) the accusation against a fugitive not having been made in good faith or in the interests of justice; (c) the passage of time since the offence is alleged to have been committed or was committed; or (d) any other sufficient cause, and having regard to the circumstances under which the offence is alleged to have been committed or was committed, it would be unjust, oppressive or too severe a punishment to surrender the fugitive, or to surrender him or her before the expiry of a particular period, the Minister must not give a notice under section 11(1) or issue a warrant under section 19(2) or (8) in respect of the fugitive, as the case may be."

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to persecution on the basis of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion. All facts will be considered by the court in an extradition hearing. Section 10 of the Extradition Act states as follows: "(1) The Minister must not give a notice under section 11(1), or issue a warrant under section 19(2) or (8), in respect of a fugitive from a foreign State or declared Commonwealth territory, if the Minister has substantial grounds for believing that — (a) the request for the surrender of the fugitive, although purporting to have been made in respect of an offence for which, but for this section, he or she would be liable to be surrendered to that State or territory, was made for the purpose of prosecuting or punishing him or her on account of his or her race, religion, sex, ethnic origin, nationality or political opinions; or (b) if the fugitive is surrendered to that State or territory, he or she may be prejudiced at his or her trial, or punished, detained or restricted in his or her personal liberty, by reason of his or her race, religion, sex, ethnic origin, nationality or political opinions."

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law does not explicitly ban refoulement on the basis of a risk of serious deprivations of fundamental human rights although section 10(2)(d) of the Extradition Act 1968 could conceivably be used to prohibit such a refoulement. The provision states that:" If the Minister is satisfied that, by reason of —(a) the trivial nature of the offence that a fugitive is alleged to have committed or has committed; (b) the accusation against a fugitive not having been made in good faith or in the interests of justice; (c) the passage of time since the offence is alleged to have been committed or was committed; or (d) any other sufficient cause, and having regard to the circumstances under which the offence is alleged to have been committed or was committed, it would be unjust, oppressive or too severe a punishment to surrender the fugitive, or to surrender him or her before the expiry of a particular period, the Minister must not give a notice under section 11(1) or issue a warrant under section 19(2) or (8) in respect of the fugitive, as the case may be."

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law does not require a person to be advised of the possible availability of asylum before being expelled or prevented entry.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in 1) the Extradition Act 1968 (2020 Rev Ed). 2) The Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Section 12, which states that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law, including migrants.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law does provide migrants with an opportunity to submit the reasons against expulsion and to have their case reviewed by the competent authority before being expelled.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law does not guarantee citizenship to migrants and children of migrants who would otherwise be stateless.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore does not explicitly provide settled migrants with legal avenues to facilitate reunification with immediate or non-dependent family members. Not all migrants are entitled to reunification with immediate or non-dependent or even dependent family members. Regulation 8 of the Immigration Regulations, provides for the various types of passes for the purpose of entitling a person to enter and remain temporarily within Singapore. Eligible regular migrants may apply for the relevant passes on behalf of their family members so that they may enter and remain temporarily in Singapore. Dependent Passes may be applied for on behalf of a legally married spouse and children below age of majority (age 21). Student Passes require acceptance into an approved full-time course.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: A judicial remedy to challenge the refusal by the authorities to allow family formation/reunification may be available by way of 1) the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Article 93. Judicial review is acknowledged by the Singapore Legislature and Executive as a key aspect of judicial power which is vested in the Judiciary under Art 93 of the Singapore Constitution. However, this judicial review is only on the decision-making process (i.e. whether it complies with administrative law requirements of legality, procedural propriety and rationality/reasonableness) rather than the substantive correctness of the decision (i.e., whether the authorities has to allow family formation/reunification). 2) The Immigration Act, Section 39A.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: Same sex marital relationships are not recognized under the family reunification framework. Same-sex civil unions or marriages are not recognised in Singapore. On 3 January 2023, the previous law that criminalised consensual male same-sex sexual relations was repealed but this does not change the non-recognition of same-sex civil unions or marriages in Singapore.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: NA

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (2020 Rev Ed), Sections 25 and 26 provide the avenues for redress through the Ministry of Manpower and civil proceedings in the Courts respectively. Besides the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, legal redress can be sought by way of personal legal action against the employer under contract law. However, ongoing civil proceedings do not entitle a migrant worker to remain in Singapore in order to attend Court, so if the migrants term of employment ends and their visa is revoked, the migrant worker will have to either engage legal counsel at his/her expense or travel into Singapore on a visit pass to attend to such civil legal proceedings.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law does noguarantee migrants’ access to health care services, independent of status, commensurate with citizens. However, national law does not, in any way, deny access to health care services to any groups, including migrants on the basis of status, but it also does not guarantee it through national law. As a matter of healthcare policy and practice, a migrant is not discriminated against where access to health care services is concerned, especially in a medical emergency.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: Being lawfully present in Singapore does not create a legal right for migrants to stand for election (run for public office). Only Singapore citizens may stand for elections, according to Article 44(2) of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While the Singapore Constitution provides equal protection of the law migrant status has not been explicitly recognized as a basis for protection.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in Article 12(1) of the Constitution of Singapore. Article 12(1) is framed at a very general level and is a declaratory statement of principles. Article 12(1) of the Constitution is concerned with equality of treatment and embodies the principle that “like should be compared with like”. It prohibits individuals “within a single class” from receiving different punitive treatment, but it “does not forbid discrimination in punitive treatment between one class of individuals and another class in relation to which there is some difference in the circumstances of the offence that has been committed” (see Ong Ah Chuan and another v Public Prosecutor [1979-1980] SLR(R) 70 (Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, on appeal from Singapore) at [34]-[35]).

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: Migrant workers are not explicitly afforded the the right to fair wages and equal remuneration for work of equal value commensurate with that afforded to citizens doing the same work.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right in the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (2020 Rev. Ed.), which states that applications for work passes must be made by both employee and employer, hence employment is tied to a specific employer and a new work pass application will need to be made in the event of a change of employer.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: The spouse/partner of the principal migrant does not have the automatic right to work (without having to apply for permission). Under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990, spouses holding Dependant Passes under the principal migrant's Employment Pass may work if issued with a Letter of Consent by the Ministry of Manpower, but spouses holding Dependant Passes where the principal migrant holds an S-Pass may only work if he/she satisfies the work pass requirements for a Work Permit, S-Pass or Employment Pass.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: No such right exists. Residency in Singapore for a migrant worker hinges on his/her employment status. The loss of employment will ordinarily and often mean the loss of residence status in Singapore. In practice, the authorities may be prepared to grant a grace period for a migrant to secure another employment.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore conditional protects this right in 1) the Employment Act 1968 (2020 Rev. Ed), Part IV. 2) The Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (2020 Rev. Ed.). 2) The Employment of Foreign Manpower (Work Passes) Regulations 2012. Migrant employment is governed by the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, while citizen employment is governed by the Employment Act which provides certain basic employment conditions and protections. Migrants have a right to most of the protection in the latter, but not the same employment conditions and protections as citizens. For example, foreign domestic workers are not covered under the Employment Act which applies to citizens and which provides for weekly rest, paid holidays, and other protections.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: Migrant workers with a valid work permitdo not have the right to social security protections commensurate with citizens. Permanent residents are able to take advantage of some social security protections, but not in the same way as citizens.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: Migrant workers with a valid work permit do not have the right to unemployment benefits commensurate with citizens. There are currently no unemployment benefits for citizens.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National lawdoes not provide temporary migrant workers with a right to become lawful permanent residents. For unskilled or low-skilled workers, no such opportunity is provided for in the work permit conditions. The conditions include: "Can not marry a Singapore citizen or permanent resident in or outside Singapore without approval from Ministry of Manpower (MOM). This applies even after their Work Permit is expired, cancelled or revoked; can not get pregnant or deliver a child in Singapore during the validity of their Work Permit unless they are already married to a Singapore citizen or permanent resident with the approval of MOM. This applies even after their Work Permit is expired, cancelled or revoked; must adhere to these and other conditions which are provided for in the Employment of Foreign Manpower (Work Passes) Regulations 2012." These work permit conditions must be agreed to before migrants are allowed entry into Singapore.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in 1) the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act (EMFA), 2) Immigration Regulations (2009 Rev. ed), Regulation 25. The 4th Schedule of the EMFA pertains to Work Permit holders (domestic workers and non-domestic workers e.g. migrant construction workers) and the 5th Schedule of the EMFA pertains to S-Pass holders (migrant workers with higher qualifications and higher salary requirements). Both the 4th and 5th Schedules have similar provisions pertaining to non-retention of work pass documents by employers.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore requires the birth registration of children of migrants regardless of their status as a migrant. This is provided for in the Registration of Births and Deaths Act 2021, 1985 (2020 Rev. Ed.).

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law requires the issuing of documents that recognize migrants’ residency status, work status, and identityprotects. This right is found in 1) the Immigration Act. 2) The Immigration Regulations (Cap. 133, Rg. 1). 2) The Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (EMFA).

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in 1) the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act (1980), s 14.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Singapore does not explicitly protect this right although Singapore has ratified the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. The Diplomatic and Consular Relations Act 2005 (2020 Rev. Ed.) does not appear to have an obligation to allow consular officials and migrants (who are nationals of the consular sending state) to communicate although this is normally done in practice.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law does not prohibit the detention of children on the basis of their status as a migrant. The Children and Young Persons Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed), Section 5 and 11, provides that undocumented migrant children are to be detained at specially designated places of detention for children only.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law does not prohibit the detention of migrants on the basis of their status as a migrant.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law allows migrants to appeal legality, conditions, or length of detention. In addition, the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Article 93, provides that judicial review of any decision is an inherent power of the judiciary. Though, the Immigration Act, Section 39A, does not explictly allow appeals on decisions made by any court, Minister or Council, judicial review of the decision-making process (but not the substantive decision) is available to migrants for conditions, length, and legality of detention.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in 1) the Immigration Act 1959 (2020 Rev. Ed.), Part II, which governs the entry and departure of individuals into and from Singapore, and entails an individualised determination for the detention of any migrant. 2) The Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Section 12, provides that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to equal protection of the law. 3) The Criminal Procedure Code, Section 123 also requires every criminal charge to state the offence with which the accused is charged. There is no distinction between migrants and citizens in this law.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law protects migrants and citizens alike with the right to be free from torture and cruel, inhumane, and degrading treatment or punishment. Any act of torture will be regarded as an unjustified use of force. Singapore is party to the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration (AHRD). Article 14 of the AHRD provides that "No person shall be subject to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment."

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in 1) Immigration Act 1959 (2020 Revised Edition) (IA), Section 38. Under the IA, Section 38, immigration officers have the authority and powers of a police officer to enforce any of the provisions of the IA relating to arrest, detention or removal. This would include the use of all reasonable means necessary (including force) to arrest the migrant, pursuant to Section 75 of the Criminal Procedural Code 2010. 2) Police Force Act 2004 (2020 Rev. Ed.). 3) Singapore Armed Forces Act 1972 (2020 Rev. Ed.). 4) Criminal Procedural Code 2010, Section 75.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law does not explicitly prohibit the use of lethal force by its officers or agents as a means of preventing migrants from entering the state's territory. Ssection 75 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (CPC) does not expressly prohibit the use of lethal force, and law enforcement officers have to use all reasonable means necessary to stop unlawful entry.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National law does not exempt trafficked and smuggled migrants from criminal prosecutions. The Prevention of Human Trafficking Act 2014 (2020 Rev Ed) does not specifically exempt trafficked and smuggled migrants from criminal prosecutions. However, the Public Prosecutor has the prosecutorial discretion to decide whether to charge migrant victims of trafficking and smuggling. This discretionary constitutional power is granted by the Constitution under Article 35(8).

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: Criminal and other convictions could affect the citizenship status for naturalized migrants. The Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Article 129, which stipulates that any person who "has, within the period of 5 years after registration or naturalisation, been sentenced in any country to imprisonment for a term of not less than one year or to a fine of not less than $5,000 or the equivalent in the currency of that country, and has not received a free pardon in respect of the offence for which he was so sentenced" can be deprived of their citizenship.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore provides such a pathway to citizenship in Articles 120 to 127 of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore. In particular, Article 123 states that, "(1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, any person resident in Singapore of or over the age of 21 years may, on application being made therefor in the prescribed form, be registered as a citizen of Singapore if he satisfies the Government that he —(a) is of good character; (b) has resided in Singapore throughout the 12 months immediately preceding the date of his application; (c) has during the 12 years immediately preceding the date of his application resided in Singapore for periods amounting in the aggregate to not less than 10 years: Provided that the Government may exempt any applicant from compliance with this paragraph — (i) where such applicant has during the 6 years immediately preceding the date of his application resided in Singapore for periods amounting in the aggregate to not less than 5 years; or (ii) where in any special case the Government considers fit to confer citizenship upon such applicant; (d) intends to reside permanently in Singapore; and (e) has an elementary knowledge of one of the following languages, namely, Malay, English, Mandarin and Tamil: Provided that the Government may exempt an applicant who has attained the age of 45 years or who is deaf or dumb from compliance with this paragraph. (2) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, any woman who is married to a citizen of Singapore may, on making application therefor in the prescribed manner, be registered as a citizen of Singapore if she satisfies the Government — (a) that she has resided continuously in Singapore for a period of not less than 2 years immediately preceding the date of the application; (b) that she intends to reside permanently in Singapore; and (c) that she is of good character." Section 127 states that, "(1) Subject to clause (4), the Government may, upon application made by any person of or over the age of 21 years who is not a citizen of Singapore, grant a certificate of naturalisation to that person if the Government is satisfied — (a) that he has resided in Singapore for the required periods and intends, if the certificate is granted, to do so permanently; (b) that he is of good character; and (c) that he has an adequate knowledge of the national language. (2) The periods of residence in Singapore or the relevant part of it which are required for the grant of a certificate of naturalisation are periods which amount in the aggregate to not less than 10 years in the 12 years immediately preceding the date of the application for the certificate and which include the 12 months immediately preceding that date. (3) A person to whom a certificate of naturalisation is granted shall be a citizen of Singapore by naturalisation from the date on which the certificate is granted. (4) No certificate of naturalisation shall be granted to any person until he has taken the Oath of Renunciation, Allegiance and Loyalty in the form set out in the Second Schedule."

citation_text_en: National law in Singapore provides a pathway to citizenship where the eligibility requirements are met. Articles 120 to 127 of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore provide the framework. In particular, Article 123 states that, "(1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, any person resident in Singapore of or over the age of 21 years may, on application being made therefor in the prescribed form, be registered as a citizen of Singapore if he satisfies the Government that he —(a) is of good character; (b) has resided in Singapore throughout the 12 months immediately preceding the date of his application; (c) has during the 12 years immediately preceding the date of his application resided in Singapore for periods amounting in the aggregate to not less than 10 years: Provided that the Government may exempt any applicant from compliance with this paragraph — (i) where such applicant has during the 6 years immediately preceding the date of his application resided in Singapore for periods amounting in the aggregate to not less than 5 years; or (ii) where in any special case the Government considers fit to confer citizenship upon such applicant; (d) intends to reside permanently in Singapore; and (e) has an elementary knowledge of one of the following languages, namely, Malay, English, Mandarin and Tamil: Provided that the Government may exempt an applicant who has attained the age of 45 years or who is deaf or dumb from compliance with this paragraph. (4) No certificate of naturalisation shall be granted to any person until he has taken the Oath of Renunciation, Allegiance and Loyalty in the form set out in the Second Schedule."

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore provides such a pathway in Articles 120 to 127 of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore. In particular, Article 123 states that, "(1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, any person resident in Singapore of or over the age of 21 years may, on application being made therefor in the prescribed form, be registered as a citizen of Singapore if he satisfies the Government that he —(a) is of good character; (b) has resided in Singapore throughout the 12 months immediately preceding the date of his application; (c) has during the 12 years immediately preceding the date of his application resided in Singapore for periods amounting in the aggregate to not less than 10 years: Provided that the Government may exempt any applicant from compliance with this paragraph — (i) where such applicant has during the 6 years immediately preceding the date of his application resided in Singapore for periods amounting in the aggregate to not less than 5 years; or (ii) where in any special case the Government considers fit to confer citizenship upon such applicant; (d) intends to reside permanently in Singapore; and (e) has an elementary knowledge of one of the following languages, namely, Malay, English, Mandarin and Tamil: Provided that the Government may exempt an applicant who has attained the age of 45 years or who is deaf or dumb from compliance with this paragraph. Section 124 states that, "(1) The Government may if satisfied that a child under the age of 21 years — (a) is the child of a citizen of Singapore; and (b) is residing in Singapore, cause such child to be registered as a citizen of Singapore on application being made therefor in the prescribed manner by the parent or guardian of such child. (2) The Government may, in such special circumstances as it thinks fit, cause any child under the age of 21 years to be registered as a citizen of Singapore." Section 127 states that, "(1) Subject to clause (4), the Government may, upon application made by any person of or over the age of 21 years who is not a citizen of Singapore, grant a certificate of naturalisation to that person if the Government is satisfied — (a) that he has resided in Singapore for the required periods and intends, if the certificate is granted, to do so permanently; (b) that he is of good character; and (c) that he has an adequate knowledge of the national language. (2) The periods of residence in Singapore or the relevant part of it which are required for the grant of a certificate of naturalisation are periods which amount in the aggregate to not less than 10 years in the 12 years immediately preceding the date of the application for the certificate and which include the 12 months immediately preceding that date. (3) A person to whom a certificate of naturalisation is granted shall be a citizen of Singapore by naturalisation from the date on which the certificate is granted. (4) No certificate of naturalisation shall be granted to any person until he has taken the Oath of Renunciation, Allegiance and Loyalty in the form set out in the Second Schedule."

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law does not allow migrants who naturalize to obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin. Dual citizenship is not permitted under Article 134 of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Article 15, which states that every person has the right to profess and practice his religion and to propagate it. There is no distinction between migrants and citizens in this regard.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law does not provide migrants with full freedom to hold opinions without interference commensurate with that afforded to citizens. Article 14, of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore provides that only citizens are guaranteed the right to freedom of speech and expression, which would broadly include the freedom to hold opinion. However, migrants generally have such rights to hold opinions without interference but their rights are not constitutional ones.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law does not provide migrants with the right to freedom of expression commensurate with that afforded to citizens. Article 14(1)(a), of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore provides that only citizens are guaranteed the right to freedom of speech and expression. However, migrants generally have such rights to freedom of expression but their rights are not constitutional ones.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law does not recognize and protect migrants’ right of freedom of association, including the right to join trade unions, commensurate with that afforded to citizens. Article 14(1)(c), of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore provides that only citizens are guaranteed the right to freedom of association. However, migrants generally have such a right to form associations, where there is no express statutory prohibition. When there is such a right, it is not a constitutional right.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: National law does not allow migrants a right to family reunification regardless of resource conditions (such as income, insurance, etc.). The sponsor must demonstrate the ability to to meet certain resource conditions for family reunification, particularly the sponsor must not be taking advantage of any welfare programs when they apply, and can provide sufficient proof of income to qualify for family reunification. Additionally, only those migrants who hold an Employment Pass may apply for certain family members to join the pass holder in Singapore; the working requirement is a policy decision, not a legislative one that requires the legislature to approve of the change.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Singapore protects this right in 1) the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev. Ed.), which stipulates that, where a person is arrested, they shall be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of their arrest and shall be allowed to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice. The individual must also be produced before a Magistrate in Court within 48 hours of arrest. 2) The Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Article 9, which states that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law, including migrants who wish to serve as complainants in criminal proceedings.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law does not provide migrant victims of crime with an avenue to immigration status or relief from expulsion as a result of being a victim of a crime. However, as a matter of policy, migrant victims of crime are granted Special Passes to allow them to remain in Singapore and assist with criminal investigations and the prosecution of offenders.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No across the board protection of this right afforded by nationa law. However, written law (see section 73 of the Penal Code 1871, the main criminal legislation) and case law recognise that female migrant domestic workers are vulnerable and the Penal Code provides for enhanced punishments where an employer commits offences against the migrant domestic worker.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: The law does not take disabilities into consideration in the context of migration. Neither does it provide special protection for migrants with disabilities in comparison to other migrants.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Jacob van Garderen and [2]: Roni Amit.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: South Africa

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. Section 17 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 provides that "everyone" has the right to peacefully assemble, demonstrate, picket and present petitions and the right is not limited to citizens. The Regulation of Gatherings Act 205 of 1993, which provides for the notice and possible prohibition of gatherings, does not contain any provision specifically targeting nonnationals. However, Regulations to the Refugees Act (implementing 2008 amendments to the Refugees Act) enacted on January 1, 2020 prohibit refugees and asylum seekers from participating "in any political activity or campaign in furtherance of any political party or political interests in the Republic."

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Political rights, including the right to vote, are limited to citizens. Section 19(3)(a) of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 provides that only citizens have the right to vote in national, provision or municipal elections. Section 6 of the Electoral Act 73 of 1998 provides that only citizens are eligible to be registered on the Voter's Roll for elections. Only persons registered on the Voter's Roll may vote in elections. Section 5 of the Local Governments'? Municipal Elections Act 27 of 2000 provides that the those portions of the National Voter's Roll applicable to the municipality in question will be used to determine who may vote in local elections. Noncitizens are excluded from registration on the Voters' Roll. There is no known example of any legislative body permitting non-nationals to vote in elections.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Constitution (No. 108, 1996) (Bill of Rights), Sections 9 (equality before the law); 33 (just administrative action); 34 (access to courts); 35 (arrested, detained, and accused persons). Section 9 states that "Everyone is equal before the law and has the right to equal protection and benefit of the law." The term "everyone" has been interpreted by the courts to include all migrants independent of the immigration status.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. While the right to have a legal practitioner assigned by the State is limited to criminal matters, Legal Aid South Africa's manual allows for legal aid to be provided to asylum seekers and this is not available in practice. Section 35 of the Constitution guarantees a right to counsel at state expense to detained individuals "if substantial injustice would otherwise result" but this has not been interpreted to apply to migrants in proceedings related to their legal status.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 35(3)(k) of the Constitution of South Africa, 108 of 1996; Section 6 of the Magistrates' Court Act (No. 32, 1944). Section 35(3)(k) provides the right "to be tried in a language that the accused person understands or, if that is not practicable, to have the proceedings interpreted in that language." Section 6 of the Magistrates' Court Act calls for an interpreter in a criminal case where "evidence is given in a language with which the accused is not in the opinion of the court sufficiently conversant."

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 37 of the Refugees Act sets out a number of criminal offenses, e.g. breaking the conditions of a permit and making false representations for the purposes of entering or remaining in the country. These offenses are governed under the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977. In similar fashion, Section 49 of the Immigration Act stipulates a number of specific offenses, e.g. Section (1) (a) "Anyone who enters or remains in, or departs from the Republic in contravention of this Act, shall be guilty of an offense and liable on conviction to a fine or to imprisonment not exceeding three months. (b) Any illegal foreigner who fails to depart when so ordered by the Director-General, shall be guilty of an offense and liable on conviction to a fine or to imprisonment not exceeding nine months. (2) Anyone who knowingly assists a person to enter or remain in, or depart from the Republic in contravention of this Act, shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a fine or to imprisonment not exceeding one year. (3) Anyone who knowingly employs an illegal foreigner or a foreigner in violation of this Act shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a fine or to imprisonment not exceeding one year, provided that such person's second conviction of such an offence shall be punishable by imprisonment not exceeding two years or a fine, and the third or subsequent convictions of such offences by imprisonment not exceeding three years without the option of a fine. (4) Anyone who intentionally facilitates an illegal foreigner to receive public services to which such illegal foreigner is not entitled shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a fine." Asylum seekers receive additional protections from sanctions. Section 21(4) of the Refugees Act 130 of 1998 provides that no proceedings may be instituted or continued against any person in respect of his or her unlawful entry or presence within the Republic if such person has applied for asylum and a final determination, which will include the right to appeal or review, has been invoked. In Ashebo v Minister of Home Affairs, the Constitutional Court narrowed this protection to require that an applicant who was being held criminally for illegal entry and presence show good cause for his unlawful entry, for not obtaining an asylum transit visa, and for remaining unlawfully in the country. Ashebo v Minister of Home Affairs and Others (CCT 250/22) [2023] ZACC 16 (12 June 2023).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right for certain categories of migrants in Section 26 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996); Section 1 of the Housing Act (No. 107, 1997); and Prevention of Illegal Eviction from and Unlawful Occupation of Land Act 19 of 1998. The Constitutional right to housing applies to everyone but only citizens and permanent residents are eligible for public housing programmes. Government subsidized housing (RDP and CRU) is limited to South African citizens. All persons, however, are guaranteed the right against unlawful eviction under section 26(3) of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 and subject to the protections of the Prevention of Illegal Eviction from and Unlawful Occupation of Land Act 19 of 1998.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 29 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996); Section 27 of the Refugees Act (No. 130, 1998); Section 4 of the National Education Policy Act (No. 27, 1996); Section 5 of the South African Schools Act (No. 84, 1996); Admissions Policy for Ordinary Public Schools (GG 19377, 19 October 1998); Proposed Admissions Policy for Ordinary Public Schools (No 38, 10 Feb, 2021). Section 29 of the Constitution provides everyone the right to basic education. The Refugees Act states that refugees are entitlted to the same "basic primary education which the inhabitants of the Republic receive from time to time." (Section 27). Under the National Education Policy Act, education policy must be directed toward protection of the Constitutional right, including the right of every person to. basic education and equal access to education institutions (Section 4). Section 4 also guarantees the right "of every person to be protected against unfair discrimination within or by an education department or education institution on any ground whatsoever." Section 4 of the South African Schools Act requires the admission of all learners without discrimination. The Admissions Policy for Ordinary Public Schools, Section 9, states that "The admission policy of a public school and the administration of admissions by an education department must not unfairly discriminate in any way against an applicant for admission." This policy further states that the "South African Schools Act, 1996 and this policy apply equally to learners who are not citizens of the Republic of South Africa and whose parents are in possession of a permit for temporary or permanent residence issued by the Department of Home Affairs" (Section 19). Section 21 states that "illegal aliens" must "show evidence that they have applied to the Department of Home Affairs to legalize their stay."

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right for certain categories of migrants in Section 29 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996); Section 27 of the Refugees Act (No. 130, 1998); Sections 39 and 42 of the Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002); Minister of Home Affairs and Others v Watchenuka and Others (010/2003) [2003] ZASCA 142 (28 November, 2003); and Refugees Regulations (27 December, 2019). Citizens, permanent residents, recognized refugees and asylum seeker visa holders have access to adult educational institutions. Asylum seekers were granted this right after the case of Minister of Home Affairs and others v Watchenuka and another 2004 (4) SA 326 (SCA) after the Supreme Court of Appeal found that a blanket ban on the right to work and study was a violation of the constitutionally protected right to human dignity for asylum seekers who often must wait years for a final adjudication on their refugee claims. Other categories of non-nationals, however, may apply for admission to adult educational facilities, but must be granted a study visa by the Department of Home Affairs under section 13 of the Immigration Act 13 of 2002 before being registered to study. Study visa holders may be charged additional international rates to study at South African institutions. The Immigration Act makes it a crime to provide instruction or training to irregular migrants.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Criminal Procedure Act, 51 of 1977; Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002), Sections 28, 29, Schedules 1, 2; Refugees Act (No. 130, 1998) Section 5 (as amended by Refugees Amendment Act, Section 6 (No. 33, 2008). Schedules 1 and 2 list a series of crimes that will result in loss of residency, including any crime for which the punishment may be longer than 6 months without the option of a fine. Following the promulgation of regulations on December 27, 2019, the amended Refugees Act took effect, establishing loss of refugee status for any crime punishable by imprisonment without the option of a fine.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Prevention of Combating and Torture of Persons Act (No. 13, 2013), Section 8. Section 8 of the Act contains a provision which includes "No person shall be expelled, returned or extradited to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he or she would be in danger of being subjected to torture." The non-refoulement provision only explicitly mentions torture, not cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Refugees Act (No. 130, 1998), Section 2. The Refugees Act adopts the language of the International Refugee Convention and also adds language from the OAU Convention, the legislation expands this protection to individuals at risk from external aggression, occupation, foreign domination or other events seriously disturbing or disrupting public order in either part or the whole of that country.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Refugees Act (No. 130, 1998), Section 2. The Refugees Act prevents refoulement where "his or her life, physical safety, or freedom would be threatened on account of external aggression, occupation, foreign domination, or other events seriously disturbing or disrupting public order."

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Neither the Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002) nor the Refugees Act (No .130, 1998) places a positive obligation on officials to advise a person on the availability of asylum before being expelled. The government has argued that once an individual has been arrested as an illegal foreigner, he cannot change that status by applying for asylum.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 2 of the Refugees Act and Section 8 of the Prevention and Combatting of Torture of Persons Act. Section 2 of the Refugees Act explains: "Notwithstanding any provision of this Act or any other law to the contrary, no person may be refused entry into the Republic, expelled, extradited or returned to any other country or be subject to any similar measure, if as a result of such refusal, expulsion, extradition, return or other measure, such person is compelled to return to or 45 remain in a country where- (u) he or she may be subjected to persecution on account of his or her race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular social group; or (6) his or her life, physical safety or freedom would be threatened on account of 50 external aggression, occupation, foreign domination or other events seriously disturbing or disrupting public order in either part or the whole of that country." Section 8 (1) of the Prevention and Combatting of Torture of Persons Act states "that No person shall be expelled, returned or extradited to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he or she would be in danger of being subjected to torture."

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act 3 of 2000; Section 34 of the Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002); and Lawyers for Human Rights v Minister of Home Affairs and Others, 2017 (5) SA 480 (CC). Section 33 of the Constitution provides that everyone has the right to administrative action that is lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair. The Promotion of Administrative Justice Act was enacted to give effect to this right. The Immigration Act lays out procedures for detention and deportation and provides a right to appeal a deportation decision. Following the 2017 Constitutional Court decision in Lawyers for Human Rights v Minister of Home Affairs, individuals must now be brought before a court within 48 hours of their detention for purposes of deportation.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Refugees Act (No 130, 1998), Chapter 4 (Sections 25 & 26); Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002), Sections 8, 34, Lawyers for Human Rights vs Minister of Home Affairs, 2017 (5) SA 480 (CC). Section 8 of the Immigration Act sets out review and appeal procedures. An individual deemed to be an illegal foreigner has three days to request that the Minister review the decision. Asylum seekers may appeal a negative decision.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa provides this right in a conditional way in Sections 18 and 27(g)of the Immigration Act 13 of 2002 ; Section 3(c) of the Refugees Act 130 of 1998. Section 18 of the Immigration Act 13 of 2002 provides for a Relatives Visa for non-nationals who are a member of the immediate family of a citizen or permanent resident. Certain temporary residence visas allow for accompanying family members to join a principal applicant. This includes a critical skills work visa (section 19(4) of the Immigration Act), an intra-company transfer work visa (section 19(5)), a retired persons visa (section 20(1A)) or a business visa (section 14). Recognised refugees may have accompanying family members joined to their file under section 3(c) and 33(1) of the Refugees Act 130 of 1998. Non-accompanying family members may also be joined to a file later if they were declared when the principal applicant first applied for asylum.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 10 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996); Dawood v Minister of Home Affairs 2000 (1) SA 997 (C); and Section 8 of the Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002). Section 8 of the Immigration Act (No.13, 2002) provides for an appeals and review process for negative decisions taken under that Act. The first stage is to appeal to the Director-General and then to the Minister of Home Affairs. This includes the rejection of any visa. Decisions under section 8 of the Act are subject to judicial review by the High Court of South Africa under the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act 3 of 2000 which implements the constitutionally guaranteed right to just administrative action under section 33 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996. In Dawood v Minister of Home Affairs 2000 (1) SA 997 (C) case, the Constitutional Court linked the right to marry and have a family to the fundamental right to human dignity. Numerous cases have challenged DHA's refusal to implement family reunification.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in a conditional way in Immigration Act 13 of 2002; Refugees act (as amended), The Civil Unions Act 17 of 2006; and Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie, 2006 (1) SA 524 (CC). The definition of "spouse" under section 1 of the Immigration Act 13 of 2002 includes both heterosexual and homosexual permanent relationships in addition to tradition marriages. The Civil Unions Act 17 of 2006 provides for unions between two spouses of the same sex to be recognized as marriages. The Refugees Amendment Act also provides the same broad definition for spouses under the Refugees Act 130 of 1998. Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie, 2006 (1) SA 524 (CC) case extended the common law definition of marriage to include same sex marriages, but immigrants from countries where such marriages are not recognized may struggle to access legal rights based on family reunification. The Refugees Act Regulations that took effect on Jan 1, 2020 includes an affidavit for parties in permanent homosexual or heterosexual relationships. Individuals must submit these forms periodically to confirm the continued existence of the relationship.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa provides temporary migrant workers with avenues to become lawfully settled in Sections 25-27 of Immigration Act 13 of 2002. This right is conditional on visa type.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in South Africa does not ordinarily allow for irregular migrant workers to regularise their stay. In exceptional circumstances. 31(2)(b) of the Immigration Act provides the Minister of Home Affairs the discretion to grant a status similar to permanent residence to any person who may not qualify for any other visa under the Act. This would include irregular migrants who would otherwise not qualify for a visa. However, in practice, the applicant's status is taken into consideration when adjudicating the application. There are no avenues for irregular migrants to become lawfully settled. In 2010, the government offered irregular migrants from Zimbabwe who met certain criteria a special permit under the Zimbabwe Documentation Process, but these permits provide no pathway for permanent residence and many Zimbabweans could not meet the requirement during the short application window.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 23 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996); Section 213 of the Labour Relations Act (No. 66, 1995); and Discovery Health Limited v CCMA & others [2008] 7 BLLR 633 (LC). The Constitution provides everyone the right to fair labour practices (Section 23). The definition of employee in the Labour Relations Act applies to everyone. Even those migrant workers who are not entitled to work under the Immigration Act are protected as employees by the Labour Relations Act. This principle was upheld by the Labor Court in the Discovery Health case.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 27 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996); Section 27 of the National Health Act (No. 61, 2003); Section 27 of the Refugees Act (No 130, 1998); and Section 44 of the Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002). Section 27(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 provides that "everyone" has the right to access health care services. Recognized refugees and permanent residents are to be treated as citizens when accessing the national health system. Temporary residents must obtain a visa for specific medical treatment which will last longer than three months under section 17 of the Immigration Act 13 of 2002. In terms of emergency healthcare, Section 27(3) of the Constitution states that no one may be refused emergency medical treatment regardless of immigration status or ability to pay. Additionally, Section 4(3)(a) of the National Health Act (No. 61, 2003) states that all pregnant or lactating women and any children under the age of 6 years old must be provided with free health care services if they are not members or beneficiaries of a medical aid (insurance) scheme, independent of immigration status.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 19(3)(b) of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 limits the right to stand for election to public office to adult citizens.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 9 of the Constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of "race, gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status. ethnic or social origin, colour, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion, conscience, belief, culture, language and birth." Section 1 of the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act lists the identical factors as "prohibited grounds". Neither law references migrant status as a prohibited ground.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 4 of 2000; and in Section 9 of the Constitution. Section 9 of the Constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of "race, gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, ethnic or social origin, colour, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion, conscience, belief, culture, language and birth." Section 1 of the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act lists the identical factors as "prohibited grounds." According to this Act, "prohibited grounds" are: (a) race, gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, ethnic or social origin, colour, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion, conscience, belief, culture, language and birth; or (b) any other ground where discrimination based on that other grounds (i) causes or perpetuates systemic disadvantage; (ii) undermines human dignity; or (iii) adversely affects the equal enjoyment of a person's rights and freedoms in a serious manner that is comparable to discrimination on a ground in paragraph (a).

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in: Section 23 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996); Labor Relations Act (No. 66 of 1995); and Discovery Health Limited v Commission For Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration and Others (2008) 29 ILJ 1480 (LC). National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 23(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 provides that "everyone" has the right to fair labour practices, which does not limit the right to citizens. Section 3 of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 requires the Act to be interpreted in line with its objects, the Constitution and the "public international law obligations of the Republic." Section 213 of the Labour Relations Act defines an "employee" as "(a) any person, excluding an independent contractor, who works for another person or for the State and who receives, or is entitled to receive, any remuneration; and (b) any other person who in any manner assists in carrying on or conducting the business of an employer, and "employed" and "employment" have meanings corresponding to that of "employee"; There is therefore no distinction between a citizen and non-citizen employee with regards to the rights under the Labour Relations Act. In the case of Discovery Health v CCMA and others ?2008? 7 BLLR 633 (LC), the Labour Court found that the CCMA (the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration) had jurisdiction to hear a matter concerning the alleged unlawful dismissal of a non-national employee whose work permit had expired. The Court found that the employee-employer relationship was not dependent on whether the employee was legally authorized to work in the country and had the right to the protections of the Labour Relations Act.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 22 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 ; Attorneys Act 53 of 1979; Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002), Section 19; and Refugees Act, 130 of 1998 (as amended), section 22(8). Work visas are limited to the specific job which was used to apply for the visa. Section 19(2) general work visas are bound to a specific job and employer. Section 19(4) Critical Skills visas permit the holder to search for employment in the general sector provided for under the visa. The list of critical skills is provided for under Government Notice 459 in Government Gazette no 37716 of 3 June 2014. A work visa holder may apply for a change of conditions of his or her visa within South Africa in terms of section 10(6) of the Immigration Act. Holders of visitor's or medical visas must apply for a change of conditions from outside of South Africa under section 10(7) of the Act. Section 22 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 restricts the right to choose one's trade, occupation or profession to citizens. It further provides that the practice of a trade, occupation or profession may be regulated by law. Many of those laws restrict access to that profession to citizens and permanent residents (for example, the Attorney's Act 53 of 1979 limits access to the legal profession to citizens and permanent residents).

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in South Africa regulates migrant spouse/partner’s right to work in the Immigration Act and Refugees Act. The holder of a Relative's Visa under section 18 of the Immigration Act 13 of 2002 may not conduct work. For spouses accompanying a visa holder, the spouse must apply for a visitor's visa and request permission to work. The spouse of a citizen or permanent resident may apply for the right to work under section 11(6) of the Immigration Act. Spouses accompanying other temporary resident visa holders may apply for the right to work (or other activity under section 11(1)(b)(iv) of the Act read with Regulation 11(4) of the Immigration Regulations 2014. Section 3(c) of the Refugees Act allows for a dependent to be included on an asylum application and be issued with an asylum seeker visa. Consequently, a dependent may also apply for the right to work to be endorsed on their asylum seeker visa.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Loss of employment will affect the validity of a temporary residence visa as any change of conditions (such as a change in employer) will require a separate change of conditions application. For instance, a work permit automatically lapses if the holder does not submit certification of employment every year.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997; Labor Relations Act (No. 66, 1995); Constitution (No 108, 1996), Sections 22, 23. The Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 gives effect to Section 23 of the Constitution and it does not make a distinction between citizen and non-citizen workers. Migrants are protected under the Labour Relations Act, but they may face restrictions in certain sectors.
