question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Constitution (No. 108, 1996), Section 27(1)(C); Social Assistance Act (No. 13, 2004), Section 5; and Unemployment Insurance Act (No. 63, 2001), Section 3. The Constitution provides everyone the right to have access to social security. Section 27(1)(c). The Unemployment Insurance Act, however, excludes migrants who are temporarily in the country for work from access to the Unemployment Insurance Fund (Section 3). Under the regulations implementing the Unemployment Insurance Act 63 of 2001, only those with a South African identity document can make a claim. The Equality Court found this practice unlawful in 2017 and ordered the government to draft new regulations. New regulations were announced in October 2019, but have not yet taken effect. Under Section 5, of the Social Assistance Act, the government (Minister of Social Development and Minister of Finance) may determine eligibility for particular grants by notice in the Gazette. The war veterans grant is limited to South African citizens and permanent residents. Refugees (holders of refugee permits) are entitled to the following: older person's grant, child support grant, care dependency grant, grant in aid (tied to receipt of disability or older person's grant), foster child grant, and disability grant. The short-term social relief of distress grant, initiated in May 2020, is available to refugees, asylum seekers, and special permit holders.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right for certain categories of migrants in Section 12 and Section 3 of the Unemployment Insurance Act 63 of 2001. Under the Act, benefits are available to all contributors, but the Act excludes temporary foreign workers (Section 3). Under the regulations, only those with a South African identity document can make a claim. The Equality Court and the North Gauteng High Court found this practice unlawful in 2017 and ordered the government to draft new regulations. New regulations were announced in October 2019, and took effect in Feb 2020. The regulations include asylum seeker and refugee permits, and valid foreign identity documents and passports, as valid identity documents. In addition, many migrants work in informal sectors that exclude them from benefits.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa provides temporary migrant workers with avenues to become lawfully settled in Sections 25-27 of Immigration Act 13 of 2002. Under Section 26 of the Immigration Act, individuals who have had work permits for five years may apply for permanent residence if they have a permanent job offer and the job meets the labor certification requirements.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Chapter 2 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996), Bill of Rights: Sections 14(c); Section 25 [Dealing with property and possessions]; Section 33 [dealing with just administrative action]. The courts have interepreted these constitutional provisions to protect this right.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 28 of the Constitution (No. 108, 1996); Section 2 and 9 of the South African Births and Deaths Registration Amendment Act (No. 18 of 2010); and Section 8 of the Regulations on the Registration of Births and Deaths, 2014. Section 28 of the Constitution includes the right to a name and a nationality from birth. The implementation of the right to a nationality is directly linked with the right to registration at birth. Children born to asylum-seekers, refugees and undocumented foreigners hold this right equally to children of citizens Section 9(1) of the South African Births and Deaths Registration Amendment Act (No. 18 of 2010) states that "In the case of any child born alive, anyone of his or her parents, or if the parents are deceased, any of the prescribed persons, shall, within 30 days after the birth of such child, give notice thereof in the prescribed manner, and in compliance with the prescribed requirements, to any person contemplated in section 4." Section 2 of the same act provides that the Act applies to South African citizens but also includes "persons who are not South African citizens but who sojourn permanently or temporarily in the Republic, for whatever purpose". The regulations to the Act deal specifically with registration of children born to parents who are not citizens, permanent residents, or refugees (Regulation 8). Regulation 8 requires that parents have a valid passport and visa, so undocumented migrants, as well as asylum seekers without documentation, may be practically be unable to register the births of their children.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Both the Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002) and Refugees Act (No.130, 1998) mandate the issuing of documents and visas recognising the different forms of status migrants may hold. However, most visas (work, study, visitors, relatives) are printed in the migrant's passport and do not provide an additional confirmation of identity. Refugee and asylum seeker permits include an ID photo, ID/file no etc which give better confirmation of identity, but these are generally folded up pieces of paper. Only refugees are entitled to receive an identity document similar to a South African identity document.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right through a patchwork of constitutional, as well as case law. Though there are no specific laws dealing with this issue, but Section 25 of the Constitution states that no one may be deprived of property except in accordance with law, and no law may permit arbitrary deprivation of property. Furthermore, although there is no specific provision prohibiting the destruction of documents, the South African courts have on numerous occasions found that the destruction of immigration-related documents are unlawful.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations of 1963, Article 2 of the Diplomatic Immunities and Privileges Act, 37 of 2001. However, sections 5 and 36 of the Refugees Act read together with Regulation 4 provides for the cessation of refugee status or re-availment to the protection of their country of origin if refugees voluntarilty seek consular services at any diplomatic mission representing their country of origin, applies for any assistance or official document, such as a travel document or citizenship related document, at any diplomatic mission representing their country of origin whether in the Republic or any other country, presents themself on the premises of any diplomatic mission representing their country of origin in the Republic or in any other territory, and/or applies for and receives any benefit afforded to citizens of their country of nationality.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 28(1)(g) of the Constitution says children may only be detained as a measure of last resort in which case the child may only be detained for the shortest appropriate period and be kept separately from adults. The courts have ruled on the detention of children in Centre for Child Law v Minister of Home Affairs 2005 (6) SA 50 (T). Court found that detention of undocumented minors unlawful as they constitute a particular vulnerable group. Instead, children should be dealt within terms of the Children's Act. The Minimum standards with regard to detention (annexed to Immigration Act Regulations) stipulate that detained minors should be kept separate from adults, kept in accommodations appropriate to their age, shall not be kept separate from their parents or guardians, and that unaccompanied minors should not be detained (Section 1(d)).

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Immigration Act lays out procedures for the detention of "illegal foreigners" in Section 32 and 34. This provision was struck down by the Constitutional Court as inconsistent with the Constitution. The Court ruled, under Lawyers for Human Rights v Minister of Home Affairs and others, 2017 (5) SA 480 (CC)., that all detainees must be brought before a court within 48 hours and called on Parliament to address this issue. While Section 34 is no longer in effect (following a two-year suspension of the declaration of invalidity to give Parliament time to address the issue), Parliament has not passed any amendments to the law. In general, asylum seekers and refugees may not be detained, except on public order and security grounds under Sections 28 and 29 of the Refugees Act.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 12(1)(b) of the Constitution; section 34 of the Immigration Act, 13 of 2002; and Lawyers for Human Rights vs Minister of Home Affairs, 2017 (5) SA 480 (CC). Section 34 of the Immigration Act lays out procedures for review and appeal of detentions for the purposes of deportation, as well as a detention ceiling of 120 days. In 2017, the Constitutional Court invalidated part of Section 34 as inconsistent with the Constitution. The Court required that anyone arrested under Section 34 be brought before a court within 48 hours. It gave Parliament 24 months to remedy the defect. It also required the Department of Home Affairs to begin bringing people before a court within 48 hours while the legislation was being amended. If the detainee is not brought before a court within 48 hours, the individual is entitled to immediate release.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Sections 12(1)(b) and 35(2) of the Constitution, 108 of 1996; Section 34 of the Immigration Act 13 of 2002, Lawyers for Human Rights v Minister of Home Affairs, 2017 (5) SA 480 (CC). Section 32(2) of the Immigration Act requires that any illegal foreigner shall be deported from South Africa. The Supreme Court of Appeal in Ulde v Minister of Home Affairs found that the arresting officer maintains a discretion whether to arrest and detain for the purposes of deportation. This discretion must be exercised in favorem libertatis. The Immigration Act further requires that an individual's immigration status be verified before being detained, and required that any detention beyond 30 days be confirmed by a warrant of the court. The Constitutional Court found that Section 34, which required that any detention beyond 30 days be confirmed by a warrant of the court, was unconstitutional. Lawyer for Human Rights v Minister of Home Affairs, 2017 (5) SA 480 (CC) Prior to the Constitutional Court case, these warrants were often issued as standard practice, without an individual appearance. Under the Constitutional Court's decision, the individual migrant must be brought before a court within 48 hours of their detention.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 12(1)d and e of the Constitution and Combating of Torture of Persons Act 13 of 2013. Section 12 of the Constitution provides that everyone has the right not to be tortured in any way. It also stipulates that no one may be treated or punished in a cruel, inhuman or degrading way. These constitutional rights are non-derogable. Although torture and cruel and inhuman treatment is covered by the Constitution, the Prevention and Combating of Torture of Persons Act 13 of 2013 goes further and makes it punishable by law. This provision applies to everyone, regardless of citizenship status.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the framework for regulating the legality of arrests in the Criminal Procedure Act, 51 of 1977 (as amended). Additional regulations are found in the Immigration Act 13 of 2002 and the Refugees Act 130 of 1998 (as amended).

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in section 49 the Criminal Procedure Act, 51 of 1977 (as amended). Lethal force would only be permitted if the officer "believes on reasonable grounds" (a) that the force is immediately necessary for the purposes of protecting the arrestor, any person lawfully assisting the arrestor or any other person from imminent or future death or grievous bodily harm; (b) that there is a substantial risk that the suspect will cause imminent or future death or grievous bodily harm if the arrest is delayed; or (c) that the offence for which the arrest is sought is in progress and is of a forcible and serious nature and involves the use of life threatening violence or a strong likelihood that it will cause grievous bodily harm."

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, Section 22(2) of the the Prevention and Combating of Trafficking in Persons Act (2013) provides exceptions for victims of trafficking in certain circumstances if during a criminal prosecution of a person, a prosecutor suspects that that person is a victim of trafficking and that the offense was committed as a direct result of that person's position as a victim of trafficking.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa provides that convictions for criminal or other offenses leads to a loss of the citizenship status of naturalized migrants in Section 20 of the Constitution, Act 130 of 1998, Section 8(2) of the Citizenship Act. Section 20 of the Constitution provides that no citizen may be deprived of citizenship. Certain exceptional circumstances can however lead to the loss of citizenship, e. g. Section 8(2) of the Citizenship Act? The Minister may by order deprive a South African citizen who also has the citizenship or nationality of any other country of his or her South African citizenship if: (a) such citizen has at any time been sentenced in any country to a period of imprisonment of not less than 12 months for any offense which, if it was committed outside the Republic, would also have constituted an offense in the Republic. Dual citizens may have South African citizenship revoked, if "such citizen has at any time been sentenced in any country to a period of imprisonment of not less than 12 months for any offence which, if it was committed outside the Republic, would also have constituted an offense in the Republic."

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa provides pathway to citizenship for certain groups of economic migrants via Section 5 of the South African Citizenship Act (No. 88 of 1995), amended by the South African Citizenship Amendment Act, 17 of 2010; and in Section 27 of the Immigration Act, 13 of 2002. The South African Citizenship Act, 1995 (Act 88 of 1995), amended by the South African Citizenship Amendment Act, 2010 (Act No. 17 of 2010) changed certain naturalization requirements. Applications for naturalization may only be made if the applicant has been on a Permanent Residence Permit for a period of ten years. Lesser-skilled economic migrants have no path to regularize their status, but skilled migrants on work and other permits may apply for permanent residence and subsequently for citizenship.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa provides pathway to citizenship for humanitarian migrants via Section 27 of the South African Citizenship Act (No. 88 of 1995), amended by the South African Citizenship Amendment Act (No. 17, 2010); Section 27 of the Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002); Section 27 of the Refugees Act (No. 130, 1998), amended in Refugees Amendment Act (No.12, 2011), Section 10. Refugees previously could apply for permanent residence after 5 years, if they obtained certification that they will remain refugees indefinitely, and may then naturalize if they meet the naturalization requirements. Amendments to the Refugees Act that took effect on January 1, 2020 changes the requirement from 5 to 10 years before a refugee could apply for permanent residence following certification that they would remain a refugee indefinitely.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa provides pathway to citizenship for family migrants through Section 5 of the South African Citizenship Act (No. 88, 1995); Regulation 3(2)(a) of the Act's Regulations (GN 1122 of GG 36054 of 28 December 2012); and Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002). Family migrants have access to citizenship if the principal family member is a citizen or permanent resident. In terms of section 5 of the South African Citizenship Act No 88 of 1995, an applicant for citizenship must have been a permanent resident for no less than 5 years prior to the application for citizenship. Regulation 3(2)(a) of the Act's Regulations (GN 1122 of GG 36054 of 28 December 2012) requires a 10 year period before a permanent resident is eligible for citizenship. The regulation also requires residency requirements for the 5 years prior to the application for citizenship. Relatives visas also provide a path to permanent residence, but are subject to financial requirements.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in South African Citizenship Act (No. 88, 1995). Individuals must get permission to retain their South Africa citizenship before acquiring another citizenship. Under the Regulations, a migrant seeking naturallzation must be a citizen of a country that allows dual citizenship: "Provided that in the case where dual citizenship is not allowed by his or her country, such person renounces the citizenship of that country and furnishes the Minister with the prescribed proof of such renunciation."

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Sections 9 (equality) and 15(1) (freedom of religion, belief and opinion) of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa (1996) (the Bill of Rights). Section 15(1) provides that "everyone" has the right to freedom of religion, belief and opinion and therefore this right is not limited to citizens.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 15 of the Constitution (No 108 1996). Section 15 guarantees everyone, including migrants, "the right to freedom of conscience, religion, thought, belief and opinion."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. Even if Section 16 of the Constitution guarantees to everyone freedom of expression, including freedom to receive or impart information or ideas, the Regulations to the Refugees Act, that took effect on Jan 1, 2020, restricts refugee and asylum seekers from participating in any political activity or campaign in furtherance of any political party or political interests in the Republic.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for all migrants. National law in South Africa protects this right in Sections 18 and 23 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996. Section 18 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 provides that "everyone" has the right of freedom of association. Section 23 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 provides that "every" worker has the right to (a) form and join a trade union; (b) to participate in the activities and programmes of a trade union; and to strike. Therefore the right is not limited to citizens. However, recent amendments to the Refugees Act, which were brought into operation by Regulations on 1 January 2020, prohibit refugees and asylum seekers from participating in any political activity or campaign in furtherance of any political party or political interests in South Africa. Doing so will lead to the "cessation" (withdrawal) of refugee status. These regulations do not affect the right of refugees to join trade unions, but they do affect freedom of association.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 18(1) of the Immigration Act 13 of 2002 regarding relative's visas requires that the citizen or permanent resident sponsor provides financial assurance for the family member. Regulation 17(2) of the Immigration Regulations GN R413 in Government Gazette 37679 of 22 May 2014 provides for the proof necessary by way of monthly pay slip or a certified bank statement not older than three months old to prove financial assurance. Government Notice 456 in Government Gazette 37716 of 3 June 2014 sets the assurance at R8500.00 per month. Section 26(b) of the Act provides for direct access to permanent residence for spouses who have been married for not less than five years. There does not appear to be any prescribed amount for financial assurance. Section 27(g) of the Act provides for permanent residence for a ???relative of a citizen or permanent resident within the first step of kinship. Regulation 23(7) of the Immigration Regulations 2014 requires the citizen or permanent resident who is sponsoring the relative under this section to satisfy the Director-General the he / she is able and willing to maintain the foreign relative making the application. There does not appear to be any prescribed amount for financial assurance.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 9 of the Constitution of South Africa, 108 of 1996; and in the Criminal Procedure Act, 51 of 1977. Section 9 of the Constitution says that "everyone is equal before the law and has right to equal protection and the benefit of the law." These rights are laid out in more detail in the "Service Charter for Victims of Crime," which sets out a series of rights based on the Constitution and South African law.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Immigration Act (No. 13, 2002), Prevention and Combatting of Trafficking in Persons Act (No. 7, 2013). Section 31(2)(b) of the Immigration act allows for the Department of Home Affairs to grant special authorization for migrant victims of crime to remain in the country. There is also a provision for victims of trafficking in the Prevention and Combatting of Trafficking in Persons Act which references this provision of the Immigration Act. Sections 15-17 of the Prevention and Combating of Trafficking in Persons Act (No. 7, 2013) provides a path for victims of trafficking to get a temporary visa for the purposes of assisting in the law enforcement investigation. If they will face a risk from repatriation, they may apply for permanent residence.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa (No. 108, 1996); Refugees Act, 130 of 1998 (as amended), Children's Act, 38 of 2005; Immigration Act, 13 of 2002 and the 2014 Regulations thereto. The Immigration Act also takes into consideration the status of children, including unaccompanied minors, in the context of migration; Section 9 of the Act read together with Regulation 5(10) prescribes the manner in which a child, including an unaccompanied child, may enter and depart South Africa.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. South Africa has a number of laws that deal with gender-based equality, but none of them consider the vulnerability of women in the context of migration.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in South Africa protects this right in Section 21A of the Refugees Act which states that individuals who are reasonably suspected to have mental disabilities should be assisted in applying for asylum. There is no provision for physically disabled individuals. Other legislation like the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 4 of 2000 also prohibit discrimination against persons with disabilities, including migrants.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Laura Garcia Juan. [2]: David Moya Malapeira and Guadalupe Begazo.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Spain

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 7. Article 7.1, of the 4/2000 Immigration Act recognizes that migrants have the right of assembly under the same conditions as Spanish citizens. 2) The Spanish Constitution Articles 21.1. Article 21.1, Spanish Constitution recognizes the right to peaceful unarmed assembly noting that the exercise of this right shall not require prior authorization. The Spanish Constitutional Court judgement 236/2007 recognized that foreign citizens, regardless of their administrative status, have the right of freedom of assembly commensurate with that afforded to citizens.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, this right is protected for some groups of migrants, in particular circumstances. For example, LO 4/2000 Immigration Act, Article 6.1. Article 6.1, Immigration Act 4/2000 states that migrants residing in Spain may hold the right to vote in municipal elections in the terms established in the Constitution, in international treaties where appropriate, and in other provisions in domestic law. LO 5/1985 on the General Electoral System, Article 176. Migrants can only vote in municipal elections (not regional or national elections) as established by LO 5/1985 on the General Electoral System, Article 176. In general, this right is available to European Union citizens residing in Spain, and migrants who are citizens of countries with reciprocity agreements (Norway, Ecuador, New Zealand, Colombia, Chile, Peru, Paraguay, Iceland, Bolivia, Cape Verde, Republic of Korea and Trinidad and Tobago) after the relevant residence requirements are met.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Spanish Constitution, Articles 13.1,, 24. Article 24 of the Spanish Constitution, in concordance to Article 13.1, extends to foreigners equal protection and remedies by judges and courts in the exercise of their legitimate rights and interests. 2) The LO 4/2000 Immigration Act, Articles 20, 21. Articles 20 and 21 of the 4/2000 Immigration Act recognizes that migrants have the right to a fair trial and to lodge an appeal against administrative decisions.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Articles 22, 62 bis 1 h), 63.3. Article 22 of the Immigration Act 4/2000 grants migrants in Spain the right to free legal counsel in the administrative and judicial procedures related to their legal status as long as said proceedings are related to expulsion, return, entry refusal, asylum, or summary removal proceedings. 2) The Free Legal Aid Act 1996. The Free Legal Aid Act 1996 establishes the procedure to apply for free legal aid in such cases including the appointment of an attorney by the bar. It is also important to point out that the LO 1/1996, de 10 de enero, de Asistencia Jur?dica Gratuita, states that the right to counsel at the government's expense is available to all foreigners who are in Spain, regardless of their immigration status, when they prove insufficient resources to litigate.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Criminal Procedure Code, Article 123. Article 123 states that migrants have the right to benefit from translation and interpretation services if the person does not understand or is not fluent in the Spanish language. This includes: a) the right to be assisted by an interpreter who uses a language that they understand during all the proceedings; b) the right to be assisted by an interpreter during conversations outside of the criminal proceedings with their own lawyer if they are directly related to the criminal proceedings. Translation and interpretation expenses will be borne by the Administration.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the LO 4/200 Migration Act, Articles 55, 57. Unauthorized entry can result in administrative sanctions, but is not punishable as a criminal offense.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 13. Article declares that only those migrants with long-term resident status are entitled to access to public housing programs on an equal basis with citizens. The possibility of access is only for migrants who are legal residents, but this right is only enforceable in exactly the same conditions as citizens once foreigners obtain a long-term resident permit.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in LO 2000 the Immigration Act, Article 9. Equality in access to education services only applies to minor migrant children according to the Immigration Act 4/2000 (amended in 2009); below 18 years of age, they have a right to access to the education system, including basic, free and compulsory education as well as post-compulsory education.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Articles 9.1 and 9.2. Article 9.2 of the Immigration Act 4/2000 states that resident foreign nationals shall have the right to education of a non-compulsory nature in the same conditions as Spanish citizens. Specifically, they "shall have the right of access to levels of education and training...to the obtainment of the corresponding qualifications in each case, as well as access to the public system of scholarships and grants." However, equality in access to education services only applies to minor migrant children according to the Immigration Act 4/2000 (amended in 2009); below 18 years of age, they have a right to access to the education system, including basic, free and compulsory education as well as post-compulsory education. Adult migrants only enjoy equal access to education services as long as they are lawful residents in Spain.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Expulsion from Spanish territory is an administrative sanction according to LO 4/2000 the Immigration Law, Article 57. Administrative sanctions can be applied in cases of administrative offenses (LO 4/2000 the Immigration Law, Article 57.1). Furthermore, the penalty of a prison sentence for criminal offenses may be replaced by expulsion in some specific cases (according to LO 10/1995 of 23 November, of the Penal Code, Article 89.1). Expulsion entails, in any case, the loss of any authorization to remain in Spain, according to LO 4/2000 the Immigration Law Article 57.4.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 12/2009, Reguladora del Derecho de Asilo y de la Protecci?n Subsidiaria, Articles 20.1 c), 20.1 d) and 44.4. 2) LO 4/2000, Additional Provision 10. Despite of these provisions, there are two land borders in Spain (Ceuta and Melilla) where this issue is very controversial. The Spanish Government considers that refoulement on the basis of risk of return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment is covered by law because of the special regime of Ceuta and Melilla, according to LO 4/2000, Additional Provision 10. In 2020 and 2021, the Constitutional Court handed down two sentences that declared Additional Provision 10 of the LO 4/2000 in accordance with the Spanish Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the 12/2009 Asylum Act, Aticles 5, 20.1 d), 36.1 a. 2) LO 4/2000 Additional Provision 10. Despite these provisions, there are two land borders in Spain (Ceuta and Melilla) where this issue is very controversial. The Spanish Government considers that refoulement on the basis of risk of return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment is covered by law because of the special regime of Ceuta and Melilla, according to LO 4/2000, Additional Provision 10. In 2020 and 2021, the Constitutional Court handed down two sentences that declared Additional Provision 10 of the LO 4/2000 in accordance with the Spanish Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the 12/2009 Asylum Act Article 5 and 6. Article 6 explicitly refers to serious violations of fundamental rights as ground to refugee protection and Article 5 provides refugees with protection against refoulement.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 64.5 of the LO 4/2000 Immigration Act and Articles 23.6 and 246.7 of the 557/2011 Royal Decree recognize the right to apply for asylum but do not introduce an obligation to public authorities to inform asylim-seekers about the possible availability of asylum before being expelled or prevented entry.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no explicit ban on chain-refoulement, and this is decided on a case-by-case basis. Article 36.1 of the Asylum Act which states that non-refoulment protections will apply in accordance with international treaties. European Court of Human Rights case-law has clearly declared that expulsion to a country that does not respect the non-refoulement prohibition is not lawful. In addtion, several articles in the LO 4/2000 the Immigration Law (36, 54.2 c), 57.6, 66.3 d)) could be read to imply a ban on the expulsion to any country where a migrant is likely to be subjected to refoulement through a subsequent expulsion, as both articles state that a transport company returning a migrant has the obligation to bring the migrant “…to any other State where their admission is guaranteed.” Despite these provisions, though, this matter has not been settled by court interpretation.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the 4/2000 Migration Act, Article 57. A migrant can only be expelled when justified by facts relevant to the individual concerned due to Protocol No. 4 to the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Convention is binding upon Member States of the Council of Europe and it expressly prohibits collective expulsion of aliens. However, in the European Court of Human Rights judgement, ND and NT v. Spain, the Grand Chamber agreed that such push-backs at the border do not need to be decided after any administrative procedure, and no guarantees are needed. Therefore, immediate removals at the borders will not be considered under the prohibition of collective expulsions.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Royal Degree 557/2011, Article 23.4. 2) The LO 4/2000 Migration Act, Articles 21, 22.3, 57.9, 65.1. During expulsion proceedings, migrants have the right to be heard and submit written comments to the administrative authority before the adjudication of the case. After the administrative decision, there is a right to an administrative appeal before going to the courts to seek judicial review.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Civil Code, Articles 17.1, 22.1. Article 17.1 states that migrants in Spain are guaranteed citizenship if they would otherwise be stateless. 2) Royal Decree 865/2001. 3) LO 12/2009.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Articles 16.2, 17, 18.1. According to Article 18, a migrant can reunite their families under the following conditions: 1) one year of prior lawful residence in Spain and authorization for another year at least; 2) showing enough income to cover the living expenses of each family member; 3) showing evidence of housing conditions to accommodate all reunited family members; 4) health insurance for each family member. Reuniting ascendants older than 65-years old is subject to additional requirements, but is still possible. 2) The Royal Decree 557/2011, Articles 17-18, 52-61.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Administrative Judicial Procedures Act of 1998. 2) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 21.1. All types of administrative resolutions concerning migrants' rights are subject to appeal before the judicial authority

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Spanish Civil Code, Article 44. 2) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 17.1. Article 44 of the Spanish Civil Code makes same-sex marriage legal in Spain, and Article 17.1 of the Immigration Act 4/2000 extends reunification to same sex spouses, since it accepts civil partnerships for family reunification.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 32. There are only a few exceptions to this rule. First, student visas or students permits are not residence permits, therefore the time spent in Spain does not contribute to a long-term residence permit. Additionally, seasonal workers are subject to a separate regime, and cannot tranisition to permanent residency in the same way as other temporary migrants.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 31.3. 2) Royal Decree 557/2011 Articles 123, 124. Irregular migrants can regularize in exceptional circumstances of special ties with the labour market or with family members regularly staying in Spain. This legal principal is called “arraigo social” (deep rooting), meaning that if a person without a legal permit residing in the country meets certain requirements by law, they can apply for a one year temporary residence authorization due to exceptional circumstances (set down in Article 123 of the Royal Decree 557/2011). Additionally, Article 124 of Royal Decree 557/2011 identifies three different types of “arraigo” related to work, social roots and family roots. The main conditions are that migrants have to prove a continued stay in Spain for a minimum period of two years, provide a lack of a criminal record in Spain and in their country of origin or in the country or countries in which they resided during the last five years, and demonstrate the existence of labor relations whose duration is not less than six months.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Spanish Constitution, Article 24. According to Article 24 of the Spanish Constitution, all persons have the right to obtain effective protection from the judges and the courts in the exercise of their rights and legitimate interests, and in no case may there be a lack of defense. 2) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Articles 20, 22, 36. Articles 20 and 22 Immigration Act 2000 guarantees the right to effective legal protection, and the right to free legal assistance, respectively. Finally, Article 36 provides for the authorization for the exercise of lucrative activities, which states that the lack of residence and work authorization, without prejudice to the responsibilities of the employer to which it gives rise, including those of Social Security, will not invalidate the employment contract with respect to the rights of the foreign worker, nor will it be an obstacle to obtaining the benefits derived from assumptions contemplated by international agreements for the protection of workers or others that may apply,

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 12. 2) National Health System Quality and Cohesion Law, Articles 3, 3bis, 3ter. Article 3.ter establishes that “Foreigners not registered or authorized as residents in Spain have the right to health protection and healthcare under the same conditions as people with Spanish nationality, as established in article 3.1." 3) Royal Decree-Law 7/2018. Article 3.1 Royal Decree 7/2018 establishes that “All persons with Spanish nationality and foreign persons who have established their residence in Spanish territory are holders of the right to health protection and health care." In addition, irregular migrants who have not registered with their local councils, but who are pregnant or suffer an accident and require emergency care are guaranteed access.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, this right is protected for some groups of migrants, in particular circumstances. Act 4/2000, Article 6.2. stipulates that citizens of the European Union and those migrants' from countries with bilateral treaties with Spain can run for public office in Spain. Most of the bilateral agreements between Spain and third countries (Norway, Ecuador, New Zealand, Colombia, Chile, Peru, Paraguay, Iceland, Bolivia, Cape Verde, Republic of Korea and Trinidad and Tobago) do not recognize the right to passive suffrage, only an active right after the relevant residence requirements are met, with the exception of Norway. Notwithstanding, EU citizens enjoy both passive and active rights as a result of them directly benefitting from the provisions of European Union Treaties on this topic.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 15/2022, Article 2. 2) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 23.2. The Immigration Act makes a distinction between legal and illegal migrants as it declares, as a principle, “the recognition of equal rights and obligations for all those who live or work legally in Spain." The concept of "migrant" must be understood as subsumed in that of "foreigner" for Spanish legislation. Spanish legislation uses the words "immigrant" and "foreigner" in its wording. It is worth highlighting the fact that LO 15/2022 does not use the words “immigrant” nor “foreigner” but that of “people.” However, according to Constitutional Court Judgement numbers 107/1984 and 115/1987, immigrants can not be discriminated against in certain fundamental rights (life, protection against torture or ill-treatment, freedom of thought and religion, freedom from arrest, etc), but the Constitution (Article 23, regarding the right to suffrage and the right to work as a civil servant) can introduce a reasonable and proportionate differential treatment on grounds of migrant status for certain rights, like the right to enter, leave or abide in the country or the right to work.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Spanish Constitution, Article 14. 2) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 23.1. 3) LO 15/2022, Article 2. The concept of "migrant" must be understood as subsumed in that of "foreigner" for Spanish legislation. Spanish legislation uses the words "immigrant" and "foreigner" in its wording. It is worth highlighting the fact that Ley 15/2022 does not use the words “immigrant” nor “foreigner” but that of “people.”

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, national law in Spain protects this right for those legally resident in Spain in LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 2.bis, (which states that the law "[recognizes]... equal rights and obligations for all those who live or work legally in Spain"), 2e), 10, 23.2, 36. Legal provisions mostly provide for equal treatment in terms of labour wages for regular migrant workers with a valid work permit, e.g., Article 10 of the Immigration Act taken together with Article 23.2 (prohibition of discrimination by employers) and Article 36 with regards to access to work and work authorization. Such provisions lay down a regime that implies equal pay and equal work conditions for all legal resident workers, without regard to their nationality.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Articles 38.5, 38.7. 2) Royal Decree of the Migration Act 557/2011, Articles 63.1 and 63.5. There are two restrictions on the free choice of employment (geographic scope and occupation) ONLY within the first one-year duration of the work permit. Additionally, a recent modification of the regulation from the Royal Decree 629/2022, has made it possible to allow the migrant to freely choose employment or self-employment after one year from granting the first work permit.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Royal Decree 55/2011, Article 58.4. 2) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 19.1. The Royal Decree 55/20011 states that the residence authorization for family reunification of the spouse, the civil partner or the reunified child will enable the holder to work so that no working authorization is needed. This authorization enables them to work for others or for their own account in any part of Spanish territory, occupation or activity sector.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain conditionally protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Articles 31.7, 38.6. 2) Royal Decree 557/2011, Articles 71.2, 71.3. There are three general scenarios that require clarification on this issue: first, immediately after arrival, if the initial visa for residence and work permit can not be transformed into a work and residence permit because the employer is not able to hire the foreign worker, there is a special speedy procedure available to the migrant to ask for administrative permission to find a similar job in a very short period of time. Second, residence and working permits requires having worked a minimum amount of time during the previous authorization for them to be renewed. Third, long-term residents do not require a work authorization so their work could be discontinuous and this does not affect their status.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO Act 4/2000 the Immigration, Articles 2bis, 2 e), 10, 14, 23. In principle, Articles 2bis and 2e) implicitly state “the recognition of equal rights and obligations for all those who live or work legally in Spain." This means migrants have a right to the same employment conditions and protections. Three other provisions of the LO 4/2000 Migration Act, on Articles 10.1, 14 and 23 taken together recognize legally resident foreigners, who meet the requirements accorded by law, the right to exercise a paid activity on their own or another's account, as well as to access the Social Security system. They are entitled to services and social benefits, both general and basic as well as specific ones, under the same conditions as Spanish Citizens and any discrimination against them under this provision is prohibited and sanctioned by the law. 2) Royal Decree 1620/2011. 3) Royal Decree 16/2022.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Immigration Act 4/2000, Articles 2.bis, 2e), 10, 14, 36.5. Article 14 states states that resident foreigners have the right to access social security benefits and services under the same conditions as Spanish citizens, both general and basic as well as specific ones, under the same conditions as Spanish citizens.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Immigration Act 4/2000, Articles 2.bis, 2e), 10, 14, 36.5.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 32. 2) Royal Decree 557/2011. As a general rule, those who have had a temporary residence permit in Spain for five years continuously and who meet the conditions established by law will have the right to switch to a long-term residence permit. Additionally, Article 148.3, Royal Decree 557/2011, also provides for several cases where long-term residence authorization can also granted: "...c) Residents who were born in Spain and, upon reaching the age of majority, have resided in Spain legally and continuously for at least the three consecutive years immediately prior to the application; d) Foreigners who have been Spanish of origin and have lost their Spanish nationality; e) Residents who, upon reaching the age of majority, have been under the guardianship of a Spanish public entity during the immediately preceding five consecutive years; f) Stateless persons, refugees or beneficiaries of subsidiary protection who are in Spanish territory and whose respective status in Spain has been recognized."

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the LO 4/2000 Immigration Act, Article 4. 2) The LO 4/2015 on Protection of Public Security, Article 13.2. Article 13.2 of the Organic Law 4/2015 states that the migrants have the right to not be deprived of their identity documents except by judicial decision in criminal proceedings.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Law of Civil Registry 20/2011, Articles 44, 45, 46, 47, 48. Registration of the birth of a child is mandatory in Spain for every child, national or foreigner, regardless of status.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the LO 4/2000 Migration Act, Articles 4, 4.2, 27.2b), 29.2, 34.2. In particular, Article 4 states that foreigners in Spanish territory have the right and the duty to keep documentation proving their identity issued by the competent authorities of the country of origin, as well as one proving their status in Spain. Moreover, all foreigners who have been issued a visa or a permit to remain in Spain for a period exceeding six months will obtain a special foreigner's identity card, which they must personally request within one month of their entry into Spain or since the authorization is granted, respectively. Holders of a residence and seasonal work visa will be exempted from said obligation. 2) LO 4/2015 on Protection of Public Security, Article 13.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Immigration Act 4/2000, Articles 4.1, 4.3. Article 4.3 of the Immigration Act 4/2000 prohibits the taking of a migrants' documents and implicitly destroy them, but it does not include any penalty. Instead, the law provides the right to keep and preserve these documents in Article 4.1, so anyone that violates this right is acting illegally.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in LO 4/2000 Immigration Act, Articles 22.3, 60.4, 62.5, 62 bis e), 64.3, which establishes that expulsion procedures that include administrative detention will be communicated to the Consular authorities. 2) The Code of Criminal Procedure, Article 520.2, which states that notice will be sent by Spanish authorities to the Consulate in the event of criminal arrest of a migrant/foreigner.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Detention of children on migration grounds is not formally prohibited in Spain. Migrant children in family units which are subjected to deportation proceedings may be sent to a detention center and kept together. In such cases, the center must provide specific facilities to accommodate the families in separate modules from other migrant detainees according to Article 7 of the Royal Decree 162/2014 of Aliens Detention centers. Also, the Supreme Court judgment of 10th February 2015 recognized the right to protect family life in migrant detention centers in application of the EU Return Directive 2008. Children falling under the category of unaccompanied foreign minors, however, are placed in foster care under the protection of the public authorities as established by the Organic Law on the Legal Protection of Minors with the regulations set forth in article 35 of the 4/2000 Immigration Act. This can be seen as an implicit prohibition of the detention of unaccompanied migrant children.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Being in Spain without a valid residence authorization is considered a serious infraction according to Article 53.1a of the LO 4/2000 Immigration Act. This may be grounds for detention and internment in a Detention Centre for Foreigners (CIE) according to Article 62 of the LO 4/2000 Immigration Act. CIEs are public establishments where the migrants may be held in detention for a maximum of 60 days.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the LO 4/2000 Immigration Act, Articles 21, 23, 62.6, 65. In particular, Article 23 states that any breach of the legal grounds and conditions for detention and interment are subject to judicial control, and in extreme cases to Habeas Corpus proceedings.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in Athe Immigration Act 4/2000, Articles 53, 57, which require individualized determination of administrative detention based on grounds relating to immigration status.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Law, Articles 3 and 62bis b). Article 3 of the LO 4/2000 states "the norms related to the fundamental rights of foreigners will be interpreted in accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights." This includes the right to be free from torture and cruel, inhumane, and degrading treatment. 2) The Spanish Constitution, Article 15. In order to provide protections of this right, Articles 3 and 62 bis b) of the Immigration Act 4/2000 must be read together with Articles 15 of the Spanish Constitution and with Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, norms which clearly prohibit any torture, cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment of all human beings. Incorporation of EU law and international law is established by the Spanish Constitution in Articles 10.2 and 96 of the Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In general, there is no express provision on the use of force. Instead, there are only general provisions and internal protocols on the proportionate use of force by police officers. In the case of Ceuta and Melilla (which are overseas territories located in the north of Morocco), the First Additional Clause of the Organic Law 4/2015 states that aliens trying to illegally enter Spanish territory can be detained at the border and immediately removed.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Criminal Code provides general provisions on crimes like homicide, and explains the penalties for officials and citizens if the use of lethal force is found to be unnecessary or unjustified. However, neither the law nor the regulation cover the use of lethal force as a means of preventing entry into the territory. See: LO 4/2000 (articles 26 and 60); Royal Decree 557/2011, articles 15 and 23. There has been at least one criminal case against police officers (Tarajal case). In a recent case, he Melilla's case (ocurred on 24h June 2022 ) instead of providing aid to several migrants when they tried to enter Spanish territory by swimming from Morocco, instead tried to prevent the migrants from entering Spanish territory by using the threat of firing their weapons. However, despite some of the migrants drowning, the Courts have not convicted any member of the police for such actions.It is an open case.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) Ley Org?nica 10/1995, de 23 de noviembre, del C?digo Penal, article 177bis 11). 2) Article 59 bis of the 4/2000 Immigration Act. 3) Chapter IV of the 557/2011 Royal Decree. Illegal entry in Spain is considered a breach of administrative law, not criminal law. However, criminal law also exempts trafficked/smuggled migrants from criminal prosecution according to Article 59 bis of the 4/2000 Immigration Act. Provided said migrants are considered victims of human trafficking in accordance with Article 10 of the Council of Europe Convention on the Fight Against Trafficking in Human Beings, immigration officials are obliged to inform the potential victim of their rights and at the same time grant them a residence authorization for a short period of time in order for that person to recover and temporally sever their ties with traffickers. Additionally, Chapter IV of the 557/2011 Royal Decree regulates the temporary residence and work permits of victims of human trafficking (Articles 140 - 146). The chapter deals with many topics such as identification of potential non-European Union victims of trafficking, the procedures to obtain the above mentioned residence and work permits, the assisted return to the country of origin if so desired by the victim, and the protection of minors who are victims of human trafficking.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Civil Code Article 25.2. Article 25.2 of the Civil Code states that naturalization obtained using false statements, concealing information, or directly by fraud, can be nullified. Nullification proceedings can only be exercised during the next fifteen years from the date a migrant is naturalized by the Public Prosecutor’s Office before the civil court. Beyond this, no crime allows authorities to stripe any Spaniard of their nationality, be it nationality by birth or through naturalization.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Civil Code, Article 22.1. The general rule to acquire Spanish citizenship is through ten years lawful and continued residence, irrespective of whether the migrant is on an economic, humanitarian, or family visa.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Civil Code, Article 22.1. The general rule to acquire Spanish citizenship is through ten years lawful and continued residence, irrespective of whether the migrant is on an economic, humanitarian, or family visa.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in the Civil Code, Articles 22.1, 22.2.d. The general rule to acquire Spanish citizenship is through ten years lawful and continued residence, irrespective of whether the migrant is on an economic, humanitarian, or family visa. Additionally, acquisition of nationality through marriage to a Spaniard only requires one year residence after marriage (Article 22.2.d Spanish Civil Code). The situation is slightly different for children born in Spain from foreign parents; after one year since birth an application for Spanish citizenship can be submitted in this case. Similarly they could submit such application when they reach their majority.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Spanish Constitution, Article 11.3. 2) The Civil Code, Article 24.1. In accordance with Article 24.1, those with citizenship of Latin American countries, Andorra, Philippines, Equatorial Guinea and Portugal, may obtain dual nationality. France has been added to this list by agreement between the Kingdom of Spain and the French Republic, done in Montauban, on 15 March, 2021 at the 26th Franco-Spanish Summit. Sephardic Jews may also obtain dual nationality according to LO 12/2015.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Spanish Constitution, Article 16.1. Article 16.1 of the Spanish Constitution recognizes the freedom of ideology, religion and worship as a guaranteed right to individuals and communities with no other restrictions on their expression than may be necessary. 2) LO Act 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 3.1. Article 3.1, of the Immigration Act 4/2000 states that, foreigners shall enjoy in Spain the rights and freedoms recognized in Title I of the Spanish Constitution in the terms established in the International Treaties, in this Act and in those that regulate the exercise of each of them. As a general interpretative criterion, it will be understood that foreigners exercise the rights recognized by this Law in conditions of equality with the Spaniards.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in Spanish Constitution, Article 20.1 a). The Spanish Constitutional Court Judgement 107/1984 and the later 115/1987 recognized that foreign citizens, regardless of their administrative status, have equal rights to freedom of opinion and expression.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in Spanish Constitution, Articles 20.1 d), 20.1 a). The Spanish Constitutional Court Judgement 107/1984 and the later 115/1987 recognized that foreign citizens, regardless of their administrative status, have equal rights to freedom of opinion and expression.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, Article 8. 2) The Spanish Constitution, Articles 22 and 28. The Spanish Constitutional Court, in judgement 236/2007, recognized that foreign citizens, regardless of their administrative status, have the right of freedom of association equal to that of Spanish citizens. As a general principle regarding rules and regulations of fundamental rights and freedoms, the Spanish Constitution recognizes they will be interpreted in accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, international treaties, and agreements ratified by Spain

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 18.2 of LO 4/2000 the Immigration Act, the sponsor must prove that he/she has adequate housing, insurance coverage, and sufficient financial means to cover his/her needs and those of their family before visas for family reunification are granted.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Spanish Constitution Article 24. Article 24 of the Spanish Constitution reads as follows, 'All persons have the right: 1) to obtain effective protection from the judges and the courts in the exercise of their rights and legitimate interests, and in no case may there be a lack of defense. 2) Likewise, all have the right to the ordinary judge predetermined by law; to defense and assistance by a lawyer; to be informed of the charges brought against them; to a public trial without undue delays and with full guarantees; to the use of evidence appropriate to their defense; not to make self-incriminating statements; not to plead themselves guilty; and to be presumed innocent. The law shall specify the cases in which, for reasons of family relationship or professional secrecy, it shall not be compulsory to make statements regarding allegedly criminal offences." 2) LO 4/2000, Article 20.1. which recognizes that migrants have the right to a fair trial and to lodge an appeal against administrative decisions.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) LO 4/2000 Immigration Act, Articles 31bis, 59, 59bis. Article 59, among other provisions, states that "1. The foreigner who is irregularly in Spain and is a victim, injured or witness of an act of illicit trafficking of human beings, illegal migration, labor exploitation or illicit traffic of labor or exploitation in prostitution abusing their situation if necessary, it will be exempt from administrative responsibility and will not be expelled if it denounces the authors or cooperators of said traffic, or cooperates and collaborates with the competent authorities, essential data or testifying, where appropriate, in the corresponding process." 2) The Royal Decree 557/2011 (Reglamento de Extranjer?a), Article 126.1. However, exceptional residence permits for humanitarian reasons are only granted to victims of certain crimes like trafficking of human beings, racism, discrimination, xenophobia, etc., if victims collaborate with public authorities, police or the judiciary in their investigations against criminal networks.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: The suggested citation would be: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) Immigration Act 4/2000, (in spanish Ley de extranjer?a) in Articles 35, 59.5, 59 bis.5, 62.4. This act introduced a specific regime for unaccompanied migrant minors that, among other provisions, includes the duty to immediately protect the child following the "best interests of the child" principle. 2) Royal Decree 557/2011 (in spanish Reglamento de extranjer?a), Article 123. 3) Organic Act on Legal Minors' Protection Act 1/1996. 4) Royal Decree 629/2022 introduced modifications to reduce the financial means required for family reunification when the family member to be reunited is a child.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) Article 31 bis of the Immigration Act 4/2000. The Immigration Act 4/2000 allows for the temporary residence and work for foreign women victims of gender violence. It states that, regardless their administrative situation, women in such situations are guaranteed the rights recognized in Organic Law 1/2004 on the Integral Protection Measures against Gender Violence, as well as protection and safety measures established in current legislation. However, in order to access temporary protection status it is not enough to simply make an application to the authorities, there has to be a decision by the Prosecutor or the Judge acknowledging that harassment and/or violence or intimidation existed. This special regime included the authorization to legally and temporary stay in Spain. Women staying irregularly in Spain are protected from deportation procedures after reporting a situation of gender based violence. In such cases, deportation procedures will not be initiated, or if already initiated, will be halted.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Spain protects this right in 1) the Royal Decree 557/2011, Article 41.2. 2) The Immigration Act 4/2000 Article 14.2, Article 17. Article 14.2 ensures a migrant's right to access and benefits from social services to all foreigners with disabilities (as well as minors) regardless of their status, including special care and medical treatment as required by their physical or psycological situation if they live in Spain (“domicilio habitual”). Additionally, Article 17 on Family Reunification, includes people with disabilities as beneficiaries of family reunification procedures as long as they are not able to provide for their own needs due to their health conditions; they shall also benefit from the same type of authorization as family member who are reuniting with them, as established in Article 41.2 of the Royal Decree 557/2011.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Teodor Bodin. [2]: Emelie Jorwall

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Sweden

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 2 section 1 and The Act (1994:1219) on The European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The national law in Sweden protects the right to vote in local elections in chapter 1 sections 7 and 8 of the Local Government Act (2017:725) but only for those who have been registered as having their domicile in Sweden in the population registry for a period of at least three years preceding the election day. Immigrants with pending applications do not have a right to be registered, even if they are legally present in Sweden, i.e. asylum seekers with ongoing investigations. The right to vote in local or regional elections is available to all citizens of EU states that have their domicile in their local or regional entity. The Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 3 section 4 states that only Swedish citizens have the right to vote in national elections.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in the Constitution, The Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 1 section 9.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 18 sections 1 and 1a.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Code of Judicial Procedure (1942:740) chapter 5 §6; and Chapter 23, section 16.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 20 section 4 criminalizes unauthorized entry into Sweden across an external border according to the codex on the Schengen borders. Unauthorized entry through an internal border according to the Schengen borders is on the contrary not criminalized and there are no civil sanctions for this.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in Social Services Act (2001:453) chapter 2 section 1, chapter 2a section 1 and chapter 4 section 1 and 3. This right is also protected in the Act on Reception of Asylum seekers, code section 3.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Education Act (2010:800) chapter 7 section 2 and 3 and chapter 29 section 2. Chapter 7 section 2 states that children residing in Sweden are obliged to attend school and chapter 7 section 3 states that all children who are obliged to attend school have the right to free primary education in a public shool. Chapter 29 section 2 states that a child is to be considered residing in Sweden if they should be registered in the population register. The National Registration Act (1991:481) regulates the population register and section 3 of the act states that a person who has moved to Sweden is conidered to be a resident if they are presumed to regularly spend their resting hours in the country for at least one year. An alien who is given a permit to reside in Sweden for a period of at least one year can therefore be registered in the population register and have te same right to primary education as Swedish citizens. The Education Act (2010:800) chapter 29 section 2 also lists a number of categories of migrant statuses that, when applying the act, should be considered residents in Sweden and enjoy the same rights. Notably, this also applies to asylum-seekers and those staying in Sweden irregularly.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Higher Education Ordinance Act (1993:100) Chapter 7 section 2, The Education Act (2010:800) chapter 20 sections 3, 3a and 20 and chapter 29 section 2 and 3 and The Ordinance Act (2010:543) on application fee and tuition fee at universities and collages section 5 and 2. Even though there is no requirement related to migration status or residence, the Higher Ordinance Education Act imposes a language requirement and application & tuition fees on migrants from non-EEA countries.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden regulates the ability of migrants' criminal and other convictions affecting residence status in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 17, chapter 7 section 6 and chapter 8a section 1, 4-7. The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 17 requires that convictions are considered when considering an application for residence permit. According to the legislative history only criminal convictions of a certain dignity should be considered, but in case law from the Supreme Migration Court (MIG 2019:23), less serious but repeated offenses can also be considered.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to torture or cruel, inuman or degrading treatment or punishment in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 12 sections 1-3; Chapter 1, section 6a and Chapter 4, section 2 of the Aliens Act; and The Act (1994:1219) on The European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms article 3.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to persecution based on race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion in Chapter 12, section 2 and Chapter 4, section 1 of the Aliens Act (2005:716).

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden bans refoulment on the basis of a risk of serious deprivations of fundamental human rights in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 12 section 1.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden bans expulsion to any country where a migrant is likely to be subjected to refoulement through a subsequent expulsion in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 12 section 1-2.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Administrative Procedure Act (2017:900) section 5, The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 8 and 8a, The Act (2022:666) on Terror Crimes and The Act (2022:700) on special control over certain aliens.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
