citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 13 sections 1-3 and The Administrative Procedure Act (2017:900) sections 23 and 25.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The Act (2001:82) on Swedish citizenship offers certain privileges to stateless persons and particularly stateless children in relation to obtaining citizenship,for example in relation to establishing identity and duration of residency requirements, but it does not guarantee citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden provides settled migrants with legal avenues to facilitate reunification with immediate or non-dependent family members in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 sections 3 and 3a, with conditions in section 3b. The Swedish legislation on family reunification is based on the European Council Directive 2003/86/EC of 22 September 2003 on the right to family reunification. There are criteria which must be met in relation to support obligations and which family members are accepted.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden provides judicial remedy to appeal the refusal by the authorities to allow family formation/reunification in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 14 sections 1 and 3.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden recognizes same sex relationships under the family reunification framework in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 sections 3 and 3a. The Marriage Code, Chapter 1, section 1, is neutral on the subject of the gender of the persons that are married or cohabitants, but in the preparatory legal documents, (prop. 2020/21:191 s. 87), the legislator states that the expressions husband/wife and cohabitant refers to both couples of opposite and same sex. This was the practice even before the amendment to the law made in 2020.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 5. Any migrant with a temporary work authorized visa has the ability to access permanent residence eventually assuming certain conditions are met.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right with very limited exceptions as explained in Aliens Act (2005: 716) chapter 6, section 4. However, there are avenues for migrants to leave the country and to apply for a work permit from outside the country.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Labour Disputes (Judicial Procedure) Act (1974:371), The Code of Judicial Procedure (1942:740) chapter 11 section 1 and The Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 1 section 9.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right for regular migrants in the Health and Medical Services Act (2017:30) chapter 8 section 2. Emergency medical care is available to all migrants, independent of status, and persons under 18 years of age have the same right to medical care as those legally residing in the region, as mentioned in The Act (2008:344) on health- and medical care for asylumseekers et.al. sections 4, 5 and 6 and the Act (2013:407) on health and medical care to certain aliens residing in Sweden without neccessary permits, sections 5, 6 and 7.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in Sweden protects the right to stand for election at the local and regional level, only for certain categories of migrants. The Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 3, section 4 states that only Swedish citizens have the right to stand for election in national elections. According to the Local Government Act (2017:725) chapter 4, section 3, only migrants who have been registered in the population registry for a period of at least 3 years (in other words, only those who have a right to vote at the local and regional elections) can vote for public office at the local/regional level.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden prohibit discrimination against migrants on the basis of their status as a migrant in The Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 2 section 12 and The Discrimination Act (2008:567) chapter 1 sections 1, 4, 5 and chapter 2.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden prohibits discrimination against migrants on the grounds of race or ethnicity in The Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 2 section 12 and The Discrimination Act (2008:567) chapter 1 sections 1, 2, 4, 5 and chapter 2.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No universal protection of this right for all migrants due to the lack of legal regulation of wages in general, even if the Discrimination Act (2008:567) chapter 2, section 1 prohibits employers from discriminating against their employees on the basis of belonging to a minority group.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 6. Section 2a of the Act indicates fewer restrictions after two years. Furthermore, aliens with a permanent residence permit (the Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 6 section 1) and certain asylum seekers have free choice of employment.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in a limited way in the Aliens Ordinance Act (2006:97) chapter 4, section 4a. When an alien applies for work permit they can apply for residence permit for family members at the same time. According to the Act, residence permit should be granted for the same period as the main applicant. If the period for the work permit for the main applicant is more than six months, the family member can also be given a work permit.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in the Aliens Ordinance Act (2006:97) chapter 5 section 3.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: The national law in Sweden protects this right in the Discrimination Act (2008: 567) chapter 2, section 1 which prohibits employers from discriminating against their employees and those seeking employment. There is no legal requirement to provide most benefits due to the Swedish system of delegating the terms of employment to the parties of the labor market (employers, employees and their representatives). However there are some benefits like the Annual Leave Act (1977:480) section 1 and 2 that applies to all. The Annual Leave Act (1977:480) section 1 and 2 states that an employee has the right to paid vacation according to the law and that this right cannot be waived through a contract between the employee and the employer. There are additional labor laws that make some work benefits mandatory.The Discrimination Act would prohibit an employer to differentiate between between citizens and migrants regarding work conditions and protection.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects migrant workers’ rights to social security protections in The Social Insurance Code (2010:110) chapter 5 sections 2, 3, and 12 as well as chapter 6 section 2.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Act (1997:238) on Unemployment Insurance section 1 and 12. The Act (1997:238) on Unemployment is neutral regarding the migration status of the individual, meaning that immigrants qualify the same way as citizens. There is a qualification period before benefits are granted; 6 moths of work during a 12 mont period, but this applies regardless of migration and citizenship status.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 3a section 3 and chapter 5 section 5. The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 3a section 3 states that an EEA-citizen has a right to reside in Sweden if they are workers or seeking employment. After five years of lawful residency they have a permanent right to reside in Sweden. Chapter 5 section 5 applies to all other aliens than EEA-citizens. The legal provision states that a permanent residence permit can be given to an alien who have had a work permit for a total of four years during a period of seven years preceding the application.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 9 section 4 and in Chapter 2, section 15 of the Constitution, the Instrument of Government.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden requires birth registration of migrant children, regardless of their status, in The National Registration Act (1991:481) § 24.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden mandates the issuing of documents that recognize migrants' recidency status, work status and identity in The Aliens Ordinance Act (2006:97) Chapter 4 section 22 and The Act (2015:899) on Identity Card for Persons Registered in the Population Register sections 1 and 3.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National Law in Sweden makes it illegal to destroy documents that recognize migrants' residency status, work status and identity in The Criminal code (1962:700) chapter 12 section 1.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this obligation in The Act (1989:152) on "Obligation to Notify etc. when Aliens are Deprived of their Liberty" (Lag (1989:152) om underr?ttelseskyldighet m.m. n?r utl?nningar ?r ber?vade friheten), sections 1 and 2.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No universal protection of this right. The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 10 section 2 states when a migrant child can be detained. There is no explicit rules prohibiting the detention of children based on their status as migrants. Children wihout guardians has stronger protection against being detained as there is a provision stating that this should only be allowed in exceptional cicumstances, The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 10 section 3. A provision stating for how long a child can be detained is in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 10 section 5.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden does not prohibit the detention of migrants on the basis of their status as a migrant. However, the circumstances in which migrants can be detained are strictly limited (the primary permitted reasons are determination of identity and execution of a decision on expulsion) but most forms of migrant detention are prohibited under the Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 10 section 1.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National Law in Sweden protects this right in relation to legality in The Aliens act (2005:716) chapter 14 § 9; it protects this right in relation to conditions in The Aliens act (2005:716) chapter 14 § 10. Decisions on detention are not defined in length, thus the length of the detention cannot specifically be appealed.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 10 section 1 and section 2.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 2 sections 4 and 5 and in the Act (1994:1219) on the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, convention article 3. Rights awarded in The Instrument of Government (1974:152) and the Act (1994:1219) on the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms are general and applies to aliens as well as nationals. Article 3 of the convention states that no one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no legal provision in Sweden that specifically regulates use of force in relation to immigrants entering the state's territory. The Police Act (1984:387) section 8 states that a police officer carrying out service duties must observe what is prescribed by law to act in a way that is justified considering the purpose of the action and the circumstances at hand; section 10 gives police the right to use force only when other means for carrying out a duty is inadequate and the use of force is justified. If the border police was acting to prevent aliens from crossing the border in an irregular way or to uphold the public order at a border, the legal provision would likely warrant the use of force.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Police Act (1984:387) section 8 and 10. The Police Act (1984:387) section 8 states that a police officer carrying out service duties must observe what is prescribed by law to act in a way that is justified considering the purpose of the action and the circumstances at hand, section 10 gives the police the right to use force only when other means for carrying out a duty is inadequate and the use of force is justified. The use of lethal force for the purpose of preventing migrants from entering the territory of Sweden would certainly not be considered justified.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in the Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 15 which provides an opportunity for authorities to apply for a temporary residence permit for an alien that has been the victim of a crime in order for them to participate in a criminal investigation and court hearing. This could be done regarding victims of human trafficking or smuggling. Such an application would legalize their stay in Sweden and likely exempt them of any liability for violating the Aliens Act (2005:716).

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Act (2001:82) on Swedish citizenship, section 14.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden provides pathway to citizenship for economic migrants via obtaining a permanent residence permit after meeting relevant requirements and then applying for citizenship after meeting further relevant requirements, in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 5 and The Act (2001:82) on Swedish citizenship section 11.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden provides pathway to citizenship for humanitarian migrants via obtaining a permanent residence permit after meeting relevant requirements and then applying for citizenship after meeting further relevant requirements, in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 sections 1a and 6 and The Act (2001:82) on Swedish citizenship section 11.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden provides pathway to citizenship for family migrants via obtaining a permanent residence permit after meeting relevant requirements and then applying for citizenship after meeting further relevant requirements, in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 3g and The Act (2001:82) on Swedish citizenship section 11.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden allows migrants to obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin in The Act (2001:82) on Swedish citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in the Constitution, the Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 2 sections 1 and 2 and The Act (1994:1219) on The European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in the Constitution, the Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 2 section 1 and The Act (1994:1219) on The European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in the Constitution, the Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 2 section 1, The Fundamental Law on Freedom of Expression (1991:1469) chapter 1 section 1 and The Act (1994:1219) on The European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 2 section 1 and The Act (1994:1219) on The European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protections of this right. Chapter 5, code section 3 b of the Aliens Act restricts the right to family reunification for some categories of migrants by imposing requirements on income and accommodation. The Swedish legislation on family reunification is based on the European Council Directive 2003/86/EC of 22 September 2003 on the right to family reunification. The legal provisions states that residence permit shall be given to a number of immediate and non-depedent family members. The legal provisions are conditional in the sense that The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 3b states that residence permit according to chapter 5 sections 3 and 3a may only be granted if the alien residing in Sweden is able to financially support themselves and the alien applicant and has housing of approprate size and standard for themselves and the alien applicant. However, according to The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 3c the conditions in section 3b does not apply if the alien residing in Sweden is a child or if they are a citizen of Sweden, another EESstate or Switzerland and the alien applicant is their husband/wife or cohabitans partner and the alien residing in Sweden and the alien applicant has been cohabiting abroad for a longer period of time or their relationship in another way is well-established. According to Aliens Act, chapter 5, section 3b, migrants that are given refugee status are given the benefit of not being required to be able to financially support family member, if an application for reunification is made within three months of being granted refugee status.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in the Constitution, The Instrument of Government (1974:152) chapter 1 section 9 and in the Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 15.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: There is no universal protection of this right. However, the Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 15 states that a temporary residence permit for the duration of at least six months shall be given to an alien staying in Sweden if needed for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation or a criminal proceeding in court, and chapter 5 section 16 of the same act provides a possibility of granting a residence permit to an alien who has had a temporary residence permit on the basis of a relationship to a partner if that relationship has ended foremost because of the alien or their child having been victims of violence or other serious violations in the relationship.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 1 section 10 and chapter 5 section 6 and through the Act (2018:1197) on The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child UN Convention on the Rights of the Child that implements the convention as law in Sweden.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Sweden protects this right in The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 16 and in Chapter 4, section 1.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: No universal protection of this right. The Aliens Act (2005:716) chapter 5 section 6 states that if a residence permit cannot be granted on other grounds, a permit may be granted to a migrant if, in an overall assessment of the migrant’s situation, there are such particularly distressing circumstances that he or she should be allowed to stay in Sweden. During the assessment, the migrants state of health must be taken into account. This usually applies only regarding life threatening conditions. There is no other legal provision that provides special protection for migrants with disabilities.

citation_text_en: Switzerland.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 22 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101), which provides that "1) Freedom of assembly is guaranteed; 2) Every person has the right to organize meetings and to participate or not to participate in meetings." However, since the revision of the Asylum and Foreign Nationals Act in 2010, the abusive use of subjective reasons to seek asylum through political exile has been punishable by law (Article 116 paragraph 1 letter c Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.31)). In its Message on the new penal provisions, the Federal Council stated that asylum-seekers who could not assert any asylum-relevant facts in the asylum procedure would repeatedly take part in demonstrations in Switzerland or publish statements critical of the regime on the Internet. According to the Federal Council, the persons concerned very often engage in these activities with the sole intention of subsequently establishing their refugee status. With the introduction of the newly proposed penal provisions, this abusive behaviour could be sanctioned (Federal Council, Message on the Amendment of the Asylum Act, 26 May 2010, p. 4469). Although the Federal Council conceded that the penal provisions affect fundamental rights such as the right to freedom of expression (Article 16 paragraph 1 BV) as well as the right to freedom of assembly (Article 22 BV) and freedom of association (Article 23 BV), it nevertheless considered the amendment of the Asylum Act to be justified. The Federal Council argued that it was in the public interest and served to maintain public order to take measures against abuse of the right of asylum. The provisions would only sanction abusive public political activity. Political activities in a private context, such as political statements within the circle of family or friends and financial support of parties or organisations, would not be covered (Federal Council, Message on the Amendment of the Asylum Act, 26 May 2010, p. 4507). Article 116(1)(c) AsylA met with criticism in the consultation procedure (Federal Office for Migration (FOM), Summary of the results of the consultation procedure from 15 January 2009 to 15 April 2009 on the draft amendment to the Asylum Act (AsylA), May 2010, pp. 41), in parliamentary debate (Official Bulletin of the Federal Assembly, Council of States, Winter Session 2011, Fifth Session, 12 December 2011, 1132; Official Bulletin of the Federal Assembly, National Council, Summer Session 2012, Sixteenth Session, 14 June 2012, 1179 f.) and later in practice (Spescha, Marc, Antonia Kerland and Peter Bolzli (2015), Handbuch zum Migrationsrecht, 3rd edition, Zurich, Schulthess, p. 378). In particular, it was criticised that the provision represented a step backwards to the times when foreigners in Switzerland were still subject to a political ban on speaking (Official Bulletin of the Federal Assembly, National Council, Summer Session 2012, Sixteenth Session, 14 June 2012, 1179; Federal Office for Migration (FOM), Summary of the results of the consultation procedure from 15 January 2009 to 15 April 2009 on the draft amendment to the Asylum Act (AsylG), May 2010, p. 42).

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. In Switzerland, according to the Federal Act on Political Rights (BPR, SR 161.1) all citizens have the right to vote. Additionally, Article 136 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) provides that "paragraph 1: All Swiss citizens over the age of eighteen, unless they lack legal capacity due to mental illness or mental incapacity, have political rights in federal matters. All citizens have the same political rights and duties ; paragraph 2 : They may participate in elections to the National Council and in federal popular votes, and launch or sign popular initiatives and requests for referendums in federal matters." However, while foreign nationals are largely excluded from political participation in Switzerland, they can participate neither in federal votes nor in federal elections, but cantons and municipalities can enact their own regulations on political participation. This right is not federally protected, though.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 29 and Article 29a of Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101). Article 29, paragraph 1 states that "Every person has the right to equal and fair treatment in judicial and administrative proceedings and to have their case decided within a reasonable time." This right therefore applies equally to citizens and migrants before administrative, civil, and criminal courts. However, in asylum and other immigration cases, access to judicial review before the Federal Supreme Court is restricted; in asylum proceedings, there is no access to judicial review before the Federal Supreme Court at all; in proceedings under the Federal Law on Foreign Nationals and Integration, there is access to judicial review only in certain cases. Article 83 paragraph 1 letters c and d Federal Act on the Federal Supreme Court, Federal Supreme Court Act (BGG, SR 173.110)

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 29 paragraph 3 of Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101), which states that, "Any person who does not have sufficient means has the right to free legal advice and assistance unless their case appears to have no prospect of success. If it is necessary in order to safeguard their rights, they also have the right to free legal representation in court." Free legal representation shall be appointed at the request of the party making the request. Representation is ordered if the requesting party does not have the necessary means (indigence), its legal claims are not futile (non-frivolousness, Aricle. 65 paragraph 1 Administrative Procedure Act (APA, SR 172.021)) and representation is necessary to safeguard its interests (necessity, Article 65, paragraph 2 APA). The necessity of representation is generally assumed if there is a particularly strong interference with the fundamental legal positions of the party making the request (serious case). If the encroachment on the legal position is not particularly severe, special factual or legal difficulties must exist in order for a claim to be affirmed (relative severe case). In this case, it is examined whether a nonindigent party would reasonably consult a lawyer under otherwise identical circumstances, because he or she is not legally competent enough and the interest in the outcome of the proceedings justifies the effort. In this context, the Federal Supreme Court takes into account, in particular, the age, social situation, language skills or health and mental/psychological condition of the person concerned (abilities of the requesting party) as well as the seriousness and complexity (factual or legal difficulties) of the case. In administrative proceedings under migration law, whether at first instance or on appeal, the criterion of the considerable scope of the proceedings (serious case or relatively serious case) is usually affirmed, at least as far as residence in Switzerland is concerned. However, this alone is often not sufficient for the appointment of free legal counsel. Particularly in first instance administrative proceedings, in addition to the criterion of the significant scope of the decision, even in serious cases, special factual or legal difficulties are also assumed and a very strict standard is applied (cf. Spescha Marc, Bolzli Peter, de Weck Fanny and Priuli Valerio, Handbuch f?r Migrationsrecht, 4th completely revised edition 2020, p. 413 f. with further references and Kayser Martin and Altmann Rahel in: Christoph Auer, Markus M?ller and Benjamin Schindler (eds.), Kommentar zum Bundesgesetz ?ber das Verwaltungsverfahren (VwVG), 2nd ed., Zurich/St. Gallen 2019, Article 65 N 68) 2) In the federal procedural codes, the right is specified for civil proceedings in Article 117 et seq. Civil Procedure Code (CPC, SR 272). 3) For criminal proceedings in Article 128 ff. Criminal Procedure Code (CPC, SR 312). 4) For proceedings before the Federal Supreme Court in Article 41 or Article 64 Federal Supreme Court Act (BGG, SR 173.110). 5) For administrative proceedings in Article 65 APA). 5) Arts. 102f to 102m (in force since 1 March 2019) of the Asylum Act. The Asylum Act contains not only special-law concretizations on the free administration of justice in proceedings before the Federal Administrative Court (Article 102m AsylA), but also special-law provisions on the free administration of justice for proceedings before the State Secretary of Migration (Article 102h Asylum Act, AsylA, SR 142.31). These special legal provisions are exceptional because they presume the necessity of legal counsel both in the first-instance proceedings (there generally, with exceptions) and in the appeal proceedings (there only under the condition of indigence and non-vulnerability).

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 32, paragraph 2, Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) according to which "Every accused person has the right to be notified as quickly and comprehensively as possible of the charge brought against them. Those accused must be given the opportunity to assert their rights to a proper defence." ; as well in Article 68, paragraph 1, Criminal Procedure Code (CPC, SR 31), that states that, "Where a party to the proceedings does not understand the language of the proceedings or is unable to express him- or herself adequately, the director of proceedings shall appoint an interpreter. In minor or urgent cases, the director of proceedings may, if the person concerned consents, dispense with appointing an interpreter provided the director of proceedings and the clerk of court have an adequate command of the foreign language concerned."

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 115 paragraph 1 letter Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20), illegal entry can be punished with a custodial sentence of up to one year or a fine, provided that there are no grounds for justification or exclusion of guilt.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right for all migrants in emergency situations in Article 12 of the Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101), any person in distress and unable to provide for himself is entitled to assistance and to the means indispensable for a dignified existence (so-called emergency assistance). Emergency assistance includes food, hygiene, clothing, shelter and basic medical care. The core right to emergency accommodation in the event of distress applies to everyone, regardless of their immigration status according to a judgment of Federal Supreme Court of 20 March 2009, 135 I 119: "The fundamental right to a minimum standard of living under art. 12 of the Swiss Constitution does not guarantee a minimum income, but only the basic needs for survival in a manner consistent with human dignity, such as food, housing, clothing and basic medical care. (....) The implementation of art. 12 Cst. can be differentiated according to the status of the assisted person. For example, for asylum seekers whose case has been dismissed, there is no interest in integration and no lasting social contact needs to be guaranteed in view of the temporary nature of the person's presence on Swiss territory. The granting of minimum benefits is also justified in order to reduce the incentive to remain in Switzerland".

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 19 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101). The right and obligation for all children to attend elementary school applies to all people residing in Switzerland, including regular migrants and undocumented migrants.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Access to adult education institutions depends on the status and the country of origin (there are differences between third country nationals and EU/EFTA nationals). For third country nationals, the principle is that migrants who came to Switzerland for work are not allowed to attend any form of educational institution. To do so, they should ask for a different kind of permit. For EU/EFTA citizens though, Article 9 paragraph 3 Annex 1 of the bilateral Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (EU/EFTA nationals) provides that "[employed person] shall also be entitled on the same footing and under the same conditions as employed national workers to attend vocational schools [...]".

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland regulates the ability of migrants’ criminal and other convictions affecting residence status in Article 62 and 63 of the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) (that enumerate the circumstances where a residence permit may be revoked, for example: dependence on social assistance). Moreover, criminal offenses (even abuse of social assistance) can lead to expulsion (Article 66a Swiss Criminal Code, SR 311.0). There is also the possibility of non-mandatory (for the judge) expulsion (Article 66a bis Swiss Criminal Code).

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 33 Refugee Convention (SR 0.142.30). 2) Article 3 Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (SR 0.101). 3) Article 25 paragraph 2 und 3 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) which state "No person may be deported to a state in which they face the threat of torture or any other form of cruel or inhumane treatment or punishment"). 4) Article 5 Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.3) 5) Article 83 paragraph 1 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20), which reiterates the rights stated in the constitutional provision.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 3 Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.3). This provides the defintion of refugee. 2) Article 25, paragraph 2, Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) ("Refugees may not be deported or extradited to a state in which they will be persecuted").

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) The provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights (SR 0.101), such as the right to life (Article 2), the prohibition of torture (Article 3), prohibition of slavery and forced labor (Article 4) and Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8). All are self-executing. 2) Article 10, paragraph 1, Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) ("Every person has the right to life. The death penalty is prohibited") combined with Article 25, paragraph 3, BV ("No person may be deported to a state in which they face the threat of torture or any other form of cruel or inhumane treatment or punishment").

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) the provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights (SR 0.101). 2) Article 25, paragraph 2, Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) and Article 5 Asylum Act. This bans expulsion to any country where a migrant is likely to be subjected to refoulement through a subsequent expulsion.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 64-69 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20). These articles provide that if a foreign national does not possess a required permit (Article 64 paragraph 1 letter a FNIA) or if a foreign national does not meet or no longer meets the entry requirements (Article 64 paragraph 1 letter b FNIA), he or she must leave Switzerland with the threat of coercive measures in case of failure to do so. An appeal (without automatic suspensive effect) can be lodged against this removal order of the competent authority (Article 64 paragraph 3 FNIA).

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 29 paragraph 2 and Article 29a of Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101). An appeal against a removal order can be made within 5, 10 or 30 days, it depends on the legal proceedings concerned (Asylum is regulated differently by the Dublin procedures or foreigner procedures).

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Switzerland ratified the Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons of 28 September 1954 (Stateless Convention, SR 0.142.40) on 3 July 1972. According to Article 28 of the Convention on Stateless Persons, Member States shall issue identity and travel documents to stateless persons legally residing on their territory. According to Article 59 paragraph 2 letter b Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) in conjunction with. Article 4 Ordinance on the Issuance of Travel Documents for Foreign Persons (RDV, SR 143.5) and Article 31 paragraph 1 FNIA, recognized stateless persons are entitled to be issued a residence permit and a travel document (i.e. a passport for a foreign person). However, The facilitation of naturalisation of stateless persons is not bindingly stated in the international convention on stateless persons.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right conditionally in 1) Article 42 et seq. and 85(7) Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) and Article 51 Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.31). Family reunification of Swiss nationals requires only a common home (Article 42 FNIA). Family reunification for foreigners with a B and C permit is in turn linked to a need-based dwelling, and the applicant must be independent from social welfare. Family reunification for provisionally admitted refugees is subject to a waiting period of at least three years and further conditions (housing that meets needs and independence from social welfare are required [Article 85(7) FNIA), while family reunification for refugees who have been granted asylum is not subject to a waiting period or further conditions (Article 85(7) FNIA and Article 51 AsylA). 2) Arts. 43-45 and 85, paragraph 7, of the Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 112 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) in conjunction with Article 44 et seq. Federal Act on Administrative Procedure (Administrative Procedure Act, APA, SR 172.021 in conjunction with cantonal procedural provisions. 2) For decisions on family reunification at the federal level Article 105 Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.31) in conjunction with Article 44 et seq. APA. An appeal can be filled against every refusal of family reunification. Decisions on family reunification are generally taken by the cantonal migration authorities, with the exception of decisions on family reunification of recognised refugees who have been granted asylum.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 52 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.2). Article 1 paragraph 1 letter e Asylum Ordinance 1 on Procedural Matters (Asylum Ordinance 1, AsylV 1, SR 142.311). Article 52 provides that "The provisions of this Chapter [family reunification] on foreign spouses apply mutatis mutandis to registered partnerships of same-sex couples." 2) Article 52 FNIA.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 34 paragraph 2 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20). Different conditions apply to different visa types but as soon as there is a visa, there is a regular path to a settled status. However, the extension of a short-term visa (less than 1 year) can only be prolonged for 2 years (Article 32 paragraph 3 FNIA). Article 30 paragraph 1 letter b Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) states that under certain conditions, the Swiss immigration authorities can provide a hardship permit to persons residing illegally in Switzerland (such as an individual case of extreme hardship). This permit is at the discretion of the authority. This is not a right (the competent authority "may" provide it if the conditions are met, according to the Ordinance, Article 31 Ordinance on admission, residence and employment (VZAE, SR 142.201)).

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 30 paragraph 1 letter b Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) states that under certain conditions, the Swiss immigration authorities can provide a hardship permit to persons residing illegally in Switzerland (such as an individual case of extreme hardship). This permit is at the discretion of the authority. This is not a right (the competent authority "may" provide it if the conditions are met, according to the Ordinance, Article 31 Ordinance on admission, residence and employment (VZAE, SR 142.201)).

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 29 and Article 29a Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101). All migrant, including undocumented migrants, can take legal action if their employment agreement is violated.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 3 Federal Law on Health Insurance (KVG, SR 832.10). 2) Article 12 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101). Article 12 BV (Right to assistance when in need) guarantees to everyone an access to basic health care. Every person living in Switzerland for more than three months is subject to compulsory health insurance. This concern Swiss nationals as well as foreign nationals, including undocumented migrants. Every insured person has access to the same care benefits.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Right afforded to all citizens under Article 136 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101), but not applicable to migrants

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Although migrants are protects on the basis ofArticle 8, paragraph 2, Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101), which provides that "No person may be discriminated against, in particular on grounds of origin, race, gender, age, language, social position, way of life, religious, ideological, or political convictions, or because of a physical, mental or psychological disability," this has not been interpreted to protect migrants on the basis of their status as migrants. Furthermore, there are legal provisions such as those in the Asylum Act, where the question arises as to whether they are discriminatory (this is disputed). The Asylum Act contains the principle that social assistance benefits for asylum seekers, temporarily admitted persons and persons with protection status S must be lower than those of the "native population" (Article 82 paragraph 3 Asylum Act, AsylA, SR 142.31). The justification for this regulation is that the persons concerned would only be staying in Switzerland temporarily and would therefore not need money to participate in society.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 8 paragraph 2 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101).

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Swtizerland protects this in 1) Article 22 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) in conjunction with Article 22 Ordinance on admission, residence and employment (VZAE, SR 142.201) (foreigners). 2) Article 7 Agreement between the European Community and its Member States, of the one part, and the Swiss Confederation, of the other, on the free movement of persons, FZA, SR 0.142.112.681 (European nationals). 3) Article 43 Asylum Act, AsylA, SR 142.31 (asylum seekers), Article 85a FNIA (temporarily admitted persons), Article 61 AsylG (refugees). 4) Article 8 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101).

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 21 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20). It should be noted that the admission of third-country nationals under the Foreign Nationals Act (FNIA) is limited to specialized and qualified workers. 2) National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 38, Article 32, paragraph 2 and 3, Article 33, paragraph 2, Article 34, paragraph 1, FNIA.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 46 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20). According to this provision, spouses and children of Swiss nationals and of persons with a settlement or residence permit may engage in self-employed or employed gainful activity throughout Switzerland. The provision does not apply to persons with a short-term residence permit.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 62 paragraph 1 letter e and Article 63 paragraph 1 letter c Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20. 2) Article 61 FNIA. If a migrant can not satisfy the requirements of their work visa, e.g., by losing their employment, they may not be able to extend their visa. However, they will not lose their visa. The only way for a migrant to lose their visa if they become unemployed would be for them to become dependent on welfare. If a person has received high financial support payments and it cannot be expected that he or she will be able to support himself or herself or his or her family in the future, they can have their visa revoked (cf. for example BGer judgment 2C_13/2018 of 16 November 2018 E. 3.2 or 2C_131/2020 of 4 Mai 2020). However, if there is a ground for revocation, according to case law, it must be examined whether the associated measure of terminating the residence permit is proportionate (cf. Article 5 paragraph 2 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101), Article 8 paragraph 2 ECHR and Article 96 paragraph 1 FNIA).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 21 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20. 2) Article 8 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101). Apart from the constitutional provision, Article 22 FNIA requires that for a foreign national from a third country (out of EU/EFTA) to be granted a work permit the "[...] employment conditions customary for the location, profession and sector are satisfied". But this condition does not apply to third country nationals who are already present in Switzerland, such as asylum seekers, refugees, people benefiting from family reunification or any citizen. Regarding EU/EFTA citizens, Article 7 Agreement between the European Community and its Member States, of the one part, and the Swiss Confederation, of the other, on the free movement of persons, FZA, SR 0.142.112.681) also provides that the same employment and work conditions must be granted.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 82 paragraph 1 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20); Article 82 paragraph 3 Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.31). Refugees who are dependent on social assistance have different amounts of money available to them in Switzerland, depending on their status and the canton. 2) Article 1a, paragraph 1, Federal Law on Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AHVG, SR 831.10). Migrants have equal access to both Old-Age insurance, and the occupational pension scheme (which is based on income, and not status) commensurate with citizens. However, migrants must meet a residency requirement (10 years) to be eligible for "supplementary benefits".

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 8 Federal law on compulsory unemployment insurance and the Insolvency Compensation (Unemployment Insurance Act, AVIG, SR 837.0) 2) Article 2, paragraph 1, of the Unemployment-Insurance Act. Every employee working for an employer in Switzerland has to pay unemployment insurance premiums and therefore is entitled to receive benefits from this insurance.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 33 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20). There is no entitlement to conversion of a short-term residence permit or cross-border commuter permit into an annual residence permit for third-country nationals. However, all migrants (excepting EU/EEA nationals, for which the situation is different), regardless of type, can switch to permanent status provided they meet certain criteria. 2) Article 34, paragraph 4 FNIA. Level of integration in the Swiss immigration system can affect immigration status, and lead to avenues where temporary migrants can transfer to a permanent residence visa.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Artcile 10 paragraph 2 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) which provides the confiscation of identity documents entails consequences on the right to personal liberty. 2) Article 141 and Article 254 of the Swiss Criminal Code (SR 311.0) indicates individuals may be punished under criminal law for confiscation of property. 3) Article 8 paragraph 3 and 4 Ordinance on Admission, Residence and Employment (VZAE, SR 142.201) creates an obligation for migrants to submit original documents to authorities and to keep such documents available to authorities.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 9 paragraph 1 1 and 15a Civil Status Ordinance (ZStV, SR 211.112.2) which states that, by law, every birth must be registered, regardless of the migration status of the parents.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 41 paragraph 1 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20), which mandates the issuing of documents that recognize migrants’ residency status, work status, and identity.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 144 Swiss Criminal Code (SR 311.0). 2) Article 254 Swiss Criminal Code, which states that "any person who damages, destroys, conceals or misappropriates a document over which he has no exclusive right of disposal, with a view to causing financial loss or damage to the rights of another or in order to obtain an unlawful advantage for himself or another is liable to a custodial sentence not exceeding five years or to a monetary penalty."

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 81, paragraph 1, Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration (FNIA, SR 142.20), which states that, ("(...) Detainees may communicate with their legal representatives as well as with their (...) consular authorities both verbally and in writing"). 2) Although not national law, Article 36 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (SR 0.191.02) is self-executing. In Switzerland, the application of monism is expressed by Article 5 paragraph 4 of the Federal Constitution ( SR 101). Approval of the conclusion of a treaty is by means of a federal decree and not by means of a federal law (Article 166 paragraph 2 in conjunction with Article 163 paragraph 2 Constitution). Furthermore, international law must be upheld by for all authorities (Article 190 Constitution) and the Federal Supreme Court is also empowered to examine violations of international law (Article 189 paragraph 1 letter b Constitution).

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Under the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act, children between the ages of 15 and 18 may be detained (Article 79 paragraph 2 and Article 80a paragraph 5; Article 81 paragraph 3 Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration (Foreign Nationals and Integration Act, FNIA, SR 142.20)). However there is an exemption for those younger than 15, outlined in Article 80, paragraph 4, of the same act, which states that, "In no event may any detention order in preparagraphtion for departure, detention pending deportation or coercive detention be issued in respect of children or young people who have not yet attained the age of 15".

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. If a person who has been ordered to leave the country allows the deadline for leaving the country to expire without taking action or otherwise evades or resists removal, the competent enforcement authority may order coercive measures. Individual coercive measures in the Federal Law on Foreign Nationals and Integration (FNIA, SR 142.20) can be ordered at an earlier stage, e.g. to establish the identity of the person or to identity or to ensure that deportation proceedings are carried out. The coercive measures for asylum cases as well as for cases are regulated uniformly in Articles 73 to 78 of the (FNIA). In this regard, the FNIA provides for the following coercive measures: (1) shortterm detention under Article 73 FNIA; (2) inclusion and exclusion under Article 74 FNIA; (3) preparagraphtory detention under Article 75 FNIA; (4) detention pending deportation under Article 76 FNIA; (5) detention under the Dublin procedure (Dublin detention) under Article 76a FNIA; (6) detention pending deportation for failure to cooperate in obtaining papers underArticle 77 FNIA; (7) Enforcement detention under Article 78 FNIA. Article 73, paragraph 1, Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration provides that: "The competent authority of the Confederation or the canton may detain persons without a short stay, residence or permanent residence permit: a. to notify them of a decision in connection with their residence status; b. to determine their identity or nationality, as far as their personal cooperation is required".

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 80 and Article 80a of the Federal Law on Foreign Nationals and Integration (Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) which determine detention and detention conditions. 2) Article 79 FNIA governs the maximum duration of the detention order, or extension of said detention. 3) Article 5, paragraph 3 and 4 European Convention on Human Rights (EMRK, SR 0.101) shown in law as Article 31, paragraph 4 of the Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101). Article 80 paragraph 4 and 5 FNIA provides the legal basis for the review of the legality and appropriateness of the detention (Article 80a paragraph 4 for the detention review under the Dublin procedure). It must be read in conjunction with Article 79 on the maximum term of detention. Those legal bases allow for the appeal against the length, the conditions and legality of the detention respectively.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 80 paragraph 2 and 4 Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20). These govern the legality and appropriateness of the detention, but also the family circumstances of the detained person and circumstances of the detention that shall be taken into account. paragraph 4 states: "When reviewing the decision to issue, extend or revoke a detention order, the judicial authority shall also take account of the detainees family circumstances and the circumstances behind the enforcement of detention."

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 10 of the Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101), which states that: “[...] (3) Torture and any other form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment shall be prohibited.”

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Force may be used by officers or agents in accordance with the principle of proportionality stated in Article 9 of the Federal Law on the Use of Coercion and Police Measures in the Area of Responsibility of the Confederation (Law on the Use of Coercion, ZAG, SR 364).

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 11 and 13 of the Federal Law on the Use of Coercion and Police Measures in the Area of Responsibility of the Confederation (Law on the Use of Coercion, ZAG, SR 364).

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Swiss criminal law is conceived on the basis of culpability and is characterized by the principle that - despite acting in accordance with the offence - a person can only be liable to prosecution if they act culpably (Article 19 Swiss Criminal Code, SR 311.0). If a victim of human trafficking commits an act that is punishable by law in order to avert an imminent harm to themself or to someone else, the requirements of self-defense and necessity under Article 15 et seq. of the Swiss Criminal Code, in particular the existence of necessity (Article 17 of the Swiss Criminal Code), must be examined (cf. Federal Council, Message on the Approval and Implementation of the Council of Europe Convention on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings and on the Federal Act on Extra-Procedural Witness Protection of 17 November 2010, p. 36 et seq). Despite these provisions, victims of trafficking and smuggling face criminal sanctions, such as under Article 115 of the Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration (illegal entry and stay) most of the time. The principle of non-punishment (convention of Council of Europe) is not applied, except for asylum applicants.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 36 and Article 42 Federal Act on Swiss Citizenship (Swiss Citizenship Act, SCA, SR 141.0). Article 42 provides that convictions for criminal or other offenses leads to a loss of the citizenship status of naturalized migrants.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Federal Citizenship Act, in force since January 1, 2018, in Article 9 f. Federal Act on Swiss Citizenship (Swiss Citizenship Act, SCA, SR 141.0), which provides that: "paragraph 1: The Confederation shall grant a naturalisation licence only if the applicant: a. holds a permanent residence permit when the application is made; and b. can prove that he or she has been resident in Switzerland for at least ten years, three of which have been in the five years prior to making the application ; paragraph 2 : When calculating the length of residence mentioned in paragraph 1 letter b, the period that the applicant has lived in Switzerland between the ages of 8 and 18 counts as double. The actual length of residence must however amount to at least six years." There are also other conditions, as well. According to Article 11 of the SCA, a person is granted a federal naturalization permit within the framework of ordinary naturalization if he or she has been successfully integrated (letter a), is familiar with Swiss living conditions (letter b) and does not pose a threat to the internal or external security of Switzerland (letter c). The focus is on the "integration" of the applicant. Article 12 paragraph 1 SCA defines how successful integration is demonstrated, namely: in observance of public security and order (letter a), in respect for the values of the Federal Constitution (letter b), in the ability to communicate verbally and in writing in a national language in everyday life (letter c), in the participation in economic life or in the acquisition of education (letter d) and in the promotion and support of the integration of the wife or the husband, the registered partner or the minor children over whom parental care is exercised (letter e). Finally, Article 18 SCA applies, each cantonal legislation may require an additional minimum or maximum residence period of two to five years.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Federal Citizenship Act, in force since January 1, 2018, in Article 9 f. Federal Act on Swiss Citizenship (Swiss Citizenship Act, SCA, SR 141.0), which provides that: "paragraph 1: The Confederation shall grant a naturalisation licence only if the applicant: a. holds a permanent residence permit when the application is made; and b. can prove that he or she has been resident in Switzerland for at least ten years, three of which have been in the five years prior to making the application ; paragraph 2 : When calculating the length of residence mentioned in paragraph 1 letter b, the period that the applicant has lived in Switzerland between the ages of 8 and 18 counts as double. The actual length of residence must however amount to at least six years." There are also other conditions, as well. According to Article 11 of the SCA, a person is granted a federal naturalization permit within the framework of ordinary naturalization if he or she has been successfully integrated (letter a), is familiar with Swiss living conditions (letter b) and does not pose a threat to the internal or external security of Switzerland (letter c). The focus is on the "integration" of the applicant. Article 12 paragraph 1 SCA defines how successful integration is demonstrated, namely: in observance of public security and order (letter a), in respect for the values of the Federal Constitution (letter b), in the ability to communicate verbally and in writing in a national language in everyday life (letter c), in the participation in economic life or in the acquisition of education (letter d) and in the promotion and support of the integration of the wife or the husband, the registered partner or the minor children over whom parental care is exercised (letter e). Finally, Article 18 SCA applies, each cantonal legislation may require an additional minimum or maximum residence period of two to five years.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 9 of the Federal Act on Swiss Citizenship (Swiss Citizenship Act, SCA, SR 141.0). 2) Article 21 Federal Act on Swiss Citizenship. Article 21 provides that: "paragraph 1 : Any foreign national may apply for simplified naturalisation following marriage to a Swiss citizen if he or she : a. has lived for three years in marital union with his or her wife or husband; and b. has resided for at least five years in Switzerland, including one year immediately prior to making the application : paragraph 2 : Any person who lives or has lived abroad may also apply provided he or she: a. has lived for six years in marital union with his or her wife or husband; and b. has close ties with Switzerland."

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) in Article 37, paragraph 1 Federal Act on Swiss Citizenship (Swiss Citizenship Act, SCA, SR 141.0). Dual citizenship has been allowed since 1992.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 15 of the Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) and Article 72, paragraph 3 BV. Article 15 states that the, "1) Freedom of religion and conscience is guaranteed. 2) Every person has the right to choose freely their religion or their philosophical convictions, and to profess them alone or in community with others. 3) Every person has the right to join or to belong to a religious community, and to follow religious teachings..."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 16 paragraph 1 Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) (freedom of expression). Article 16 states that, "1) Freedom of expression and of information is guaranteed. 2) Every person has the right freely to form, express, and impart their opinions. 3) Every person has the right freely to receive information to gather it from generally accessible sources and to disseminate it." However, since the revision of the Asylum and Foreign Nationals Act in 2010, the abusive use of subjective reasons to seek asylum through political exile has been punishable by law (Article 116 paragraph 1 letter c Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.31)). In its message on the new penal provisions, the Federal Council stated that asylum-seekers who could not assert any asylum-relevant facts in the asylum procedure would repeatedly take part in demonstrations in Switzerland or publish statements critical of the regime on the Internet. According to the Federal Council, the persons concerned very often engage in these activities with the sole intention of subsequently establishing their refugee status. With the introduction of the newly proposed penal provisions, this abusive behaviour could be sanctioned (Federal Council, Message on the Amendment of the Asylum Act, 26 May 2010, p. 4469). Although the Federal Council conceded that the penal provisions affect fundamental rights such as the right to freedom of expression (Article 16 paragraph 1 BV) as well as the right to freedom of assembly (Article 22 BV) and freedom of association (Article 23 BV), it nevertheless considered the amendment of the Asylum Act to be justified. The Federal Council argued that it was in the public interest and served to maintain public order to take measures against abuse of the right of asylum. The provisions would only sanction abusive public political activity. Political activities in a private context, such as political statements within the circle of family or friends and financial support of parties or organisations, would not be covered (Federal Council, Message on the Amendment of the Asylum Act, 26 May 2010, p. 4507). Article 116(1)(c) AsylA met met with criticism in the consultation procedure (Federal Office for Migration (FOM), Summary of the results of the consultation procedure from 15 January 2009 to 15 April 2009 on the draft amendment to the Asylum Act (AsylA), May 2010, pp. 41), in parliamentary debate (Official Bulletin of the Federal Assembly, Council of States, Winter Session 2011, Fifth Session, 12 December 2011, 1132; Official Bulletin of the Federal Assembly, National Council, Summer Session 2012, Sixteenth Session, 14 June 2012, 1179 f.) and later in practice (Spescha, Marc, Antonia Kerland and Peter Bolzli (2015), Handbuch zum Migrationsrecht, 3rd edition, Zurich, Schulthess, p. 378). In particular, it was criticised that the provision represented a step backwards to the times when foreigners in Switzerland were still subject to a political ban on speaking (Official Bulletin of the Federal Assembly, National Council, Summer Session 2012, Sixteenth Session, 14 June 2012, 1179; Federal Office for Migration (FOM), Summary of the results of the consultation procedure from 15 January 2009 to 15 April 2009 on the draft amendment to the Asylum Act (AsylG), May 2010, p. 42).

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Arts. 43-45 and 85, paragraph 7, Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.2) state that there are conditions for family reunification, which depends on the type of permit the migrant holds. Among other conditions the person applying for family reunification must live with the person; have a suitable accommodation; or do not depend on social assistance. In addition, the family must be able to communicate in the national language spoken at their place of residence.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in Article 29a of the Federal Constitution (BV, SR 101) ("In a legal dispute, every person has the right to have their case determined by a judicial authority"). However, due to the principle of territoriality according to the OHG (Article 17 Victim Assistance Act (OHG, SR 312.5)), persons who are victims of human trafficking abroad and who were not yet resident in Switzerland at the time of the crime are excluded from the scope of the OHG (Article 3 paragraph 2 in conjunction with Article 17 OHG).

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 30 paragraph 1 letter e Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA, SR 142.20) in conjunction with Article 36 Ordinance on Admission, Residence and Employment (VZAE, SR 142.201). The cantonal immigration authorities grant victims of human trafficking a short-term residence permit for the expected duration of the police investigation or court proceedings. As long as the law enforcement authorities deem the presence of the victim necessary, the migration authority of the canton in which the crime was committed grants a short-term residence permit. Article 36 paragraph 6 VZAE provides for the possibility of granting a residence permit in these cases, provided there is a serious case of personal hardship.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 3 paragraph 1, of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC, SR 0.107). 2) Article 11, paragraph 1, of the Federal Constitution, SR 101 ("Children and young people have the right to the special protection of their integrity and to the encouragement of their development"). 3) Article 17 of the Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.31) provides for special procedural provisions for minors (paragraph 2) and notably unaccompanied minors (paragraphs 2bis, 3, 3bis and 6.4) The Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration (FNIA, SR 142.20) provides for special provisions in case of detention (Articles 79, paragraph 2; 80, paragraph 4; 81, paragraph 3), deportation (Article 69, paragraph 4) and admission for education or training purposes (Article 27, paragraph 2) of foreign minors.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 3, paragraph 2, the Asylum Act (AsylA, SR 142.31), in which motives for seeking asylum specific to women must be considered. 2) Article 6 o of the Asylum Ordinance 1 (AsylV 1, SR 142.311), states that in the case of gender-specific asylum motives, the asylum-seeker must be heard by a same-sex person. 3) Article 50 of the Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration (FNIA, SR 142.20) provides that migrant women who have been victims of marital violence have the right to be granted a residence permit after the dissolution of the marriage. Other important provisions that do not technically only apply to women, but in practice overwhelmingly protect women are special rules regarding victims of human trafficking (Article 30 paragraph 1 letter e of the Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration (FNIA, SR 142.20) and Article 35-36a of the Ordinance on admission, residence and employment (VZAE, SR 142.201).

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Switzerland protects this right in 1) Article 58a paragraph 2 Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration (FNIA, SR 142.20) where appropriate consideration must be given to the situation of persons who are unable to meet the integration criteria of paragraph 1(c) (language skills) and (d) (participation in economic life or in the acquisition of education) due to a disability or illness or other serious personal circumstances, or who are only able to do so under more difficult conditions. 2) Article 77f of the Ordinance on admission, residence and employment (VZAE, SR 142.201), according to which a deviation from the integration criteria is possible if the foreigner cannot fulfill said criteria or can only fulfill the criteria under difficult conditions due to a physical, mental or psychological disability (subparagraph a), a serious or long-term illness (subparagraph b) or other weighty personal circumstances such as a pronounced learning, reading and writing disability, poverty or the performance of care duties (subparagraph c). 3) Article 49a FNIA provides for explicit exceptions from the requirement of proof of language proficiency if there are important reasons, including disability. 4) Article 31 paragraph 5 VZAE; cf. also Article 77f VZAE, which applies in the context of the integration criteria found in Article 58a FNIA). If participation in economic life or the acquisition of education was not possible due to age, state of health or the asylum laws prohibition to work, this must also be taken into account when examining financial circumstances of the migrant.
