question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: Turkey

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Pursuant to Article 3 of Assembly and Demonstration Law, foreigners should obtain a permit by Ministry of Interior prior to organizing an assembly or demonstration whereas citizens do not need to obtain such permission. Foreigners who wish to address the public, carry signs or tools during a demonstration should inform the administration 48 hours prior to the demonstration. These conditions are not set for citizens. However, pursuant to Article 28 of the Turkish Citizenship Law, migrants who acquired Turkish citizenship by birth but renounced their citizenship later, have equal rights with citizens except some certain rights listed in the same article. Right to assembly and demonstration is not one of the rights excluded for these migrants. Therefore they constitute an exception to Article 3 of the Assembly and Demonstration Law. Similarly, long term residence permit holders, pursuant to Article 44 of Foreigners and International Protection Law and Article 41(2) of Implementation Regulation of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection, are provided with similar rights. However, these migrant groups may be deemed as exceptions, and therefore, the freedom of assembly is not a right granted to migrants, in general, commesurate with those afforded with citizens.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 67 of Turkish Constitution, Article 6 of Law on Fundamental Conditions of Elections and Electoral Registers (Law No. 298, entry into force date: 02.05.1961) and Article 10 of Law on Elections of Members of the Parliament (Law Nr. 2839, entry into force date: 13.06.1983), only Turkish citizens have the right to vote in local/regional or national elections.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in the 1) Turkish Constitution, Articles 10, 12, 36, 40 and 74. The Constitution provides the equality principle for 'everybody' including foreigners (migrants)under articles 10 and 12. Article 36 of the Constitution stipulates that: 'Everyone has the right of litigation either as plaintiff or defendant and the right to a fair trial before the courts through legitimate means and procedures. No court shall refuse to hear a case within its jurisdiction’. Further Article 40 of the Constitution provides that: "Everyone whose constitutional rights and freedoms have been violated has the right to request prompt access to the competent authorities." 2) The Law on Human Rights and Equality Institution of Turkey (Law No. 6701, entry into force date: 20.04.2016), Article 3.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Civil Procedural Code (Law No. 6100), Article 334. The right to have a counsel at government expense (legal aid) is provided on the condition of reciprocity under Article 334 of Turkish Civil Procedural Code in relation to civil law cases. 2) The Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 57(7) and 81(2). Article 81 of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP) specifically indicates that applicants and beneficiaries of international protection, provided that they are in financial hardship, would be provided legal aid in accordance with the relevant provision of Attorneyship Law (Article 176). 3) Temporary Protection Regulation (Bylaw), Article 53. The Temporary Protection Bylaw, provides a similar designation for temporarily protected persons (Article 53). Although, it cannot be clearly stated that all migrants have such a right under the Turkish Civil Procedural Code as it is conditioned on reciprocity and LFIP provides this right only to a specific group, the Attorneyship Law can be used for all migrants to have access to such a right. 4) Attorneyship Law (Law No. 1136), Article 176. Article 176 of the Attorneyship Law on the other hand, provides this right without any limitations based on nationality. 5) The Law of Criminal Procedures (Law No. 5271), Article 150.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in the Turkish Penal Procedure Code (Law No. 5271), Article 202, which states that if the individual doesn't speak sufficient Turkish, an interpreter is appointed by the court. In such cases, the interpreter can be appointed at the investigation stage by the prosecutor. According to the Article 324(5) of the Turkish Penal Procedure Code, The expenses of an interpreter assigned for a suspect, defendant, victim or witness who does not speak Turkish or is disabled shall not be considered as costs of the proceedings and shall be covered by the State Treasury.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP), Articles 54 and 102. 2) Passport Law (Law 5682), Article 34. 3) International Labor Force Law, Article 23. Unauthorized entry is considered an administrative offense in Turkish law (LFIP, Article 102). It does not result in civil or criminal sanctions but results in administrative sanctions (administrative fines, deportation decisions and detention). Working without a work permit is also considered as an administrative offence and subjected to an administrative fine and deportation decision (International Labor Force Law, Article 23 and LFIP Article 54).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 3 of the Regulation on the Housing Account and State Aid (No. 2016/8559), only Turkish citizens may benefit from housing aid.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Turkish Constitution,Article 42. Article 42 of the Turkish Constitution stipulates that no one shall be deprived of the right of education. 2) The Primary Education Law (Law No. 222), Article 42. 3) The Fundamental Law on National Education, Article 4. Right to access to primary education is regulated to be compulsory to Turkish citizens under the provisions of the Fundamental Law on National Education and Law on Primary Education. 4) The Regulation on the Education of Children of Migrant Workers, Article 9. Furthermore, the Regulation on the Education of Children of Migrant Workers, in consistency with Article 30 of the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families and with Article 28 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, provides that children of migrant workers should have equal access, free of charge (for state schools) to primary education. 5) The Circular (Ministry of National Education) No. 2014/21, dated 23.09.2014, which regulates the procedure for humanitarian migrant children's access to primary education. However, national law of Turkey stipulates the submission of an official permit and/or foreigner ID number for registration to schools. Therefore, this right is accessible for only migrants who have a legal permit to stay (this could be based on either humanitarian status, regular residence status or temporary status).

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Foreigners who have obtained one of the residence permits listed in Article 30 of the Turkish Law Number 6458 on Foreigners and International Protection (short-term residence permit; family residence permit; student residence permit; long-term residence permit; humanitarian residence permit; victim of human trafficking residence permit); or those who are exempted from the obligation to obtain a residence permit according to Article 20 of the Turkish Law Number 6458 on Foreigners and International Protection; or those who have been granted temporary protection in line with Article 91 of the Turkish Law Number 6458 on Foreigners and International Protection, can enroll at Turkish public education institutions other than universities. However, irregular migrants are not granted access to public adult education according to the Circular (Ministry of Education Circular) of 2014. Further, Pursuant to Higher Education Law, the Higher Education Council of Turkey has the discretion to determine the conditions of access for migrants to higher education institutions. Article 46 of said Law further designates that the Council also has the discretion to determine tuition fees for foreign students.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. A deportation decision could be rendered if the person has been convicted, served a sentence, and deemed necessary to be deported (Article 54(1)(a) of Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP) and Article 59 of Turkish Penal Code) or if the person poses a threat to public order, security or health [Article 54(1)(d) of the LFIP]. Article 60 of the Implementation Regulation (Bylaw) of the LFIP (IR) further implies that the administration has the discretion to review the deportability of the foreigners who are convicted. Therefore, it is possible for the administrative authorities to consider even minor convictions as a threat to public order and render a deportation decision which would cause the cancellation of a residence permit. However, for long term residence permits, it is explicitly indicated that the permit would be cancelled if it is considered that the person poses a serious threat to public order or security. In these cases, the administrative authority has the discretion on determining what poses a serious threat to public order or security, including the power to claim that any conviction may result in loss of residence status.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Article 4. 2) Implementation Regulation of LFIP, Article 4. 3) Temporary Protection Regulation, Article 6.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Article 4, which provides that within the scope of this of this Law no-one shall be returned to a place where he or she may be subjected to torture, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment or, where his/her life or freedom would be threatened on account of his/her race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. 2) Implementation Regulation (Bylaw) of LFIP, Article 4. 3) Temporary Protection Regulation (Bylaw), Article 6. The cited articles prohibit refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to persecution on the basis of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Article 4. 2) Implementation Regulation of LFIP (IR), Article 4. 3) Temporary Protection Regulation (TPR), Article 6. According to the cited articles of the LFIP, IR and TPR; the right to life and freedom is protected within the framework of nonrefoulement principle, only on the basis of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion. The aforementioned provisions are designated as follows: "[n]o one within the scope of this of this Law shall be returned to a place where he or she may be subjected to torture, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment or, where his/her life or freedom would be threatened on account of his/her race, religion, nationality, membership of particular social group."

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Although Article 4 of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection together with Article 4 of the Implementation Regulation of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection provides that 'foreigners cannot be deported or removed to a country, where it is understood that they may face threats as a result of the conducted research and proceedings shall be constituted for these persons pursuant to the provisions related to international protection (...),' the law does not explicitly stipulate any requirement for persons to be advised of the possible availability of asylum before being expelled or prevented entry.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Although this protection is explicitly provided for applicants of international protection (in Articles 73, 74, 76, 77 of the Implementation Regulation (Bylaw) of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP)), the general rule of non-refoulement (Article 4 of the LFIP), which is applicable to all migrants regardless of their status, does not include an explicit protection from chain-refoulement. The landmark decision in Abdolkhani and Karimnia v. Turkey(Abdolkhani and Karimnia v. Turkey, European Court of Human Rights App. No. 30471/08,22.09.2009, paras. 88-89 ), The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) emphasized the significance of the protection from chain refoulement and indicated that an "indirect removal of an alien to an intermediary country does not affect the responsibility of the expelling Contracting State to ensure that he or she is not, as a result of its decision to expel, exposed to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention."

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 53(2), 54 and 55 (2). Article 54 of the LFIP provides an exhaustive list for the grounds of deportation decisions. Article 55 lists the situations for which the deportation decisions cannot be rendered. This Article also provides that such determination should be done individually. Article 53(2) stipulates that the decision should include the grounds. 2) The Implementation Regulation of LFIP (IR), Article 54 requires that the deportation decisions should be issued individually for each migrant.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 53(2) and (3). According to Article 53 (2) and (3), the deportation decision together with its reasons shall be notified to the migrant, with respect to whom a removal decision has been issued or, to his/her legal representative or lawyer. If the migrant with respect of whom the removal decision has been issued is not represented by a lawyer, the migrant or his/her legal representative shall be informed about the consequence of the decision, procedures and time limits for appeal. The migrant, their legal representative or lawyer may appeal against the deportation decision to the administrative court within fifteen days as of the date of notification. The person who has appealed against the decision to the court shall also notify the authority that has ordered the removal regarding the appeal.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Turkish law does not provide a right to acquire citizenship for all migrants and children of migrants who would otherwise be stateless, but it does provides such a right for those who are born in Turkey. Pursuant to Article 8 of the Turkish Citizenship Law (TCL), a child born in Turkey who cannot acquire citizenship of any country by birth due to foreign parents is a Turkish citizen from birth. Also, a child who was found unaccompanied in Turkey is deemed to have been born in Turkey, unless otherwise proven, therefore such a child could also acquire Turkish citizenship.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey conditionally protects this right, in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 34 and 35. Family reunification is allowed under Turkish law only for spouses, minor children and dependent children pursuant to Article 34 of the LFIP. The supporter and the family member should meet certain conditions for the issuance of the residence permit for family members. These conditions are listed under Article 35 of the LFIP. It should also be noted that conditional refugees (this is a type of an international protection status in Turkish law) are excluded from being a supporter under Article 34(1) of the LFIP. These rules are also enshrined in Article 30 of Implementing Regulation of LFIP. 2) The Temporary Protection Regulation, Article 49. For temporarily protected persons, a separate provision in the Temporary Protection Regulation is applicable (Article 49). However family reunification of these migrants are subjected to the discretion of the administration.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protectst this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Article 25(2). Article 25(2) provides that refusal, nonrenewal or cancelation of an application for a residence permit in general should be notified to the concerned foreigner or to her/his representative or lawyer in order to allow the foreigner to be able to appeal a negative decision. Moreover, rejection or cancelation or non-renewal of a family residence permit or rejection of a family reunification request is considered to be an administrative decision. 2) The Administrative Judicial Procedure Law (Law No. 2577), Article 2. According to Article 2, parties who claim that their interests are infringed because of a decision of administration, may brought annulment actions before the courts. 3) The Turkish Constitution, Article 125 states that "[r]ecourse to judicial review shall be available against all actions and acts of administration."

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Turkish law only recognizes marriages that are between a man and a woman (as stated in the law). Therefore, a valid same sex marriage or a marital relationship concluded in a foreign country is likely to be considered to be in violation of Turkish public policy and would not be recognized. Therefore, although there are no specific provisions in the relevant regulations (concerning family reunification), it is not likely in the practice to provide family reunification to same sex marital relationships.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 29 and 42. There is no distinction in law in regards to visa type for the access to permanent residence status (long term residence permit). However, this pathway is not available to refugees working on the basis of a work permit exemption whose residence is considered based on humanitarian reasons.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Pursuant to Articles 42 and 54 of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection, there is no avenue for irregular migrant(s) (workers) become lawfully settled in Turkey, and an irregular (work) situation is a valid reason for deportation.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law inTurkey protects this right in 1) the Labor Law (Law No. 4857, entry into force date: 10.06.2003), Articles 5 and 24. According to Article 1 of the Labor Law no. 4857 (4857 say?l? I? Kanunu), the law is applicable to anyone who is legally employed in Turkey, and that the aim of the law is to regulate the working conditions, the working environment and the working obligations within the employment relation. Article 5 states that within the employment relation, all discrimination for reasons of language, race, color, gender, handicap, political ideas and philosophical beliefs, religion, denomination and for similar reasons. 2) The Law on the Human Rights and Equality Institution of Turkey (Law No. 6701, dated 06.04.2016), Article 6. Article 2 of that law defines the employment relation as the relation between the employer and the employee. Therefore, migrants who are legally employed in Turkey are entitled to the same treatment as Turkish citizens in the same position; this also applies to redress.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 52 of Social Security and General Health Insurance Law, migrants start benefiting from general health insurance following a minimum 1 year legal residence in Turkey. Also, according to Article 89 of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection, international protecton beneficiaries may enjoy general health care up to one year. Continuation of this right is subjected to the discretion of the administration.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 67 of Turkish Constitution, Article 6 of Law on Fundamental Conditions of Elections and Electoral Registers (Law No. 298, entry into force date: 02.05.1961), Article 10 of Law on Elections of Members of the Parliament (Law No. 2839, entry into force date: 13.06.1983), Article 10 of the Law on the Election of Local Administrators (Law No. 2972) guarantees the right to stand for election only for Turkish citizens.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 10 of the Turkish Constitution stipulates that everyone is equal before the law without distinction as to language, race, colour, sex, political opinion, philosophical belief, religion and sect, or any such grounds. The constitution does not refer to migrant status or nationality. The term ‘any such grounds' may be interpreted to include migrant status, however such interpretation has not yet been provided in case-law. Further, Article 3 of the Law on Human Rights and Equality Institution (LHEI) states that within the scope of this Law, gender, race, color, language, religion, belief, sect, philosophical and political discrimination based on opinion, ethnicity, wealth, birth, marital status, health status, disability and age is prohibited. This article also does not mention migrant status or nationality as a basis for prohibited discrimination.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Turkish Constitution, Article 10. Article 10 of the Turkish Constitution stipulates that 'everyone' (including migrants) is equal before the law without distinction as to language, race, colour, sex, political opinion, philosophical belief, religion and sect, or any such grounds. 2) The Law on Human Rights and Equality Institution, Article 3 states that within the scope of this Law, gender, race, color, language, religion, belief, sect, philosophical and political discrimination based on opinion, ethnicity, wealth, birth, marital status, health status, disability and age is prohibited. This article is also applicable to ‘everyone' including migrants.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Labor Law (Law No. 4857), Articles 1, 2, 5, and 102. Article 5 prohibits discrimination for reasons of language, race, color, gender, disability, political views and philosophical opinions, religion, denomination and for similar reasons. Neither the scope of this Law (Article 1), nor the employment relation defined in this Law (Article 2) excludes the foreigners. Therefore, in principle migrant workers would have the equal right of payment. Article 102 obliges a minimum wage, and does not exclude foreigners for the payment of "minimum wage" either. 2) The Law on the Human Rights and Equality Institution of Turkey (LHEI, Law No. 6701, dated 06.04.2016), Article 6. Moreover, Article 6 provides that "the employer or a person authorized by the employer may not discriminate against an employee of the employer or a person applying for this purpose, a person who is in a workplace to obtain practical work experience or a person applying for this purpose, and a person who wants to obtain information about the workplace or work to work in any capacity or to obtain practical work experience, in any of the work-related processes, including information, application, selection criteria, recruitment criteria, recruitment conditions, employment and termination of employment."

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in the International Labor Force Law (ILFL, Law No. 6735, entry into force date: 13.08.2016), Articles 10 and 11. According to Article 10 of the ILFL, if the application is approved, a work permit for a maximum of one year shall be granted to the foreigner at the first application provided that this period does not exceed the duration of the labor or service contract. During this time the migrant can be employed at a specific job in a specific work place which belongs to a real person or legal entity or public organization, and other institutions or workplaces of these organizations in the same line of business. If an extension is requested and approved, a work permit for a maximum of two years at the first extension application and a maximum of three years in the following applications shall be granted for the same employer. However, applications to be employed by a different employer shall be evaluated within the scope of the above mentioned paragraph. Therefore, if the employee would like to change their employer it would be deemed as a new work permit application. The ILFL provides the right to apply and receive permanent work permits on some exceptional conditions. Holders of these permits together with Turquoise Card Holders (Article 11 of the ILFL) are subjected to equal rights with citizens provided that the special provisions in the laws are observed.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 6 of International Labor Force Law, all foreigners should obtain a work permit to access the labor market. Article 13 of the Law sets forth the exemptions from work permit and Article 16 provides the conditions of obtaining a work permit in an exceptional way, however the spouse of the principal migrant is not listed in any of these provisions. Therefore, spouses are subject to the general procedure to obtain a work permit.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Pursuant to Article 27 of Foreigners and International Protection Law, a valid work permit is considered a residence permit. Hence, Article 25 of the Implementation Regulation of the LFIP, states that for such cases, the loss of work permit would result in loss of residence permit. For migrants who stay in the country with a certain long term residence permit, loss of work permit does not automatically result in the loss of residence permit. On the other hand, loss of work permit might have an indirect effect for the loss of residence permit in some cases. For instance, one of the reasons to obtain a short-term residence permit is to establish business in Turkey. In that case, loss of work permit would invalidate the justification of the residence permit and would result in loss of the permit pursuant to Articles 32 and 33 of the Law.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Labor Law (Law No. 4857), Articles 1, 2, and 5. Article 5 prohibits discrimination for reasons of language, race, color, gender, disability, political views and philosophical opinions, religion, denomination and for similar reasons. Neither the scope of this Law (Article 1), nor the employment relation defined in this Law (Article 2) excludes the foreigners. Therefore, in principle migrant workers would have the equal rights in terms of work conditions. 2) The Law on Human Rights and Equality Institution (LHEI, Law No. 6701, dated 06.04.2016), Article 6 prohibits discrimination in relation to working conditions.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in Social Security and General Health Insurance Law (Law Nr. 5510, entry into force day by Turkey: 16.06.2006), Article 4 (2) (c), 5 and 6(e), 50, 52. 2) International Labor Organization (ILO) Convention concerning Equality of Treatment of Nationals and Non-Nationals in Social Security (entry into force date by Turkey 10.08.1971). Article 90 of the Turkish Constitution which states that: "International agreements duly put into effect have the force of law. No appeal to the Constitutional Court shall be made with regard to these agreements, on the grounds that they are unconstitutional. (Sentence added on May 7, 2004; Act No. 5170) In the case of a conflict between international agreements, duly put into effect, concerning fundamental rights and freedoms and the laws due to differences in provisions on the same matter, the provisions of international agreements shall prevail". According to the cited provisions, as long as the migrant is not insured in another country, they can be insured and have equal access to rights to social security protections.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in the Unemployment Insurance Law (Law No. 4447, entry into date: 08.09.1999), Article 46. According to Article 48 of the Unemployment Benefits Law, Unemployment Insurance is obligatory to those who fall within the scope of the law. Article 46 of the same law defines to whom the law is applicable. It refers to Articles 4 and 50 of the Law No. 5510 on Social Security and General Health Insurance for the scope; these articles provide that the law is applicable to those who are legally employed and those who voluntarily join an insurance scheme (irrespective of nationality). The law is therefore equally applicable to Turkish citizens and foreigners that are legally residing in Turkey.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 10, and 42. Pursuant to Article 42, following a minimum of 8 years of regular residence, migrants can acquire a long-term residence permit. 2) Article 10(3) of the International Labor Force law, states that foreigners holding a legal work permit for a minimum of eight years may apply for a permanent work permit. Permanent work permits provide the same rights as a permanent residence permit.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families (entry into force date by Turkey 09.05.2001), Articles 16(3) and 21. The Convention is the only source that directly provides such safeguard specifically for migrant workers. As the relevant Convention is ratified and properly put into force pursuant to Article 90 of the Turkish Constitution, it is considered to have the equal power of a Law enacted by Parliament and also part of national law. Article 21 of the Convention is of a self executing (operative) nature. Therefore, it can be directly applied by public authorities and it is binding just like a domestic law rule. 2) Articles 135, 136 and 205 of the Turkish Penal Code respectively designates the crimes of confiscation of personal data by unauthorized individuals and destroying of official documents. 3) Article 20 of the Turkish Constitution provides the right to private law and prohibits the search and confiscation of private belongings unless there is a legal ground. Although these provisions are applicable to all, including foreigners, they are not specific for migrant workers.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right, in 1) the Law on the Civil Registration Services (LCRS, Law No. 5490), Articles 3(1)(??), 8, 15, and 40. Article 15 states that every child who is born alive in Turkey shall be notified to civil registration offices within thirty days as of the date of birth in Turkey. However, this Article might create some confusion. Article 15 states that "every child born alive is required to be notified within 30 days starting from the date of birth in Turkey, if the child is born abroad, notification shall be done within 60 days starting from the birth". Article 40 designates that "notification of births for foreign children in Turkey are accepted by civil registration offices .(...).These notifications are not registered in family registries. They are kept in a special folder". It should also be noted though, according to the cited article of Temporary Protection Regulation, all children who are born in Turkey while under temporary protection should be registered. Article 40 of the Implementation Regulation of the LCRS specifically designates notification of birth of foreign children. 2) Regulation on the Civil Registration of Foreigners Residing in Turkey (RCRF, No. 2006/11057), Articles 5 and 9(1). Article 9(1) of the RCRF also states that foreigners who are registered should notify about their civil matters (including births) and that registration should be made according to these notifications. As a result of these provisions, it can be concluded that the registration of the births of migrant children is only obligatory for those whose parents are already registered in the Foreigners' Registry (and obtained Foreigner ID Numbers). 3) Temporary Protection Regulation, Article 21(3) and 33(2)(d).

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) Foreigners and International Protection Law, Articles 23 (residence permits), 50 (for stateless person IDs), 76 (International Protection Applicant ID Cards), and Article 83 (International Protection Beneficiary ID Card). 2) Temporary Protection Regulation, Article 22 (Temporary Protection ID Card). 3) International Labor Force Law, Articles 11 (Turquiose Card), and 24. (Work permits). 4) Implementing Regulation of International Labor Force Law, Article 24. 5) The Passport Law. 6)Turqoise Card Regulation (dated 14 March 2017), Articles 5 and 18. According to the cited articles, documents recognizing migrants' residency status, work status and identity should be issued. These include; residence permits, international protection applicant ID Document, International Protection Beneficiary Document, Work permits, Stateless Person ID Document, Temporarily Protected Person ID Document and Passports Stamped for Foreigners. Turquiose Card for high-skilled migrants is included in this legislation but reportedly not issued so far in practice.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Turkish Penal Code (Law No. 5237), Article 205. Destroying official documents is designated as a crime under article 205 of Turkish Penal Code. This rule is a general one; it covers the documents of migrants as they are official documents, but it does not explicitly refer to migrants. In its decision on 4 April 2016 (application number2014/16383E), the Turkish Court of Cassation has interpreted this Article to mean that this crime can be committed by anyone, and furthermore that this Article is applicable to any official document (including identity papers), and that the Article applies as soon as the perpetrator changes, destroys or hides an original official document in order to prevent its owner to exercise rights attached to the official document.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) Foreigners and International Protection Law, Article 59. 2) Turkish Penal Procedure Law, Articles 95(2) and 107(3). 3) The Law on Imprisonment and Security Measures (Law No. 5275), Article 84. 4) Regulation (Bylaw) on The Establishment, Administration, Management and Supervision of Reception and Return Centers (Official Gazette No. 28980), Article 11 (1)(h).

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no explicit and specific prohibition in the Turkish legislation in regard to the detention of children on the basis of their status as a migrant. Considering provisions of the Turkish legislation [(Articles 59(1)(?) and(d) of Foreigners and International Protection Law together with articles 4(1)(c) and (?) of The Bylaw on The Establishment, Administration, Management and Supervision of Reception and Return Centers)], which regulate the best interest of the child and access to education issues for the children in return/removal centers, it can be concluded that the Turkish law allows the detention of children provided that certain safeguards are available. However, unaccompanied minors are not subjected to detention in removal centers.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There is no prohibition of detention of migrants on the basis of their status as a migrant in Turkish law. Article 57 of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP) allows detention of irregular migrants (who are subjected to removal) when certain conditions are met. Article 68(1) does state that international protection applicants shall not be subject to administrative detention solely for lodging an international protection claim, but there is no other prohibition of detention of migrants on the basis of their status as a migrant in Turkish law.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP) (Law No. 6458), Articles 57(5), (6), 68(4), (7), 80. 2) Law on Administrative Jurisdiction Procedures (Law No. 2577), Article 2. 3) The Turkish Constitution, Article 125. 4) Regulation on Alternatives to Detention (dated 14 September 2022), Article 18. According to the cited articles of the LFIP, migrants have the right to appeal to Judge of the Criminal Court of Peace for the legality of the detention decision. In relation to appeals regarding conditions of the detention (centers), there is no explicitly and specifically determined remedy. However, pursuant to the Constitutional Court's decision for the B.T. Application (Application No.2014/15769, Decision Date: 30.11.2017, Publication in the Official Gazette Date: 16.02.2018) the right to file a full remedy action provided under Law on Administrative Jurisdiction Procedures(Law No. 2577) is sufficient to be accepted as an effective remedy for the conditions of detention(in the removal centers) (B.T. Application, paras. 54, 55). The law stipulates the duration of the detention for 6 months, and this duration may be extended only for 6 additional months. Although there is no explicit provision in the migration law providing for a possibility to appeal against the decision on the duration of the detention, in general, since the decision to prolong the detention is a new administrative decision, and administrative decision can be appealed against to the Administrative Court under Turkish law, appeals against decision affecting the duration of detention are on paper also possible under Turkish law.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 57(1), 57(2) and 68(1), 68(2) and 68(3). 2) Implementation Regulation of the LFIP, Regulation on Alternatives to Detention (dated 14 September 2022), Articles 59 and 96. The cited articles provide that a determination should be done individually, and on case by case basis. The cited articles also provide an exhaustive list for the grounds for a detention decision. With the amendments made on the LFIP Article 57 (entry into force date 24.12.2019) and with the enactment of the Regulation on Alternatives to Detention, it is also possible to implement alternatives to detention, following an individual determination.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Turkish Constitution, Article 17. Article 17 provides the right to be free from torture and cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment and punishment for everybody including migrants. 2) Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 4, 55(1) (a), 73, 74. 3) Implementation Regulation (Bylaw) of LFIP, Articles 4, 75, 76 and 77. 4) The Temporary Protection Regulation (Bylaw), Article 6.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 2(1) of the Law on Protection and Security of Land Borders (Law No. 3497), Articles 4(C)(8,9), 5 of the Coast Guard Command Law (Law No. 2692), Articles 87-90 of the Law (Law No. 211)on Turkish Armed Forces Internal Services, Regulation (By-law) regarding Cooperation and Coordination Among Institutions on Border Management (dated 01.02.2016, No. 2016/8520)and Article 13 (D) of Law No. 2559 on the Duties and the Competences of the Police Forces, allow the use of force for attempts of illegal entry to the country. There is no legal provision that prohibits the use of force on this matter. However, the cited sources also provide that the use of force should be proportional and comprehensively detail the conditions where the use of weapons are allowed.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 2(1) of the Law on Protection and Security of Land Borders (Law No. 3497), Articles4(C)(8, 9), 5 of the Coast Guard Command Law (Law No. 2692), Articles 87-90 of the Law (Law No. 211) on Turkish Armed Forces Internal Services, Regulation (By-law) regarding Cooperation and Coordination Among Institutions on Border Management (dated 01.02.2016, No.2016/8520)and Article 13(D) of Law No. 2559 on the Duties and the Competences of the Police Forces, weapons may be used provided that it should be proportional. There is no provision in the law that explicitly prohibits the use of lethal force as a means of preventing migrants from entering the state's territory.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Human trafficking crime is defined and regulated under Article 28 of the Turkish Penal Code. Human trafficking as a criminal offense is defined and regulated under Article 79 of the Turkish Penal Code. Pursuant to this provision force, violence, intimidation and threat are among the essential elements of the crime, whereas Article 28 of said Law provides that a person who commits a crime as a result of force and violence that s/he cannot resist or get rid of, or a certain and severe intimidation or threat, is not punished. Additionally, Articles 79 and 80 of the Turkish Penal (Criminal) Code (Law No. 5237), Law on Combatting Smuggling (Law No. 5607), Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nation Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime (date of entry into force by Turkey: 13.12.2000), Council of Europe Convention on Action Against Trafficking in Human Beings (entry into force date for Turkey: 01.09.2016), Regulation on Combatting Human Trafficking and Protection of Victims of Human Trafficking (No 29656) also penalize migrant smuggling and human trafficking. Despite these provisions, while trafficked victims are exempt from criminal prosecutions related to trafficking, there is no explicit applicable provision in the same manner for smuggled migrants.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in the Turkish Citizenship Law (Law No. 5901), Article 29. Loss of Turkish citizenship without the consent of the individual is designated under Article 29 of the Turkish Citizenship Law. This Article provides an exhaustive list of circumstances where a person might be deprived of their citizenship. This list includes major convictions. Further, a person who cannot be reached as they are abroad and for whom an investigation is being conducted based on Articles 302, 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314, 315 (these are major convictions) of the Turkish Penal Code is notified within one month from the start of the investigation to the Ministry of Interior in terms of deprivation of nationality. If the person does not return to Turkey within 3 months they might be deprived of their nationality subjected to the decision of the President.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Turkish Citizenship Law (TCL), Articles 5, 9, 10 and 11. Pursuant to Articles 5, 9, and 10, economic migrants may acquire Turkish citizenship through a decision of the competent authority. Article 11 of the TCL is applicable to all foreigners including economic migrants who would like to be naturalized by a decision of competent authority. Pursuant to Article 11, in order to be naturalized, the person needs to be of the age of consent, have been resident in Turkey for five years without interruption prior to the date of application for citizenship, have the intention to settle in Turkey and prove this intention with action, not have any disease that constitutes a danger to public health, be a person of good morals, speak an adequate level of Turkish, have an income or profession to provide for his own livelihood and those dependent on him/her in Turkey, and not pose a threat to national security and public order. 2) Article 20 of the Implementation Regulation of the TCL, Article 12.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 25(1) of The the Temporary Protection Regulation (TPR) hinders temporarily protected individuals' (currently the Syrians) access to citizenship through the regular way of acquisition of Turkish citizenship designated under Article 10 and 11 of the Turkish Citizenship Law (TCL). However, there is no prohibition provided in law for these individuals to acquire Turkish citizenship through extraordinary means of acquisition under Article 12 of the TCL (such as through marriage with or adoption (for minors) by a Turkish citizen), respectively pursuant to Articles 16 and 17 of the TCL. With regards to other humanitarian migrants (international protection beneficiaries and humanitarian residence permitholders), there is no explicit provision that either prohibits or allows their acquisition to Turkish citizenship. In these cases, it is legally consistent to conclude that these individuals have access to Turkish citizenship through the regular acquisition procedure. However, Article 16(2)(c) of the Implementation Regulation of the the Turkish Citizenship Law (TCL) has an ambiguous provision regarding the lack of "intention to settle" for these migrants which is sought as a condition under the TCL for citizenship applications. It should also be noted that according to Article 44(4) of the Implementation Regulation of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (IR), The duration of stay in the country with a humanitarian residence permit shall not count towards the total duration of residence permits stipulated in the Law. Therefore, it is also not likely for humanitarian residence permit holders to acquire Turkish citizenship through ordinary way (based on the duration of residence). However, just like temporarily protected individuals these migrants may also acquire Turkish citizenship through extraordinary means, such as marriage or adoption.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP, Law No. 6458), Articles 34-37. 2) Implementing Regulation of LFIP, Article 30. 3) The Turkish Citizenship Law (Law No. 5901), Articles 10-11. As a rule, pursuant to Article 20 of the Turkish Citizenship Law (TCL) the acquisition of Turkish citizenship by the decision of the competent authority does not automatically affect the citizenship of the spouse. The children of the mother or father in custody can acquire Turkish citizenship if the other spouse (who does not have custody of the child) consents. If consent is not given, action is taken according to the decision of the judge in the country where the mother or father has his habitual residence. The children of parents who acquire Turkish citizenship together also acquire Turkish citizenship. Therefore, spouses and adult family migrants can be subject to the general rules of citizenship acquisition provided under Articles 10 and 11 of the TCL which requires, inter alia, 5 years of uninterrupted residence.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in Turkish Citizenship Law (TCL, Law No. 5901), Articles 11 and 44. Before 2017, Article 11(2) of the TCL provided discretion to a Board of Ministers to require renunciation of the applicant's current citizenship in order to acquire Turkish citizenship. However, this provision is abrogated with an amendment made on 19.10.2017. Therefore, Turkish law without any exceptions allows dual nationality.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Turkish Constitution, Articles 10, 12, 24, and 25, 26. The Turkish Constitution provides relevant rights to "everybody" without making distinction between citizens and foreigners. 2) The Law on the Human Rights and Equality Institution of Turkey (LHEI, Law No. 6701, dated 06.04.2016), Article 3(2), which prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender, race, color, language, religion, faith, sect, philosophical or political opinion, ethnic origin, wealth, birth, civil status, medical condition, disability or age.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Turkish Constitution, Article 25. The Turkish Constitution provides this right to "everybody" without making distinction between citizens and foreigners. There is no specific restriction provided for foreigners in the current legislation. 2) The Law on the Human Rights and Equality Institution of Turkey (LHEI, Law No. 6701, dated 06.04.2016), Article 3(2), which prohibits discrimination on the basis of philosophical or political opinon for everybody.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in the Turkish Constitution, Article 26. The Turkish Constitution provides this right to "everybody" without making distinction between citizens and foreigners.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Turkish Constitution, Article 33, which states that everyone has the right to form associations, or become a member of an association, or withdraw from membership without prior permission, and further that no one shall be compelled to become or remain a member of an association. Freedom of association may only be restricted by law on the grounds of protecting national security and public order, or prevention of crime commitment, or protecting public morals, public health.2) The Association Law (Law No. 5253), Article 3 defines the right of establishments of associations, and lists the conditions. According to this article, any person that is of legal age is able to establish an association. The terminology of the law encapsulates also legal persons and foreigners. 3) The Turkish Civil Code (Law No. 4721), Article 93, explicitly provides that any foreigner that is legally residing in Turkey can establish an association or become member of an association.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. According to Article 35 of the Law on Foreigners and International Protection, 'with regard to family residence permit applications, the following conditions shall apply to the sponsor to: a) have a monthly income in any case not less than the minimum wage in total corresponding not less than one third of the minimum wage per each family member; b) live in accommodation conditions appropriate to general health and safety standards corresponding to the number of family members and to have medical insurance covering all family members; c) submit proof of not having been convicted of any crime against family during the five years preceding the application with a criminal record certificate; ?) have been residing in Turkey for at least one year on a residence permit'. However, family reunification of temporarily protected persons are subject to the discretion of the administration, therefore, it is likely that the family reunification of these migrants could be provided without the requirements related to income and/or insurance. However, considering the fact that this is based on the discretion and even if it applies, it is only effective for ‘some’ migrants

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) Articles 10, 12, 36, 40 of Turkish Constitution. According to Article 10 of the Turkish Constitution, everyone is equal before the law without distinction as to language, race,...or any such grounds, and that State organs and administrative authorities are obliged to act in accordance with the principle of equality before the law in all their proceedings. Furthermore, Article 36 provides that everyone has the right of litigation either as plaintiff or defendant and the right to a fair trial before the courts through legitimate means and procedures. 2) Articles 3(2) and 73 of the Turkish Penal Code (Law No. 5237). Articles 3(2) and 73 of the Turkish Criminal Code states that the law shall apply to all, regardless of... race, nationality, faith... and that in case of an offense of which the investigation and prosecution is bound to a complaint, no investigation or prosecution is proceeded unless a complaint is brought by the victim of an offense. 3) Article 237 of the Turkish Penal Procedural Code (Law No. 5271), which provides that victims who have been victims of a crime, as well as the individuals liable for compensation, are entitled to intervene in the public prosecution during the prosecution phase at the court of the first instance at any stage, until the judgment has been rendered. All of these laws and provisions provide equal access to criminal proceedings with citizens.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP) (Law No. 6458), Articles 46(c), 48, 55(?), and 55(d). Although there is no general rule for all victims of crimes that relieve them from expulsion, this relief is possible for human trafficking victims or other individuals who are subjected to violence. Human trafficking victims are allowed to have a special residence permit under Article 48.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP) (Law No. 6458), Articles 25(1), 46(1)(a), 59(1)(?) and (d), 66, 67(1), 75(3), 79(4), 89(1), 95(3). Article 25(1) of the LFIP states that "the decision of the residence permit may be postponed in consideration of elements such as ... the best interest of the child during these actions." Additionally, Article 46(1)(a) states, "when best interest of the child is of concern, a humanitarian residence permit may be granted without seeking the conditions for other types of residence permits." Furthermore, Article 75(3) states, "interviews with minors may be conducted in the presence of a psychologist, child development specialist, social worker or their parent or legal representative." 2) Implementation Regulation of the LFIP, Articles 22(18), 65(2), 82(1)(?) and (d), 105, 113, 116(8), 122, 123. 3) Temporary Protection Regulation, Articles 23(2), (3) and (4), 28, 48(2), 49(2). Articles 23(2), (3) and (4) of the Temporary Protection Regulation, states, "the foreigner's family status and his or her special needs (which include being an unaccompanied minor) shall be taken into consideration" and "unaccompanied children shall be accommodated in coordination with the Ministry of Family and Social Policies and Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency." 4) Regulation on the Establishment, Management, Operation and Supervision of Reception and Removal Center, Article 4(1)(c) and (?). 5) Regulation on Combatting Human Trafficking and Protection of Victims, Article 24. 6) Unaccompanied Children Directive (dated 20.10.2015).

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP) (Law No. 6458), Articles 3(1)(l), 46(1)(c), 48, 55(1)(b), 67, 75(3), 95(3). Article 3(1)(l) includes considerations for, "Persons with Special Needs (PwSN)" include "pregnant women," "single mothers," "persons subjected to sexual violence and rape." Additionally, Article 113 states that Persons with Special Needs (PwSN), including "pregnant women," "single mothers," "persons subjected to sexual violence and rape," should be registered and given priority with respect to the rights and actions concerning international protection. 2) Implementing Regulation of the LFIP, Articles 34(6), 55(1)(?) and (d), 113; Temporary Protection Regulation, Articles 23(2) and (3), 38(3), 48. 3) Regulation on the Establishment, Management, Operation and Supervision of Reception and Removal Centers, Article 4(1)(c) and (?). 4) Regulation on Combatting Human Trafficking and Protection of Victims, Article 18(10).

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in Turkey protects this right in 1) the Law on Foreigners and International Protection (LFIP) (Law No. 6458), Articles 3(1)(l), 67(1), 75(3), 95(3). According to Article 3(1)(l) migrants with disabilities are considered Persons with Special Needs (PwSN). Article 67(1) states that Persons with Special Needs (PwSN) are prioritized with respect to the rights and actions regarding international protection. Finally, Article 95(3) states that Persons with Special Needs (PwSN) should be given priority in terms of accommodation. 2) Implementation Regulation (IR) of the LFIP, Articles 30(5), 65(2), 81(4), 85(3), 113. 3) Temporary Protection Regulation, Articles 23(2), 23(3), 38(3), 48(2). 4) Regulation on the Establishment, Management, Operation and Supervision of Reception and Removal Centers, Article 4(1)(c) and (?). 5) Law No. 5378 on Individuals with Disabilities.
