question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: United States

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in the U.S. Constitution at Amendment I. This is a basic protection for all individuals in the U.S.A., including migrants regardless of their status.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA criminalizes non-citizens voting in federal elections in Title 18 of U.S. Code Section 611.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in Amendment V of the U.S. Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Immigration is considered a civil law matter, rather than criminal law, and therefore there is no right to appointed counsel under federal law, although some local jurisdictions have created a right to counsel in certain scenarios. Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1362 only provides a right to counsel at the noncitizen's expense.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in Amendments V, VI, and XIV of the U.S. Constitution as well as in Title 42 of U.S. Code Section 2000d; Title 28 of U.S. Code Section 1827.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA does not protect migrants from civil or criminal sanctions for unauthorized entry. llegal entry is a criminal offense, for example Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1325 (misdemeanor entry without inspection).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in a limited way, for certain categories of migrants, in Title 42 of U.S. Code Section 1436a, even if this protection varies by jurisdiction. Housing is one of the most restrictive public benefits for immigrants in the USA. While there are some local shelters, federal funds are only used to support housing for lawful permanent residents and certain humanitarian migrants.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in the court case Plyler v. Doe, 457 U.S. 202 (1982) and U.S. Constitutional Amendment XIV (Equal Protection).

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No universal protection of this right. Education is generally regulated by the states, not the federal government. Although results are mixed, one federal appeals court recently held that colleges were not required to admit irregular migrants in Estrada v. Becker, 917 F.3d 1298 (11th Cir. 2019).

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA provides that certain criminal convictions will render an otherwise lawfully present immigrant deportable at Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1227. Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1182 also provides certain criminal convictions or conduct that bar eligibility for immigrants to adjust to lawfully present status in the United States. This is an extremely complicated area of law in the United States that is very actively litigated case by case. Seemingly minor offenses, including administrative offenses, can be considered "aggravated felonies" or "crimes involving moral turpitude" and a basis for removal.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in Title 8 of U.S. Code Sections 1158(b)(1)(A), 1101(a)(42) and Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations Section 208.18. Even if barred from asylum status, individuals may qualify for Withholding of Removal or protection under Convention Against Torture (CAT).

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to persecution based on race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1101(a)(42)(A), Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1158(b)(1)(A), and Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations Sections 1208.13, 1240.8(d). There are exceptions to the ban based on particularly serious crimes, although those cases may still receive protection under the Convention Against Torture regardless of nexus to a protected ground. Approval of asylum applications varies dramatically by judge and denials have risen as the administration attempts to expedite cases. Under Title 42 of the U.S. Code, a public health authority, the government has claimed the exceptional authority to circumscribe this right and therefore, many recently arrived migrants have been subjected to expulsions without access to this protection.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The USA does not offer general protection beyond the Convention Against Torture and asylum based on persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion. The USA does offer a limited status called Temporary Protected Status for residents of specifically designated countries experiencing humanitarian crises, but many countries are excluded and cutoffs to register for this status are restrictive.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA requires a person to be advised of the possible availability of asylum before being expelled or prevented entry in Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations Section 235.3(b)(2)(i) and Form I-867A. Under Title 42 of the U.S. Code, a public health authority, the government has claimed an exceptional power to ignore this obligation and therefore many recently arrived migrants have been subjected to expulsions without access to this protection.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA addresses refoulement in Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations Sections 208.16 and 208.17. While this arguably could be read into the general prohibition on refoulement (as UNHCR has done), it is not explicitly written into the law.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA historically has protected this right in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1229a. However, courts have effectively upheld the U.S. government's interpretation that it has the lawful authority to expel individuals without a screening under Title 42, a purported public health authority. See: Arizona et al v. Mayorkas, 598 U.S. __ (2022) (decision on application for stay).

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA historically has protected this right in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1229a(a)(4). However, courts have effectively upheld the U.S. government's interpretation that it has the lawful authority to expel individuals without allowing them to submit reasons against expulsion under Title 42, a purported public health authority. See: Arizona et al v. Mayorkas, 598 U.S. __ (2022) (decision on application for stay).

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA does not guarantee citizenship to migrants who would otherwise be stateless, but it does provide citizenship to their children if born in the USA under Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1401.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA provides settled regular migrants with legal avenues to facilitate reunification with immediate or non-dependent family members in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1153, Chapter 9 of the Foreign Affairs Manual Section 502.2; 8 of U.S. Code Section 1157(c)(2)(asylee family reunification). Family migration is limited to immediate relatives of individuals with lawful immigration status. Naturalized citizens may file for spouses, parents, children and siblings. Permanent residents may file for spouses and unmarried children. Some categories take so long (20 years) that they are not effective in practice.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA provides judicial remedy to appeal the refusal by the authorities to allow family formation/reunification in Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations Section 103.3 and with regard to family members of refugees in Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations Section 207.7(g). However, this does not apply to all stages of the process. In particular, consular decisions on application are non-reviewable under the Supreme Court case Kleindienst v. Mandel.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in the USA recognizes same sex relationships under the family reunification framework based on the court case United States v. Windsor, 570 U.S. 744 (2013), which held that it is illegal to discriminate against same-sex couples. However, family unification requires proof of a legal marriage. Since some countries do not have legal same-sex marriage, not all same-sex relationships may be recognized.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: Migrant workers' switch to permanent status in the U.S.A after certain conditions are met is dependent on visa type. See 8 USC Sec. 1255

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right for irregular migrants unless through an unrelated family or humanitarian mechanism.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1324 and U.S. Constitutional Amendment XIV. Authorized workers have same rights as citizens. Unauthorized workers have right to wages but contract is generally invalid given their lack of work authorization. There are additional options for victims of trafficking (T nonimmigrant status) and victims of certain crimes (U nonimmigrant status).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right for certain visa types and migrant statuses in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1641. Low-income families may qualify for medicaid, but limited groups of migrants are eligible for these programs and there may be negative immigration consequences for relying on Medicaid. Healthcare in the U.S. is largely privatized. Rules vary by state program. All people are eligible for emergency medical coverage.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA does not allow migrants to stand for election vote, as seen for example in U.S. Constitution Article 1(2), Article 1(3), and Article II(1).

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA prohibits discrimination against migrants on the basis of nationality in U.S. Constitution, Amendment XIV (Equal Protection). See also Espinoza v. Farah Mfg.Co., 414 U.S. 86 (1973).

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA generally prohibits discrimination on account of race or ethnicity in U.S. Constitution, Amendment XIV (Equal Protection).

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA generally prohibits discrimination on account of race or ethnicity in U.S. Constitution, Amendment XIV (Equal Protection). Worker's are entitled to wages earned even if they do not have work authorization. However, there are certain visas where someone can be paid less than minimum wage.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA varies in its protection of this right depending on the type of visa. Some categories of migrant workers can freely change employers and some cannot. People who obtain permanent residence through employment can eventually change employers. People who have temporary work visas generally must apply for a new visa if they change employers. Employment visas category H, L, E, TN are tied to jobs. Other types of immigrant visas that allow entry then enable immigrants to apply for jobs once issued an Employment Authorization (EAD). See: 8 USC 1184(n); 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii).

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA varies in its protection of this right depending on the type of visa. For example, the spouses of those with H-1B visas (temporary nonimmigrant visas for specialty occupations) can apply for employment authorization. See Employment Authorization for Certain H-4 Dependent Spouses final rule (H-4 rule), effective on May 26, 2015. Meanwhile, a spouse of an F-1 student visa holder is not eligible for employment without applying for a different immigration status. A spouse also may be ineligible for any kind of derivative status and therefore related empoyment authorization due to their own immigration history. See: 8 CFR 214.1(e).

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: The protection of this right in the U.S.A. is dependent on migrants' visa category. See e.g. 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). For visas in categories where the visa is resulting from employment, i.e., H, G, J, F, E categories, loss of job usually means a migrant must leave (in 30 days) or apply for a new visa.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1324 and U.S. Constitutional Amendment XIV.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA addresses migrant workers’ rights to social security protections on Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1611. Some categories of migrants are eligible for certain social security protections and some are not. There is a complex set of criteria that must be met.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA addresses this right in Title 8 of U.S. Code § 1611. Some categories of migrants are eligible for unemployment benefits and some are not. There is a complex set of criteria that must be met. This also varies by state. Also, unemployment is largely handled as an insurance scheme in the U.S. rather than a true public benefit.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1255. A temporary worker can seek to adjust status to permanent residence through an employer (in addition to the unrelated family or humanitarian applications) so long as they are in valid immigrant status.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right under Title 18 of U.S. Code Section 1597. It is illegal to knowingly destroy, conceal, remove, confiscate, or possess, an actual or purported passport or other immigration document of another individual.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right at the national level and there is sub-national variation. The USA does not have a national birth registry and those born in the U.S. are U.S. citizens, not migrants under the law.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right at the national level; there is sub-national variation. Documents are issued when someone is granted work authorization, immigration status, etc., but there is no right to a document unless you have been granted a status. Identity documents are issued by states; and not all states issue documentation for all types of immigrants.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right and makes it illegal to destroy documents that recognize migrants’ residency status, work status, and identity in Title 18 of U.S. Code Section 1324.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this obligation in Title 28 of the Code of Federal Regulations Section 50.5 ; Bureau of Consular Affairs, U.S. Department of State, Consular Notification and Access 47 (2003), and the court case Medell?n v. Texas, 552 U.S. 491 (2008).

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA addresses the detention of children on the basis of their status as a migrant in the William. Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of. 2008 Section 235(b)(1); Stipulated Settlement Agreement, Flores v. Garland, Case Number CV 2:85- 4544-DMG-AGR (C.D. Cal. 2022).

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The detention of migrants is regulated under Title 8 of the U.S. Code Section 1226.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in the USA allows review of the length and conditions of detention through a writ of habeas corpus under U.S. Constitution Article 1, § 9, clause 2 as well as bond requests for certain immigrants under Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1226(a). However, the right was limited by Johnson v. Arteaga-Martinez, 142 S. Ct. 1827 (2022) and Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez, 213 L. 142 S. Ct. 2057 (2022). In addition, access to habeas courts has proven to be onerous and there are some situations that may render detention mandatory under Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1226(c).

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Detention is statutorily mandated for arriving noncitizens without status, including asylum seekers, under Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1226(c)(1), without any consideration of individualized circumstances.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in U.S. Constitutional Amendment 8; The Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, adopted by unanimous agreement of the United Nations General Assembly on December 10, 1984, and signed by the United States on April 18, 1988, and Title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations Section 208.18 (implementing the convention). The U.S. definition of torture under 8 U.S. Code §§ 2340 does not use the international definition and also relies on caselaw for interpretation.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right in law. The United States continues to allow "reasonable" use of force, although it encourages alternatives. See the Memorandum from Acting Deputy Secretary Claire M. Grady, Department of Homeland Security Policy on the Use of Force (Sept. 7, 2018).

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National policy in the USA protects this right in Memorandum from Acting Deputy Secretary Claire M. Grady, Department of Homeland Security Policy on the Use of Force (Sept. 7, 2018); but see Supreme Court Case, Hernandez v. Mesa, No. 17?1678 (Feb. 25, 2020).

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA permits criminal prosecutions in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1325 (Criminalizing "Improper entry by alien") and Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1326 (illegal reentry).

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA provides that citizenship is not affected by criminal offenses, other than a conviction for knowingly obtaining citizenship through fraud under Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1451 .

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA provides a pathway to citizenship for economic migrants via a number of pathways ending with Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1427. Economic migrants must become lawful permanent residents before naturalizing. However, economic migrants may have no way to become permanent residents if they entered without inspection or overstayed their visa.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA provides pathway to citizenship for humanitarian migrants via various means ending in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1427. Humanitarian migrants must become lawful permanent residents before naturalizing. Certain classes of humanitarian migrants qualify for permanent residency by virtue of their humanitarian status but not all categories do (e.g. Temporary Protected Status, withholding of removal, deferral of removal under CAT).

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA provides a pathway to citizenship for family migrants via a family petition and period of permanent residents in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1427 and Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1158. Adult immediate family members may petition for each other to obtain permanent residence for 3- 5 years and then the permanent resident may apply for citizenship. However, the wait time can be prohibitively long, especially for siblings (20 years in some cases), and there are not provisions for extended family such as grandchildren or nephews/nieces. Prior entry without inspection and overstaying a visa also can be a barrier for certain categories of relatives. Waivers based on hardship are available in some cases. Family members also may be unable to achieve citizenship due to general bars related to criminal record and other grounds.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA allows migrants to obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin in the court decision of Kawakita v. U.S., 343 U.S. 717 (1952). However, they may relinquish their nationality under Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1481 (a).

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in the U.S. Constitution at Amendment I. This is a basic protection for all individuals in the US and these rights apply to migrants regardless of status.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in the U.S. Constitution at Amendment I. This is a basic protection for all individuals in the U.S.A., including migrants regardless of their status.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in the U.S. Constitution at Amendment I. This is a basic protection for all individuals in the U.S.A., including migrants regardless of their status.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in the U.S. Constitution at Amendment I. This is a basic protection for all individuals in the U.S.A., including migrants regardless of their status. However, this right is undermined in practice due to the inability of migrants to collect backpay for retaliation due to union activities if they did not have legal authorization to work, as determined in the Supreme Court case Hoffman Plastic Compounds, Inc. v. NLRB.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the USA lays out financial restrictions in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1182(a)(4); Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1183a and recently updated them through Volume 87 of the Federal Register page 55472 (Sept. 9, 2022) and in the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Policy Manual at Volume 8, Part G. Although the current administration rolled back the previous administration's tougher financial requirements, longstanding financial requirements remain in place. However, most humanitarian family reunification categories do not require this.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in Title 42 of U.S. Code Section 1981; Title 42 of U.S. Code Section 2000d.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA provides migrant victims of crime an avenue to immigration status or relief from expulsion as a result of being victim of a crime in Title 8 of U.S. Code Section 1101(a)(15) (U). U nonimmigrant status is available for victims of certain crimes, but not all crimes. Additionally, U nonimmigrant status is only available to those who can obtain certification from a law enforcement official to show they cooperated with prosecution of the crime. There also are separate provisions for victims of trafficking and certain victims of domestic violence.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 (TVPRA), Public Law Number 110-457, 122 Statutes at Large 5044 (2008); 8 U.S. Code Section 1101(a)(27)(J). The TVPRA resulted in several special protections for children throughout immigration law, although they are most focused on unaccompanied migrant children. Treatment of children is also addressed through a longstanding court settlement that was updated in 2022 (Flores Settlement). In 2022, the government also agreed to limit the practice of transferring immigrants taken into custody as children into adult detention upon reaching their 18th birthday. Garcia Ramirez v. ICE Settlement. Unaccompanied children are detained in facilities run by the U.S. Department of Health & Human Services as opposed to the Department of Homeland Security, and minors have special exemptions and procedures that are meant to make the asylum process less adversarial.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the USA protects this right in the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 (VAWA), Public Law Number 103-322, 108 Statues at Large 1902 (1994) (codified as amended in scattered sections of 8, 16, 18, 20, 28, and 42 U.S. Code). Special protections are primarily focused on women who are victims of domestic violence. Matter of A-B-, a decision of the U.S. Board of Immigration Appeals, allows for decisions about gender and gender based violence in asylum claims. There are other provisions, like eligibility for certain visas, etc. that may take into consideration vulnerability of women, but not explicitly so under law.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law protects this right by prohibiting discrimination, mandating program accessibility and requiring a combination of certain circumstances in Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, Pub. L. 93-112, 87 Stat. 355, 394 (September 26, 1973), codified at 29 U.S.C. 794(a). Regulations at 6 CFR 15.3 provide applicable definitions relating to enforcement of nondiscrimination on the basis of disability in federal immigration programs or activities. This right is also addressed, to some extent, in the court case Matter of MAM-, 25 I & N Dec. 474 (BIA 2011). Significantly, Title 8 of the U.S. Code Section 1182(A)(1)(A)(III) continues to make certain physical or mental disorders a ground for inadmissibility.
