citation_text_en: Coder 1: Kathryn Lewis Coder 2: Murtaza Ali Khan

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: United Arab Emirates

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 33 of the UAE Constitution stipulates that the freedom of assembly is guaranteed, but that the guarantee is limited. It should be noted, though, that migrants face the same restrictions as citizens.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are elections for the Federal National Council, and only citizens have the right to participate in these elections (they must hold a family book) according to the National Elections Committee Decision 25-2023.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates Protects this right in Article 25 of the UAE constitution.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, while not protected under national law, migrants can sometimes receive counsel at government expense, for example via legal advisors at Tasheel Service Centers.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Federal Law 38-2022 on the Issuance of the Criminal Procedure Law, which provides that interpretation can be provided to a migrant at no expense.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in 1) Cabinet Resolution 65-2022 On the Issuancde of the Implementing Regulation for Federal Decree-Law 29-2021 on the Entry and Residence of Foreigners. 2) Federal Decree-Law No. 31/2021 On the Issuance of the Crimes and Penalties Law.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right, as public housing programs are only available to UAE citizens.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right as free primary education programs are only available for citizens. Access to private institutions is unlimited but subject to high tuition fees.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right. National law does not directly address the topic of migrant's right for accessing educational institutions in the UAE. In general, access to private institutions is available but subject to high tuition fees. State funded education is generally not available for migrants. As per the respective education authority in the respective emirate, i.e. Knowledge and Human Development (KHDA), in the emirate of Dubai and Department of Education and Knowledge (ADEK), in the emirate of Abu Dhabi, it is mandatory for all students attending educational institutions for their enrolment to be approved, by providing a copy of their passport and Emirates Identity Card.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates provides that only major convictions lead to loss of residence status in 1) Article 10 of the Federal Law 29-2021 on the Entry and Residence of Foreigners, which states that the authorities may, at any time, cancel any visa or residence permit for reasons related to the public interest, or if the foreign national violates the law. Minor convictions (administrative offenses) do not typically lead to loos of the residence status. 2) Federal Decree-Law No. 31/2021 On the Issuance of the Crimes and Penalties Law, which specifies which crimes relate to loss of residency status and deportation.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. No legal framework exists to govern the relationship between UN's High Commissioner for Refugees and the Government of the UAE which is not a signatory of international conventions relating to refugees and stateless persons.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. No legal framework exists to govern the relationship between UN's High Commissioner for Refugees and the Government of the UAE which is not a signatory of international conventions relating to refugees and stateless persons.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. No legal framework exists to govern the relationship between UN's High Commissioner for Refugees and the Government of the UAE which is not a signatory of international conventions relating to refugees and stateless persons.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The UAE is not a signatory of international conventions relating to refugees and stateless persons and there is an absence of a national framework regulating issues related to asylum.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. The UAE is not a signatory of international conventions relating to refugees and stateless persons and there is an absence of a national framework regulating issues related to asylum.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Articles 65 and 70 of the Cabinet Decision 65-2022. Article 65 provides that a foreigner may be expelled by an order of the immigration authority. Article 70 provides that an individual will be deported from the UAE if a court deportation ruling is issued against her/him. As an exception to the expulsion provisions in any law, Article 126 of Federal Law 31-2021 on the Issuance of the Crimes and Penalties Law, which provides that a foreigner may not be expelled from the UAE if, at the time they committed the crime, he/she was a spouse or first-degree relative to a UAE national, unless the conviction issued relates to crimes against the security of the state.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are no regulations related to obtaining citizenship for those that would otherwise be stateless. The UAE is also not party to 1961 UN Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness and the 1954 UN Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates conditionally protects this right in Cabinet Decision 65- 2022 on the Issuance of the Implementing Regulation for Federal Law 29-2021 on the Entry and Residence of Foreigners Articles 46 and 54-57. Reunification with immediate family members is conditional but generally widely available and accessible to migrants. Reunification with non-dependent family members is restricted.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: No formal protection of this right. However, general practice and procedural rules allow foreign nationals to seek reconsideration, in some cases, with the UAE's immigration authorities' humanitarian committee set in Chairman Resolution No. 74 of 2022 Concerning the Conditions and Controls Implementing Cabinet Resolution No. 65 of 2022 on the Implementing Regulations to Federal Decree-Law No. 29 of 2021 regarding the Entry and Residency of Aliens.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Same sex or unmarried couples are not recognised by the Sharia Law and therefore not recognised in the UAE.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: NA

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. However, irregular migrants are sometimes offered a pathway to regularize their immigration status. This is sometimes possible through amnesty programs or other similar initiatives, although only from time to time, or simply through settlement of any fines.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Federal Law 33-2021 on Regulation of Labor Relations, Articles 50, 54, and 56. These articles regulate matters related to illegal suspension of work, as well as individual and collective labour disputes as the way to address employment related violations.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 19 of the UAE constitution guarantees the right for medical protection and treatment to all citizens, but it is not extended onto migrant workers. Migrant workers do require health insurance to access private and public medical facilities, while citizens enjoy freedom of access to public medical facilities based on a national insurance scheme they rolled into by default.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are elections for the Federal National Council, and its members must be citizens of the UAE and permanently reside in the Emirate they represent in the Council, according to Article 70 of the UAE Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Federal Law No 2 of 2015 on Combating Discrimination and Hatred prohibits any forms of discrimination based on one's religion, creed, doctrine, sect, caste, race, colour or ethnic origin.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates allows migrant workers to change their employer, but this requires new work permit application, which is laid down in Federal Law 33-2021 on Regulation of Labour Relations.

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 6 of the Federal Law 33-2021 on Regulation of Labour Relations provides that work can be practiced in the UAE only after obtaining a Work Permit from the UAE labour authorities.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates stipulates that loss of employment implies loss of immigration status unless a new job is found within a specified time period in Article 5 of the Federal Law 29-2021 on the Entry and Residence of Foreigners. Residency status of foreign nationals holding a self-sponsored residence permit (e.g., a Golden Visa) is not affected if they lose employment (effectively, only their work authorization is cancelled). However, those who hold a standard employment residence permit sponsored by an employer in the UAE, must secure an alternative visa within a specified time should they wish to continue to reside in the UAE once their employment relationship has ended (effectively, their work and residency authorizations are cancelled).

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates stipulates that migrants have a right to most of the employment conditions and protections for citizens in Federal Law 33-2021 on Regulation of Labour Relations. While the UAE labour law applies to both migrant workers and citizens equally, the latter category enjoys slightly wider protection in regards to protection against dismissal.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates Federal provides migrants access to some, but not all types of social security protections in Law 7-1999 concerning the issuance of the law on pensions and social security, and Federal Law 33-2021 on Regulation of Labour Relations. The UAE pension scheme is available only to citizens of the UAE and other Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, and only select jurisdictions, i.e., free zones, provide alternative pension schemes which migrant workers employed in that jurisdiction can access. Health insurance is mandoatry for all citizens, and migrants are covered under the same system as UAE nationals.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates provides migrants with access to some, but not all types of unemployment benefits in Federal Law 13-2022 Concerning Unemployment Insurance, and Federal Law 33-2021 on Regulation of Labour Relations. Workers employed in the private sector must subscribe to an Involuntary Loss of Employment Scheme which aims to provide financial support in the case of loss of employment. However, UAE nationals enjoy far wider benefits and assistance from the government should they become unemployed.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in the Decree Law 33-2021, Article 13, which provides that employers cannot seize official documents of their workers.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in 1) Cabinet Resolution 65-2022, Article 6. 2) Article 12 of the Decree Law 29-2021, which requires that a foreign national must register their child within four months from the date of birth, obtain documents to prove the child’s identity, and obtain a UAE residence permit. 2) Federal Law No. 3/2016 On Child's Rights (Wadeema's Law), Article 9, that states that "The child shall be registered in the birth register immediately after his/her birth according to the legal system prescribed in this regard." and article 6 of the Cabinet Resolution 65-2022

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in the Federal Law 9-2006, Articles 3 and 5 Concerning the Population Register and the Identity Card, which provides that each national and non-national residing inthe UAE and registered in a population register will have a fixed identity number and an Identity Card issued.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: There is no specific citation which refers to destroying documents, however, there are regulations which penalise for document forgery, including Article 251 of Federal Law 31-2021 on the Issuance of the Crimes and Penalties Law, Article 5 of Cabinet Resolution 65-2022, and Article 24 of Federal Law 29, are broad enough to allow for a foreign national to face legal consequences for tampering or destroying documents that recognize migrant’s status and identity.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Federal Law 4-1971 concerning the diplomatic and consular privileges and immunities, which incorporates the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, as well in the Constitution. Additionally, Article 24 of the Federal Law No (6) for 1973, concerning entry and residence of foreign nationals provides that an "Order of deportation issued for an alien may include the members of his family, who are depending on him in their living." While the deportation is usually preceded by a detention, the latter, although not clearly stated in the law, may be extended to children.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 15 of the Federal Law 29-2021 on Entry and Residence of Foreigners and article 72 of the Cabinet Decision 65-2022 provide that an order of deportation may include the family members of the deportee. While the deportation is preceded by a detention, the latter, although not clearly stated in the law, may be extended to children.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 65 of the Cabinet Decision 65-2022 provides that a foreign national may be expelled from the country if they have been caught attempting to enter the UAE illegally, or if they don’t hold a visa or entry permit (where required), among other circumstances. Deportation is preceded by a detention.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Cabinet Decision 65-2022 determined that Federal Law 29-2021 on Entry and Residence of Foreigners does not provide a legal pathway for appeal in the case of detention.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in the Cabinet Decision 65-2022, Article 70, provides that a foreigner will be deported from the UAE if a court deportation ruling is issued against her/him. Deportation is preceded by detention. Federal Decree-Law No. 38-2022 under criminal law and Federal Decree-Law No. 42-2022 of Civil Procedure in the UAE.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Federal Decree 73-2012 concerning the accession of the State to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment for 1984. Article 40 of the Constitution stipulates that "Foreigners shall enjoy, within the Union, the rights and freedom stipulated in international charters which are in force or in treaties and agreements to which the Union is party. They shall be subject to the corresponding obligations." While Articles 26 and 29 of the Constitution do prohibit torture and degrading treatment as well as physical and moral abuse, they have not been formally interpreted to apply to migrants.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Federal Law 12-1976 on the Police and Security Forces provides that the police and security forces and their affiliates, may use force within the limits required to complete the duties assignedto them; however, there are no specific references to use of force in relation to migration. Additionally, the UAE Penal Code imposes specific sanctions on public servants using force, dishonouring, or causing bodily pain of a person, by taking advantage of the power granted to public servants by virtue of their position.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Federal Law 12-1976 on the Police and Security Forces provides that the police and security forces and their affiliates, may use force within the limits required to complete the duties assigned to them. It sets out use of non-fatal means only unless if it is justifiably feared that the danger will lead to death or serious injury.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection for smuggled migrants. National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right for trafficked migrants in Federal Law 51-2006 on Combating Human Trafficking Crimes, which provides that a victim will not be held liable (civilly or criminally) for any of the crimes if they are directly connected or related to a victim’s situation as trafficked person, unless the victim has personally participated in the commission of the crime; or is a foreign resident in the UAE non-compliant with employment and residence regulations; or if he/she fails to notify the authorities of the crime.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates stipulates that only major convictions can lead to loss of citizenship status in Federal Law 17-1972 concerning Nationality and Passports. Individuals may be deprived of UAE nationality if they have been involved in terrorism or they are considered a threat to the external or internal security of the country (Art. 14 and 15.bis); or if they engage in an unauthorized military service for a foreign state, or act for a benefit of a hostile country, or if they willingly become naturalised nationals of a foreign country (Art. 15). However, those who have been naturalized, may also be deprived of the UAE nationality if they are convicted of offenses involving moral turpitude or dishonesty, or reside abroad without an excuse continuously for a period of 2 years (Art. 16).

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Federal Law 17-1972 concerning Nationality and Passports (articles 7, 8, and 9). Article 8 states that, "the Nationality of the State may be granted to any person, other than those mentioned in Articles 5 and 6, who enjoys full legal capacity if he has continuously and legally resided in the member Emirates for a period of no less than 30 years of which he has spent 20 years at least after the effective date of this Law; provided that he has lawful source of income, is of a good reputation and good conduct, and not convicted for an offence involving moral turpitude and dishonesty, and is proficient in Arab language." Article 2 of Federal Decree-Law No. 16/2017 empowered the President to waive the residency requirement for any person having provided outstanding service to the State.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are no regulations related to obtaining citizenship by humanitarian migrants. However, per article 46.9 of the Cabinet Decision 65-2022, foreign nationals may obtain a residence permit based on humanitarian considerations.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates provides a pathway to citizenship for family migrants in Articles 10 and 10.bis of the Federal Law 17-1972 concerning Nationality and Passports. Article 10 and 10bis state that, "Applicable to wife and minor children by naturalization; sons and daughters of a UAE national who is married to a foreign national after no less than six years from the date of birth (provided that the mother has the nationality at the time of birth until the date of application for nationality); a daughter of a UAE female citizen, from a father of foreign nationality, and who is married to a foreigner."

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Article 11 of the Federal Law 17-1972 concerning Nationality and Passports states that 'No one may be naturalised without renouncing the nationality of origin.'

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in 1) Articles 30 and 32 of the UAE Constitution, guarantees the freedom of opinions, communication, and expression withinthe limits of the law. However, as the interpretation of the UAE Constitution may be subjective, and it remains unclear whether these provisions apply to citizens and foreign nationals alike. 2) Articles 1 and 4 of the Federal Law 2-2015 on Combating Discrimination and Hatred, which prohibits discrimination based on one’s religion and beliefs.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in the UAE protects this right in Articles 30 and 31 of the UAE Constitution, which states that, "the freedom to hold opinions and express them orally, in writing or by other means of expression will be guaranteed within the limites of the law," and that "freedom of communication by means of the posts, telegraph or other means of communication and their secrecy shall be guaranteed in accordance with the law."

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in the UAE protects this right in Articles 30 and 32 of the UAE Constitution.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. As per Cabinet Resolution 65-2022, Article 55 a Foreign national must demonstrate that they have a residence permit in the UAE, financial solvency, and adequate housing for family members.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in the UAE protects this right in Article 28 of the UAE Constitution, which guarantees the right to counsel, right to fair trail and presumption of innocence in trials.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. There are no laws in the UAE that guarantee victims of crime an avenue to immigration status. However, a victim will not be held liable (civilly or criminally) for any of the crimes if they are directly connected or related to the victim’s situation as a trafficked person (with some exemptions)per Federal Law 51-2006 on Combating Human Trafficking Crimes.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in 1) Federal Law 3-2016 on Child’s Rights. 2) Federal Law 51-2006 on Combating Human Trafficking Crimes (as amended). 3) Federal Law 33-2021 on Regulation of Labour Relations. 4) Federal Law 29-2021 on Entry and Residence of Foreigners (together with its implementing regulations), which provides very limited special protection rights to migrant children,including the eligibility for a residence permit in certain cases of parents being divorced or fatherbeing deceased, and other unspecified circumstances on humanitarian grounds. 5) Federal Law No. 3/2016 On Child's Rights (Wadeema's Law).

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in Federal Law 51-2006 on Combating Human Trafficking Crimes (as amended), and Federal Law 33-2021 on Regulation of Labour Relations, and Federal Law 29-2021 on Entry and Residence of Foreigners (together with its implementing regulations), which provides very limited special protection rights to migrant women, including the eligibility for a residence permit in certain cases of being divorced or widowed, and other unspecified circumstances on humanitarian grounds.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Arab Emirates protects this right in 1) Federal Law 8 of 1980 on Labor Law, as amended. 2) Resolution No. 43 of 2018 in support of the people of determination. 3) Federal Law No. 29 of 2006 Concerning the Rights of People with Special Needs.

question_text_en: What is your name?
citation_text_en: [1]: Sonia Morano-Foadi. [2] Colin Yeo (original) ; Maja Grundler for backcoded questions.

question_text_en: What country are you coding?
citation_text_en: United Kingdom

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to vote in local and/or regional elections.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1, Art 11.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to stand for election.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not protect the legal right to vote in local/regional/national elections based on lawful presence. Under the Representation of the People Act 1983, the City of London (Various Powers) Act 1957, the Local Government Act 1972, the Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009, the Police Reform and Social Responsibility Act 2011, the Electoral Law Act (Northern Ireland) 1962, the Local Government Act (Northern Ireland) 1972, and the Elected Authorities (Northern Ireland) Act 1989, all amended by the Elections Act 2022, Schedule 8, certain non-nationals can vote in national and regional elections: resident Irish citizens and resident qualifying Commonwealth citizens can vote in all national and regional elections; resident EU citizens can vote in all local elections in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland; anyone legally resident can vote in local elections in Scotland, as well as in elections for the Welsh Parliament and the county and community councils. Settled migrants in the UK, who are recognized as having indefinite leave to remain or permanent residence, generally have the right to vote in local government elections and certain other elections. Qualifying EU citizens or an EU citizen with retained rights can still vote and be a candidate in local election as regulated the Withdrawal Agreement, Part 2 - Citizens' Rights.

question_text_en: Right to equal protection of the law before courts.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right before all courts and tribunals in the Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1, Article 6. Other relevant legislature includes the Equality Act 2010. See also case Khawaja v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1983] UKHL 8.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided counsel in proceedings related to migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not protect this right, however, legal aid is available for certain types of cases under the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012.

question_text_en: Right to government-provided interpretation in criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Article 6 ECHR (incorporated into domestic law by the Human Rights Act 1998); Directive 2010/64/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 October 2010 as implemented by Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE) Code C: Revised Code of Practice for the Detention, Treatment and Questioning of Persons By Police Officers (August 2019), chapter 13. Section 10 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 Code C (PACE Code C). R v West London Youth Court, ex p. N. [2000] 1 W.L.R. 2368.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from prosecution for unauthorized entry.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not protect migrants from civil or criminal sanctions for unauthorized entry. There are a large number of criminal offences that can only be committed by migrants such as under section 24(1)of the Immigration Act 1971, 'illegal entry' is a criminal offense. Please see Immigration Act 1971 Section 24(1) as is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 15 February 2023, as per Nationality and Borders Act 2022; Appendix Sponsor guidance appendix B: immigration offenses and sponsorship - list of offenses and list of offenses as per Crown Prosecution Service.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to public adult education institutions.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK regulates this right in the Housing Act 1996, sections 115, 159 and 185. Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, Section 115 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 10 March 2023 and Housing Act 1996 as amended with all changes known to be in force on or before 09 March 2023. The Housing Act 1996, sections 159 and 185 formulate this right in negative terms, stating that persons subject to immigration control under the Asylum and Immigration Act 1996 are not normally eligible for housing assistance. Migrants not caught by this provision, and therefore eligible for housing assistance, include Irish nationals and their family members, EEA nationals with status under the EU Settlement Scheme (and their family members), as well as refugee and beneficiaries of humanitarian protection. Access to public housing programs in the UK is therefore not guaranteed on an equal basis for all migrants. The eligibility for public housing, also known as social housing, is determined by various factors, including immigration status, residency status, and local authority policies. UK citizens and individuals with settled status or indefinite leave to remain in the UK generally have the same access to public housing as citizens. They can apply for social housing and are included in the same eligibility criteria as citizens. However, the eligibility and access to public housing for migrants with temporary or limited immigration status, such as those on work visas or student visas, can be more restricted. These individuals may face limitations or exclusions from accessing public housing programs, depending on the specific rules and policies of the local authority. Additionally, irregular migrants or those without lawful immigration status may face significant challenges in accessing public housing. They are generally not eligible for social housing, and their options for housing assistance may be limited. It's important to note that housing policies and eligibility criteria can vary across different local authorities in the UK. Some local authorities may have more inclusive policies that provide housing support to a broader range of migrants, while others may have stricter criteria.

question_text_en: Right of access to public adult education institutions regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in section 14 of the Education Act 1996; Equality Act 2010; and Human Rights Act 1998.

question_text_en: Right to be free from discrimination on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Education (Fees and Awards)(England) Regulations 2007, section 4 and Schedule 1. While UK law does not guarantee unconditional access to public adult educational institutions and services for all migrants, individuals with settled status or indefinite leave to remain generally have similar access as citizens, while those with temporary immigration status may have certain conditions or restrictions. The specific eligibility and access can also depend on the policies of individual institutions and the type of educational program being pursued.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Civil penalties issued for failing to comply with an administrative rule may affect residence status, but it is unlikely in practice. National law in the UK regulates the ability of migrants’ criminal and other convictions affecting residence status in a) the Immigration Act 1971, sections 3(5), 3(6) and 5; b) the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002, section 76; c) the UK Borders Act 2007, section 32; d) the Immigration Rules, paras 339AA, 339AB, 339D and 339GD.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of torture or inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in the Human Rights Act 1998, section 6, in conjunction with Schedule 1, Article 3 and Art 33 of Refugees Convention (1951) as applied in the UK.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a risk of persecution.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK bans refoulement on the basis of a risk of return to persecution based on race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion in the Nationality and Borders Act 2022, section 30 and in the Immigration Rules Part 11 Asylum (paragraphs 326A to 352H), as updated on 30 January 2023.

question_text_en: Right to not return to a deprivations of fundamental human rights.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in Section 6 of the Human Rights Act (HRA) 1988. This Act guarantees the right to life and consequently if there is a real and imminent risk of loss of life, the migrant cannot be returned. See article 2 ECHR and 2 HRA.

question_text_en: Right to be advised of availability of asylum before expulsion.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not require a person to be advised of the possible availability of asylum before being expelled or prevented entry.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from chain refoulement.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK bans expulsion to any country where a migrant is likely to be subjected to refoulement through a subsequent expulsion in the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002, section 80B (as amended by the Nationality and Borders Act 2022, section 16.). This Act's Part 5, exceptions and limitations section 94 is also relevant.

question_text_en: Right to protection against expulsion except following a legal judgment.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in a) the Immigration Act 1971, sections 3(5), 3(6) and 5; b) the UK Borders Act 2007, section 32; c) the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, section 10; d) Immigration Rules part 13: Deportation (paragraph 363) as updated 30 January 2023 and paragraph 336 of the Immigration Rules.

question_text_en: Right to submit reasons against expulsion and have case reviewed before deportation.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in a) the Immigration Act 1971, sections 15 and 16; b) the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002, sections 82 and 84.

question_text_en: Right of settled migrants to family reunification.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Rather than a right to citizenship, under section 36 of the British Nationality Act 1981, in conjunction with Schedule 2, sections 3 and 3A, children born in the UK who have always been stateless and are over the age of 18 and under the age of 22, who are living in the UK at the time of applying to be registered and at the date of application have spent the last five years living in the UK, can apply to register as British citizens. Under section 3A, stateless minors additionally have to show that they are unable to acquire another nationality.

question_text_en: Right to judicial remedy for denials of right to family reunification.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK conditionally protects this right for regular migrants based on the nature of family relationship, in the Immigration Rules, Part 11 (for refugees) and Appendix FM. General 1.2. For the purposes of this Appendix “partner” means- (i) the applicant’s spouse; (ii) the applicant’s civil partner; (iii) the applicant’s fianc?(e) or proposed civil partner; or (iv) a person who has been living together with the applicant in a relationship akin to a marriage or civil partnership for at least two years prior to the date of application, unless a different meaning of partner applies elsewhere in this Appendix. Hence, General 1.2 excludes non-dependent and non-immediate family members.

question_text_en: Right to recognition of same-sex marital relationships.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Kingdom provides judicial remedy to appeal the refusal by the authorities to allow family formation/reunification in the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002, section 82.

question_text_en: Right to family reunification without resource conditions
citation_text_en: National law in the UK recognizes same sex relationships under the family reunification framework in the Immigration Rules Appendix FM and Part 11 and Para 352A(II) Immigration Rules.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services.
citation_text_en: The opportunity for temporary migrant workers to switch to permanent status (indefinite leave to remain) after meeting certain conditions is generally conditional on the visa type and specific immigration category they are under. The conditions and requirements for switching to permanent status can vary depending on the visa route and the rules set by the UK government. For example, there is an indefinite leave to remain after 5 years of residence in the U.K. for Skilled Worker or Tier 2 (General), T2 Minister of Religion or Tier 2 (Minister of Religion), International Sportsperson, T2 Sportsperson or Tier 2 (Sportsperson). In relation to Workers and Temporary Workers and seasonal workers, the latter cannot switch visa or settle in the UK as seen in the guidance updated on January 2023.

question_text_en: Right of access to health care services regardless of status.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Immigration Rules, Appendix Private Life, para PL5.1; and Rule 276ADE. See also section 24B of the Immigration Act 1971 as amended for a definition of illegal working. Para PL 5.1. of the Immigration Rules, Appendix Private Life states that an individual can apply for limited leave to remain in the UK on the ground of long residence where s/he has resided continuously for at least 20 years (lawfully or not) and fulfills certain conditions. An irregular migrant who has been resident in the UK for more than 20 years (and a shorter period for younger applicants) can obtain limited permission then after a further 10 years obtain settlement. The Private Life route is for a person seeking permission to stay in the UK on the basis they have developed a Private Life in the UK.

question_text_en: Right of access to public housing programs.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right for migrants with valid employment contracts in the Employment Tribunals Act 1996; the The Employment Tribunals Rules of Procedure 2013; and Equality Act 2010, part 5, chapter 1, section 55 "Employment Services." See also Patel v Mirza [2016] UKSC 42; Okedina v Chikale [2019] EWCA Civ 1393.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to free primary education for migrant children.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK regulates this right in National Health Service (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015 and (Amendment) Regulations 2023: Date Legislation considered: 10 February 2023; Date Legislation in Force: 18 February 2023. Migrants with Indefinite Leave to Remain, including EEA citizens with settled status, have free access to health care services on the same basis as citizens. The 2023 Regulations have amended the National Health Service (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015 (“the Principal Regulations”). These regulations introduce charges for overseas visitors who wish to access the national health service (which is free to access for UK citizens), but the same regulations exempt EU nationals exercising their free movement rights from this provision (section 12), a right which is retained for EU nationals with rights under the European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020.On the other hand, some public health services are only available to certain category of migrants. For example, irregular migrants do not have access to all public health services, and therefore access to non-urgent or elective treatments may be limited for irregular migrants. Emergency health care is available to all.

question_text_en: Right to equal pay for the same work.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK does not protect migrants’ legal right to stand for election. Elections Act 2022, Part 2, Schedule 8 regulates voting and candidacy rights of EU citizens. Additionally, under the Representation of the People Act 1983, the City of London (Various Powers) Act 1957, the Local Government Act 1972, the Greater London Authority Act 1999, the Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009, the Police Reform and Social Responsibility Act 2011, the Electoral Law Act (Northern Ireland) 1962, the Local Government Act (Northern Ireland) 1972, the Elected Authorities (Northern Ireland) Act 1989, the Northern Ireland Assembly (Elections) Order 2001, certain non-nationals can stand for election. Being lawfully present as a migrant does not automatically create a legal right for individuals to stand for election or run for public office. The eligibility criteria for running for public office are determined by specific laws and regulations that vary depending on the level of government and the position being sought. Generally, to be eligible to stand for election in the UK, individuals must meet certain requirements, which often include being a British citizen, a citizen of Ireland, or a qualifying citizen of Commonwealth countries. Settled migrants who are not British citizens typically do not have the automatic right to run for public office. The eligibility criteria for running for public office can differ for different positions and levels of government. Some positions may have additional requirements, such as residency qualifications or membership of a political party. It is necessary to refer to the specific laws and regulations governing the particular election or public office being considered to determine the eligibility requirements for candidacy.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of choice of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in the United Kingdom protects this right in Article 14 of the Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1 which implements ECHR Art 14 stating that "the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms set forth in this Convention shall be secured without discrimination on any ground such as sex, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, birth or other status." Other status has been interpreted by the courts to inlude immigration status (see e.g. (Hode and Abdi v. the United Kingdom, 2012, para 47; Bah v. the United Kingdom, 2011, para 46).

question_text_en: Right of spouse/partner of principal migrant to work.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK prohibits discrimination against migrants on the ground of race or ethnicity in the Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1, Article 14 and in the Equality Act 2010, sections 4, 9, 13 and 19; and Chapter 1- protected charachteristics.

question_text_en: Right to maintain immigration status after loss of employment.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the the National Minimum Wage Act 1998; the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015; and the UK Equality Act Selection 39 and Immigration Rules, Part 6, Para 245AAA to 254ZZE (UK Point Based System). While irregular migrant workers are entitled to the right to fair wages and remuneraton for work of equal value, they may face additional challenges in asserting their rights compared to those with regular immigration status. Additionally, migrant workers and refugees working in the UK with leave to remain have the right to be paid annual leave and statutory sick pay, and must pay tax and national insurance.

question_text_en: Right to equal employment conditions and protection.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK regulates this right in Immigration Rules, Appendix Skilled Workers, Rules, SW 1.1-SW 46.2. Overseas Domestic Worker; Immigration Rules Appendix Domestic Workers in a Private Household ; immigration Rules Appendix Temporary Work - Seasonal Worker' other schemes. Some migrant workers, such as resident EU citizens with settled and pre-settled status, have the right to free choice of employment. Other workers from non-EU countries hold visas tied to specific employers but can change their employer if they submit a new visa application (see Immigration Rules, Appendix Skilled Worker, SW 1.2. and SW 18.2; Appendix Overseas Domestic Worker, ODW 8.3).

question_text_en: Right to form trade unions and other associations.
citation_text_en: National law in the U.K. protects this right for certain category of migrants, depending on the principal migrant's immigration status, in the Immigration Rules, Appendix Skilled Workers, Rules, SW 26.1. -SW 46.2. Partners and children of skilled workers can work, except as a sportsperson or coach. Different rules apply for temporary workers. Some schemes do not permit family to join. Irish citizens and EU nationals with pre-settled or settled status, as well as those waiting for a decision have a right to work, as do individuals with a family permit under the EU Settlement Scheme and those with a right of abode or indefinite leave to enter or remain in the UK.

question_text_en: Right of regular migrants to redress before deportation or withdrawal of residency permit.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Immigration Rules, Appendix Skilled Workers, Rules, SW 1.1-SW 46.2. , updated 30 January 2023. Skilled workers on Tier 2 who lose their job, no longer meet the requirements of the original Skilled Worker visa, which usually gives up to 2,5 years of leave in the U.K. for the holder to work. However, if he employment has been brought to an early end, this will shorten the time the worker can stay in the country. The worker has 60 days leave in the U.K. or until the end of the visa, whichever is shorter. If they plan to stay in the U.K. and continue working, they need to apply for a new visa. To do so, all of the same eligibility requirements will have to be met. They must have received a new job offer to apply from a company that has a sponsor license to be able to offer the worker the role. If they do not have another job offer, they will not be accepted onto a new visa. For temporary workers, if they receive a job offer from a company without a sponsor licence, they may be able to get a licence within 60 days, however, this will be difficult as the process can be long-winded. If the company is willing to make the application, they can seek immigration law advice to do so. As long as the company has their licence within their 60-day time limit and offer the migrant a role with the required salary, it is possible to make a new application. The migrant will not be asked to leave the country if an application is in process. They can continue to work in their current job and finish their notice period while they make a new application if they are able to. They shouldn’t start their new job until they get a decision on their new application.

question_text_en: Right to equal access to social security protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in 1) the Employment Rights Act 1996; 2) the Employment Relations Act 1999; 3) the Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999; 4) the Part-Time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000; 5) the Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006; 6) the Agency Workers Regulations 2010. 7) Section 39 of the Equality Act 2010.

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to become lawfully settled.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects migrant workers’ rights to social security protections in the Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992 and Section 39 of the Equality Act 2010. Migrant workers with a valid work permit have the right to social security protections commensurate with citizens as they are protected by U.K. employment laws. The Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992 applies to workers in the U.K. regardless of nationality. However, section 21 of the Act makes receipt of certain benefits subject to the condition that an individual has paid sufficient social security contributions. As such, migrant workers with a valid work permit will gain equal access to certain benefits only after a certain duration of stay (and contribution).

question_text_en: Right of temporary migrants to settle regardless of initial status.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right for some categories of migrants in the Jobseekers Act 1995, and the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, Section 115. Access to public benefits may be conditional on immigration status. For example, some visa categories have restrictions on accessing unemployment benefits.

question_text_en: Right to redress following employer breach of employment contract.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right for certain categories of migrants in paragraph 276B of the Immigration Rules; Appendix Skilled Workers, Rules, SW 1.1-SW 46.2. Immigration Rules Appendix Temporary Work: GAE 1.1.-GAE 21.3. Paragraph 276B of the Immigration Rules states that an individual can apply for indefinite leave to remain in the UK on the ground of long residence where s/he has resided lawfully for at least 10 years and fulfills certain conditions. There is an indefinite leave to remain after 5 years of residence in the U.K. for Skilled Worker or Tier 2 (General), T2 Minister of Religion or Tier 2 (Minister of Religion), International Sportsperson, T2 Sportsperson or Tier 2 (Sportsperson). In relation to Workers and Temporary Workers and seasonal workers, the latter cannot switch visa or settle in the UK as seen in the guidance updated on January 2023.

question_text_en: Right not to have identity documents confiscated.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Section 52 Immigration Act 2016 - Seizure of nationality documents by detainee custody officers- which states that only law enforcement officers (police or immigration officers ) have powers to seize identity documents; and Section 17 of the Asylum & Immigration (Treatment of Claimants etc) Act 2004 which gives the power to retain documents, such as a passport, where the Secretary of State or an immigration officer suspects a migrant is liable to removal and the retention of the document may facilitate removal. The 2004 Act does not allow for the indefinite retention of documents. Where a person is later granted leave, in whatever capacity, the document must be returned to the holder unless it is a forgery, in which case it must be sent to the National Document Fraud Unit (NDFU).There is no power for private citizens to confiscate ID documents. Other relevant legislation authorizing public officials to confiscate migrants' identity documents when necessary include the UK Borders Act 2007, section 44; the Immigration Act 2016, sections 48 and 52; and the Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015, section 1.

question_text_en: Right to birth registration.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK requires birth registration of migrant children, regardless of their status, in section 2 of the Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953 and section 14 of the Births, Deaths and Marriages (Scotland) Registration Act 1965.

question_text_en: Right to government document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not mandate the issuing of documents that recognize migrants’ residency status, work status, and identity. The UK Borders Act 2007 provides legislative powers that allow but do not require the Home Office to issue "biometric immigration documents" (BID). In practice, many regular migrants are given a form of biometric permit. These permits can only be used to provde one's identity, right to study, and right to public services or benefits, but not the right to rent or work. In R (The 3million Ltd) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2021] EWHC 1159 (Admin), the High Court refused permission for a judicial review challenge to the government’s policy of giving digital-only proof of immigration status, rather than physical residence permits, to EU citizens.

question_text_en: Right against destruction of document recognizing residency, work status, and identity.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK makes it illegal for anyone to destroy documents that recognize migrants’ residency status, work status, and identity in section 1 of the Criminal Damage Act 1971. Other legislation relevant includes Identity Documents Act 2010 (IDA), and section 2 Asylum (Treatment of Claimants etc) Act 2004.

question_text_en: Right to communicate with consular officials.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Even though the U.K. is a party to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (1963), it has not directly incorporated this right in national law. For migrants detained in an Immigration Removal Centre there is no provision directly addressing consular access, but there is a general obligation to permit visits and communications under Rule 26 of the Detention Centre Rules 21. The Prison Service Instructions, Immigration Repatriation and Removal Service (PSI 52/2011) in section 3.3. provide for prisoners’ rights to consular access. Thus, the obligation to allow consular officials and migrants to communicate is protected through policy, but not law.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not prohibit the detention of children on the basis of their status as a migrant. However, section 5 of the the Immigration Act 2014 puts restrictions on detention of unaccompanied children and the Home Office Guidance on "Detention: General instructions" sets out special conditions and procedures for the detention of unaccompanied young persons and families with children under the age of 18.

question_text_en: Right of migrants to be free from detention on the basis of migrant status.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not prohibit the detention of migrants on the basis of their status as a migrant.

question_text_en: Right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects migrants' right to appeal legality, conditions, and length of detention in the Human Rights Acts 1998, Schedule 2, Article 1(5) (f) and through judicial review such as R(Hardial Singh) v Governor of Durham Prison [1984] WLR 704. In addition, detainees may apply for bail to the First Tier Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum Chamber) under Section 61 of the Immigration Act 2016. Bail hearings do not determine the legality of detention, but may involve consideration of the lawfulness of detention.

question_text_en: Right to an individualized detention decision.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Immigration Act 1971 (as amended), Schedule 2, paragraph 16 (2) Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002, section 62 Immigration Act 1971, Schedule 3, paragraph 2, and the UK Borders Act 2007, section 36. Chapter 55, Enforcement and Instructions Guidance; Rule 9 of the Detention Centre Rules 2001. This right is also protected, in policy, more specifically with the Home Office Guidance on 'Detention: General instructions'.

question_text_en: Right to be free from torture and inhumane treatment.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Human Rights Act 1998 Sections 1 and 6, implementing Article 3 of the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR).

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. Section 146(1) of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 allows Immigration Officers to use reasonable force where necessary in the exercise of any power conferred by the Immigration Acts. Section 3(1) of the Criminal Law Act 1967 allows reasonable use of force when an arrest is being made in the prevention of crime. Under section 24(1) of the Immigration Act 1971, migrants who enter the UK irregularly commit a criminal offence.

question_text_en: Right to be free from use of lethal force to prevent entry to territory.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in Section 146 of the Immigration Act 1999 and in Section 2, Article 2(1) of the Human Rights Act 1998 which incorporates the right to life at Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law. Article 2(1) states that 'Everyone’s right to life shall be protected by law. No one shall be deprived of his life intentionally save in the execution of a sentence of a court following his conviction of a crime for which this penalty is provided by law.' However, Article 2(2) states that 'Deprivation of life shall not be regarded as inflicted in contravention of this Article when it results from the use of force which is no more than absolutely necessary: (a)in defence of any person from unlawful violence; (b)in order to effect a lawful arrest or to prevent the escape of a person lawfully detained; (c)in action lawfully taken for the purpose of quelling a riot or insurrection.' While it is conceivable that the exception in para b) may apply in the context of preventing entry, lethal use of force would not be 'reasonable' under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 or the Criminal Law Act 1967.

question_text_en: Right to be protected from trafficking or smuggling.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not exempt trafficked and smuggled migrants from criminal prosecutions. Both trafficked and smuggled person may be prosecuted for irregular entry under sections 24 and 24A of the Immigration Act 1971. Trafficked persons may also be prosecuted for offenses committed in the context of trafficking, however, they may have a defense under section 45 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015.

question_text_en: Right to maintain citizenship status after convictions.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. This issue is regulated in Section 40 British Nationality Act 1981, as amended by the 2014 Immigration Act, up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 18 February 2023. Section 40(2) provides that the Secretary of State may by order deprive a person of a citizenship status if the Secretary of State is satisfied that deprivation is conducive to the public good. In practice, this is likely to only be the case where the individual in question has committed a serious criminal offense, but the law can be used more widely against those with minor convictions.

question_text_en: Right of economic migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK provides pathways to citizenship for economic migrants in the British Nationality Act 1981, section 6 in conjunction with Schedule 1. The acquisition of citizenship by naturalization is open to economic migrants who have fulfilled the requirements as specified in Schedule 1 of the British Nationality Act. Under certain work visa routes such as the Skilled Worker (formerly Tier 2) category, there may be provisions for workers to apply for settlement (indefinite leave to remain) after a specific period of continuous residence in the UK, typically five years. This is subject to meeting other requirements, such as having a valid and eligible job offer, meeting the relevant salary thresholds, and fulfilling any English language and knowledge of life in the UK requirements. After obtaining indefinite leave to remain, such migrants can apply for citizenship 12 months after getting indefinite leave to remain.

question_text_en: Right of humanitarian migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK provides pathways to citizenship for humanitarian migrants in the British Nationality Act 1981, section 6 in conjunction with Schedule 1.

question_text_en: Right of family migrants to citizenship.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK provides pathways to citizenship for family migrants in the British Nationality Act 1981, section 6(2) in conjunction with Schedule 1.

question_text_en: Right to dual nationality.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK allows migrants to obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin in the British Nationality Act 1981.

question_text_en: Right to freedom to hold opinion.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1, Art 9, Art 13 and in the Equality Act 2010, section 10. Article 9 ECHR is incorporated into domestic law by the Human Rights Act 1998.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of expression.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Article 10 ECHR (incorporated into domestic law by the Human Rights Act 1998).

question_text_en: Right to freedom of association.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1, Art 10.

question_text_en: Right to freedom of assembly.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1, Art 11.

category: Thought, conscience, and religion or belief
question_text_en: Right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion or belief.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. National law in the UK does not protect this right in the Immigration Rules. Appendix FM of the Immigration Rules, sectionsE-ECP.3.1., E-LTRP.3.1., E-ECC.2.1. and ELTRC. 2.1. require evidence of income and savings. Sections E-ECP.3.4, E-LTRP.3.4., E-ECC.2.4 and E-LTRC.2.4. require evidence of adequate accommodation.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to access criminal proceedings.
citation_text_en: No protection of this right. While access to justice is a core constitutional right and includes access to courts and tribunals, there is no specific recognition that migrants who are victims of crime must receive protections equal to that of citizens. Furthermore, the UK does not protect the right to an effective remedy as codifed in Article 13 ECHR, as it has been omitted from the list of Convention rights protected underthe Human Rights Act. In practice, however, migrants have access to criminal proceedings although migrants taking part in criminal proceedings does not protect them from removal.

question_text_en: Right of victims of crime to immigration status or relief from expulsion.
citation_text_en: National law in the U.K. protects this right in relation to certain group of migrants, such as victims of domestic violence, modern slavery, and trafficking in the Modern Slavery Act section 45 (defense for victims but not immigration status; Section 53 (leave for overseas domestic workers who are victims); Nationality and Borders Act 2022, PART 5, Section 61 (2) and 65; Immigration Rules 289A, 289B and 289C.

question_text_en: Right of child migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Borders, Citizenship and Immigration Act 2009, section 55. "Duty regarding the welfare of children" contains a mandatory duty on the Home Office and others making immigration decisions to safeguard and promote the welfare of children in the UK as they carry out their functions. The scope of the duty is broad, meaning that any immigration decision taken within the UK should include a consideration of this duty. The Home Office decision maker will need to assess a child's best interests at all stages of decision-making. This duty is referred as "the best interest of the child" in jurisprudence such in ZH (Tanzania) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2011] UKSC 4. See also the Children Act 1989, which makes explicit reference to the best interests of children and therefore require decision-makers, tribunals and courts to consider this when reaching decisions.

question_text_en: Right of women migrants to special protections.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right in the Immigration Rules, Appendix FM, Section DVIL which provides for indefinite leave to remain in the UK as a victim of domestic abuse; Section E-DVILR sets out the relevant eligibility requirements. The Immigration Rules also contain an 'Appendix Domestic Worker who is a Victim of Modern Slavery' which grants a right to remain for up to two years to domestic workers conclusively identified as victims of modern slavery (as long as certain conditions are met) - see also Modern Slavery Act 2015, section 53. The Immigration Act 2016 in section 16 puts limits on the detention of pregnant women. Finally, courts and tribunals have highlighted the vulnerability of trafficked women and how this contributes to a risk of re-trafficking, e.g., in AM and BM (Trafficked women) Albania CG [2010] UKUT 80 (IAC) or TD and AD (trafficked women) CG [2016] UKUT 92 where the claimants were granted refugee status.

question_text_en: Rights of migrants with disabilities to special protection.
citation_text_en: National law in the UK protects this right through the Equality Act 2010, section 149 which relates to equal treatment for people with disabilities. Thus, the law takes disability into account in all fields, including migration. Disabled migrants do benefit from the protections accorded to all disabled persons under equality law and migrants can secure different treatment that takes their disability status into account vis a vis other migrants. Several migrants in immigration detention have won legal challenges to their detention in part based on their special needs, see section 96(1)(a) of Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 with all the changes to be in force on or before 09 February 2023.
